papers.abstract: Dynamic object manipulation requires robots to anticipate target motion while replanning fast enough to avoid executing outdated actions. Existing approaches either rely on fast reactive control without an explicit future target state or encode anticipated motion only implicitly. World Action Models (WAMs) offer a promising alternative by coupling future visual prediction with action generation, but scene-level video objectives may underrepresent target dynamics that are critical for manipulation, while iterative video-action denoising introduces substantial latency. We present TrajWAM, a trajectory-guided world action model for efficient dynamic robotic manipulation. Our key insight is to explicitly ground future visual imagination in predicted target-object motion and use the resulting future representation to condition action generation, while preserving this anticipation pathway after acceleration. Given a short history of object masks, a history-conditioned motion predictor forecasts future masks encoding the target object's trajectory. A lightweight Trajectory ControlNet then steers a pretrained video model toward trajectory-consistent futures. The resulting future representation conditions an action expert to predict executable action chunks. To enable one-step inference without breaking this interface, we introduce a decoupled distillation scheme that combines distribution matching for the video backbone, Trajectory ControlNet realignment, and action rollout distillation to support accurate one-step action prediction conditioned on the compressed future representation. Comprehensive evaluations in simulation and the real world show that TrajWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on dynamic object manipulation tasks while enabling efficient one-step video-action inference. Project page: https://kevingeng3.github.io/TrajWAM/.
bullets: Addresses the need to anticipate moving targets while replanning quickly enough to avoid stale actions.
Predicts future object masks from short mask histories to encode target motion explicitly.
Uses a lightweight Trajectory ControlNet to guide a pretrained video model toward trajectory-consistent future representations.
Conditions an action expert on these representations to generate executable action chunks.
Introduces decoupled distillation for efficient one-step video-action inference, with strong simulation and real-world results reported.

papers.abstract: World models predict how an environment responds to actions, so that candidate actions can be evaluated before execution. Executed actions, or decisions, taken in this manner are only as reliable as the model's predictive capabilities, and predictions in turn are only reliable within the model's experience. Epistemic uncertainty (EU) is the signal that marks where that experience ends. In this work we offer an extensive empirical study on how training objectives and architectures shape epistemic uncertainty of world models. More precisely, we present a controlled comparison of post-hoc EU (last-layer Laplace and ensembles) between two dominant models of different paradigms: 1) LeWorldModel (LeWM): A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), which predicts the next embedding without a decoder, and 2) DreamerV3: A recurrent state-space model (RSSM), which reconstructs the observation from a recurrent latent state. In ten simulated visual-control environments, we follow a controlled state perturbation of the environment state through every stage of the models up to the final EU estimate. We find that the RSSM attenuates the state perturbation through two mechanisms before it reaches an estimator on the predictor feature. Its recurrent update averages over context, so a change in a single frame reaches the state at a fraction of its size and recovers only as the change persists. Its reconstruction objective weights an entity by the pixels it covers, so a small object can be lost due to the training objective. The JEPA has neither mechanism and passes the change through all stages to the uncertainty. We further show that this translates to gaps in five uncertainty related downstream tasks, from unfamiliar-state detection to uncertainty-penalised planning: the RSSM uncertainty misses deviations that its own posterior registers, whereas the JEPA uncertainty reports what its model sees.
authors: Simon Baur, Wojciech Samek, Jackie Ma
bullets: Epistemic uncertainty should indicate when a world model encounters states beyond its experience.
The study compares post-hoc Laplace and ensemble uncertainty in a JEPA model (LeWM) and an RSSM model (DreamerV3).
Across ten simulated visual-control environments, controlled state perturbations are traced through each model to its uncertainty estimate.
RSSM recurrence can dilute transient changes, while its pixel-based reconstruction objective can overlook small objects; JEPA lacks these attenuation mechanisms.

These differences affect downstream tasks including unfamiliar-state detection and uncertainty-penalized planning: RSSM uncertainty can miss deviations recorded by its posterior, whereas JEPA uncertainty better reflects model-visible changes.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of epistemic uncertainty in JEPA and RSSM world models, directly relevant to world models.
papers.title: Not all world models can doubt: how training objective and architecture shape epistemic uncertainty in JEPA and RSSM world models
papers.tldr: Training objective and architecture strongly shape whether world models detect epistemic uncertainty: JEPA-based uncertainty preserves state deviations better than RSSM-based uncertainty in the studied tasks.

papers.abstract: World models are evaluated by predicting future observations from actions. These evaluations assume that actions are prepared the same way as during training, but an unchecked mismatch can make a model appear less accurate than it is. We audit this assumption in Navigation World Models (NWM) and find three interacting differences between its training and rollout code. Correcting the inputs, without retraining, reduces mean visual prediction error by 42%, measured with DreamSim on the RECON navigation dataset. The correction also changes the ranking of NWM checkpoints in an exploratory analysis and removes or reduces two alternative models' measured advantages. Correcting only the normalization offset instead increases error, showing why interacting mismatches must be checked together. To test whether sensitivity to input preparation extends beyond NWM, we deliberately introduce encoding errors into two alternative models; both become less accurate. We introduce ActRosetta, a tool that checks whether action encoding matches training, identifies supported causes of disagreement, and repairs inputs when sufficient information is available. Repair helps little where predictions barely respond to actions, the tool's diagnosis has limited coverage, and improved control remains unproven. For any action-conditioned world model, the lesson is the same: before reporting rollout error, verify that evaluation encodes actions exactly as training did.
authors: Ajmain Istiak Apon, Md Mehedi Hasan, Sejuti Rahman
bullets: Auditing NWM rollout code revealed three interacting differences from training-time action preparation.
Fixing the mismatches reduced mean visual prediction error by 42% on the RECON navigation dataset, measured with DreamSim.
Repairs changed checkpoint rankings and removed or reduced apparent advantages of two alternative models.
ActRosetta diagnoses supported action-encoding mismatches and repairs inputs when sufficient information is available.
Scope: repair helps little when predictions are weakly action-sensitive; diagnostic coverage is limited, and improved control is unproven.

papers.abstract: Video world models aim to create interactive physical worlds that capture how diverse materials move and interact. Yet material-dependent dynamics remain underexplored in controllable video generation, limiting reliable control in scenes with different materials. We present WorldInteract, a streaming video generation framework that decomposes cross-material interaction into material-dependent behavior generation and contact response computation. External pushes and contact impulses are expressed through a shared velocity-increment interface, allowing material behaviors learned from interaction-free videos to be reused in interacting scenes. A physics controller predicts contacts and computes velocity increments from estimated masses and restitution coefficients, while a causal generator executes these increments using learned material behaviors. This separation enables cross-material interaction without supervised contact videos spanning diverse material pairings and contact configurations. We train the generator on 30k simulated interaction-free videos spanning 22 material classes and introduce Material-Aware RL, using verifiable physical rewards to refine material behavior and control execution. WorldInteract substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods on Physics-IQ and delivers more reliable push control on real-world images.
authors: Ahmed Hatem, Caoliwen Wang, Robert Hoang, Siyuan Chen, Spencer Szabados, Zike Wu, Xiyang Tan, Shenyifan Lu, Rafael Bischof, Bernd Bickel, Renjie Liao, Peter Yichen Chen
bullets: Targets reliable control of scenes containing different interacting materials.
Decomposes interactions into material-dependent behavior generation and contact-response computation.
Uses a shared velocity-increment interface so behaviors learned from interaction-free videos can handle contacts and external pushes.
Combines a physics controller with a causal video generator and refines control using Material-Aware RL.
Reports substantially better Physics-IQ performance and more reliable push control on real-world images.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models must generate video continuously while responding promptly to user actions. Real-time throughput alone leaves input latency unresolved: coarse generation blocks delay action updates, and generation after input adds work to the response path. We introduce ShowNow, a fine-grained speculative streaming framework that uses computation available during playback to prepare action-conditioned futures before input arrives. Single-latent commitment enables frequent decisions, while configurable preparation covers one to eight actions. We construct a matched multi-future dataset to train alternative continuations from a common state; shared-history tree execution and fused commitment make their preparation efficient. On a single H100, our 5B model sustains 480p generation at 16 fps with eight prepared futures. In ViZDoom, the complete ShowNow deployment reduces median input-to-display latency from 620 to 208 ms relative to the native-block SolarWM-FT deployment. Matched-policy experiments reduce restart empty ticks from 1.56% to 0.09% (94%) and improve on-time responses to action changes. These results establish complementary roles for fine-grained commitment and advance preparation, with measured trade-offs in visual fidelity and long-horizon consistency. ShowNow turns playback-time computation into responsive visual interaction. Project: https://github.com/showlab/ShowNow.
authors: Yiren Song, Guian Fang, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Targets input latency caused by coarse, blocking video generation and post-input computation.
Uses fine-grained single-latent commitment with configurable preparation for one to eight possible actions.
Trains on matched multi-future continuations and accelerates preparation through shared-history tree execution and fused commitment.
On a single H100, a 5B model generates 480p video at 16 fps with eight prepared futures.
In ViZDoom, latency falls from 620 ms to 208 ms, while restart empty ticks decrease from 1.56% to 0.09%; trade-offs remain in visual fidelity and long-horizon consistency.

papers.abstract: Dexterous mobile manipulation is essential for robots to perform useful tasks in complex, unstructured environments. However, existing systems face two challenges. First, navigation remains too coarse for downstream manipulation, which often requires a precise base position and approach orientation rather than merely reaching a meter-scale goal region. Second, navigation and manipulation are commonly trained in isolation, lacking a feedback loop that enables the two capabilities to co-evolve. These limitations prevent current systems from reliably executing long-horizon dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks in real-world environments. To address them, we introduce Nav4Manip, a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation. It comprises two complementary architectures: Nav4Manip-N learns long-horizon navigation and refines its policy through manipulation feedback, while Nav4Manip-M trains a world-action model (WAM) for downstream dexterous manipulation. We train Nav4Manip-N in three stages: multi-task co-tuning learns navigation behavior and manipulation-aware affordance prediction; rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) rejects low-quality policy-generated paths and fine-tunes the model on retained trajectories; and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) uses counterfactual preferences to further improve navigation decisions. To support this framework, we establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs from benchmark rollouts, providing large-scale paired navigation--manipulation trajectories and affordance supervision. Extensive experiments on public vision-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, while real-world evaluations show that Nav4Manip completes diverse dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://nav4manip.github.io/.
authors: Yusen Feng, Zixi Kang, Zhijun Yin, Changxiao Liu, Tianhong Gao, Jiazhao Zhang, Jiahang Liu, Libin Liu, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
bullets: Targets navigation that must achieve manipulation-ready base positions and orientations, not just coarse goal regions.
Uses two coupled components: Nav4Manip-N for manipulation-aware navigation and Nav4Manip-M with a world-action model for dexterous manipulation.
Trains navigation through multi-task co-tuning, rejection-sampling fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from AI feedback.
Introduces the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and paired navigation–manipulation trajectories with affordance supervision.
Reports state-of-the-art results on public VLN benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip, plus successful real-world task execution.

The two experts are coupled through a 30-block Mixture-of-Transformers.

papers.abstract: We present $\mu$MPC, a fast model predictive control (MPC) framework that reduces online computation using learned Koopman-linearized dynamics. By precomputing finite-horizon control-to-output maps, $\mu$MPC eliminates lifted-state trajectories, yielding an action-only Koopman-Compiled QP (KC-QP) with $Hn_u$ decision variables, independent of lifted dimension. A fixed, precomputed primal operator enables efficient primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, accommodating changing goals and constraints without refactorization. This efficiency also enables control-aware dynamics learning through differentiable KC-QPs in the training loop and batched DAgger-style data aggregation. $\mu$MPC achieves solve times as low as $23\mu$s on a desktop CPU and 24 ms onboard a 168 MHz Crazyflie microcontroller. It scales to 4096D quadruped control in under 5 ms, visual planning with 2048D world models in 0.4 ms, and collision-aware planning for 200 quadrotors at over 30 Hz on the GPU. Across these benchmarks, $\mu$MPC achieves up to $108\times$ faster constrained MPC and $1907\times$ faster visuomotor planning than competing methods.
bullets: Precomputes finite-horizon control-to-output maps, removing lifted-state trajectories and making optimization size depend only on the control horizon and input dimension.
Uses a fixed primal operator for fast primal-dual iterations with matrix-vector products and projections, while supporting changing goals and constraints without refactorization.
Enables differentiable KC-QPs for control-aware dynamics learning and batched DAgger-style data aggregation.
Reports solve times from 23 μs on a desktop CPU to 24 ms on a 168 MHz Crazyflie, with scaling to high-dimensional quadruped, visual-planning, and multi-robot tasks.
The abstract reports up to 108× faster constrained MPC and 1907× faster visuomotor planning than competing methods.

papers.abstract: Modern video generators excel at producing visually plausible futures guided by text and image prompts. Yet their emphasis on semantic plausibility does not guarantee fidelity to the physical consequences of specific actions. Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), in contrast, aim to simulate how the world responds to robot actions, enabling scalable policy evaluation and improvement without costly real-world rollouts. The challenge is not merely to generate a plausible future, but to predict what follows from a specific physical action. As video priors grow stronger, we ask how little adaptation is truly needed to bridge this gap. We introduce Dianjing, a minimal recipe that preserves and unlocks the capabilities of strong video priors through unified physical action conditioning, training concentrated at the high noise levels where motion and layout, and thus the consequences of actions, are decided, and native history conditioning. Built upon MiniMax H3, a 33B video foundation model, Dianjing freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only 0.34% of its parameters using approximately 65 hours of robot video across two embodiments, without additional robot-specific pretraining or camera calibration. Controlled ablations show that where training is allocated across noise levels matters more than how actions enter the network. On WorldOracle, which evaluates predictions against paired real-world executions, Dianjing achieves the best scores on four of the five evaluation tracks and ranks second on AgiBot-Long. Our findings suggest that strong video priors already bring us most of the way to world modeling; lightweight physical action grounding can unlock their potential for real-world prediction.
authors: Zanyi Wang, Xia Chen, Liu Liu, Xianglong Guo, Dengyang Jiang, Haodong Li, Tingyang Xiao, Wenhao Hu, Zhizhong Su
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually plausible video generation and predicting the physical consequences of specific robot actions.
Freezes the MiniMax H3 backbone and trains only 0.34% of parameters using about 65 hours of robot video from two embodiments.

Ablations indicate that allocating training toward high noise levels matters more than the specific action-injection mechanism.
Achieves the best WorldOracle scores on four of five tracks and ranks second on AgiBot-Long.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Dianjing: minimal adaptation of a strong video prior for action-conditioned world modeling. (b) High-noise sampling: training emphasizes high noise levels to improve action-conditioned adaptation. (c) Native references: the clean latent tail of the generated past is passed to the next chunk through the pretrained reference pathway, without a specialized memory module.

(c) The zero-shot TI2V prior generates a visually plausible but action-inconsistent future, whereas Dianjing grounds its predictions in temporally aligned robot actions with only 0.34% trainable parameters, improving the episode-level SV from 31.99 to 76.74 and producing a prediction more faithful to the paired real-world execution.

papers.abstract: Embodied world models aim to predict future interactions that are both visually realistic and physically consistent. Yet explicit 3D motion prediction alone does not guarantee that object structure and contact relationships are preserved. Beyond motion prediction, 3D representations provide an explicit state space for imposing structural and physical constraints. Building on this insight, we introduce RehearsalWorld, an editable robot world model driven by 3D Interaction Rehearsal (3DIR). Given an initial RGB-D observation and robot actions, Interaction-Consistent Rehearsal (ICR) uses a pretrained 3D point-flow model as a motion prior. It refines the predicted trajectories through response-aware object grouping, persistent grasp memory, and contact structure refiner, preserving scene stability, object structure, and grasp attachments. Rehearsal-Aligned Video Generation (RAVG) then uses geometric projections of the rehearsal as temporal conditioning. We fine-tune a video generator on projection-video pairs to synthesize realistic interaction videos. Thanks to the decoupling of physical response from visual synthesis, RehearsalWorld also supports independent editing of material properties and camera viewpoints. Compared with PointWorld on real DROID grasping sequences, RehearsalWorld reduces gripper-relative offset by approximately 79% to 84% across deformable, articulated, and rigid objects and lowers reference motion error. For video prediction, it achieves a PSNR of 23.92 dB and an FVD of 149.

On real DROID grasping sequences, reduces gripper-relative offset by approximately 79–84% versus PointWorld and reports 23.92 dB PSNR and 149 FVD for video prediction.

papers.abstract: Predicting the outcomes of robotic manipulation requires modeling both visual appearance and evolving 3D geometry. This poses two challenges: video compression can obscure fine-grained robot motion, while jointly predicting RGB and geometry demands sufficient generative capacity. We introduce Loop4D, a framework that addresses these challenges through motion-preserving 4D representations and recurrent generative refinement. Our 4D VAE encodes RGB and pointmap sequences into compact spatiotemporal latents while preserving motion details and geometric structure. Our RGB VAE combines geometry-guided supervision with predictive reconstruction to reduce compression-induced motion artifacts. Our geometry VAE uses lightweight adapters to adapt pretrained RGB representations while preserving their priors. Building on these representations, our Dual-Stream Looped Diffusion Transformer maintains separate appearance and geometry streams with shared Transformer weights and cross-modal connections. By reusing Transformer blocks across loops, we increase effective depth without replicating backbone parameters, enabling models with fewer parameters to improve joint RGB-geometry prediction through additional computation. Experiments demonstrate high-quality 4D generation and validate Loop4D in simulated robotic manipulation tasks.

Uses a dual-stream diffusion Transformer with separate RGB and geometry streams, cross-modal connections, and looped block reuse for greater effective depth without duplicating parameters.
Demonstrates high-quality 4D generation and validation in simulated robotic manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used in robotics to improve the performance of embodied models. Compared with general-purpose video generation, robotics places more stringent requirements on world models. Generated videos must satisfy fine-grained physical constraints on robot motion and object interactions. However, existing world model benchmarks can overlook robotics specific physical details and struggle to assess them accurately. To address this problem, we introduce WorldPhy, a world model benchmark for accurate, fine-grained evaluation of physical plausibility in robotics. Our benchmark contains 300 tasks, each consisting of an initial-frame image and a task instruction, covering diverse robotics scenes, task categories, viewpoints, and robot configurations. We further collect over 12K high-quality human annotations, and use them to train WorldPhyReward to accurately provide scores and reasons across six fine-grained physical dimensions and an instruction-following dimension. Comparisons with general VLMs and existing reward models show that WorldPhyReward better aligns with human ratings. We system- atically evaluate 13 frontier open and closed-source world models. The results reveal that current world models struggle to consistently maintain fine-grained physical plausibility across different robotics scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/chuziyuan139/ WorldPhy.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) couple future imagination with action generation, but they execute every action chunk while ignoring the potential risk. To fill this gap, we present WAtcher, a safety-aware world-action framework in which the policy imagines the outcome of the candidate chunk before execution. For fast future preview, WAtcher builds on a compact WAM whose video expert imagines the visual outcome in only two denoising steps. In addition, we propose Safe-Guard, a lightweight module kept outside the WAM that scores each candidate chunk from its imagined outcome and triggers a bounded retreat when the risk is high. Safe-Guard is detachable and can be applied to other WAMs. To train Safe-Guard, we build an autonomous pipeline to collect hazard data from RoboTwin, LIBERO, and a real robot. Specifically, the pipeline perturbs expert demonstrations and labels each candidate chunk from the physical events recorded when it is executed, such as contacts and losses of support. Using the ~25,000 labeled windows from this pipeline, Safe-Guard reaches 92.1% balanced accuracy on a blind set, and cuts hazardous closed-loop trials on training tasks from 27.0% to 10.8% without lowering task success. On a held-out 300-question benchmark, it scores 94.2%, against 72.5% and 63.3% for zero-shot GPT-6-Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. WAtcher also reaches 90.4% and 82.4% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ManiSkill3, on par with or above leading WAMs, and 74.0% on five real-world tasks with Safe-Guard on, against 59.5% for $\pi_{0.5}$. Safe-Guard achieves 92.1% balanced accuracy and reduces hazardous trials from 27.0% to 10.8% without lowering task success.
The system reports strong results across RoboTwin 2.0, ManiSkill3, and five real-world tasks, including 74.0% success with safety enabled.

papers.abstract: We present SPARC, a geometry-guided attention pruning framework that turns the native self-attention of pretrained video diffusion transformers into a unified mechanism for camera control and persistent scene memory. Our key insight is that attention connectivity can simultaneously serve as geometric conditioning for camera control and spatial addressing for historical memory retrieval. Motivated by the asymmetric contextual requirements of reconstructing observed content and synthesizing novel regions, SPARC restricts observed tokens to geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context, while preserving dense attention for unobserved regions. Correspondence-aware attention biasing and order-invariant historical positioning further enable stable retrieval across long temporal gaps. Without introducing additional learnable control or memory modules, SPARC achieves precise camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation while substantially reducing attention computation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of aggressive attention pruning in improving camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity, with an inference speedup of over 50x when combined with four-step distillation. Project page is available at https://zju3dv.github.io/SPARC.
authors: Zesong Yang, Weikai Chen, Liyuan Cui, Yuan Li, Jiaxin Huang, Lutao Jiang, Runze Zhang, Yingda Yin, Xiaoyang Huang, Kai Yan, Keyang Luo, Xin Wang, Hujun Bao, Zhaopeng Cui
bullets: Addresses camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation in long-horizon camera-controlled video generation.
Uses geometric correspondences to guide attention and retrieve relevant historical scene content.
Restricts observed regions to matching historical tokens plus local context, while retaining dense attention for novel regions.
Adds correspondence-aware attention biases and order-invariant historical positioning for stable retrieval across long temporal gaps.
Reports improved camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity while substantially reducing attention computation.

figures.caption: Figure 3. System Overview. For each target chunk, SPARC establishes token-level correspondences with historical observations through local geometric projection, and then prunes the backbone’s native self-attention to focus on geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context for previously observed regions, while newly revealed regions retain dense attention for flexible content synthesis. Historical RoPE re-indexing is employed to eliminate artificial temporal ordering biases among retrieved historical observations. The generated observations are subsequently appended to the history bank for continuous rollout.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on DL3DV-Eval. Given the same input image and camera trajectory, we show frames generated with different methods along the roaming time. Explicit-3D baselines drift from the target trajectory or accumulate geometric distortions, and implicit baselines fail to follow the prescribed camera path, whereas SPARC preserves scene appearance and accurate camera control throughout the rollout. See Supp. for additional scenes and video comparisons.

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison of revisitation on WorldScore-Static. Each scene follows a closed-loop camera trajectory (top view), and frames are sampled along the roaming time. Baselines either distort the scene or fail to recover the originally observed content upon revisiting, whereas our SPARC faithfully restores the scene at both revisits. See Supp. for additional scenes and video comparisons.

Figure 9. Additional long-horizon generation results. Without any degradation-aware augmentation, SPARC generates high-fidelity, minute-long videos with precise camera adherence and persistent scene consistency.

Figure 7. Ablation on attention pruning and historical RoPE indexing. The bottom rows visualize the pixel-wise difference |∆| between outputs generated using the original and shuffled history orders: sequential history RoPE yields discrepancies that grow along the trajectory, whereas our shared indexing remains invariant.

Figure 2. Redundancy of dense full self-attention. Most target regions have been observed in historical frames and require only sparse geometric correspondences for faithful reconstruction, while newly revealed regions benefit from broader contextual interactions.
Figure 8. Attention weight visualization. Given target queries, dense attention with the camera adapter exhibits attention peaks that deviate from geometrically corresponding historical regions.
Figure 5. Camera alignment. SPARC achieves the best camera alignment on DL3DV-Evaluation.

Figure 10. Training-free dynamic scene generation. We segment the foreground object and shift its correspondence locations along a prescribed motion trajectory, allowing SPARC to synthesize natural object motion consistent with the specified trajectory.

papers.abstract: Planning with latent world models requires both accurate multi-step predictions and latent distances that reflect physical proximity to the goal. However, models are typically trained on ground-truth observations but must rely on their own imaginations during planning, while closer latent distances do not necessarily correspond to better task outcomes. Existing methods resort to auxiliary training objectives or additional task-cost readouts, which respectively incur extra training overhead or leave the latent geometry itself misaligned with task cost. We introduce CARE-WM, a drop-in training method that meets both requirements without additional supervision, a separate cost model, or any change to LeWM's architecture and Euclidean-cost planner. CARE-WM trains the predictor on its own predictions and adaptively calibrates the strength of latent regularization. With a single hyperparameter configuration, CARE-WM improves mean planning success over LeWM across all evaluated continuous-control tasks and matches or exceeds the best results of other LeWM-family methods on most tasks. Further analyses show lower open-loop latent prediction error and closer agreement between latent-cost rankings and physical task costs.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between training on real observations and planning with model-generated imagined states.
Uses same-horizon self-conditioning plus constraint-adaptive latent regularization.
Requires no auxiliary supervision, separate task-cost model, or changes to LeWM’s architecture and Euclidean-cost planner.
Improves mean planning success over LeWM across all evaluated continuous-control tasks and matches or exceeds competing LeWM-family methods on most tasks.
Also reduces open-loop latent prediction error and better aligns latent-cost rankings with physical task costs.

papers.abstract: World-Action Models (WAMs) are a promising new paradigm of robot manipulation policies that jointly generate future video and actions. Successful manipulation requires both identifying where to interact and modeling how the robot and objects move. Yet standard adaptation methods, such as full fine-tuning and LoRA, do not explicitly select parameters aligned with these manipulation-specific capabilities. Motivated by this challenge, we discover two functionally specialized families of attention heads: Next-Interaction Heads, which localize upcoming grasp-and-release targets, and Motion Heads, which track movement across frames. Furthermore, we introduce HeadLight, a parameter-efficient refinement method that jointly adapts Next-Interaction Heads and Motion Heads. On RoboTwin tasks unseen during fine-tuning, HeadLight achieves 62.28% success, compared with 57.89% for full fine-tuning and 58.66% for LoRA, while updating only 1.1% of parameters. Inference-time ablations further validate the functional importance of these heads: ablating Motion Heads reduces manipulation success from 57.89% to 0.94%, while ablating Next-Interaction Heads lowers it to 40.61%, both substantially more than ablating equally many random heads. Finally, we show that our approach is effective across multiple WAM architectures and real-robot manipulation settings.
authors: Yuze Zhu, Jacky Li, Yusen Luo, Ken Jiankun Zheng, Chancharik Mitra, Trevor Darrell, Roei Herzig
bullets: World-action models must both identify where to interact and model how robots and objects move.

HeadLight jointly adapts these specialized heads instead of broadly fine-tuning the model.
On unseen RoboTwin tasks, it achieves 62.28% success versus 57.89% for full fine-tuning and 58.66% for LoRA.
Ablations show both head families are functionally important, with effectiveness demonstrated across architectures and real-robot settings.

papers.title: Targeted Adaptation of World-Action Models via Interaction and Motion Heads

papers.abstract: Robot world models are increasingly used to evaluate and plan policies, yet robot training data are dominated by successful demonstrations. Off the happy path, when a grasp is misaligned or mistimed and the object is pushed, tilted, or slips, their predictions break down. Across five pretrained action-conditioned models, object-motion error is at most 10.4% lower than that of a static baseline that copies the first frame, and two models are worse than this baseline. We present WorldReforge, which teaches world models what happens when manipulation goes wrong. We construct the Reforge dataset of 62k simulated trajectories by perturbing reference grasps in position, orientation, and closure timing, recording each resulting push, slip, or failed pickup with ground-truth object pose, contact, and surface points. WorldReforge turns this ground truth into two training signals without additional inference cost. Interaction Alignment focuses reconstruction on the small object and contact regions that a global loss underweights, and Surface Correspondence trains backbone features to follow the same physical surface points across frames. On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and by 35.0% on unseen objects, and it lowers the error in predicting how two actions' outcomes diverge by 43.3%. Although trained only in simulation, it also improves reconstruction on DROID and on real failure videos. Controlled data studies show that failed contact and successful holding teach complementary physics: failed contact teaches how objects respond, and holding teaches how a grasped state persists. Our code, data, and models are available at aim-uofa.github.io/WorldReforge/.
authors: Zhiyue Zhao, Mingyu Liu, Bolin Zhang, Liyang Li, Guangyu Huang, Canyu Zhao, Jinchuan Shi, Haokai Zhang, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen
bullets: Existing action-conditioned world models struggle off the happy path, with some performing no better than—or worse than—a static first-frame baseline.
The Reforge dataset contains 62k simulated failure trajectories covering pushes, slips, and failed pickups with ground-truth object motion and contact geometry.
Interaction Alignment emphasizes object and contact regions, while Surface Correspondence tracks physical surface points across frames without extra inference cost.
On Cosmos3 Nano, WorldReforge reduces object trajectory error by 28.2% overall and 35.0% on unseen objects, and reduces action-outcome divergence error by 43.3%.
Simulation-trained models also improve reconstruction on DROID and real failure videos; failed contact and successful holding provide complementary learning signals.

papers.abstract: A world model lets an agent anticipate the consequences of its actions and use imagined futures to make decisions. We introduce Normalizing-Flow World Model (NFWM), which pairs an invertible observation encoder with an action-conditioned probabilistic predictor. Because the encoder is invertible, the predicted distribution over latent states defines a distribution over future observations. Maximizing the exact conditional likelihood of those observations therefore trains the representation and dynamics jointly. An agent can plan directly in the learned latent space and decode sampled trajectories to inspect possible futures. On Teleport, these samples capture the two possible outcomes of the same action. In Flappy Bird, a world model trained by likelihood alone supports reward-based planning that reaches 100 pipes in all ten evaluated games. For goal-conditioned control, an auxiliary inverse-dynamics objective shapes the coordinates used to compare predicted states with a goal. On LIBERO, NFWM uses this distance to select successful action sequences more often than LeWM and SMWM. In Atari Boxing, training on imagined trajectories improves a policy beyond its behavior-cloned initialization. Together, these results establish normalizing flows as capable world models.
authors: Zijia Li, Yong-Hyun Park, Shusheng Yang, Jiatao Gu
bullets: Pairs an invertible observation encoder with an action-conditioned probabilistic dynamics predictor.
Trains representations and dynamics jointly by maximizing exact conditional likelihood over future observations.
Produces interpretable samples of possible futures and enables planning directly in latent space.
Supports successful reward-based planning in Flappy Bird, goal-conditioned control on LIBERO, and policy improvement in Atari Boxing.
The approach is evaluated across Teleport, Flappy Bird, LIBERO, and Atari Boxing; the abstract does not specify broader limitations.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) support robot control through visual prediction, but dense future modeling repeatedly encodes static context already available in the current observation, while action-relevant changes are often spatially sparse. We study sparse dynamic representation learning, retaining the current observation as a contextual anchor and using a small set of compact dynamic tokens to represent anticipated changes. We develop CompactWAM, a sparse-dense joint predictive framework that enables sparse representation learning within a video-supervised shared backbone, without requiring a reconstruction objective for the sparse pathway. Since a limited token budget alone does not specify which information to retain, we introduce Dynamic Forcing, which pairs direct action supervision with privileged dense future guidance to promote action relevance and dynamic fidelity. While action prediction gradients directly drive compact tokens to capture control-relevant cues, dense future guidance further shapes them via action functional guidance that matches sparse and dense contributions to the action expert, and dynamics-aware distribution matching, which aligns temporal relational changes relative to a static reference. At inference, a single visual forward pass encodes current observations and compact dynamic tokens for action generation, eliminating dense future modeling. CompactWAM achieves 98.4\% success on LIBERO and 77.9\% on LIBERO-Plus, retaining respective success rates of 98.3\% and 76.6\% with only 9.2\% of the dense future token budget. Evaluations on RoboTwin~2.0 and real-world manipulation further demonstrate the effectiveness of the learned sparse predictive representations.
authors: Ziqiang Li, Shisheng Chen, Yunnan Wang, Wenyao Zhang, Zili Lin, Yuyang Zhang, Xudong Yang, Fangzhuo Jin, Chenyu Zhou, Wenjun Zeng, Xin Jin
bullets: Addresses redundant encoding of static context and the spatial sparsity of action-relevant changes in world action models.
Retains the current observation as context while representing anticipated changes with a small set of dynamic tokens.
Introduces Dynamic Forcing: action supervision plus action-functional and dynamics-aware guidance from dense future representations.
Achieves 98.4% success on LIBERO and 77.9% on LIBERO-Plus, while using only 9.2% of the dense future token budget with minimal reported performance loss.
Additional evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and real-world manipulation support the effectiveness of the sparse representations.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) unify future video prediction and action generation for robotic control, but their reliance on iterative denoising incurs substantial inference costs. Distilling these models into few-step generators offers a promising route to efficient deployment, yet maintaining task performance under aggressive step reduction remains challenging. Existing methods rely on point-wise trajectory consistency distillation, which pursues high visual fidelity while leaving downstream action information unexploited in optimizing video generation, and also lacks explicit distribution-level alignment. To address this, we propose DriftWAM, a few-step WAM distillation framework that incorporates the actions induced by predicted videos into video learning. Specifically, DriftWAM integrates action-aware video drifting, which performs video distribution matching through a joint visual--action similarity kernel to steer sample evolution under the guidance of these induced actions, with action-guided video regularization, which leverages the compatible teacher--student matches identified by the joint kernel to backpropagate action-level gradients directly into the video generator. Evaluations on the RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO benchmarks, as well as in real-world robotic manipulation tasks, show that DriftWAM consistently outperforms prior consistency distillation methods across few-step settings at the same inference speed.
authors: Minyang Li, Siyu Xu, Yunke Wang, Ying-Cong Chen, Chang Xu, Daochang Liu
bullets: WAMs are costly at inference because they require iterative denoising, while aggressive step reduction can hurt task performance.
DriftWAM uses action-aware video drifting to match video distributions with a joint visual–action similarity kernel.
Action-guided video regularization transfers action-level gradients from compatible teacher–student matches into the video generator.
Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real robotic manipulation tasks show consistent gains over prior consistency-distillation methods at matched inference speed.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Training Overview of the video branch in DriftWAM. On the left, the teacher generates reference video–action pairs offline, while the student produces video candidates under the same context c. Sharing the same frozen parameters, the teacher in the middle extracts visual features and computes action responses for both student and teacher videos. The resulting visual and action-response distances feed the joint kernel, whose attraction and repulsion weights determine the targets for LV drift in the upper branch. In parallel, the lower branch uses the same kernel to select student–teacher pairs for LV reg, which aligns the paired videos’ action responses and directly backpropagates action-level gradients to the video generator.

papers.abstract: Optimizing indoor climate systems plays a critical role in achieving the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 13. However, indoor delayed thermodynamic responses and partial observability severely hinder existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods, which are primarily limited by implicit thermal inertia, occupancy dynamic prediction, and cumulative prediction errors during long-horizon rollouts. Thus, we propose a novel occupant-centric indoor climate control framework. It develops indoor environmental world models to predict future physical thermal baselines and dynamic occupancy, explicitly capturing latent thermal inertia. By formulating adaptive regulation as counterfactual advantage learning against future environments via a Branching Dueling Q-Network, and integrating a Held-Action TD-{\lambda} target, it effectively mitigates delayed credit assignment. Additionally, a proposed physics-aligned smoothness regularization suppresses high-frequency actuator fluctuations, potentially extending equipment service life. Experiments on SemiBuildingSim and Sinergym demonstrate that our method achieves a superior multi-objective trade-off. Compared to the best-performing methods, it further reduces energy consumption by 11.2%, occupant discomfort by 44.2%, and action fluctuation by 47.3%, achieving better sample efficiency and cross-region effectiveness. This interdisciplinary study offers an energy-efficient, occupant-centric AI solution for control science, building science, and energy sustainability.
authors: Xu Yang, Kailai Sun, Dianyu Zhong, Irfan Qaisar, Yu Yang, Qianchuan Zhao, Jian Kang
bullets: Addresses delayed thermal responses, partial observability, occupancy dynamics, and long-horizon prediction errors in indoor climate control.
Builds world models for future thermal baselines and dynamic occupancy while explicitly modeling latent thermal inertia.
Uses counterfactual advantage learning with a Branching Dueling Q-Network and Held-Action TD-λ targets to improve delayed credit assignment.
Adds physics-aligned smoothness regularization to suppress high-frequency actuator changes.

In SemiBuildingSim and Sinergym, reports reductions of 11.2% in energy consumption, 44.2% in discomfort, and 47.3% in action fluctuation, with improved sample efficiency and cross-region effectiveness.

papers.abstract: World models predict what happens under an action, but choosing between actions requires comparing their outcomes in the same physical situation. Factual transitions alone determine action-wise marginal futures and average effects, but not individual effects or the probability that switching actions causes harm. We introduce WhatIf, a counterfactual world model for manipulation that couples candidate futures through shared latent physics and transition noise inferred from factual history. Each candidate action induces a sparse object-factor causal graph describing the physical pathways it activates. Rolling out these graphs under the shared situation anchors predictions to observed outcomes and confines action contrasts to the objects each action reaches. Shared type-conditioned functions support varying numbers of objects, while a round-trip loss enforces action-invariant abduction without counterfactual labels. We show that replacing an individual effect with its conditional mean incurs mean-squared error equal to its conditional variance, motivating comparisons between coupled futures. Building on these comparisons, Counterfactual Advantage Planning (CAP) ranks plans by their advantage over an incumbent within shared situations and constrains the probability of harm. Paired advantages reduce estimator variance by a factor of $1-\rho$, where $\rho$ is the correlation between branch outcomes, and cancel model errors shared by both branches. Each executed transition provides hindsight advantages to update the physics posterior, the next plan, and an amortized policy without a learned critic. We further establish when observational transitions identify interventional dynamics. Paired simulator interventions evaluate counterfactual accuracy, graph recovery, compositional generalization, and decision quality.
authors: Xu Yang, Kailai Sun, Qianchuan Zhao
bullets: Factual transitions alone cannot estimate individual action effects or the risk that switching actions causes harm.
The model couples candidate-action rollouts through shared latent physics and inferred transition noise, using sparse action-grounded causal graphs.
A round-trip loss enables action-invariant abduction without counterfactual labels, while type-conditioned functions support varying numbers of objects.

Counterfactual Advantage Planning ranks plans against an incumbent, controls harm probability, reduces variance through paired advantages, and updates from executed transitions without a learned critic.
Paired simulator interventions assess counterfactual accuracy, graph recovery, compositional generalization, decision quality, and conditions for identifying interventional dynamics.

The current action changes the successor through graph topology and edge strength.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in world models for game interaction and control have increased the demand for large-scale gameplay videos paired with camera trajectories. However, capturing synchronized camera trajectories often requires game-specific pipelines, limiting scalability. We therefore propose GameWeaver, a unified diffusion framework that automatically produces paired video--camera data through three complementary tasks: camera pose estimation from observed video, video generation along a prescribed camera trajectory, and joint video--camera generation from a reference image and text. First, each tipxel stores the normalized 3D coordinates of a pixel ray's endpoint in a reference coordinate frame. The resulting three-channel tipxel fields and RGB frames share the pretrained video model's VAE. Next, a fully trainable dual-stream Transformer exchanges appearance and geometry features through bidirectional gated attention and conditions both streams on shared text features. Finally, deterministic fitting recovers camera intrinsics and normalized trajectories from generated tipxel fields. In our evaluation tasks, GameWeaver achieves a normalized translation MSE of 0.0029 for camera control; for joint generation, it scores 85.48 out of 100 on instruction adherence versus 64.71 for the best cascade on that metric, validating the feasibility of the proposed approach.
authors: Lifan Jiang, Yifan Huang, Jixuan Zhang, Peifeng Wang, Yuying Ma, Dehai Zhao, Deng Cai, Boxi Wu
bullets: Addresses the scalability challenge of collecting synchronized gameplay videos and camera trajectories with game-specific pipelines.
Represents geometry using three-channel tipxel fields sharing a pretrained video model’s VAE with RGB frames.
Uses a dual-stream Transformer with bidirectional gated attention and shared text conditioning.
Supports camera-pose estimation, trajectory-conditioned video generation, and joint video–camera generation from an image and text.
Reports 0.0029 normalized translation MSE for camera control and 85.48/100 instruction adherence for joint generation, compared with 64.71 for the best cascade.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires historical context, yet retaining extensive visual histories incurs growing storage and retrieval costs, while aggressive compression risks losing fine-grained information needed for subsequent decisions. Moreover, executed action histories capture intermediate behaviors that sparse visual observations may miss. Preserving this complementary context efficiently calls for modality-specific memory mechanisms that balance recent detail with long-term retention. To this end, we introduce $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM, a world-action model equipped with hierarchical visual and interaction memories. $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM preserves recent visual observations in dense short-term memory while consolidating entries evicted from this window into fixed-size associative long-term memory through gated delta updates. Within the same short- and long-term hierarchy, interaction memory encodes executed action prefixes into compact temporal representations, complementing visual observations with behavioral context. These complementary memories are integrated into world-action modeling through layer-wise retrieval, enabling memory-augmented action generation with a bounded online memory footprint independent of episode length. On the memory-dependent simulation benchmarks MIKASA-Robo and RMBench, $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM achieves +53.2% and +61.2% absolute improvements in average success rates over Fast-WAM, respectively. These gains extend to real-world manipulation, where $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM achieves a +29.3% absolute improvement over LingBot-VA in average success across three tasks. These results suggest that $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM offers a promising approach to efficient memory-augmented world-action modeling.
authors: Xiaopeng Zhang, Weiqi Yuan, Xin Zhu, Jiaxi Huang, Yueqi Hu, Yin Zhang, Jian Yao, Yanjie Li
bullets: Addresses the storage, retrieval, and information-loss challenges of retaining long visual histories, while capturing behavioral context missing from sparse observations.
Uses dense short-term visual memory and fixed-size associative long-term memory updated through gated delta consolidation.
Encodes executed action prefixes in a matching short-/long-term interaction-memory hierarchy.
Integrates visual and interaction memories through layer-wise retrieval for memory-augmented action generation with episode-length-independent online memory.
Reports absolute average-success improvements of 53.2% and 61.2% over Fast-WAM on MIKASA-Robo and RMBench, and 29.3% over LingBot-VA across three real-world tasks.

papers.title: $\mathrm{M}^{2}$-WAM: Efficient Hierarchical Memory Across Modalities and Timescales for World-Action Models
papers.tldr: M²-WAM enables long-horizon robotic manipulation with bounded-memory world-action modeling by combining hierarchical visual and interaction memories across timescales.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon video generation is key to interactive world modeling, physical intelligence, and spatial reasoning, yet maintaining geometric consistency and accurate camera control remains challenging without 3D grounding. We introduce \textbf{VivaWorld}, a framework for generating geometry- and view-consistent long videos from an image. We first construct a compositional hybrid 3D representation that combines reconstructed point clouds, which preserve observed scene geometry and appearance, with generated textured meshes, which provide complete object geometry across $360^\circ$ novel views. We also introduce a connected-region filter removing inconsistent floating components for robust cross-view reconstruction and propose a hybrid camera embedding that combines global and object-anchored Pl\"{u}cker rays to capture both scene-level camera motion and camera-object relationships, and inject it together with the visual guidance into a video generation model via a control adapter. Extensive experiments show VivaWorld achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and camera control, while supporting controllable novel-view synthesis, long-horizon scene exploration, and physical AI. Project page is available at: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/sil/projects/vivaworld/
authors: Ying Jiang, Donglai Xiang, Anita Hu, Masha Shugrina
bullets: Targets geometric inconsistency and inaccurate camera control in long-horizon video generation.
Combines reconstructed point clouds with textured meshes to preserve observed details and complete unseen object geometry.
Uses connected-region filtering to remove inconsistent floating components during reconstruction.
Introduces hybrid global and object-anchored Plücker-ray camera embeddings injected through a control adapter.
Reports state-of-the-art visual quality and camera control, with controllable novel-view synthesis and long-horizon scene exploration.

A compositional control adapter injects those signals into a pretrained video diffusion model, and generated frames update visual guidance to condition the next chunk for long-horizon generation.

We compare full conditioning (including imperfect meshes, such as extra chairs or a misplaced bear) with missing meshes, mesh misalignment, incomplete point clouds, and fewer object anchors (left: point-cloud rendering; right: predicted frame). All variants generate videos with good overall visual quality. Accurate point-cloud guidance prevents incorrect background chair meshes from causing artifacts in the final video. Insufficient mesh guidance can distort fine structures such as chair legs, while incomplete point clouds reduce foreground and background detail. papers.abstract: World models typically predict future observations in pixel or latent space, limiting their ability to directly represent true 3D scene evolution. We present SplatWAM (Splatting World Action Model), a generative world model that learns action-conditioned dynamics directly over compact 3D Gaussian primitives. A tokenizer SplatWAM-T first encodes a variable number of unposed views into a fixed budget of Gaussian tokens. A dynamics model SplatWAM-D then predicts future Gaussian states in a single forward pass per action, using log-Euclidean covariance coordinates and differentiable rendering supervision to facilitate learning in an explicit 3D space. Each predicted state can be rasterized from arbitrary viewpoints, enforcing a shared 3D representation across views by construction. On OGBench Scene, SplatWAM renders novel views 12x faster than video world models (~80 FPS on an RTX 5090) with up to 2.0 dB higher PSNR. We further introduce SplatWAM-P, a lightweight flow-matching policy head jointly trained with the dynamics model. Across 8 task suites, model-free Gaussian-token policies outperform pixel-based counterparts by up to 24.8 percentage points. SplatWAM-P improves over Latent Particle World Model (LPWM) by 12 percentage points and matches HIQL without a learned value function. On LIBERO, our ~1B model outperforms WorldVLA (~7B) and the robot-pretrained OpenVLA (~7B), while matching OpenVLA-OFT when both are trained without large-scale robot pretraining. Code and checkpoints will be released.
authors: Frank Tsu-Fang Lu, Karthik Sundar Senthilkumar, Christopher Thirgood, Oscar Mendez, Simon Hadfield
bullets: Encodes variable numbers of unposed views into a fixed set of Gaussian tokens, then predicts future Gaussian states per action.
Uses explicit 3D dynamics, log-Euclidean covariance coordinates, and differentiable rendering to maintain consistent representations across viewpoints.
Renders novel views about 12× faster than video world models at roughly 80 FPS, with up to 2.0 dB higher PSNR on OGBench Scene.
Its jointly trained flow-matching policy improves over LPWM by 12 percentage points and reaches performance comparable to HIQL across task suites.
On LIBERO, the roughly 1B-parameter model outperforms larger WorldVLA and robot-pretrained OpenVLA models under the reported settings.

papers.abstract: Tracking motion capture with a whole-body musculoskeletal model means coordinating hundreds of muscles through contact, and current controllers take hours to days of GPU time to train, so every tuning decision is expensive. SuperMimic trains a tracking policy by backpropagating through the rollouts of a learned world model. We extend it to MS-Human-700 (700 muscles) and MyoFullBody (354 muscles), with MuJoCo's activation dynamics inside the world model. To make its training fast, our recipe takes the speedups developed for the Unitree G1, replaces three of their settings that fail on muscles, and adds four changes of our own: observations without muscle geometry, data collection concurrent with the updates, Beta exploration noise that keeps every excitation in $[0,1]$, and 50 Hz control. On one RTX 5090 it trains MS-Human-700 in 6.3 minutes to the held-out return that SuperMimic's published hyperparameters reach in 3.9 hours, 37$\times$ sooner, and in 20 minutes to lower tracking errors than theirs after 10 hours. It trains MyoFullBody 34$\times$ sooner without retuning. Ablations show what is specific to muscles: a higher policy learning rate stalls half of the runs, and clipped Gaussian noise adds a tonic co-contraction that Beta noise avoids. Finally, refining the policy's actions through the world model at test time lowers the position error by a further 26% with no held-out clip failing, and reaches the same return after 5.1 instead of 6.3 minutes of training. Code, the training recipe and videos are on the project page https://muscle-supermimic.beanpow.top.
authors: Kaibo He, Maciej Bakowicz, Shihe Zhou, Yusen Feng, Yanan Sui, Dhanush Radhakrishnan
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of coordinating hundreds of muscles under contact for motion-capture tracking.
Extends SuperMimic with MuJoCo activation dynamics to MS-Human-700 and MyoFullBody, plus muscle-specific training changes including Beta exploration noise and 50 Hz control.
Trains MS-Human-700 37× faster than the published SuperMimic setup and MyoFullBody 34× faster, without retuning.
Test-time action refinement reduces position error by a further 26% and reaches the same return with less training.
Ablations identify muscle-specific failure modes: overly high policy learning rates can stall training, while clipped Gaussian noise causes tonic co-contraction.

papers.abstract: World-action models combine action generation with future prediction, allowing visual transitions to serve as supervision for policy learning. Our controlled study of prediction spaces shows that spatially structured semantic features support better overall generalization under visual perturbations and make motion information more readily recoverable from learned predictive representations. Building on these observations, we introduce PreWAM, a world-action model that organizes future supervision around state changes in a prediction space defined by pretrained DINO features. Specifically, Residual World Prediction jointly learns source-relative changes and their resulting future states to emphasize dynamic information while preserving future-state semantics. Temporal-Scale Prediction conditions world queries on temporal distance to capture both short-term local motion and longer-horizon state evolution. These predictive objectives jointly shape a shared vision-language backbone with action supervision during pretraining and downstream policy learning. Experiments across the LIBERO benchmark family, SimplerEnv, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic manipulation demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved generalization and robustness under diverse distribution shifts.
bullets: A controlled study finds spatially structured semantic features improve generalization under visual perturbations and preserve recoverable motion information.
PreWAM represents future supervision through source-relative changes and resulting future states in pretrained DINO feature space.
Residual World Prediction emphasizes dynamic information while retaining future-state semantics.
Temporal-Scale Prediction models both short-term motion and longer-horizon state evolution.
Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation show strong performance and improved robustness under diverse shifts.

figures.caption: Figure 2. PreWAM overview. A shared Qwen VLM processes current observations and language instructions to provide features for the action expert and world predictor. The predictive branch uses paired-frame features from frozen DINOv3 as visual states, learning source-to-future changes through Residual World Prediction across short, medium, and long horizons through Temporal-Scale Prediction. Joint supervision of changes and future states trains the VLM alongside action learning; deployment uses only the VLM and action expert.

papers.abstract: Real-world egocentric videos capture multi-step household procedures, but their recorded trajectories leave alternative actions and recovery from the learner's own mistakes largely unexplored. We introduce EgoVine, a post-training framework that turns a fixed demonstration set into interactive experience for long-horizon planning. EgoVine operates in executable symbolic environments compiled from real-world video annotations, where an agent must coordinate object manipulations under partial observation and account for delayed consequences. Restoring a decision state allows the learner to explore alternative actions and compare their eventual outcomes. Union jointly trains action generation and consequence prediction in one model, using the same executions to supervise candidate comparison and recovery. Verified repairs add recovery targets from failed attempts, while comparisons among sampled continuations guide policy updates. The updated planner then returns to the environments, with its own decisions and mistakes shaping the next round of experience. On a shared benchmark, EgoVine-1.5B achieves 81.8% success on Main planning tasks and 66.7% on longer task compositions, outperforming all evaluated Flash LLM baselines on both. EgoVine connects real demonstrations to an iterative learning process that trains compact planners on choices and futures beyond the recorded trajectories.
bullets: Converts annotated egocentric videos into executable symbolic environments with partial observation and delayed consequences.
Restores decision states to compare alternative actions and their eventual outcomes beyond recorded trajectories.
Jointly trains action generation and consequence prediction, while verified repairs provide recovery targets from failures.
Iteratively feeds the planner’s own decisions and mistakes back into subsequent experience.
EgoVine-1.5B reaches 81.8% success on main tasks and 66.7% on longer compositions, outperforming evaluated Flash LLM baselines.

papers.abstract: Whole-body motion tracking enables humanoid robots to reproduce diverse skills from human demonstrations. Existing model-free reinforcement learning methods either distill motion specialists into a single policy at the cost of performance or train a generalist policy directly using cluster-scale computation. SuperMimic reduces this computational cost through a differentiable world model that implicitly learns the physics shared across motions by predicting the next state from the current state and action. However, this implicit formulation may not fully capture the underlying physical processes. Errors around changes of support can accumulate over imagined rollouts used to train the tracking policy. To address this challenge, we introduce DynaMimic, a differentiable world model that explicitly incorporates shared physics into state prediction. Specifically, its network predicts a contact wrench at each candidate support link and a residual generalized force. DynaMimic then uses these predictions to compute the next state through closed-form Lagrangian forward dynamics. Across 60 full LAFAN1 motions, DynaMimic reduces mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 18.6% relative to SuperMimic. For terrain tracking, we give both methods the same local height maps. Relative to terrain-conditioned SuperMimic, DynaMimic reduces MPJPE by 14.9% on A3 Parkour (66.15 to 56.28~mm) and by 10.8% on GRAIL terrain clips (141.88 to 126.57~mm). On a real A3 humanoid, the learned policies can perform diverse skills, such as floor recovery, cartwheel and a box vault.
authors: Chaoyue Xing, Linyi Huang, Yiting He, Yixuan Yin, Siqi Hou, Yi Zhang, Liyuan Pan, Miaomiao Liu, Daqi Liu

Predicts contact wrenches and residual generalized forces, then computes state updates using closed-form Lagrangian dynamics.
Reduces MPJPE by 18.6% across 60 LAFAN1 motions compared with SuperMimic.
With terrain conditioning, lowers MPJPE by 14.9% on A3 Parkour and 10.8% on GRAIL terrain clips.
Demonstrated diverse skills—including floor recovery, cartwheel, and box vault—on a real A3 humanoid.

papers.abstract: World models support embodied decision-making by predicting future environment states. In embodied visual tracking, uncertain target motion and robot-induced viewpoint changes jointly affect visual observations, making future-state prediction challenging. We propose Motion-Conditioned World Modeling, which incorporates predicted target-motion distributions and robot ego-motion into latent state transitions. A Geometry--Progress module jointly models geometric paths and single-step travel distances through shared motion modes and path-conditioned progress distributions. This formulation captures uncertainty in route selection and motion progress while preserving their dependence. Action-induced coordinate transformations express predicted paths in the next robot frame, providing geometrically grounded conditions for future visual-state prediction. Future visual feature reconstruction supervises the motion predictor through the conditioned transition branch, linking explicit motion representations to subsequent observations. The model is jointly optimized with motion likelihood, feature reconstruction, and expert-action supervision, enabling the tracking policy to combine visual context with predictive motion cues.Experiments on three embodied tracking benchmarks demonstrate improved tracking performance and cross-environment generalization with a lightweight $0.5$B backbone.

papers.abstract: Computers and their interfaces are usually treated as fixed, so a person, or increasingly an AI agent, must adapt to whatever the operating system presents. This is limiting when someone needs a different workflow, or an interface suited to hands-free use or a disability. We explore an overlooked alternative. Rather than training an agent to operate an existing computer, we train a generative model to be the computer, predicting each next screen from past screens and the user's mouse and keyboard actions. Treating a desktop as an interactive world model raises problems that natural-video world models largely avoid. Without a camera pose to index memory, the model must remember content that has left the screen without any geometric cues. Arithmetic in a terminal has to be exactly right, not merely plausible. Small interface text must also stay legible at interactive frame rates. Our Interactive Neural Computer is structured like a Neural Turing Machine and starts to address these problems with three modules trained end to end from pixels and actions. A surprise-gated slot memory, supervised by latent next-frame prediction (MEMORY-JEPA), stores what is off screen. An exploratory query bridge brings in the reasoning of a pretrained VLM, and a residual renderer predicts only the latent changes between frames. In long closed-loop rollouts, our model recalls occluded files in 64.2% of trials (chance is 33.3%), compared with at most 56.0% for recurrent and sliding-window baselines. It also raises terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3% to 50.1%. Finally, because the memory is explicit, it can be transplanted at test time to causally change what the model renders.

bullets: Addresses fixed interfaces by exploring computers that adapt through generative screen prediction.

Improves terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3% to 50.1%.

papers.abstract: Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy of the scene, on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. We present SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model): given a calibrated camera, it represents, from the first frame alone, the robot by its 3D model and the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points; a rule-based simulator with no trained parameters moves them under the actions, and a video model renders the result. SimPWM returns the realistic video together with the simulated state. We then freeze the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded and check whether the video still shows the object lifted. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, the answer differs for the arm and for the objects. With each of three base video models, the arm follows the proxy (robot IoU 0.75-0.78, against at most 0.69 for end-to-end models); rendering the robot alone already gives this. What the simulated objects add is the object state: against a robot-only proxy, they cut missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%, and the video follows them only with some base models: on rigid objects, freezing them lowers the lift rate of MiniMax-H3, fine-tuned on episodes whose simulation agrees with the real video, from 42% to 10%, but that of LTX-2.3, trained on the same episodes, only from 57% to 49%, as if it inferred the grasp from the arm motion; more than half of the remaining lifts of MiniMax-H3 are of cloth and rope, which the simulator carries rigidly. With any base model, the simulated state records what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state.
authors: Tingting Liao, Mingjia Huo, Hao Li, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric P. Xing, Guangyi Liu
bullets: Represents the robot with a 3D model and potentially contacted objects as 3D points from the first frame and calibrated camera.
A parameter-free rule-based simulator applies actions, while a video model renders realistic video alongside the simulated state.
Across unseen DROID setups, robot motion follows the proxy more closely than end-to-end models, while rendering the robot alone is often sufficient.
Adding simulated objects reduces missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%; object-state adherence varies substantially by base video model.
Rigid-object lift behavior is more sensitive to freezing simulated objects for MiniMax-H3 than LTX-2.3, while rigidly modeling cloth and rope remains a limitation.

papers.abstract: Recently developed World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions, providing predictive context for control. However, existing WAMs typically learn implicit attention allocation with limited explicit action-relevant attention guidance, leading to limited performance. To unleash strong capabilities of WAMs, we introduce explicit attention guidance as a unifying principle and propose our Attention-Guided WAM (AG-WAM), an end-to-end framework with three plug-and-play attention guidance modules that directly reformulate internal attention paradigm in WAMs: the Content-Adaptive Predictive Attention module, the Guidance-Point Visual Attention module, and the State-Conditioned Text Attention module. Without any external plugin module adopted, our end-to-end framework with the unifying principle of explicit attention guidance boosts the accuracy and efficiency of WAMs. Without using any private embodied training data, our AG-WAM establishes new state-of-the-art performance on multiple public robotic manipulation benchmarks including LIBERO-X, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin-2.0, significantly outperforming other methods, even those using massive private embodied training data by a notable margin, meanwhile notably improving training and inference efficiency.
authors: Hongcheng Zhang, Lei Sun, Songxuan Liu, Tengteng Pan, Yuqiang Zhai, Xianglong Xu, Jianya Guo, Xiao Song
bullets: Existing WAMs rely on implicit attention, limiting action-relevant prediction and control.
AG-WAM introduces three plug-and-play modules: content-adaptive predictive, guidance-point visual, and state-conditioned text attention.
The framework is end-to-end and requires no external plugin modules or private embodied training data.
It reports state-of-the-art results on LIBERO-X, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin-2.0, with improved training and inference efficiency.
The abstract does not specify quantitative gains or detailed limitations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong results in arm-centric manipulation, yet humanoid whole-body control (WBC) requires dynamic balance and tightly coupled full-body coordination. Existing hierarchical humanoid VLAs typically decouple motion generation from physical execution, leaving tracking and balance errors unable to directly optimize the VLA generator. We propose DiffGR00T, an end-to-end differentiable training framework that couples GR00T N1.7 with SONIC, a pretrained whole-body behavior foundation model. To enable execution-aware differentiable training, we replace the non-differentiable simulator with a learned, action-conditioned world model, allowing multi-step body-execution losses to backpropagate through the frozen whole-body controller and the flow-matching sampler directly into the VLA action head. On four HumanoidArena simulation tasks, DiffGR00T improves average task success by 12.5 percentage points over the supervised base VLA (59.2% to 71.7%), demonstrating that execution-aware gradients effectively align high-level motion generation with closed-loop whole-body dynamics.

bullets: Addresses the mismatch between high-level motion generation and physical execution in humanoid whole-body control.

On four HumanoidArena simulation tasks, average success rises from 59.2% to 71.7%, a 12.5-point improvement over the supervised base VLA.
