papers.abstract: Can artificial intelligence reproduce the economic dynamics that emerge as households, firms and governments interact and adapt through markets and institutions? To answer this question, we define an economic world model (EWM) as an agent's internal representation of how an economic system works, enabling counterfactual simulation and decision-making under resource constraints. We then propose a general framework for studying EWMs that links three tasks: simulating agent behaviour, learning economic transitions and systematically evaluating the dynamics. As an initial implementation, we learn household policies from microeconomic data and calibrate a structural economic transition model using macroeconomic data, linking individual decisions to aggregate dynamics. Our micro-to-macro evaluation framework compares simulated individual actions and group distributions with observed microdata and assesses macroeconomic dynamics through forecasting and counterfactual experiments. Results show that simulated and observed household consumption distributions overlap by 94.9%, while EWM forecasts closely track real GDP and several other aggregate levels. In government-borrowing counterfactuals, the EWM reproduces the benchmark life-cycle model's short-run transmission from borrowing to consumption. For ex ante planning, the EWM enables an LLM agent to achieve 10.29% higher simulated GDP under the epidemic shock than direct LLM decisions. This initial EWM is only a starting point. We invite economists and AI researchers to build a stronger EWM together. Economists can contribute richer economic models and knowledge, while AI researchers can develop stronger data-driven methods for simulating agent behaviour and learning economic transitions. Together, we aim not only to reproduce real economic dynamics, but also to discover and test new mechanisms that support better decisions and benefit society.

papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world-action models (WAMs) extend vision-language-action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions and future observations, yet this predictive ability serves only as an auxiliary loss for policy learning. Meanwhile, most policy improvement methods learn dynamics and values in separate models, increasing training overhead and limiting representation sharing between these complementary objectives. We introduce DexWAC, a unified world-actor-critic model that jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage. Our key insight is that visual prediction encourages control-relevant features, while value supervision promotes task-relevant representations; together, they shape a representation suited to policy learning. Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts, for each action chunk, the visual latent and proprioception at its endpoint together with its reward and continuation, so the world model alone efficiently yields complete imagined transitions without generating intermediate video frames. After adapting the world model and critic on real rollouts, we improve the pretrained actor through either PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-$N$ selection. DexWAC surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and achieves 75% average success on two real-world tasks, compared with 45% for $\pi_{0.5}$. Its world model is more accurate and faster than video-based baselines, and ablations confirm that learning dynamics and value together improves the policy.
authors: Hongjia Liu, Dacheng Zhou, Minghao Fu, Chuanjun Guo, Tianze Wang, Qingtao Liu, He Wang, Li Yi

Predicts endpoint visual latents, proprioception, reward, and continuation for action chunks, avoiding intermediate video-frame generation.
Adapts the world model and critic on real rollouts, then improves the actor with imagined-rollout PPO or critic-guided best-of-N selection.
Outperforms large-scale VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and reaches 75% average success on two real-world tasks versus 45% for π₀.₅.
World-model accuracy and speed, plus ablations, support jointly learning dynamics and value for better policies.

papers.abstract: Driving world models anticipate action consequences through representations of how the world evolves. For autonomous driving, these representations must capture both the surrounding scene and the ego vehicle's motion under a candidate plan. We propose CodeWAM, a driving world model that incorporates executable code as part of its world representation. Code represents ego dynamics by expressing how the vehicle state evolves under plan execution, while a learned visual model captures scene-dependent consequences. Executing the code produces a candidate-conditioned motion sequence, which is evaluated relative to the prior plan and recorded motion history. The resulting execution consequences and learned scene outcomes jointly represent the candidate's future, enabling the planner to assess both what a plan may lead to and how the vehicle transitions into that future. The selected plan becomes part of the next decision's execution context, linking successive choices within the model. CodeWAM achieves 93.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, 92.1 EPDMS on v2 navtest, and 50.6 EPDMS on NAVHARD. Further experiments demonstrate improved pairwise execution consistency and gains on Hydra-MDP and DrivoR without additional training, supporting executable code as a complementary representation for driving world models.

Reports 93.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, 92.1 EPDMS on v2 navtest, and 50.6 EPDMS on NAVHARD.
Shows improved pairwise execution consistency and gains on Hydra-MDP and DrivoR without additional training.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.
authors: Zhilu Zhang, Xiaoyu Liu, Wenxi Liu, Shengfeng He
bullets: Addresses the mutation or disappearance of moving objects after they leave and re-enter the camera view.
Couples perspective video generation with low-frame-rate panoramic evolution without auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs.
Uses Geometric Anchoring for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation for temporal aggregation.
Supports both latent-level and attention-level camera conditioning architectures.
Experiments on a new dynamic benchmark show gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

GeoAnch transfers spatially aligned features at synchronized timestamps, while TemComp aggregates features across neighboring timestamps for intermediate observations. For illustration, we depict a temporal sampling interval of s = 4 in image-space indices.

papers.abstract: Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object's frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).
authors: Joonghyuk Shin, Alex Trevithick, Katar\'ina T\'othov\'a, Liyuan Zhu, Shengyu Huang, Jaesik Park, Shalini De Mello, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Riccardo de Lutio, Haithem Turki
bullets: Video world models often lose long-term visual consistency, while explicit 3D worlds lack photorealistic appearance.
M2R stores rendered features on mesh surfaces in each object’s coordinate frame and retrieves them by rasterizing visible surfaces.
This makes appearance move with objects, persist across revisits, and remain shared among observing agents, with memory tied to surfaces rather than frames.
Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and coding-agent-authored worlds.
It more than doubles object permanence, nearly doubles cross-agent consistency, and renders 720p video at 40 FPS.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. M2R renders each agent’s view from the initial frame and renderings of a shared scene mesh. As agent A explores, it stores generated keys and values in a surface memory, indexed by the mesh surfaces they depict. When agent B encounters the same surfaces, it retrieves and renders them as agent A saw them (a). We train our renderer on rollouts that revisit earlier views. With a one-chunk window, it must render each revisit from the memory it wrote, supervised by a frozen teacher that sees the full past (b).

Figure 8. Multiple agents. We show a rollout in MutableWorlds in which two agents look from the same viewpoint (A) and meet twice (B). AgentGarten and Code World Model show agent 2 a different building (A2) and fail to preserve agent 2 across meetings (B). M2R is the only method to share appearance between agents.

Figure A14. MutableWorlds. We show a bakery drawer that is reopened after 39 s (top) and a room that is revisited from two views (bottom). Code World Model moves from a quay into a room and changes the furniture, and AgentGarten changes the drawer, its contents, and the view through the window, while M2R preserves all of them.

Figure A13. HSSD. We show a drawer that is reopened after 41 s (top) and a vase that is moved from a counter (A) into a fridge (B) while the camera looks away (bottom), in the layout of Fig. 6. Code World Model and AgentGarten change the contents of the drawer and keep the vase on the counter or draw a darker one, while M2R preserves both. The frame at the bottom left is the reference render at the first visit.

Figure A16. Multiple agents with a dynamic object. In a harbor workshop, we show cross-agent consistency for a place (A) and for a tool drawer that agent 1 opens and agent 2 reopens 38 s later (B), and agent persistence from both cameras at two meetings 34 s apart (C, D). AgentGarten and Code World Model show agent 2 another place, draw the drawer without its tools, and change or lose the other agent in at least one view, while M2R keeps the place, the tools, and both agents. papers.abstract: Long-horizon panoramic video wandering aims to continuously synthesize scene-consistent $360^\circ$ observations along user-specified camera trajectories from an initial equirectangular projection (ERP) panorama. Existing panoramic video models have achieved promising results in camera-controlled generation, while recent 3D-guided approaches further provide geometric guidance for improving scene consistency. However, stable long-horizon wandering remains challenging due to diverse motion--orientation relationships and imperfect memory guidance induced by accumulated generation artifacts and depth inaccuracies. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PVWander}, a 3D-memory-guided framework that accumulates generated observations into an online point-cloud memory and reprojects it to guide subsequent generation, with two complementary designs: \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} for motion--orientation alignment and \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} for adaptive memory guidance. \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} exploits the horizontal cyclic symmetry of ERP panoramas to uniformly align each clip's ERP orientation with its principal translation direction, yielding more consistent, forward-like relative motions while preserving the prescribed camera path. \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} exploits the coarse-to-fine nature of diffusion denoising to adaptively regulate reprojected memory guidance through timestep-dependent channel-wise gates, preserving its structural benefits while mitigating visual artifacts from imperfect projections. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PVWander achieves improved long-horizon generation quality, while ablations validate the effectiveness of both designs.
authors: Chuanxin Song, Xiaodong Wang, Shijie Chen, Junliang Xie, Zhanmi Zhong, Suiying Wu, Peixi Peng
bullets: Targets scene-consistent panoramic video synthesis along user-specified camera trajectories from an initial ERP panorama.
Accumulates generated observations in an online point-cloud memory and reprojects it to guide future frames.
Path-Facing canonicalization aligns ERP orientation with the principal translation direction while preserving the camera path.
Timestep-aware gating adaptively controls memory guidance during diffusion denoising to reduce artifacts from imperfect projections.
Experiments and ablations report improved long-horizon generation quality and validate both design components.

papers.abstract: Visual world models enable goal-directed planning by predicting action outcomes. Gradient-based planners optimize actions to lower predicted goal cost, but continued optimization can exploit prediction errors after execution stops improving. Comparing plans requires informative relative scores; improving them also requires reliable update directions. Exact-state execution reveals that a frozen hierarchical world model ranks goal-conditioned proposals even when its rankings among outputs of prolonged gradient search are uninformative. Effective planning pairs goal-directed candidates with predictions that distinguish their outcomes. We introduce CriticJEPA, which learns goal-conditioned flow proposals from reward-free trajectories and uses frozen rollouts to select among them at every hierarchy level. Forward selection forms a complete planner; short anchored updates refine candidates before selection. Across visual navigation and manipulation, CriticJEPA increases success at a fraction of the planning compute, transferring shared settings across independently trained models, hierarchy depths, and unseen tasks while keeping every world-model weight fixed.
authors: Xvyuan Liu, Jianjie Fang, Honglin Zhang, Zhaolu Wang, Xin Zhang, Wei Wu, Fengli Xu, Chen Gao, Yong Li
bullets: Gradient-based planning can exploit world-model prediction errors without improving real execution.
The method learns goal-conditioned flow proposals from reward-free trajectories and selects among them using frozen hierarchical rollouts.
Forward selection creates a complete planner, while short anchored updates refine candidates before selection.
Experiments in visual navigation and manipulation show higher success with less planning compute across models, hierarchy depths, and unseen tasks.
World-model weights remain fixed during planning and transfer.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) aim to construct a unified architecture capable of understanding world state evolution and guiding action generation. However, existing visual branches focus on predicting static visual observation, rather than reflecting potential transition information that captures the evolution of world states under motion interactions. This leads to representational entanglement between high-level physical condition evolution and low-level action trajectory generation within the Action Model, creating a structural bottleneck while weakening the predictive capability of world evolution modeling for action generation. We propose PILOT (Physical Inference for Latent Optimized Trajectories), whose core Representational Deduction (RD) bridges this gap by integrating motion chain-of-thought (CoT) guidance as a native model capability. Specifically, RD aims to encourage the action branch to explicitly model potential state transition tokens, which are retained as CoT in the reasoning space to guide fine-grained motion trajectory. Experiments demonstrate that RD not only improves the success rate and generalization ability of WAMs in complex robotic manipulation tasks but also enhances the model's physical interpretability by decoupling high-level motion semantics from low-level trajectory details. Furthermore, the abundant state transition supervision signals introduced by RD effectively alleviate the sparse supervision in action generation, supporting data-efficient real-robot adaptation with reduced demonstration sets.
authors: Xiangkai Ma, Xinyi Wang, Junjie Wang, Sheng Xu, Mingyang Li, Yue Ma, Han Zhang, Yuzheng Zhuang, Wenzhong Li, Zhihao Yuan
bullets: Existing World Action Models mainly predict static visual observations, limiting their ability to model evolving world states during interaction.
PILOT’s Representational Deduction encourages action branches to infer and retain potential state-transition tokens as reasoning guidance.
These motion CoT representations guide fine-grained trajectory generation while decoupling physical motion semantics from action details.
Experiments report improved manipulation success, generalization, and physical interpretability.
Additional transition supervision supports data-efficient adaptation to real robots with fewer demonstrations.

Simultaneously, we leverage a Causal Dynamics Engine (c) to supervise the motion semantics by learning physical state transition information. papers.abstract: Evaluating the physical plausibility of generated videos is critical for reliable robotic planning with world models. These videos inform action proposal and assessment before real-world execution, so undetected physical violations can lead to erroneous assessments of action feasibility and safety. Yet current video generators often produce physically implausible interactions. Detecting such violations directly with vision-language models (VLMs) remains challenging as physical verification requires evidence-grounded spatiotemporal reasoning beyond high-level semantic understanding. We develop five law-specific metrics for evaluating physical plausibility by combining spatiotemporal evidence from segmentation, tracking, 3D geometry, or appearance comparisons with targeted VLM reasoning: Contact fidelity, Object persistence, Solidity, Robot deformation, and Object deformation. Building on this metric suite, we introduce RoboProbe, an agentic evaluation framework that coordinates metric execution and selectively refines evaluations through constrained actions. To evaluate the physical plausibility of robot world models, we further introduce RP-Bench, with 761 human-labeled generated videos and 130 real demonstrations of 239 manipulation tasks from 12 robot datasets. On RP-Bench, all five metrics achieve AUROCs above 0.85 and outperform the evaluated learned judges, prior evaluators, and a frames-only Gemini baseline. Applying these metrics to five video generators reveals distinct patterns of physical violations across models, in both violation types and frequencies.
authors: Zhuoying Yang, Jiachen Ni, Yichen Guo, Xiaoshan Wu, Mengyu Wang
bullets: Motivation: Physically implausible generated videos can cause unsafe or incorrect robotic planning decisions.
Method: Combines segmentation, tracking, 3D geometry, and appearance evidence with targeted VLM reasoning across five law-specific metrics.
Framework: RoboProbe is an agentic evaluator that coordinates metrics and selectively refines assessments through constrained actions.
Benchmark: RP-Bench contains 761 human-labeled generated videos and 130 real demonstrations covering 239 manipulation tasks from 12 robot datasets.

Results: All five metrics exceed 0.85 AUROC and outperform the evaluated learned judges, prior evaluators, and a frames-only Gemini baseline; analyses of five generators reveal distinct violation patterns.

papers.abstract: Surgical scene understanding is constrained by data scarcity and long-tail class imbalance, as annotating surgical videos demands scarce clinical expertise while rare procedural events remain underrepresented. We tackle this through data generation and propose SurgGenesis, a generative surgical world model that learns future surgical state transitions in a latent space from visual observations and textual procedural descriptions, serving as a scalable surgical data engine. To adapt a large-scale video diffusion model to the data-scarce surgical domain without catastrophic forgetting, we introduce a three-stage progressive LoRA strategy that incrementally injects endoscopic visual priors, procedural semantics, and spatial motion cues. Rather than judging generation by visual fidelity alone, we validate SurgGenesis along two axes that separate a world model from a generic generator: (i) future-awareness, by comparing predicted futures against the real future through a GT-latent prediction gap and temporal-horizon analysis, and (ii) action-faithful usefulness, by checking that generated clips contain the commanded surgical triplet and that using them to rebalance long-tail events and drive downstream understanding (segmentation, triplet recognition, 3D reconstruction) yields action-specific gains. Conditioned futures therefore complement conventional long-tail sampling. Code: https://zh-qr.github.io/SurgGenesis
authors: Qirui Zhong, Quande Liu, Yang Chen, Cheng Xue
bullets: Learns latent future surgical state transitions from endoscopic observations and textual procedural descriptions.
Uses a three-stage progressive LoRA adaptation to inject visual, procedural, and spatial-motion knowledge into a video diffusion model.
Evaluates both future awareness against real future states and whether generated clips follow commanded surgical actions.
Generated data supports long-tail rebalancing and improves downstream segmentation, triplet recognition, and 3D reconstruction.
Scope: designed for data-scarce surgical video understanding, with usefulness assessed through action-specific downstream gains.

papers.tldr: SurgGenesis is a future-aware generative surgical world model that creates action-faithful video data to address scarce annotations and long-tail procedural events.

papers.abstract: World-action models connect visual prediction with executable robot control. We present EffectWAM, which develops this connection through three complementary components: Effect, camera positional encoding (CaPE), and Action Grounding. Effect represents visual change as the difference between independently encoded future observations and a shared current-observation anchor. CaPE conditions endpoint pooling on relative camera pose when reliable extrinsics are available, while sharing the same learned parameters with pose-free pooling for uncalibrated trajectories. Action Grounding trains the visual representation to retain measured changes in end-effector pose and gripper state. An exponential moving average of the observation encoder supplies Effect targets. A shared generation expert learns to jointly predict Effect and an executable action chunk through flow matching, and reuses the sampled pair to generate future video on demand. This allows the controller to execute actions without waiting for video synthesis. We train on more than 20,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data, excluding unused chain-of-thought data, and accommodate dataset-specific joint, end-effector, and hand-pose representations. Our evaluation uses the Small (8B) configuration on all five benchmarks and additionally evaluates the Large (26B) configuration on RoboDojo. Experiments examine closed-loop manipulation across complementary benchmarks, and comparisons across multiple baseline policies show consistent improvements from Action Grounding.
authors: Yuan Zhang, Hao Cui, Jingfei Ni, Meiyi Wang, Xin Nie, Chi Liu, Wenjie Xu, Lin Gao, Hao Li, Xianhe Zhang, Jiajia Wu, Diyuan Liu, Jia Pan, Chao Ji
bullets: Represents visual effects as future–current observation differences using a shared current-state anchor.
Uses camera positional encoding when extrinsics are available while supporting pose-free, uncalibrated trajectories.

A shared flow-matching expert predicts both visual effects and executable action chunks, enabling control without waiting for video synthesis.
Evaluations across five benchmarks report consistent improvements from Action Grounding; training uses over 20,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data.

papers.abstract: Occupancy world models predict future 3D scenes conditioned on ego actions, yet their predictions may not faithfully follow the specified trajectory under counterfactual actions. Because driving datasets provide sparse coverage of alternative trajectories for each scene, existing models learn the spatial effect of ego motion implicitly from observed scene--trajectory combinations, which may entangle action effects with scene--trajectory correlations. We propose ReCast, an ego-trajectory-guided transformer that grounds future prediction in action-induced geometric correspondence across ego-centric frames. ReCast decouples historical encoding from future decoding and aligns deformable interactions using relative ego transformations, while retaining flexibility for non-rigid scene evolution. We also introduce a counterfactual action-faithfulness benchmark covering in-distribution, tail, and out-of-distribution trajectories. On Occ3D-nuScenes, ReCast achieves competitive standard forecasting performance while improving counterfactual forecasting, with particularly clear gains under out-of-distribution trajectories.
bullets: Existing models can entangle action effects with scene–trajectory correlations because driving data sparsely covers alternative trajectories.
ReCast uses an ego-trajectory-guided transformer with relative ego transformations to align future predictions across ego-centric frames.
The model separates historical encoding from future decoding while preserving flexibility for non-rigid scene changes.
The proposed benchmark evaluates counterfactual action faithfulness on in-distribution, tail, and out-of-distribution trajectories.
On Occ3D-nuScenes, ReCast maintains competitive standard forecasting and improves counterfactual forecasting, particularly out of distribution.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models enable action- and camera-controlled exploration, yet struggle to maintain consistent spatial geometry and appearance when revisiting previously explored locations. Historical KV caches help auto-regressive video diffusion models maintain long-term consistency, but their retrieval and attention computation introduce substantial latency as history grows. We propose DraftKV, a training-free framework that retrieves historical KV caches based on geometric grounding and query-conditioned relevance, while combining CPU offloading with tile-wise streaming attention to reduce GPU memory usage and inference latency. Theoretically, we show that draft relevance reproduces the mean branch of full-resolution block relevance exactly, so its deviation is confined to the $\beta$-weighted max branch, and we bound retrieval utility loss in terms of the measured Top-K selection overlap. We further show that draft relevance cannot distinguish blocks with similar pooled descriptors regardless of camera pose, motivating geometric grounding before refinement. Then, we introduce streaming CG-Attention, which overlaps CPU-to-GPU KV transfers with attention computation through tile-wise streaming, hiding transfer latency while maintaining bounded GPU memory usage. Experiments across diverse model families show that DraftKV achieves superior generation quality and consistency while achieving $3.27\times$ end-to-end speedup and 42.2% peak GPU memory reduction over other CPU-offloaded KV cache retrieval methods. Notably, DraftKV enables high-quality interactive world generation with historical KV retrieval on a single H100 GPU using SolarWM-33B.
authors: Xiaoling Zhou, Haopeng Li, Yufa Zhou, Rui Ding, Yu Li, Jun Lin, Enze Xie, Chunhua Shen, Xuan Shen
bullets: Addresses spatial and visual inconsistency when revisiting locations, while reducing the latency and memory cost of growing KV histories.
Uses geometric grounding and query-conditioned draft relevance to retrieve the most useful historical KV cache blocks.
Introduces tile-wise streaming attention with CPU offloading to overlap KV transfers and computation under bounded GPU memory.
Reports 3.27× end-to-end speedup and 42.2% lower peak GPU memory than other CPU-offloaded retrieval methods.
Supports high-quality historical-KV world generation on a single H100 GPU with SolarWM-33B.

papers.abstract: Visual self-models learn from images how a robot moves under motor commands. Continuum robots need them even more, as they bend continuously without measured joint angles or fixed link geometry. Existing continuum self-models predict point clouds, image-space curves, or future images, but not the next 3D shape, appearance, and tip pose together from an observed body. 3D Gaussians offer a renderable representation of shape and appearance, yet articulated Gaussian self-models rely on joint angles to drive deformation. In this work, we propose BendGS, which uses a virtual backbone estimated from observation to drive command-conditioned Gaussian deformation, enabling next-state prediction for continuum robots without measured joint angles. In Gaussian modeling, a feed-forward network reconstructs the robot as 3D Gaussians from multi-view images, and the backbone, a chain of coordinate frames, is fitted to back-projected depth points to estimate the bending state. In transition, a network predicts its change under a relative motor command to deform the bound Gaussians. The deformed Gaussians render the next images and the 3D shape, and the distal frame gives the tip pose. Training losses use RGB-D images and masks, without bending or tip labels. On simulated and real robots, BendGS achieves the lowest Chamfer distance, best image quality, and lowest tip errors among the compared methods.

On simulated and real robots, reports the best Chamfer distance, image quality, and tip errors among compared methods.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) adapt pretrained video generators for robot control by jointly predicting future camera frames and actions, transferring physical priors learned from video into manipulation policies. However, generating future frames before every action makes test-time inference too slow for closed-loop control, while most existing policies remain restricted to short observation histories. Building on Fast-WAM, which showed that video prediction shapes policy representations during training so that future frame synthesis can be skipped at deployment, we present G0.7, a generalist world action model scaled along two axes: extending the context window from a single observation to up to five minutes of history, and scaling pretraining to a large-scale corpus of robot teleoperation and human egocentric (ego) video. Across public simulation suites and real-robot deployments, direct action decoding (Fast mode) matches imagine-then-act (IDM) inference from the same checkpoint while running in 60 ms per 16-step action chunk on a single RTX 5090 (7.6x faster than IDM) and supporting pause-free real-time chunking. Performance scales consistently with pretraining data, with human ego video driving the largest gains in out-of-distribution generalization: G0.7 achieves a 70.8 mean score across five simulation benchmark suites, 48% and 54% zero-shot pick-and-place success on Galaxea R1 Pro and R1 Lite, 96.7% in-distribution and 93.3% out-of-distribution success on video-conditioned in-context learning tasks, and 86.9% mean task progress across seven real-world post-training tasks including multi-minute box folding, drink preparation, and product bagging.
authors: Tianyuan Yuan, Baijun Ye, Shicheng Cao, Xing Nie, Xiaopeng Yu, Ke Dong, Zijie Zhao, Shenling Qiu, Yizhao Xu, Feiyang Xue, Haonan Liu, Haoyu Zhang, Haobo Jia, Zheng Liu, Anqi Yang, Jiahui Niu, Yue Sun, Tailai Cheng, Jianpeng Yu, Yang Wen, Longhao Wei, Zibin Dong, Shiduo Zhang, Yicheng Liu, Hang Zhao

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models generate navigable worlds frame by frame, but a persistent world requires previously observed scenes to remain recoverable as users move away and return. Existing memory evaluations, however, often focus on seen-view revisits and full rollouts, leaving cross-view scene recovery underexplored while entangling memory with trajectory-following errors and accumulated generation degradation. We introduce SceneMemBench, a benchmark for scene memory in interactive video world models. It evaluates two complementary dimensions: seen-view recall versus novel-view recovery, and controlled diagnosis versus end-to-end interaction. We introduce Continued Rollout from a shared ground-truth observation history, alongside Full Rollout over complete model-generated interactions. SceneMemBench contains 600 controlled trajectories across 33 Unreal Engine scenes and 60 Full Rollout cases, covering eight representative open- and closed-source models. We evaluate scene recovery along subject consistency, appearance fidelity, and geometric consistency. Results show that novel-view recovery is generally more challenging than seen-view recall, while model profiles under controlled histories can differ markedly from those observed in full interaction. Together, these findings reveal complementary failure modes obscured by seen-view revisits or end-to-end rollouts alone.

Finds novel-view recovery is generally harder, and that controlled-history model profiles can differ substantially from full interactions.

papers.abstract: Bimanual dexterous manipulation relies on multimodal inputs that capture visual context and non-visual physical interaction cues for precise and coordinated control. To address the challenge of effectively integrating these modalities for policy learning, we propose HiMoDex, a two-stage framework centered on hierarchical multimodal world-state representations. In Stage 1, we pretrain a hierarchical representation network on the collected dataset of 1.19 million synchronized multimodal time steps. The network integrates visual context with tactile, force-torque, and audio cues into unified world-state embeddings. In Stage 2, we freeze the pretrained network and use its embeddings to condition a shared world-action transformer. The transformer jointly learns action generation and action-conditioned future-state prediction. Experiments across five real-world tasks show that HiMoDex achieves an average success rate of 78.7\%, representing an absolute improvement of 32.0\% over the strongest evaluated baseline. Extensive ablations validate the benefits of hierarchical representation learning and two-stage training. Failure analysis helps explain performance differences across variants. Code, data, and demos will be released at https://anonymous.4open.science/w/research-website-BAB4/.
authors: Jin Yang, Youlin Wang, Ping Wei

Across five real-world tasks, it achieves a 78.7% average success rate, 32.0 percentage points above the strongest evaluated baseline.

papers.abstract: To manipulate a moving object, a policy must predict the scene at the moment its action executes, yet every millisecond spent predicting pushes that moment further away. Scene-level forecasts are computationally expensive, whereas target-centric forecasts can omit nearby objects that affect contact. Our key insight is that what a policy must predict decouples by role: only the target's pose, which determines contact, requires millimeter precision, while the surroundings matter primarily through the clearance they leave and the motion they impart. We present FoveaWAM, a native 4D world-action model that allocates precision according to these roles. Specifically, it models the target's past and future motion as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and relies on the current frame for everything static. This compact representation lets FoveaWAM act in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10 times faster than video world-action baselines, leaving substantially less time for the scene to evolve before action execution. To evaluate each policy under its own latency, we introduce OnTimeBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark in which the scene keeps moving while the policy computes. FoveaWAM reaches 82.1% success on OnTimeBench, 20.8 points above the strongest baseline, and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks. Project page: https://foveawam.github.io/
authors: Jiaqi Yin, Baoyue Zhang, Jiyuan Zhang, Wenxuan Liu, Zhaofei Yu, Yue Deng, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Addresses the latency–accuracy trade-off in manipulating moving objects: prediction time can let the scene change before action execution.
Uses role-aware 4D modeling: metric SE(3) trajectories for the target, sparse 3D flow for surroundings, and the current frame for static content.
Runs in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10× faster than video world-action baselines.
Introduces OnTimeBench, which evaluates policies while scenes continue moving during computation.
Achieves 82.1% success on OnTimeBench and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks.

At inference, the decoders are skipped, and the world stream runs once per query and caches its keys and values for the action stream.

papers.abstract: Direct visual world models predict the effects of candidate action sequences without recursive latent rollout, yet they leave the temporal structure of action effects unspecified. We introduce Zhengrong (Zhengrong-PoleWM), a world model that decomposes a latent trajectory into an initial-condition anchor, a free response, and delayed responses to action innovations. Nonlinear networks map visual history and causal action prefixes to response coefficients. A shared bank of stable conjugate poles determines how each response evolves with elapsed time. This factorization preserves nonlinear interactions across actions, anchors predictions exactly at the initial state, prevents future actions from affecting earlier predictions, and yields bounded responses to finite control plans. We derive an exact re-anchoring identity that identifies the additional basis direction $\Psi_\kappa(s)$ needed to represent shifted trajectory tails. Across four offline image-goal control benchmarks (Cube, TwoRoom, PushT, and Reacher), Zhengrong-PoleWM achieves $90.83\% \pm 0.47\%$ macro-average success over two training seeds at epoch 20, exceeding the strongest baseline (QQWorld) by 6.08 percentage points. Selecting checkpoints by validation loss yields $91.21\% \pm 1.00\%$. In a controlled first-epoch Cube study without restart regularization, neural and pole response heads outperform a generic direct predictor by 20.67 and 23.34 percentage points, respectively. On an NVIDIA A100 GPU, median latency for a full 30-iteration cross-entropy method search ranges from 74 to 87 ms across the four tasks. The mean of these medians is 77.5 ms, a 15.8% latency reduction relative to Fast-LeWM and a $7.1\times$ speedup over autoregressive LeWM.

papers.abstract: Learning how actions change visual states is essential for prediction and decision-making in embodied tasks. Existing action-conditioned JEPA world models typically predict future representations at discrete observation intervals, leaving the temporal evolution of action effects implicit. We introduce ActField, a continuous-time JEPA world model that explicitly models latent state evolution through an action-conditioned vector field integrated over physical time. ActField separates action-independent evolution from action-induced changes, with the latter modulated by the latent context. A reference-conditioned representation and multi-step dynamics loss further support accurate long-horizon prediction. Together, these components provide a structured and temporally continuous formulation for predicting action-conditioned visual dynamics. Experiments across LIBERO, DROID, and BEHAVIOR demonstrate improved visual prediction fidelity and more accurate action-induced motion prediction over existing world models. Further evaluations on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate the utility of ActField in improving downstream policy planning through VLM-guided action selection.

papers.abstract: 4D occupancy forecasting predicts the 3D semantic occupancy of a driving scene seconds ahead. Over a few seconds, the scene changes little while the vehicle moves, so most of the space ahead has already been seen. Sorting the future into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, we find that current camera-based world models fall short on the unchanged part: they fail to hold on to what they have already seen, rather than to forecast what will change. We therefore make what the model has seen its state. PersistWorld streams camera frames into a persistent 3D world state anchored in the scene, writing each frame once instead of rebuilding the state from past frames. The state is learned end to end with the forecast, and an evolver predicts it at any queried time along the ego trajectory. On Occ3D-nuScenes, PersistWorld raises the IoU of the best camera-based world model by 19 points at 1-3 s and by 18 to 24 points up to 8 s, while running more than twice as fast. Code and models: https://github.com/wangzian828/PersistWorld. Project page: https://wangzian828.github.io/PersistWorld
authors: ZiAn Wang, Tianyi Wang, Zhihao Chen, Manni Cui, Junkai Chen, ZhiJin Chen, Ruiqi Liu, Junfei Wu, Huanyu Zhang, Shu Wu
bullets: Targets a key weakness of current world models: forgetting scene regions that remain unchanged.
Streams each camera frame into a scene-anchored 3D state, writing information once rather than reconstructing history.
Jointly learns the persistent state with forecasting and uses an evolver to predict it at queried times along the ego trajectory.
On Occ3D-nuScenes, improves the best camera-based baseline by 19 IoU points at 1–3 seconds and 18–24 points through 8 seconds.
Runs more than twice as fast as the compared camera-based world model.

To forecast, the Evolver predicts the state at a queried time tk from S and the ego trajectory, and the Reader, marked R, decodes it in the queried ego frame. Bottom: the internal operations of each component, Secs. 3.2–3.4. The grid loss supervises the current and future occupancy, and the ray loss supervises the ray-depth sections of the Writer. papers.abstract: Navigation systems in colonoscopy are advancing from guiding the endoscopist to steering the scope autonomously. Since an incorrect motion can injure the patient, developing and evaluating these systems calls for a world model of colonoscopy. Such a model must follow a commanded scope motion, keep the colon anatomy consistent, and show lesions and procedural events. Yet camera-controlled generators trained on general scenes lose the colon's structure under motion, and endoscopic generators offer no camera control. We present ColonoWorld, a colonoscopy world model conditioned on a camera trajectory and a coarse 3D tube of the colon, trained on in vivo videos. From a whole-colon tube, it generates a full cecum-to-rectum procedure, even for unseen colon shapes. It also places polyps, instruments, and irrigation at specified locations and times. ColonoWorld outperforms state-of-the-art video generators, reducing camera trajectory error by 32% and FVD by 29%. Our code and annotations will be released at https://aidaslab.github.io/ColonoWorld.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot embodied systems are typically designed to collaborate by coordinating actions, sharing trajectories, or learning joint policies. We ask a complementary question: can collaboration emerge before decision-making, by first building a shared understanding of the environment? We introduce Shared Environmental Understanding, a policy-agnostic representation that aggregates partial egocentric observations from multiple robots into a shared latent world model. This shifts collaboration from the policy space to the representation space, enabling decentralized decision-making with shared environmental context. To this end, we propose Shared Environment Encoding and Retrieval (SEER), a framework that organizes multi-robot observations into a shared memory, retrieves relevant context via spatio-temporal similarity, and encodes it using a predictive latent world model. The resulting representations are injected into downstream navigation agents as tokens. Experimental results demonstrate that SEER captures action-relevant environmental structure and consistently improves navigation performance across both specialized VLN agents and general vision-language model agents, while preserving single-agent capabilities.

papers.abstract: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.

papers.abstract: World action models guide robots by predicting the effects of actions or generating commands from observations. A model may compare hundreds of candidate futures before acting, repeatedly reading weights that must fit in device memory. Post-training quantization reduces the number of bits used to store pretrained weights, but a smaller model is not necessarily a deployable one: temporary tensors can exceed graphics processing unit (GPU) memory limits, while even small prediction errors can change the selected action. This creates two coupled challenges: identifying bit assignments that preserve task performance and determining which of them meet real execution constraints, without exhausting costly task trials. We present PTQ4WAM, a framework for choosing layer-wise bit assignments and execution routes under memory, latency and task-evaluation budgets. Calibration measurements guide candidate proposals, optionally with a language model agent. We profile full-model routes on the GPU before spending task trials on feasible assignments. Fusing group rescaling and reading visual history in place can make an otherwise infeasible assignment deployable. Across 15 workloads from four model families, the median task score is 99.2% of the corresponding 32-bit floating-point (FP32) score. On fixed GPU replays, the median speedup over FP32 is 2.36 times and the median reduction in peak allocated memory is 71.5%. The code will be released soon.

Scope: results focus on fixed GPU replays; code release is forthcoming.

papers.abstract: Edge cases are not the long tail; they are the norm. An embodied system deployed across changing environments, bodies, objects, and tasks will routinely encounter combinations that were absent from its training data. General-purpose physical intelligence therefore requires world models that reuse prior knowledge, predict consequences, and adapt with little or no additional training. Yet current evaluations of conditional video generation emphasize visual quality, prompt alignment, or isolated physical plausibility, leaving systematic generalization difficult to measure. We introduce AxE Bench, a benchmark that organizes condition changes along eight factors of the acting agent and of its environment, and pairs every original condition with controlled variants that change one side or both. WBench-plus applies the same structure to an existing multi-turn benchmark, pairing each WBench scenario with variants on the environment side, through its world setting or camera behavior, or on the agent side, through its interaction instructions. Additionally, to score generated futures, we develop an evaluation harness that combines vision-language reasoning with targeted computer-vision evidence, converting each video into temporally localized events and comparing generated events with reference events in both time and semantics. We summarize each model with the AxE Score, event Fidelity weighted by its Stability across original-variant pairs. Across twenty models, generated events match reference events far more often in timing than in content: no model exceeds a Fidelity of 13.01, the highest Stability is 0.55, and the highest AxE Score is 7.10. Together, these components turn world-model generalization from an informal aspiration into a falsifiable evaluation program for real and simulated interactions. Our project website can be found at: AxEBench.github.io
authors: Haiyu Xu, Yiyang Chen, Jiayi Zhou, Jiaming Ji, Juntao Dai, Yaodong Yang, Boyuan Chen

papers.abstract: World models support planning by predicting how the environment evolves under candidate actions. However, one-step predictive accuracy alone does not characterize multi-step planning utility, which depends on distinguishing candidate futures. This raises a natural question: How does latent transition geometry shape planning? We investigate this through an action-conditioned transition-field view, using curvature regularization as a controlled intervention. Across four continuous-control tasks, appropriately tuned regularization improves planning, while excessive regularization can be detrimental. By decomposing the transition field into affine and non-affine components, we find that regularization reduces action sensitivity mainly through the non-affine component. To assess its role in planning, we directly manipulate the non-affine action response in frozen models and show that it affects candidate selection and closed-loop success. Further analysis shows that curvature generally brings predicted futures closer together, while preserving more of the differences along the goal direction. This helps explain why the planning effects vary across tasks. We observe broadly consistent planning trends across five sampling- and gradient-based solvers on LeWM and similar rollout-geometry trends on DINO-WM. Qualitative attention visualizations reveal accompanying shifts toward task-relevant visual structure. Together, these findings clarify how latent transition geometry influences multi-step planning.
authors: Xuanya Zhu, Da Li, Xiatian Zhu
bullets: The study examines how curvature in action-conditioned latent transition fields affects multi-step planning.
Moderate curvature regularization improves planning across four continuous-control tasks, whereas excessive regularization can hurt.
Regularization mainly reduces action sensitivity in the non-affine transition component.
Directly manipulating non-affine action responses changes candidate selection and closed-loop success in frozen models.
Curvature brings predicted futures closer together while preserving more goal-relevant differences, helping explain task-dependent effects across multiple planning solvers and world models.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models generate virtual environments autoregressively from player actions and visual history. However, visual history alone cannot reliably capture the evolving states of independently acting non-player characters (NPCs) in real games, particularly when they are outside the camera view. Recent multi-agent world models address this challenge through joint multi-view generation or persistent shared state, but often rely on external observations, like maps or scene geometry, or predefined state transitions. We present SWAM, a State-aware World Action Model that separates agent-state evolution from autoregressive visual generation in interactive 3D environments. A lightweight state model propagates character dynamics from actions without consuming generated frames, combining motion priors with learned scene-dependent corrections. The predicted states then guide an autoregressive diffusion transformer alongside visual history through a novel conditioning scheme. Rather than requiring an explicit scene geometry map or visibility tests, the conditioning indicates where characters may appear, allowing the diffusion model to learn their appearance and occlusion. This design enables NPCs to evolve independently of visual generation while maintaining consistent observations across visibility changes, interactions, and respawns. Evaluations in a custom Godot-based first-person shooter game demonstrate improvements in visual fidelity, NPC consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing approaches.
authors: Jenna Kang, Bingxuan Li, Colin Groth, Anatolii Evdokimov, Sai Zhang, Qi Sun
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of tracking independently acting, off-screen NPCs from visual history alone.
Uses a lightweight state model to propagate character dynamics from actions, motion priors, and learned scene-dependent corrections.
Conditions an autoregressive diffusion transformer on predicted states and visual history without requiring scene maps or visibility tests.
Supports consistent NPC appearance and behavior across visibility changes, interactions, and respawns.
Experiments in a custom Godot first-person shooter show improved visual fidelity, NPC consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing approaches.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how the world responds to actions and offer a promising path toward general embodied intelligence, but they are large and run the network many times per plan, so they are hard to deploy on robots. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) compute with sparse binary spikes and use additions instead of multiplications, which saves power. However, existing WAMs use dense videos as the world state, so a spiking version would spend most of its computation on the background. We therefore introduce SpikingWAM, the first spiking WAM, which uses a sparse task skeleton as the world state. Inspired by biological motor control, which attends only to the key positions of a task, the Task Skeleton State (TSS) keeps the keypoints of the arm and the task objects, and a small spiking front end estimates the object keypoints from images. Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA) keep millimetre precision, and the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR) runs the network once per plan. On the simulated benchmarks LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, SpikingWAM achieves competitive success rates with far less energy than ANN methods and surpasses all compared methods on LIBERO-Plus. Real robot experiments further confirm its effectiveness. These results show that a task skeleton lets spiking networks implement WAMs at very low energy, offering a new solution for low power embodied intelligence. Project page: https://wxqnl.github.io/spikingwam/
authors: Mingquan Liu, Peng Zhou, Shanming Yao, Shuai Wang, Simo Wu, Malu Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high computational and energy costs of large world-action models that repeatedly process dense video observations.
Represents the world with a sparse Task Skeleton State containing arm and object keypoints, estimated from images by a spiking front end.
Introduces Body Frame Spike Coding, Grid Coincidence Attention, and Persistent Single Step Readout for precise, efficient planning.
Achieves competitive simulated-task success with substantially lower energy than ANN methods, surpasses compared methods on LIBERO-Plus, and works in real-robot experiments.

papers.abstract: Residual world models forecast a driving scene through its temporal change, so feature components that stay constant over time vanish from the residual pathway. We ask whether evidence with weak temporal change, such as a waiting pedestrian or a stopped vehicle, can be used more effectively for planning, and introduce MOVER, a complementary event-routing mechanism. A training-time teacher measures how each spatially grounded event query responds when a past frame is removed from shared history and contrasts that sensitivity with the event's pooled temporal residual, prioritizing events that depend on history but receive weak residual evidence. A student predicts the resulting priorities from unperturbed history, so the teacher adds no inference cost. Under fixed total routing mass, one distribution scales a low-rank future bird's-eye-view update and biases trajectory-conditioned event reading. On nuScenes, MOVER reduces ResWorld's UniAD-style average L2 from 0.65 to 0.55 m and its collision rate from 0.23% to 0.12% without direct planner ego status (0.50 m and 0.09% with it), adding 4.1 ms per frame. Matched controls show that the complementary teacher outperforms either signal alone and that the allocation acts mainly during training. Adapted to BridgeDrive-LEAD, MOVER reaches a 96.52 +/- 0.65 driving score over three seeds on the 220-route Bench2Drive closed-loop benchmark, exceeding matched controls in each paired seed by a margin within seed variation.
authors: Xiangyu Li, Yu Jiang, Tianyi Wang, Liang He, Qixing Huang, Zhaomiao Guo
bullets: Residual world models may underrepresent static or slowly changing evidence, such as waiting pedestrians and stopped vehicles.
A training-time teacher identifies events that depend on past frames but receive weak temporal-residual evidence; a student predicts their routing priorities at inference.
The priorities allocate a fixed routing budget between low-rank future bird’s-eye-view updates and trajectory-conditioned event reading, adding no teacher cost at inference.
On nuScenes, MOVER reduces average L2 from 0.65 to 0.55 m and collision rate from 0.23% to 0.12%, with 4.1 ms/frame overhead.
On Bench2Drive, adapted MOVER achieves a 96.52 ± 0.65 driving score across three seeds and exceeds matched controls within paired-seed variation.

During training, a history-occlusion teacher produces complementary priorities from history sensitivity and residual evidence; a single-view student router distills these priorities. papers.abstract: Terraforming Mars is a long-horizon, action-conditioned control problem that requires predicting atmospheric responses to interventions over centuries to identify effective policies. This position paper argues that physics-regularized recurrent state-space world models are the most promising foundation for this setting. Data-driven climate emulators lack action-conditioning, and physics-based general circulation models (GCMs) are too expensive for policy search. Among learned world models, recurrent state-space architectures with physics constraints are better suited than transformer-based alternatives: they provide native uncertainty quantification through their stochastic-deterministic decomposition, remain stable under sparse non-terrestrial training data, and enforce physical consistency at each rollout step. To make this position concrete, we describe a potential architecture combining JEPA-inspired latent encoding, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-lineage planning head. We also introduce MarsWorld, an open benchmark proposal for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, and discuss broader implications and objections.
authors: Sameera S Kashyap, Akshitha Nagaraj, Razvan Marinescu
bullets: Terraforming requires long-horizon, action-conditioned predictions of atmospheric responses.
Climate emulators often lack intervention conditioning, while physics-based GCMs are too costly for policy search.
The paper favors recurrent state-space models over transformers for uncertainty estimation, sparse-data stability, and stepwise physical consistency.
A proposed design combines JEPA-inspired latent representations, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-style planning head.
The paper proposes MarsWorld, an open benchmark for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, but presents a position and architecture proposal rather than experimental validation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Proposed Mars atmospheric world model architecture. S1: A two-stage training strategy separates synthetic pre-training data (MCD v6.1) from observational fine-tuning sources (EMARS, OpenMARS; with TES/MCS as the underlying retrievals); intervention actions at enter the transition model as continuous vectors. S2: A state encoder maps atmospheric fields to a latent z; PINN constraints and UDE residuals regularize the latent and downstream dynamics, merged at the concatenation node. S3: An RSSM propagates stochastic latent zt and recurrent memory ht under action-conditioned transitions ρ(z | h, a) with physics enforced at every step; ht is updated from (ht−1, zt−1, at−1) via the recurrent backbone. S4: An actor-critic head trains within imagined latent rollouts; the actor π(a | z, h) outputs intervention policies, the critic V (z, h) estimates returns from (∆P,∆T,∆O2), and a decoder reconstructs gridded fields against EMARS as an auxiliary signal. S5: Outputs are a learned policy trajectory, a long-horizon atmospheric forecast, and a rollout uncertainty map from stochastic latent samples.

Table 1: Requirements for Mars terraforming simulation vs. existing systems. (i) Mars physical accuracy; (ii) tractable for policy search; (iii) action-conditioned rollouts; (iv) century-scale stability; (v) trainable on sparse non-terrestrial data.

papers.abstract: Safety-critical scenarios are rare in recorded driving and must be generated to test and train motion planners of automated vehicles. In guided diffusion models, each scenario type needs its own weighted objective, separate from the validity check. Optimized together with the attacker, the vehicle under test can cancel the attack or draw it toward itself. We state each scenario as a signal temporal logic specification with clauses typed by role. Every clause names the agent it may change and the agents it may read, and the vehicle under test reads the attacker only from the attack onset. A large language model drafts the specification from a description, and a type checker accepts it. A compiler derives the optimization: it edits a diffusion model's samples by the smallest change that satisfies the specification, each clause moves only its owner, the attacker is solved against the unreacted vehicle under test before its response, and the monitor of the same specification decides acceptance. On nuScenes and CommonRoad, judged independently of the specification, one parameter set produced valid scenarios at a rate 0.14 above a weighted objective tuned per scenario type, and descriptions yielded at least one valid scenario for 11 of the 16 pre-crash types expressible in the public data. Learned planners fail more often on the generated scenarios than on their seeds. Fine-tuning on them lowers a planner's failure rate on critical scenarios, and the time headway one clause of the label requires, not the generator, sets the size of the gain.
authors: Zifan Zeng, Qunli Zhang, Peng Wang, Shiming Liu, Feng Liu, Zheng Hu
bullets: Targets the scarcity of rare, safety-critical driving scenarios for testing and training automated-vehicle motion planners.
Uses role-typed signal temporal logic: clauses specify which agents may be changed or observed, with restricted attacker–vehicle interactions.
An LLM drafts specifications; a type checker validates them, and a compiler derives constrained diffusion optimization and acceptance monitoring.
Across nuScenes and CommonRoad, one parameter set achieved a 0.14 higher valid-scenario rate than objectives tuned per scenario type.
Generated scenarios caused more learned-planner failures than their seeds; fine-tuning reduced failures, with gains limited by the labeled time-headway requirement.

figures.caption: FIGURE 2. Overview of the method for the description of a lead-vehicle braking scenario. Middle: an LLM drafts a role-typed specification, a type check returns errors for repair (contribution 1), and the compiler turns every clause φk into four objects. The exact robustness ρ, a minimum and maximum over time and agents, yields the monitor’s verdict ρ ≥ 0 and, for the observation clause, the onset t⋆. Its smooth lower bound ρ̃ enters a hinge loss whose gradient moves only the clause’s owner. Right: the solver runs in stages derived from the roles (contribution 2): the attacker keeps its seed during its hold time and is then edited against the unreacted seed of the ego, then the ego’s response is edited with the attack fixed, and the ego keeps its seed until the release t⋆ + δ. A specification may name a further guided role, such as a bystander that blocks the ego’s escape lane: it owns its clauses, whose gradients move only that role, and is solved in its own stage after the ego’s. All other agents are context agents and keep their seed trajectories. The monitor of the compiled specification accepts the result or restarts the role from maneuver primitives, and the K seeds of many windows are solved in one batch (contribution 3). Thumbnails (nuScenes, bird’s-eye view, true vehicle sizes): left, a seed scene with every agent’s trajectory (boxes at t = 0); bottom right, the generated scenario at t = 3 s: the lead vehicle brakes into the path of the ego’s unreacted seed (dashed), and the generated ego, identical to its seed until the release (circle), stays behind the lead vehicle.

In every panel the attacker’s seed (dashed red) did something else, the attack is turned against the unreacted seed of the ego vehicle (dashed black), with which it collides, and the generated ego vehicle responds from the release on with the smallest edit that keeps it clear of the attacker, by 0.1 to 0.7m at the closest point: it brakes in (a), (c), (e) and (f) and swerves in (b) and (d). The six pass the independent judges of their types. The drafted road clauses, which confine the attacker to the ego vehicle’s road corridor, are not met at the junctions, which is why the specification’s own monitor accepts only (b), (c) and (f) (Section VI). Footprints every 0.5 s (0.4 s on CommonRoad), light to dark; context agents in grey.

FIGURE 1. (a) Without ownership, the ego vehicle’s clauses also move the attacker and cancel the attack. (b) Without the stage order, the attacker is optimized against the responding ego vehicle: it chases the response, cuts in and brakes to a standstill, the unreacted seed collides with it, and the monitor rejects the output, since the specification asks for an unsafe gap and not a collision. (c) Ours: the attacker cuts in against the unreacted seed and slows down ahead of it, and the ego vehicle keeps its seed until the release t⋆ + δ and then brakes at 2.8m/s2. papers.abstract: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control enable teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. We propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.
bullets: Targets cooperative transport in environments requiring obstacle detours and changing team configurations.
Models humanoids, shared objects, and obstacles as interacting entities in a relational latent world model.
Imagines outcomes of alternative waypoint commands using offline counterfactual simulator rollouts.
Selects guidance commands using predicted progress, failure, contact risk, and long-horizon value.

Evaluated on three obstacle-constrained transport tasks, with generalization from four-humanoid training to teams of two to ten and unseen configurations; experiments report improved success over evaluated baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Uses a counterfactual latent world model for multi-humanoid cooperative manipulation, fitting robot learning and interactive/latent action world models.
papers.title: CarlHOI: Counterfactual Predictive Imagination for Generalizable Multi-Humanoid Object Interaction under Constrained Environments
papers.tldr: CarlHOI uses counterfactual world-model predictions to adapt pretrained multi-humanoid object-transport skills to unseen obstacles, team sizes, objects, and constraints without retraining.

papers.abstract: Learning to predict the effects of contact-rich manipulation skills requires models that represent distinct outcome modes rather than a single expected result. Even for basic skills such as pushing, picking, and placing, small variations in contact conditions or object geometry can produce qualitatively different object motions under nearly identical states and actions. Deterministic and Gaussian models tend to average over these alternatives or represent them as a single broad distribution, obscuring distinct modes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating. We study probabilistic skill-effect models that learn multimodal distributions over object pose changes given partial point clouds and actions. We instantiate this abstraction with three representative model classes: mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching, each paired with latent dynamics for next-step prediction. Across diverse objects and skills, explicitly multimodal models predict which outcome occurs more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines. In planning, flow matching significantly improves task success over the deterministic baseline on every skill and achieves the highest success on every multi-step sequence. On a real robot, probabilistic models succeed at pick about twice as often as the deterministic baseline, providing evidence that probabilistic skill effects offer a practical abstraction for reasoning and planning under uncertainty.
authors: Siyeon Kim, Mohanraj Devendran Shanthi, Joseph C. Liechty, Tucker Hermans
bullets: Contact variations and object geometry can produce distinct outcomes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating from similar states and actions.
The study models distributions over object pose changes from partial point clouds and actions using mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching with latent dynamics.
Explicitly multimodal models identify outcome modes more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines across diverse objects and skills.
Flow matching improves task success over the deterministic baseline for every skill and performs best on all evaluated multi-step sequences.
On a real robot, probabilistic models achieve roughly twice the pick success rate of the deterministic baseline.

papers.title: Grounded in Contact: Reducing Floating and Interpenetration Artifacts with Multimodal Skill-Effect Models
papers.tldr: Multimodal probabilistic models better predict contact-rich manipulation outcomes and improve planning and real-robot performance over deterministic baselines.

papers.abstract: Latent world models enable planning from images, but their predictions do not directly establish whether a robot will satisfy physical constraints. We present JEPA-Shield, which connects a frozen action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model to task-space safety enforcement. Two downstream models predict relative motion from imagined latent rollouts and decode unsafe geometry from the current image. Split conformal prediction turns end-to-end motion-prediction errors into multi-horizon uncertainty tubes. A backup-based shield checks these tubes against physical constraints and screens both candidate trajectories and final proposals in diffusion-inspired sampling-based model predictive control. Under the stated exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, we establish probabilistic constraint satisfaction at action-block boundaries for a returned plan executed without replanning. We also introduce VParkBench, with geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks and a editable photorealistic Gaussian-splatting environment. In closed-loop evaluation, JEPA-Shield achieves success rates of 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, respectively, with no observed constraint violations. Ablations show complementary benefits from shielding and uncertainty calibration. The results demonstrate the importance of grounding latent world-model predictions in task-space quantities and explicitly accounting for prediction uncertainty in safety-critical planning.
authors: Taekyung Kim, Ege Yuceel, Steven Hong, Georgios Fainekos, Dimitra Panagou, Bardh Hoxha
bullets: Motivation: Image-based latent predictions alone do not guarantee that robot plans satisfy task-space safety constraints.
Method: A frozen action-conditioned JEPA predicts imagined rollouts, while downstream models estimate motion and unsafe geometry; split conformal prediction forms multi-horizon uncertainty tubes.
Safety mechanism: A backup-based shield checks candidate and final diffusion-inspired MPC trajectories against physical constraints.
Guarantee: Under exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, the returned plan satisfies constraints probabilistically at action-block boundaries without replanning.

Evaluation: On geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks in VParkBench, success rates were 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, with no observed constraint violations; shielding and calibration provided complementary benefits.

papers.title: JEPA-Shield: Safe Diffusion Planning with Latent World Models via Conformal Shielding
papers.tldr: JEPA-Shield makes latent-world-model planning safer by calibrating imagined motion uncertainty and rejecting trajectories that may violate physical constraints.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies complete most benchmark tasks but often violate safety constraints. Since they are stochastic, one remedy is to sample several candidate action chunks and execute one that a world model predicts is safe. We ask what such a model must do. In simulation, a lookahead safety filter with the simulator as an exact world model raises the safety rate of three VLA policies on LIBERO and of pi0.5 on LIBERO-Plus by 11.5 to 25.7 points. It also helps pi0.5 on three RoboCasa tasks. Learned critics trained on one policy's data detect dangerous states (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates at one state close to chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551-0.560), and the learned dynamics and video models we test do no better. When the simulator's state is perturbed, selection degrades long before detection. In the loop, a median position error of 3.18 mm removes 70% of the gain on LIBERO-Spatial, partly because the error also corrupts the displacement check. On LIBERO-10 the loss is smaller, and the intervals overlap. The median does not predict the cost: a pixel reader with a 0.56 mm median error keeps 6.5 points less of the gain than Gaussian error of a similar median. A world model for safety should thus be judged by within-state ranking, and its state must be accurate in the tail and on handled objects, not only in the median.
bullets: VLA policies can violate safety constraints despite strong benchmark performance, motivating safety filtering over sampled action chunks.
An exact-simulator lookahead filter improves safety rates by 11.5–25.7 points across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and selected RoboCasa tasks.
Learned critics detect dangerous states well (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates nearly at chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551–0.560).
Safety-selection gains degrade substantially when the world model’s state is perturbed; median position error can remove most of the benefit.
Evaluation should emphasize within-state ranking and state accuracy in tail cases and on handled objects, not just median error.
