papers.selection_reason: Analyzes what a world model must do to keep VLA policies safe via action-conditioned lookahead prediction, matching interactive world models and VLA safety.
papers.title: Detecting Is Not Choosing: What a World Model Needs to Keep a VLA Policy Safe
papers.tldr: A safety world model for VLA policies must accurately rank candidate actions within each state—not merely detect dangerous states—and remain reliable under state-estimation errors.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) excel at robot manipulation by imagining future observations and decoding actions from them, yet remain confined to a single embodied agent. In practice, manipulation often requires multiple robots to collaborate across disjoint workspaces, coupled timing, and heterogeneous embodiments. Such coordination demands both spatiotemporal alignment of future interactions and awareness of individual embodiment and role identities, whereas existing decentralized per-robot policies, flat centralized models, and multi-robot VLAs fail to unite both. To bridge this gap, we present MAWAM, a multi-agent world action model that jointly predicts the future observations of multiple embodiments and decodes each agent's actions from them for collaborative manipulation. Through an agent-axis curriculum, MAWAM expands a single-agent WAM along an agent dimension to coordinate teams under shared weights. Within one unified causal sequence, joint self-attention spans all agents to spatiotemporally align their imagined futures, while hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks bind each stream to its role, identity, and embodiment. We further formalize multi-agent-necessary manipulation along three axes (why, when, and who) and develop MA-Task Harness, a coding-agent pipeline where mutually constraining generators and evaluators co-evolve customizable simulation-data and evaluation packages. Using this pipeline, we build MA-Bench across all axes with seven tasks, pairing joint success rate with role and collaboration scores for fine-grained analysis. On MA-Bench, MAWAM reaches 82.7% mean joint success, 30.7% above the strongest baseline, and achieves real-time closed-loop collaboration on a real heterogeneous robot team.
authors: Rongze Tang, Chenyu Zhou, Jianjie Fang, Ziming Liu, Zhaolu Wang, Ziyou Wang, Xvyuan Liu, Wei Wu, Chen Gao, Yong Li, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Addresses multi-robot manipulation requiring spatial-temporal coordination, role awareness, and embodiment awareness.
Expands a single-agent world action model across an agent dimension using shared weights and an agent-axis curriculum.
Uses joint self-attention, hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks to coordinate agent-specific behavior.
Introduces MA-Task Harness and MA-Bench, covering seven tasks with joint success, role, and collaboration metrics.
Achieves 82.7% mean joint success on MA-Bench and real-time closed-loop collaboration on a heterogeneous robot team.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan toward a goal by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions, but under the distribution shift, prediction errors can lead the planner astray. Test-time training using executed actions helps, yet what it corrects and whether its updates should persist across episodes remains unclear. We address both by analyzing the world model's prediction error. On PushObj, an object-pushing task, we probe multiple actions from the same state and decompose the error into an offset shared across actions and an action-dependent component. The offset effectively shifts the planner's goal, and AdaJEPA mainly tracks it: the common shift alone recovers 91% of its planning gain. Part of the offset is episode-specific, so carrying its correction into the next episode does not help and may even hurt. The remaining offset recurs across episodes and action-dependent error can be or needs to be learned and retained from many episodes. Our sft-JEPA therefore uses two learners on different timescales: a fast learner that tracks the offset and resets each episode, and a slow LoRA learner that accumulates recurring knowledge across episodes. Across PushObj, PointMaze, zero-shot planning on RoboCasa (with DINO-WM), and OGBench (with LeWAM), sft-JEPA leads all benchmark averages, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.
authors: Shuaicheng Niu, Guohao Chen, Kevin Z. Shen, Yunbei Zhang, Peilin Zhao, Yinan Zhang, Cyril Leung
bullets: Problem: Distribution-shifted prediction errors can mislead latent-world-model planners, and it is unclear which corrections should persist across episodes.
Method: Decompose prediction error into an action-shared offset and an action-dependent component.
Key finding: The shared offset shifts the planner’s goal; tracking it alone recovers 91% of AdaJEPA’s planning gain, while episode-specific corrections should not persist.
Contribution: sft-JEPA combines a fast, episode-resetting learner for transient offsets with a slow LoRA learner for recurring and action-dependent errors.
Results: It leads benchmark averages across PushObj, PointMaze, RoboCasa, and OGBench, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes test-time training in latent world models and proposes a slow-fast approach for planning under distribution shift.
papers.title: What Test-Time Training Corrects in Latent World Models? A Slow-Fast Approach
papers.tldr: A slow-fast test-time training method separates transient from recurring world-model errors, improving planning across diverse benchmarks.

papers.abstract: World models support robotic manipulation by predicting how the scene evolves under a planned action. For garments this prediction is notoriously difficult: deformations are complex, and self-occlusion leaves much of the cloth unobserved. Planned gripper trajectories provide a useful motion prior because cloth held by a gripper moves with it, while the remaining deformation must be predicted. We introduce ClothCast, a world model that applies this prior to the cloth's points and learns the residual motion. ClothCast takes one RGB-D observation, the camera pose, the robot's own model and the planned gripper trajectories, with no cloth mesh or material parameters. It lifts the observation to a layered point set that includes hypothesized occluded layers, carries the points with a blended rigid prior derived from the gripper poses, and predicts the residual motion with a video-diffusion point-flow model. Over entire 4- to 11-second episodes at 10 Hz, the moved points are rendered into depth, from which a geometry-conditioned completion model synthesizes RGB; after release, a hand-designed settling step replaces the learned motion. We further release ClothCastBench, 10,000 simulated dual-arm cloth-manipulation episodes with the ground-truth cloth mesh, including occluded layers, at every frame. On 492 held-out episodes, ClothCast achieves 2.5x lower sequence-averaged visible-surface Chamfer distance than Flex-{\pi}, the strongest baseline in geometry (14.0 mm vs. 35.6 mm), and 3.7 dB higher cloth-region PSNR than Cosmos-Predict2.5, the strongest baseline in cloth PSNR. On a 50-episode ablation subset, the rigid prior alone, applied to ClothCast's learned initial geometry with the same post-processing, already outperforms both geometry-capable baselines, and the learned residual lowers its error by about a third.
authors: Yushen Hu, Yilong Song, Zhen Zhou, Apurv Kushwaha, Harshvardhan Chandirasekar, Zhu-Tian Chen
bullets: Addresses cloth world modeling from a single RGB-D observation despite complex deformation and self-occlusion.
Uses camera pose, robot model, and planned gripper trajectories without requiring a cloth mesh or material parameters.

ClothCastBench provides 10,000 simulated dual-arm cloth-manipulation episodes with ground-truth meshes and occluded layers.

On 492 held-out episodes, it reports 14.0 mm visible-surface Chamfer distance and higher cloth-region PSNR than the cited baselines; a rigid prior alone already outperforms geometry-capable baselines, while residual learning further reduces error.

papers.abstract: Deep learning has shown promise for estimating human pose with multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) radar through walls. Building paired radar and pose datasets demands considerable time and manual effort, while large visual pose datasets provide no corresponding radar echoes. Physical simulation can supply synthetic signals, but requires expertise in scattering models and can leave a gap between simulated and real data. To address this challenge, we introduce MIMORPHEUS, a framework that generates radar echoes from 3D human poses through conditional diffusion. To prepare echo and pose representations, MIMO-VAE compresses the echoes according to their channel and fast time sample structure, while SkeleCoder learns pose features through contrastive alignment with echo features. These pose features then guide diffusion in the MIMO-VAE latent space, and the VAE decoder reconstructs echoes from the generated latents. Once trained, the generator augments radar data by producing different echoes for a recorded pose and supplies the radar modality for pose annotations in existing visual datasets. In data augmentation experiments, our method reduces MPJPE by 6.8%-11.2% across four radar pose estimators. Transfer experiments with three public pose datasets also show that visual pose annotations can supply useful radar training data. Code will be made publicly available on GitHub.
authors: Shizhao Zhang, Yanyan Zhang, Deshui Yu, Jun Pan, Guangyou Fang
bullets: Addresses the cost of collecting paired radar–pose data and the simulation-to-real gap.
Compresses radar echoes with MIMO-VAE and learns pose features via contrastive alignment in SkeleCoder.
Generates radar echoes conditioned on 3D poses through diffusion in the VAE latent space.
Augmentation reduces MPJPE by 6.8%–11.2% across four radar pose estimators.
Transfer experiments indicate that visual pose annotations can provide useful radar training data.

papers.abstract: World Action Models anticipate visual outcomes to guide robot actions, yet humanoid interaction also depends on how the robot's body responds. Visual foresight alone can miss body motion, while latent-distance losses do not directly supervise action responses. We present $\zeta_0$, a framework that turns vision-language-action policies into World Action Models by foreseeing future visual features and measured joint trajectories in a shared latent representation. During training, a teacher conditioned on recorded futures provides a reference action response, and dual-response transfer trains the causal predictor to match it through the teacher and the executing policy. All components are trained jointly, and deployment uses only causally predicted futures. On seven HumanoidArena tasks, $\zeta_0$ built on $\Psi_0$ and GR00T N1.7 reaches 63.6% and 79.5% mean success, 18.8 and 9.0 points above these bases. On six real-world tasks, it reaches 78.3% and 85.0%, gains of 16.7 and 10.0 points. On GR00T, its 79.5% tops all compared seven-task joint policies. Project page: https://chenyizhi123.github.io/zeta0-project/
authors: Yizhi Chen, Zhanxiang Cao, Yitong Wang, Junyu Liu, Hongchu Zeng, Xinyi Peng, Chuxuan Huang, Yicheng Su, Zihao Zhou, Shengcheng Fu, Haoyang Li, Liyun Yan, Tianyue Zhan, Jianming Ma, Yang Zhang, Keqi Zhu, Xiaxi Si, Jinming Yao, Qiao Sun, Shizeng Zhang, Jiangwei Zhong, Yue Gao
bullets: Addresses the gap between visual foresight and accurate body-response prediction in humanoid interaction.
Transforms vision-language-action policies into World Action Models with shared-latent visual and joint-trajectory foresight.
Uses a future-conditioned teacher and dual-response transfer to train causal predictions without requiring future observations at deployment.
Improves mean success on seven HumanoidArena tasks to 63.6% and 79.5%, and on six real-world tasks to 78.3% and 85.0%, depending on the base policy.
Scope: evaluation covers seven simulated and six real-world humanoid tasks.

papers.abstract: Agents in complex, stochastic environments must contend with dynamics that can exceed their world models' predictive capacity and randomness that obscure the consequences of their actions. We hypothesize that, compared to imagining entirely new trajectories in such complex environments, it can be easier to transform observed trajectories with alternative actions. Counterfactual world models condition on observations to predict alternative outcomes under the same underlying environmental randomness, using experience as a reference for predicting action-dependent changes. We present a policy gradient estimator, REINFORCE Look Back (RLB), that uses counterfactual returns as baselines to distinguish action effects from environmental luck, and prove conditions for unbiasedness and variance reduction. In settings where environmental evolution is harder to predict than action-induced changes, we show that counterfactual world models are easier to learn and support better policy learning than ordinary world models. Our findings suggest that counterfactual thinking can help agents learn effective behavior without independently reproducing the full complexity of their worlds.
authors: Jinwoo Kim, Toghrul Abbasov, Lucius E. J. Bynum, Aahlad Puli, Stephanie Milani, Hyunwoo Ryu, Seunghoon Hong, Kyunghyun Cho, Rajesh Ranganath
bullets: Targets stochastic, complex environments where accurately predicting full future trajectories is difficult.
Introduces REINFORCE Look Back (RLB), which uses counterfactual returns as policy-gradient baselines.
Provides conditions guaranteeing unbiased estimates and reduced variance.
Shows counterfactual models can be easier to learn and improve policy learning when action effects are easier to predict than environmental evolution.
Scope: benefits depend on the environment having this relative predictability structure.

papers.abstract: Physical counterfactual video editing turns a source video and a language-specified physical edit at a given execution frame into a counterfactual video that shows how the scene would evolve after the edit. Existing evaluations with counterfactual target videos mainly cover object removal or specific rigid-body motions, although real scenes also involve elastic deformation, fluid flow, and interactions among rigid bodies, elastic solids, and fluids. We introduce PhyCoVE, a benchmark of 533 cases on 110 source videos that covers rigid, elastic, and fluid dynamics in five interaction patterns, with edits that remove an object, change a physical quantity, or insert a new object. For the simulated cases, a language model proposes scene designs, coding agents build them with solvers suited to each material and physically based rendering and then simulate each edit from the source scene state, and humans check every stage. For the real cases, we record continuously from one camera position before and after each edit. We also propose counterfactual fidelity, a metric that applies across materials and their interactions and measures how much of the physical change from the source video to the target video a generated video reproduces. We evaluate seven open-source and commercial video editing models and find that counterfactual fidelity ranks them nearly as human preference does, but even the best model reproduces only about one seventh of the physical change. The models change how a scene looks but rarely how it evolves, whereas a physical edit requires understanding the dynamics that it changes. Physical counterfactual video editing thus remains far from solved, and PhyCoVE provides a foundation for developing and evaluating methods for it.
authors: Conghan Yue, Yuanjie Chen, Yunyan Xiao, Zeyu Peng, Xingsong Ye, Ya Gao, Yanglin Huang, WeiYao Zhang, Yue Han, Zhineng Chen, Yu-Gang Jiang
bullets: Introduces 533 benchmark cases from 110 videos spanning rigid, elastic, and fluid materials across five interaction patterns.
Covers object removal, physical-quantity changes, and object insertion in simulated and real-world videos.
Proposes counterfactual fidelity, a cross-material metric that measures how much of the physical change is reproduced.
Evaluates seven open-source and commercial models; the metric closely matches human preferences.
Even the best model reproduces only about one seventh of the physical change, showing that the task remains largely unsolved.

papers.abstract: World-action models learn from future prediction, but accessing their future representations directly at test time can require costly frame generation. Methods that generate future frames before planning incur additional forward passes, while future co-training methods omit explicit future predictions at inference. We introduce \method, a planner that reads the hidden states of masked future tokens without decoding future frames. We pretrain MMaDA-Parallel-M on driving video using frame-level masked world modeling, which predicts a masked suffix of future frames and explicitly includes inputs with all future frames masked. Learned planning queries attend to these masked positions and the observed context, and a continuous head predicts the trajectory in the same forward pass. With a single front camera, \method reaches 92.0 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, with an end-to-end latency of 60.3\,ms.
authors: Ziyu Zhao, Casey Sun, Zeyu Wang, Shicong Ma, Emily T Zhang, Cheng Lu
bullets: Addresses the inference cost of generating future frames before planning.
Pretrains a masked world model on driving video, including inputs where all future frames are masked.
Uses planning queries over masked future states and observed context, with a continuous trajectory head in one forward pass.
Achieves 92.0 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 using a single front camera.
Runs with 60.3 ms end-to-end latency.

papers.abstract: Marine robots face partial observability, non-stationary dynamics, and sparse communication, motivating WMs that learn compact predictive states for planning. This review develops a functional taxonomy of WMs for ocean engineering, focusing on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) and AdaJEPA's test-time adaptation within model predictive control, mapping them to navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring, and separating demonstrated evidence from prospective applications. The synthesis identifies key Gaps: benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, safe adaptation and proposes a research agenda for physics-informed, deployment-adaptive marine WMs validated through simulation and field missions.
authors: Basma Dokkara, Esteban W. G. Cluab, Luiz M. G. Goncalves, Paolo Spagnolo, Cosimo Distante
bullets: Marine robots must operate under partial observability, changing dynamics, and limited communication.
It provides a functional taxonomy spanning navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring.
The review focuses on JEPAs and AdaJEPA-style test-time adaptation integrated with model predictive control.
It distinguishes demonstrated evidence from prospective applications.
Key gaps include benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, and safe adaptation; it proposes physics-informed, deployment-adaptive validation in simulation and field missions.

papers.abstract: A world model should tell us not only what will happen, but what would happen under a different action. Learned Earth models now forecast remarkably well, yet forecast skill says little about what their state means or how it responds to a changed driver. We build LandWM, a world model of land-surface water in which rain is the action, learned from seven years of SMAP and CYGNSS observations: physical observation operators tie its latent state to soil water, and a mass-conserving balance governs how that state responds to rain. Over the U.S. Southern Great Plains, the model, never shown a soil-moisture value, tracks 28 in-situ probes as well as the operational SMAP Level-4 product, even from CYGNSS alone, and a storm added to the forcing of a station's cell wets its soil as natural storms wet the probes. Replace either piece and the forecasts stay, but the meaning goes: with neural operators, only a probe fitted to the stations finds the soil water; with a generic recurrent transition, rain on a single cell barely moves it. Yet when the same rain covers the whole region the two transitions swap roles, and the conserving one responds too weakly. Grounding makes a world model readable; its response to actions must be tested under more than one kind of intervention.
authors: Suya Li, Zekun Qi, Xiaochong Xu, Duo Zhang
bullets: Addresses the gap between accurate forecasting and understanding what model states mean or how they respond to changed rainfall.
Learns from seven years of SMAP and CYGNSS observations, using physical observation operators and a mass-conserving water-balance transition.
Over the U.S. Southern Great Plains, it tracks 28 in-situ probes comparably to operational SMAP Level-4, including from CYGNSS alone.
Adding a storm to a station cell produces soil wetting consistent with natural storms, demonstrating action-response behavior.
Intervention tests show that both state grounding and transition design matter, with responses depending on the spatial scale of rainfall.

papers.abstract: Visual world models enable goal-conditioned planning by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions in latent space. However, planning depends on how well a model ranks candidates, whereas training optimizes how accurately it predicts each one. We identify the Decision-Relevant Residual (DRR), the part of the cost error that can reorder candidates, and show that the more training reduces the DRR, the more it improves selection (Spearman $\rho = 0.82$, vs. $0.61$ for prediction error). Building on this insight, we introduce Decision-Aligned Selection (DAS), a plug-in selection rule that scores candidates by the standardized consensus of several independently trained checkpoints, which averages out their checkpoint-specific residuals. Across two model families (LeWorldModel and DINO-WM) and five tasks, DAS selects better actions than single checkpoints in 12 of 18 configurations and outperforms training one model three times longer in 14 of 18. In closed loop, DAS improves success over single checkpoints in 6 of 9 pre-registered LeWM comparisons.
authors: Chan Aristella Lu, Arya Fayyazi, Junil Yeo, Jin Lu, Kyu Hyung Lee, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
bullets: Prediction error can differ from decision quality because only residual cost errors that reorder candidates affect action selection.
The Decision-Relevant Residual (DRR) correlates more strongly with selection quality than overall prediction error (Spearman ρ = 0.82 vs. 0.61).
Decision-Aligned Selection (DAS) scores actions using standardized consensus across independently trained checkpoints.
DAS selects better actions than single checkpoints in 12/18 configurations and beats training one model three times longer in 14/18.
In closed-loop evaluation, DAS improves success over single checkpoints in 6/9 pre-registered LeWM comparisons.

papers.abstract: Existing surgical world models often leave implicit how instrument motion drives localized tissue responses and how interaction history informs subsequent actions. We introduce KineState-SWAM, a surgical world-action model coupling action prediction and video generation through a persistent interaction state, separating kinematically determined instrument motion from learned scene evolution. A flow-matching policy predicts joint trajectories conditioned on interaction state, robot configuration, and task instruction. Kinematic Geometry Conditioning converts these trajectories into surface-motion tokens and spatially aligned instrument renderings using calibrated URDF kinematics. Causal Interaction Dynamics recurrently updates the state through geometry-guided attention and motion-aligned feature transport, carrying interaction history into subsequent action predictions without intermediate video synthesis. The State-Geometry Adapter combines state-dependent spatial modulation with localized geometric residuals to guide video generation. Interaction-aware supervision emphasizes tissue responses near instrument working regions. We introduce dVRK-Chole5.2k, comprising 5,255 videos spanning 17 surgical tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved action accuracy and video fidelity over evaluated baselines within matched action-conditioning settings. Ablations support preserving and transporting interaction states for long-horizon prediction.
authors: Rulin Zhou, Yujie Ma, Rui Tang, Qiujie Song, Wanhao Liu, Guoheng Ma, Liangjing Shao, An Wang, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses the missing link between instrument motion, localized tissue response, and interaction history in surgical world models.
Uses a flow-matching policy to predict joint trajectories from interaction state, robot configuration, and task instructions.
Converts trajectories into geometry-aligned motion tokens and instrument renderings via calibrated URDF kinematics.
Maintains interaction history through recurrent geometry-guided dynamics and guides video generation with state and geometric residuals.
Introduces dVRK-Chole5.2k with 5,255 videos across 17 tasks; reports improved action accuracy and video fidelity over evaluated baselines, with ablations supporting state preservation and transport.

papers.abstract: Two visually identical animated characters can respond differently to the same action command because their body dynamics differ. For example, a stiff blob and its bouncy twin reach different heights when both receive the jump command. Given only the first frame and the action command, a visual world model has no information to distinguish these twins, because their initial appearances are identical. We therefore propose an in-context world model that encodes clips of a character's other actions into a body representation, using a contrastive loss to separate look-alike characters. We introduce ToonTwins, a benchmark of 144 2D cartoon characters that run, jump, fall, turn and crouch. Its characters form look-alike groups of four that differ only in their dynamics profile, and we also evaluate the model on 32 animated animals from DeformingThings4D. Even with a body code from these clips, the latent pixel world model we tested recovered at most 25 percent of the twins' jump height difference. On new shapes, our model identified the correct twin in 85.9 percent of cases, compared with 76.7 percent for a transformer baseline that reads the same clips without a body summary, and in a controlled ablation the contrastive loss gave more than half of this gain. On the animated animals, it reduced the mean path prediction error by 8.5 percent against a model without body information.
bullets: Problem: Identical-looking characters can respond differently to the same action because their body dynamics are unobserved from a single frame.
Method: Encode clips of a character performing other actions into a body representation using an in-context world model and contrastive loss.
Benchmark: ToonTwins contains 144 cartoon characters in look-alike groups with differing dynamics; evaluation also uses 32 animated animals from DeformingThings4D.
Results: The model identified the correct twin in 85.9% of new-shape cases versus 76.7% for a transformer baseline, while contrastive learning accounted for more than half the gain.
Scope: The model recovered at most 25% of twins’ jump-height differences, indicating substantial limitations in predicting dynamics.

papers.abstract: Learning deformable physical world models requires dynamics that generalize beyond observed motion. Accurate reconstruction alone does not ensure accurate future prediction, motivating us to learn how observations should influence physical identification. However, visual reliability alone does not determine how informative an observation is about physical dynamics. We propose ViTrust to learn 3D observation trust, determining how strongly each tracked point influences physical identification. Its key design is a visual-contact trust adapter that combines pointwise spatiotemporal evidence with interaction history on a persistent contact graph to predict time-varying observation weights. A single-stage, shared-forward objective jointly optimizes these weights and physical parameters through weighted geometry and correspondence losses, with constraints to prevent observation-weight collapse. All learning uses only the observed prefix. The fitted physics remains fixed for future prediction under supplied controls. Experiments on real-world sequences demonstrate improved future prediction over the evaluated baselines, alongside qualitative demonstrations of novel-control rollouts and cross-object transfer.
authors: Zhihao Guo, Zhihao Li, Xu Ge, Lijian Zhong, Yu Lu, Haitao Wu, Longqing Zhao, Yue Ma
bullets: Addresses the gap between reconstructing observed motion and identifying dynamics that generalize to unseen future motion.
Uses a visual-contact trust adapter combining pointwise spatiotemporal evidence with persistent contact-graph history.
Jointly learns observation weights and physical parameters from weighted geometry and correspondence losses, while preventing weight collapse.
Trains only on the observed sequence prefix, then keeps the fitted physics fixed during controlled future prediction.
Real-world experiments show improved future prediction over evaluated baselines, with qualitative novel-control and cross-object transfer results.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of VITRUST. (a) Pointwise Spatiotemporal Evidence. Depth-consistent sampling of frozen VideoMAE features, combined with depth and motion cues, forms pointwise spatiotemporal descriptors. (b) Visual–Contact Observation Trust. Contact graph message passing and a temporal GRU encode interaction history on persistent patches defined by fixed point-to-anchor assignments. Patch-level contact adjustments are broadcast back to points and fused with pointwise visual scores to predict relative observation weights Wψ for physical identification. (c) Single-Stage Training. A regularized objective jointly updates physical parameters θ and adapter parameters ψ through trust-weighted geometry and tracking losses from a shared forward simulation on the observed prefix. (d) Future Prediction. Frozen physical parameters predict motion under future controls without refitting or future object observations, with 3D Gaussians used for rendering. papers.abstract: World models hold great promise for autonomous driving planning, yet their ability to imagine the future often comes at a formidable computational cost. Efficiency efforts, such as knowledge distillation and domain-specific pre-training, often shift this burden to costly teachers or training pipelines, leaving lightweight world modeling an open challenge. We introduce FastWorld, a natively lightweight world-model framework for efficient autonomous driving planning. FastWorld reduces computation through compact scene representations, short-horizon action-conditioned prediction, and selective candidate verification and score refinement. These designs support efficient future-informed planning without teacher distillation or additional domain-specific pre-training. On NAVSIMv1, FastWorld achieves 92.2 PDMS at 132 FPS on a single 4090 GPU. It also achieves 89.4 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2 and an average L2 of 0.40 over 3 seconds at 17 FPS on nuScenes. Code and models can be found at https://github.com/MoyangSensei/FastWorld.
authors: Feiyang Jia, Lin Liu, Zhicheng Bao, Caiyan Jia, Ziying Song, Shengkai Zhang, Lina Han, Yan Zhao, Xiaoshuai Hao
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of imagining future driving scenarios for planning.
Uses compact scene representations, short-horizon action-conditioned prediction, and selective candidate verification with score refinement.
Avoids costly teacher distillation and additional domain-specific pre-training.
Achieves 92.2 PDMS at 132 FPS on NAVSIMv1, 89.4 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2, and 0.40 average 3-second L2 at 17 FPS on nuScenes.
Scope is demonstrated on NAVSIM and nuScenes benchmarks; the abstract does not report broader deployment limitations.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools.
authors: Chendong Xiang, Chengwen Zhang, Ruowen Zhao, Zeyuan Wang, Shuhe Huang, Rongxu Cui, Min Zhao, Fan Bao, Hengkai Tan, Jun Zhu
bullets: Addresses temporal misalignment between human demonstrations and robot actions, plus shortcut reliance on scene or task identity.
Generates matched human contexts from recorded robot videos and supplements them with real paired recordings.
Uses variable-length video windows and intra-task contrastive learning to make actions track the provided human context.
Achieves 83.5/100 across six unseen Astribot S1 tasks and 69.5% success on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, surpassing Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points.
Transfers context-specified behaviors to rearranged layouts and substituted tools despite training only on scene-aligned pairs.

papers.abstract: Searching from high altitude and navigating to a target instance specified by a reference image is a common application for UAVs. In such tasks, high-altitude observations provide broad ground coverage for efficient search, but targets occupy fewer pixels, making instance verification and action selection more difficult. We present AERIN, a visual world model that uses action-conditioned prediction to guide the UAV toward the target while adjusting its viewpoint to obtain higherquality observations for subsequent instance verification. Highaltitude navigation requires fine-grained target details and scene context relevant to visibility, but repeatedly predicting dense visual representations of this information is computationally expensive. AERIN addresses this challenge with a compact, fixedsize, target-conditioned latent state that separately represents both for efficient action evaluation. Experiments demonstrate that AERIN outperforms the evaluated baselines in target approach and observation quality, while requiring substantially less decision time than similar world models.
authors: Zhenzhen Jiao, Rui Tian, Zhineng Chen
bullets: High-altitude UAV search offers broad coverage but makes target recognition and action selection harder because targets appear small.
The model predicts action-conditioned outcomes to guide target approach and select viewpoints that improve subsequent observations.
AERIN uses a fixed-size latent state that separately encodes fine-grained target details and visibility-relevant scene context.
Experiments show better target approach and observation quality than evaluated baselines, with substantially lower decision time than similar world models.

papers.abstract: Video world models generate plausible novel views but often lack persistent memory, failing to preserve a place's geometry and appearance when an agent revisits a scene. A central challenge is how previous views should be effectively used for creating memory. Reconstructing them independently underutilizes geometric constraints between nearby views, while repeatedly reconstructing a growing history can propagate later prediction errors into earlier geometry. We introduce RecallWorld, a persistent embodied video world model that jointly reconstructs short multi-view episodes into Scenelets while keeping geometry independent across episodes. Starting from a single source image, camera-aware ray lifting places perspective and native fisheye images in a common world frame, retaining wide-field content for perspective generation. Each generated segment extends the Scenelet memory and conditions subsequent generation. Coverage-based retrieval selects complementary Scenelets from the full history, while target-view visibility is resolved geometrically before appearance fusion, providing consistent memory conditioning for guiding subsequent generation. Across four datasets, RecallWorld improves revisit PSNR over the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.6 dB on partial revisits and 3.9 dB on full cycles, demonstrating substantially stronger preservation of scene identity across exploration and return.
authors: Sarosij Bose, Gitika Karumuri, Chenqi Li, Allen Tu, Srikumar Sastry, Mellon Zhang, Avinash Ravichandran, Alexander Schwing, Konstantinos Karydis, Amit K. Roy Chowdhury
bullets: Addresses the problem of world models forgetting scene geometry and appearance across revisits.
Jointly reconstructs short multi-view episodes into independent Scenelets to avoid error propagation across the full history.
Uses camera-aware ray lifting to unify perspective and fisheye views in a common world frame while preserving wide-field content.
Retrieves complementary Scenelets by coverage and resolves target-view visibility geometrically before fusing appearance.
Improves revisit PSNR by 2.6 dB on partial revisits and 3.9 dB on full cycles across four datasets.

papers.abstract: Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is central to online planning for model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), but its iterative refinement incurs planning latency. Reducing refinement iterations often degrades performance, motivating stronger policy guidance learned from the planner. However, existing methods typically learn from the planner through action-level alignment, which does not directly capture the complete $H$-step planner proposal. Moreover, planner imitation leaves further target improvement to online refinement. To address these limitations, we propose FaSt World PlANner (SWAN), an advantage-aware MPPI-based MBRL framework that explicitly represents and improves the complete $H$-step planner proposal to improve policy guidance for efficient online planning. For proposal representation, SWAN combines k-MPPI, a multimodal MPPI extension, with a mixture of factor analyzers (MFA) action-chunk policy to capture multiple modes and correlations across time and action dimensions. For proposal optimization, we introduce Advantage-Guided Proposal Optimization (APO), which reuses MPPI evaluations to construct an improved target using advantage estimates and trains the policy toward this target while preserving planner alignment. Experiments across 31 high-dimensional continuous-control tasks from DMControl, HumanoidBench, and MyoSuite show that SWAN substantially improves control performance and sample efficiency while using 50% fewer MPPI refinement iterations than state-of-the-art planning-based MBRL methods. Finally, SWAN demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical Unitree Go2, achieving stable velocity-tracking locomotion with high-frequency control. (see our demo at https://swanfastworldplanner.github.io/)

bullets: Targets the latency of iterative MPPI planning and the limitations of action-level planner imitation.
Represents complete H-step proposals using k-MPPI and a mixture of factor analyzers to model multimodality and temporal/action correlations.
Introduces Advantage-Guided Proposal Optimization, which uses MPPI evaluations and advantage estimates to improve policy targets while maintaining planner alignment.
Improves control performance and sample efficiency across 31 continuous-control tasks while reducing MPPI refinement iterations by 50%.
Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go2 for stable, high-frequency velocity-tracking locomotion.

papers.abstract: Payload-carrying robots, such as delivery robots and autonomous trucks, must choose motions that keep them and their payload safe, so their planners predict the outcome of each candidate motion. Modern planners compare thousands of candidates per step on a GPU, using world models such as batched simulators or learned predictors. Most of them assume a rigid payload, but a liquid payload keeps moving after a maneuver, and its state is rarely measured. Near a safety limit, small prediction errors can make an unsafe plan look safe. Coupled fluid simulations are accurate but too costly for every candidate, while low-order slosh models are cheap but accurate only away from resonance. We study this trade-off on a ground vehicle with a partly filled tank near its rollover limit. First, we build PLiMB (Parallel Liquid-MultiBody), a GPU-parallel slosh simulator that, to our knowledge, couples FLIP liquid two-way with many multibody vehicles for the first time. It provides training data and a high-fidelity reference. Second, we propose a scalable physics-anchored world model that combines a modal-slosh and roll prior, an estimate of the hidden liquid state from the vehicle's own motion history (no sensor in the tank), and a learned correction. Without simulating the fluid, it scores thousands of candidate plans in one batched pass within a 20 Hz control tick on one GPU. We judge each world model by the plans it leads a planner to choose. Near the rollover limit, planners that treat the liquid as a rigid payload or use published low-order slosh models repeatedly pick unsafe plans when a safe one exists. Ours never does in our standard tank and makes about half as many in a wide tank whose sloshing mode lies in the maneuver band. There, the liquid state left by earlier driving can change the best plan, and reading it from the vehicle's history halves our model's near-limit prediction error.
authors: Yicheng Zhu, Linfeng Tian, Yang Chen, Tao Li, Zilin Bian
bullets: Liquid payloads can continue sloshing after maneuvers, making rigid-payload and simple slosh assumptions unsafe near rollover limits.
PLiMB is a GPU-parallel, high-fidelity simulator coupling FLIP fluid dynamics with many multibody vehicles to generate training data and references.
The proposed model combines modal slosh and roll physics, history-based hidden-state estimation, and a learned correction without requiring tank sensors.
It evaluates thousands of candidate plans in one GPU-batched pass within a 20 Hz control cycle.

Near rollover limits, it never selected an unsafe plan in the standard tank and made about half as many unsafe choices in a wide tank; history-based state estimation halved near-limit prediction error there.

papers.title: Knowing What You Carry: Scalable Physics-Anchored World Models for Robotic Planning with Liquid Payloads
papers.tldr: A physics-anchored world model infers hidden liquid motion from driving history and enables fast, safer robotic planning with liquid payloads.

papers.abstract: JEPA world models are trained to predict logged transitions but used to compare counterfactual actions from one state. The logged behavior data show one action per state, and under a local linear approximation we prove the action response is unidentified along any direction the policy never varies within a state. We therefore supplement behavior data with measured outcomes of alternative actions from the same state. Our fork futures execute two actions from one restored state, and their outcome difference cancels the state term, identifying the action response on the sampled span. The resulting model, Fork-JEPA, matches predicted to measured differences, anchors the logged successor with behavior prediction, and adds a lookback head that keeps the predecessor recoverable, all at training time, leaving planning unchanged. On three visual control tasks, behavior-only training leaves the predicted action effect no better than a constant guess. Fork-JEPA makes it readable and raises planning success by up to 14\% over LeWM, its base model. Where the action response changes across hidden zones, it nearly doubles cross-zone success, and 1,024 fork pairs beat 1.2M extra behavior steps. Our project is available at https://fork-jepa.github.io/.
authors: Yihao Wu, Runjia Zeng, Tongyan Wang, Renzhong Huang, Chongzhou Fang, Qifan Wang, Fan Heng, Dongfang Liu
bullets: Behavior logs contain only one action per state, leaving action responses unidentified where the policy does not vary.
Fork futures execute two actions from one restored state; subtracting their outcomes cancels the shared state effect.
Fork-JEPA combines measured action differences with logged-transition prediction and a lookback head that preserves predecessor information.
Across three visual-control tasks, it improves planning success by up to 14% over LeWM; 1,024 fork pairs outperform 1.2M extra behavior steps.
When action effects vary across hidden zones, it nearly doubles cross-zone success; scope is limited to sampled action-response directions and tested tasks.

papers.title: Two Actions from One State: Fork Futures Teach JEPA World Models to Compare

papers.abstract: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.
authors: Inkyu Sa, Gaurav Kuppa, Steve Van der Hoeven, Konstantin Stulov, Rajat Bhageria, Luis Rayas
bullets: Learns from 61,773 automatically labeled production picks using pre-pick heightmaps, actions, food, and utensil information.
Predicts post-pick heightmaps and picked mass with uncertainty; mass is evaluated on 12,294 held-out picks across nine foods.
Achieves 10.93 g RMSE, outperforming commanded-target/per-food-mean baselines and the controller’s internal estimate.
Rejecting the most uncertain picks yields 89.4% coverage with 10.28 g RMSE.
Performance is weakly sensitive to commanded volume/depth and can fail without warning on unseen target weights; broader food and utensil coverage is needed.
papers.selection_reason: Learns an action-conditioned food-picking world model from production data for robot planning and mass prediction.
papers.title: Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data
papers.tldr: A production-trained food-picking world model predicts both the next pan state and picked mass, enabling uncertainty-aware planning for assembly robots.

papers.abstract: Beckmann Transport Models (BTM) learn one-step generative maps end-to-end from data, without a teacher, a distillation stage, or pretrained features. We introduce Scalable Beckmann Maps (SBM), which bring to BTM the two ingredients behind the quality of modern multistep generators: classifier-free guidance (CFG) and a training recipe that scales, while keeping sampling at a single network evaluation. CFG combines conditional and unconditional velocity or score predictions, which a Beckmann map does not have. Our guidance rests on one observation: the BTM current is a positive multiple of an autonomous denoising field, to which CFG applies as it does to a velocity. With exact denoisers this gives guided BTM. In practice we substitute the map's own conditional and null predictions for the denoisers, which requires no additional network and introduces a bias that we characterize. We show that the guided update is consistent with a guided conservation equation, and that guidance can move the boundaries between basins, sending more noise to the modes a condition favors. Trained from scratch in the latent of a representation autoencoder, SBM reaches a one-step FID of 1.6 on ImageNet 256x256 without a teacher or a feature loss, outperforming the Improved-MeanFlow baseline with 3.2x fewer FLOPs. In text-to-image generation it reaches a GenEval score of 0.86 with one network evaluation. As a world model, where we train without guidance, the recipe alone outperforms DriftWorld on all five metrics of two robot-manipulation benchmarks, with 1.9-2.8x less training compute and no pretrained auxiliary feature encoder.
authors: Ulrik Unneberg, Shiyi Wang, Lee Cheuk-Kit, Felix Berg, Boris Kozinsky, Yilun Du, Michael S. Albergo, Eric Vanden-Eijnden
bullets: Extends Beckmann Transport Models with guidance by applying classifier-free guidance to their autonomous denoising field.
Uses the model’s conditional and null predictions, requiring no additional network, while characterizing the resulting bias.
Provides a guided conservation-equation interpretation in which guidance shifts basin boundaries toward condition-favored modes.
Achieves 1.6 one-step FID on ImageNet 256×256 and a 0.86 GenEval score for text-to-image generation.
Also improves world-model performance across five metrics on two robot-manipulation benchmarks with lower training compute.

Figure 2 Flow matching, BTM and Equilibrium Matching on the same two-dimensional problem: noise is transported to five data points, whose weights are given in the legend. (a) Flow matching learns a time-dependent velocity; arrows show the field at t = 0.5. Because the velocity changes over time, trajectories can bend sharply and even reverse direction, and this curvature makes the ODE hard to integrate in few steps. (b) BTM assumes an autonomous flow. Its flow lines are fixed and never cross, the endpoint map is constant along each of them, and the separatrices of the map (solid) divide the plane into one basin per data point, each receiving source mass equal to that point’s weight. (c) Equilibrium Matching (Wang and Du, 2025) also learns a time-invariant field, whose magnitude is set by a schedule ct, here ct = (1− t)0.8; the shaded bands are a potential reconstructed from the current, ∆ϕ = ∇ · J . A nonconstant schedule ct can bias the endpoint distribution by shifting the basin boundaries: the separatrices of its map (solid) depart from those of BTM (dotted), and the basins of the two lower modes shrink, so these modes receive too little mass. At ct = 1 the autonomous field is identical to that of BTM.

papers.abstract: Aging is characterized by continuously evolving health states, yet most existing prediction models focus on static health risk at isolated time points rather than explicitly modelling how health trajectories unfold over time. We developed a health world model based on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture to represent evolving health states and simulate future trajectories under specified actions. The model combines a state encoder, an action- and context-conditioned predictor, a stop-gradient target encoder, and clinical outcome heads. We trained the model on the US Health and Retirement Study (HRS) and evaluated it without refitting in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). Open-loop evaluation assessed discrimination and calibration for mortality and worsening of activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). In the held-out HRS test set, the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) for mortality, ADL worsening, and IADL worsening were 0.89, 0.93, and 0.93 at the first horizon and 0.84, 0.84, and 0.85 at the fifth horizon, respectively. Predicted risks stratified subsequent outcomes across horizons. Across the evaluated horizons, mortality AUROC ranged from 0.867 to 0.881 in ELSA and from 0.796 to 0.801 in CHARLS. Simulated trajectories preserved the expected risk ordering across predefined action regimes. In counterfactual simulations, changes in lifestyle actions shifted predicted risks in directions consistent with observed associations. The model provides a framework for longitudinal risk prediction and action-conditioned simulation in older adults.
authors: Jingyi Wu, Chenghua Guo, Qianlin Zuo, Pengfei Li, Luxia Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of static, single-time-point risk models by representing longitudinal health-state evolution.
Uses a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with state encoding, action/context-conditioned prediction, target encoding, and clinical outcome heads.
Trained on the US Health and Retirement Study and evaluated without refitting in English and Chinese aging cohorts.
Showed strong discrimination for mortality and ADL/IADL worsening in HRS, with meaningful risk stratification across future horizons and cross-cohort performance.
Action-conditioned and counterfactual simulations preserved expected risk ordering and produced lifestyle-related risk shifts consistent with observed associations.

papers.abstract: Two centuries ago, an early cinema-like theater called the Diorama could already control its scenes at will. Today's video generation models produce videos of near-cinematic quality, yet they still lack this controllability. This limitation stems from the inherent semantic gap between text and pixels, since a prompt can describe a video only coarsely and leaves its details and relations beyond control. We bring this ability to video generation with Causal Dioramas, modules that decompose a video into a concept graph of variables that can be intervened on individually. Each instruction is translated into an intervention on the concept graph, modifying the specified concepts and their dependents. A connector then conveys this intervention to the video generator, which reuses the original noise to produce a counterfactual video while preserving all other content. Building on Causal Dioramas, we develop a unified framework for controllable generation, counterfactual revision of generated videos and editing of real videos. We outperform both open-source and commercial models in controllability on T2V-CompBench, CoVEBench and OpenVE-Bench.
authors: Yifan Shen, Xinyi Yang, Peiyuan Zhu, Yichang Jian, Jinyuan Hu, Xilin He, Fengming Zhu, Guangyi Chen, Kun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited detail and relational control of text-to-video prompts caused by the semantic gap between text and pixels.

papers.abstract: Current leading video generation models can synthesize highly realistic videos, while still frequently violating physical and logical constraints in multi-step reasoning and planning, even after training with large-scale reasoning data or existing diffusion RL methods. We attribute these failures to the conventional video training paradigm, which treats a solution as a fixed-length clip rather than a chain of decisions. We present ViDecide, a decision-centric framework that trains video diffusion models to predict state transitions causally and decide when to stop, with a decision-focused training schedule. We further propose Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT), which corrects failed decisions by mapping their noise to the model's own successful continuations, achieving stable improvement without policy-gradient optimization. Across abstract games, planning tasks, and a new benchmark of multi-step robot planning, ViDecide achieves an average strict success rate of 83.8%, far above 23.3% for standard fine-tuning and 67.8% for the strongest prior method, and generalizes to larger puzzles and unseen layouts. Our framework therefore unlocks greater potential for video generation models as reliable reasoners and planners in the visual world. Project page: https://kevin-thu.github.io/ViDecide.
bullets: Targets physical and logical failures in multi-step video reasoning and planning.
Models solutions as causal state transitions with an explicit stopping decision.
Uses decision-focused training and Corrective Fine-tuning to repair failed decisions without policy-gradient optimization.
Reports an 83.8% average strict success rate across games, planning tasks, and robot-planning benchmarks, with generalization to larger puzzles and unseen layouts.

(c) From the state hd before a failed decision, CFT resamples a successful continuation and trains the noise ϵ−d that produced the failed decision to generate the successful decision X+ d , shifting the decision distribution toward solvable moves.

papers.abstract: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .
authors: Yuhang Dai, Yinwei Wu, Ziyue Lin, Han Ji, Xingyi Yang
bullets: Introduces NoPeBench to evaluate obstacle interactions in interactive video world models.

papers.abstract: When a robot is damaged, it must decide which routes it can still afford, and the amount of risk it may accept can change from one mission to the next. We argue that whether a learned model helps such a robot depends on its decision interface, that is, on what the model hands to the planner. A decision policy tells the planner what to do, whereas an outcome model, a kind of world model, predicts the consequences of each route. We study simulated Unitree Go2 quadrupeds and H1 humanoids with weakened motors, added payloads, or reduced foot friction. We compare four interfaces. The first is a decision policy, and the second is the same policy trained with fixed penalties for infeasible routes. The third is an outcome model that predicts the feasibility and travel time of each route. The fourth, which we call a capability contract, is an outcome model that predicts the chance of success and the travel time of the robot on each terrain and composes them along a route. All share the same collected experience, matched tuning and risk calibration, and an uncertainty guard. Two comparatively low-risk probes let the capability contract rank hazardous terrains about as well as four new trials on every hazard. At a calibrated 5% limit on selecting empirically infeasible routes, outcome models cut declined missions from about 32% to 7-8% on Go2 and from 57% to 35-36% on H1 compared with the plain policy. Fixed penalties narrow this gap, but the best penalty changes with the risk target. Predicting outcomes lets the planner preserve missions by changing routes as risk requirements tighten.
bullets: Robot damage changes which routes are feasible and how much risk is acceptable per mission.
The study compares decision policies, fixed-penalty policies, generic outcome models, and capability contracts that compose terrain-level success and travel-time predictions.
Capability contracts rank hazardous terrains using two low-risk probes, avoiding the need for four new trials per hazard.
At a calibrated 5% infeasibility limit, outcome models reduce declined missions from about 32% to 7–8% on Go2 and 57% to 35–36% on H1.
Fixed penalties help but require retuning as the target risk changes; scope is simulated damaged quadruped and humanoid robots.

papers.abstract: Autonomous racing requires an accurate vehicle dynamics model near the limits of handling, yet a mismatch between the nominal and actual dynamics inevitably remains. To reduce this mismatch, existing methods learn from on-track data, i.e., data collected while the vehicle drives on the track under racing conditions, by adapting the physical parameters of the nominal model or by learning a residual that captures the remaining mismatch. However, these on-track learning methods typically handle either the physical parameters or the residual separately, which restricts their ability to resolve the mismatch. To address this limitation, we propose an interactive semi-parametric learning framework that learns both the physical parameters and the residual under a single shared prediction-error objective. Since updating one changes the learning target of the other, they are recursively updated in turn, each guided by the other's latest update. Each update is then accepted only if it does not increase the shared objective, so that the objective is guaranteed to be non-increasing and convergent over the recursion. Numerical simulations and hardware experiments show that the proposed framework outperforms the baselines. Compared with the nominal model, it reduces the one-step prediction errors of lateral velocity and yaw rate by 90.0% and 81.6% in simulation and by 54.0% and 59.4% on hardware.
authors: Jungbin Kim, Youngim Nam, Cheolhyeon Kwon
bullets: Addresses mismatch between nominal and actual vehicle dynamics during on-track racing.
Jointly learns physical parameters and residuals under one shared prediction-error objective.
Recursively alternates updates, accepting only changes that do not increase the objective.
The objective is guaranteed to be non-increasing and convergent over the recursion.
Simulations and hardware experiments show large reductions in lateral-velocity and yaw-rate one-step prediction errors versus the nominal model.

papers.abstract: Visual world models can now generate compelling interactive worlds, but visual realism does not guarantee faithful dynamics. We systematically compare how categorical and continuous prediction shape learned dynamics under both next-token and iterative whole-frame generation. These choices are often bundled in approaches such as autoregressive token models and whole-frame flow matching. We design controlled 2D and 3D environments and evaluate dynamics validity, calibration, and visual quality. In 2D with lossless visual encoding, categorical models achieve higher rollout validity with less training compute, particularly for stochastic entities. Among categorical models, greedy decoding produces the highest rollout validity, while sampling from a next-token model yields the best-calibrated stochastic predictions. Failures in continuous models, such as disappearing game characters, echo those seen in more complex environments. Here, known dynamics let us measure their impact. In 3D, categorical models also achieve stronger long-horizon performance with less training compute. Even models with lossy tokenization remain competitive on semantic accuracy and FVD, despite lower next-frame RGB accuracy. Together, these findings make a strong case for categorical prediction as a compute-efficient route to learning world dynamics.
authors: Sarah Parisot, Melanie Fernandez Pradier, David Bignell, Sergio Valcarcel Macua, Katja Hofmann
bullets: The study separates prediction type—categorical versus continuous—from generation strategy using controlled 2D and 3D environments.
Categorical models achieve higher rollout validity in 2D and stronger long-horizon performance in 3D, particularly for stochastic entities.
Greedy decoding gives categorical models the highest rollout validity, while sampling provides the best-calibrated stochastic predictions.
Continuous models exhibit dynamics failures such as disappearing characters; categorical models remain competitive even with lossy visual tokenization.
Results support categorical prediction as a compute-efficient approach to learning world dynamics, beyond matching next-frame appearance.

papers.abstract: Training a humanoid motion tracker by backpropagating imagined returns through a learned world model is fast, because the model gives a first-order policy gradient. We ask how much of that gradient holds in the simulator. On a tracker for the Unitree G1, the $0.5\%$ of imagined rollouts with the largest gradients carry $22\%$ of the summed gradient norm, yet neither a second rollout from the same state nor the simulator confirms them. When the actions are moved along the model's gradient, the simulator returns 94% of the predicted change in return where the gradient norm is below the batch median, 48% between 3 and 10 times the median, and 1% above 30 times; the part of a gradient that either check confirms stops growing at a few times the median. We therefore cap each rollout's action-gradient norm at 10 times the batch median, draw imagination starts in proportion to their predicted gradient norm so that the cap removes less, and reset episodes where the world model and critic predict the lowest return. Trained on 223 hours of motion and tested on 353 motions that no actor performed in training, the method raises the normalized return of SuperMimic, the baseline it builds on, from 0.953 to 0.967 and the lowest $1\%$ of test clips from 0.65 to 0.76, halves the test clips that fall persistently, from 15--18 to 7--10, and reaches the baseline's final return in 40% of the baseline's iterations and half its training time. On LAFAN1, trained and evaluated on the same clips as prior work, it reaches 0.935 against 0.906.
bullets: Very large imagined gradients are poorly validated: simulator-confirmed return changes fall from 94% at low norms to 1% above 30× the batch median.
The method caps each rollout’s action-gradient norm at 10× the batch median, samples starts by predicted gradient norm, and resets episodes with the lowest predicted returns.
On unseen Unitree G1 motions, normalized return improves from 0.953 to 0.967, while the lowest 1% of clips improve from 0.65 to 0.76.
Persistent-fall clips decrease from 15–18 to 7–10, and baseline final performance is reached in 40% of its iterations and half the training time.
On LAFAN1, the method achieves 0.935 versus 0.906 for prior work.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can improve pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies through imagined experiences. However, existing VLA-MBRL methods primarily rely on large-scale image or video generation world models, incurring large computational overhead. Latent world models offer a more efficient alternative but face two challenges: compounding errors during recursive prediction and incompatibility with VLAs' visual input interfaces. In this work, we propose LS-MBPO, a lightweight residual MBRL framework that leverages latent world models to improve upon pretrained VLAs. LS-MBPO introduces two key techniques: (1) Hierarchical Forcing, which combines dense causal supervision with autoregressive feedback to mitigate compounding prediction errors; and (2) Latent Subchunk Rollouts, which leverage action chunks from a frozen VLA policy and a latent residual policy for successive subchunk refinement, bridging the gap between latent imagination and VLA policy execution. We further introduce a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum that progressively shifts rollout starting points from later to earlier task stages, enabling effective policy learning from short imagined rollouts. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot show that LS-MBPO achieves superior task performance and training efficiency compared to existing methods.
authors: Nan Tang, Han-Tao Zhang, Jing-Cheng Pang, Hao-Nan Wang, Hao-Xiang Ren, Yi-Fei Sheng, Jun-Yin Ye, Tian Xu, Fan-Ming Luo, Hao-Xin Lin, Yang Yu
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of image/video-based VLA model-based reinforcement learning.
Uses Hierarchical Forcing to mitigate compounding errors in recursive latent predictions.
Introduces Latent Subchunk Rollouts to connect latent imagination with frozen VLA action-chunk execution.
Applies a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum for learning from short imagined rollouts.
Reports strong task performance and training efficiency across LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan by rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences through a transformer predictor, so a single decision can take tens of seconds. Existing accelerations prune spatial tokens as in vision-language models, yet a sampling-based planner uses predicted costs only to rank candidates, so a rollout can be compressed freely as long as the ranking survives. We propose SOAR, a training-free method that adapts rollout compression to each planning decision. At every decision, SOAR probes a few candidates under several token budgets and keeps the smallest budget that preserves their ranking, so it compresses as far as the current decision allows, without task labels. A closed-loop study of more than 80,000 episodes fixes the rest of the rollout: the first step, which alone reads a real observation, stays exact, and the context frame is cached rather than recomputed. On seven navigation and manipulation tasks with frozen checkpoints, SOAR matches dense-level planning success at 2.3x speedup and retains 98% at 2.5x. Our code is available at https://github.com/starrywiki/SOAR.
authors: Anqi Li, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets the high cost of rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences for each decision.
Probes a few candidates at multiple token budgets and selects the smallest budget that maintains their ranking.
Requires no training or task labels; the first observation-processing step remains exact and context frames are cached.
Across seven navigation and manipulation tasks, matches dense planning success at 2.3× speedup and retains 98% at 2.5×.
Evaluated in a closed-loop study spanning more than 80,000 episodes with frozen checkpoints.

papers.abstract: We present Ego4Gen (Egocentric 4D Future Generation), a world model for 4D future generation in robotic manipu lation. Given a single egocentric image and a text prompt, Ego4Gen jointly generates temporally aligned RGB frames, dense point maps, and dense scene flow, explicitly pre dicting the evolution of scene appearance, spatial struc ture, and motion. Built on Cosmos3-Nano, Ego4Gen ex tends the pretrained generative backbone through modality routed LoRA and asymmetric attention, using geometric pseudo-labels from MotionCrafter to learn to predict future geometry and motion latents. These latents can either be decoded into explicit 3D structure and motion or mapped to robot actions. To this end, we also introduce FlowIn verse, a lightweight inverse dynamics network trained in two stages to translate predicted 4D latents into robot ac tions. Experiments show that these geometry and motion latents outperform the evaluated latent-action and video latent baselines in out-of-distribution settings. Closed loop policy evaluations further demonstrate their utility for translating predicted 4D futures into robot control. To gether, these results support geometry-grounded motion to kens as a world-action interface, connecting 4D future gen eration with robotic manipulation and suggesting a path to ward reduced reliance on action-labeled data.

Geometry and motion latents outperform evaluated latent-action and video-latent baselines in out-of-distribution settings.
Closed-loop policy evaluations demonstrate that the predicted futures can support robot control and reduce reliance on action-labeled data.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation(VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through unseen 3D environments, where the target spaces often lie beyond the current observation. Navigation world models address this challenge by predicting future views either as pixels or latent representations, providing valuable look-ahead information for action decision. Both paradigms define the future primarily through what the agent may observe, raising a fundamental question: is predicting future views the ultimate form to represent the future for VLN? Cognitive studies show that the human hippocampus prospectively represents both future goals and intervening locations along planned routes. Inspired by this predictive-map view, we organize the navigation-relevant future around goal-directed spatial states and route structure. We instantiate this perspective with two complementary abstractions: a short-horizon waypoint that specifies the next local state to reach, and a mid-horizon corridor that captures the spatial support of the upcoming route. Based on this design, we propose FS-Nav, a future-state world modeling framework that predicts waypoint-corridor states from spatial memory and language instructions, and communicates them to a VLM navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces. Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks demonstrate that FS-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance. This highlights navigation-relevant future-state modeling as a promising direction for representing the future in VLN.
authors: Kangyi Wu, Pengna Li, Yucheng Wang, Yance Fang, Xihan Ma, Zhizhong Su, Yang Wu, Ye Deng, Jinjun Wang, Jianyi Liu
bullets: VLN agents must plan beyond their current visual observation while following language instructions.
The paper argues that future representation should include goal-directed spatial states and route structure, inspired by predictive-map views of navigation.
FS-Nav predicts short-horizon waypoints and mid-horizon corridors from spatial memory and language instructions.
These future states are communicated to a vision-language navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces.
Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, though the abstract provides no further experimental details.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of FS-Nav. The Future State World Model encodes the accumulated spatial memory and navigation instruction, fuses their geometry and language features, and predicts a short-horizon waypoint together with a mid-horizon corridor. The Future State Renderer deterministically renders the same prediction as either a top-down canvas or a first-person overlay. Conditioned on the instruction, observation history, and rendered guidance, the Future-State-Guided Navigator generates an action chunk and interacts with the environment in a closed loop. (b) On a single RTX 4090, future-state prediction takes 66.7 ms, over 500× faster than generating a five-frame future observation with Wan2.2-TI2V-5B. papers.tldr: FS-Nav models future navigation states as waypoints and route corridors—not just future views—to improve vision-language navigation in unseen environments.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) often generate future visual states alongside robot actions, introducing substantial computational overhead during inference. During closed-loop execution, consecutive inference cycles often predict similar action sequences, leading to redundant computation. However, reducing this redundancy requires distinguishing consistent actions from changes that demand fresh computation. To address these challenges, we propose ReActWAM, a training-free framework that combines action-intent-guided prefix skipping with inner-chunk prediction reuse. A coarse-to-fine assessment evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action prediction conflicts. For eligible chunks, we draw on first-step differences to adapt the cached latent and network features to the current condition, providing an estimate at a later denoising step that bypasses the redundant prefix. Subsequent inference refines this estimate while reusing stable denoising predictions within the chunk. Experiments across LingBot-VA, FastWAM and the Cosmos family on LIBERO-Long and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate $1.41\times$--$5.44\times$ GPU inference speedup, with minimal degradation in task success rates. Real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot further achieve $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining success rate.
authors: Zhaochen Guo, Yunke Wang, Siyu Xu, Zijian Wang, Chenghao Xia, Chengbin Du, Shinan Liu, Chang Xu
bullets: Addresses redundant computation in closed-loop WAM inference caused by similar consecutive action-sequence predictions.
Uses training-free action-intent-guided prefix skipping and inner-chunk prediction reuse.
Evaluates motion changes, visual consistency, and action conflicts to determine when cached computation is safe.
Reports 1.41×–5.44× GPU inference speedups with minimal task-success degradation across several WAMs and benchmarks.
Achieves 1.46× end-to-end speedup on a Franka Research 3 robot while maintaining success rate.
