papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video world models imagine future observations under candidate robot actions, providing a promising visual tool for robot policy evaluation and interaction simulation. However, existing video world models often optimize global reconstruction errors instead of emphasizing interaction-relevant regions. As a result, they may preserve overall scene appearance but overlook local interaction details, leading to physically implausible outcomes such as hallucinated contact effects and inconsistent robot-object interactions. We introduce MoReWorld, a unified motion-region-guided framework that uses a shared motion region, the part of the environment that moves in response to the robot's actions, to focus dynamics learning and video generation on interaction-relevant regions. The same motion region guides local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning. At inference time, the motion region is predicted as a motion probability map from visual history and robot actions, without requiring future observations or ground-truth motion labels. On WorldSimProbe, MoReWorld achieves the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score, with the strongest performance on local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics. These results indicate that motion-region guidance helps the model preserve scene-level consistency while more faithfully predicting action-conditioned interaction dynamics.
authors: Yongkang He, Xiaofen Xing, Xiangmin Xu
bullets: Existing models can preserve global appearance while missing local interaction details, causing implausible contact effects and robot-object behavior.
MoReWorld uses a shared motion region to guide local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning.
The motion region is inferred at test time from visual history and robot actions, without future observations or ground-truth motion labels.
On WorldSimProbe, it achieves the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score, with strongest results in local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics.

figures.caption: Figure 2. An overview of MoReWorld. (b) During training, WAFT optical flow yields moving/static labels m, s, and URDF rendering yields the environment mask E = 1− ρ that excludes the robot region; their product gives the motion-map labels. (c) The gated future motion Ck and the robot appearance r are injected into the Wan input. (d) A shared Wan denoising transformer jointly processes RGB and VGGT latents and predicts the RGB velocity, clean future VGGT features, and an auxiliary flow velocity, supervised with the motion-region weighted loss.

Columns show, from left to right, the ground truth, MoReWorld (Ours), MVA, Ctrl-World, and LingBot-VA. All models receive the same initial frame and action trajectory. The four panels show a pear painting (top left), a real tabletop photograph (top right), an illustrated still life (bottom left), and another painted still life (bottom right). Within each panel, columns show input actions as black-background URDF renderings, MoReWorld (Ours), MVA, LingBot-VA, and Ctrl-World, from left to right. The top row shows the supplied initial image; subsequent rows advance in time. Red boxes and the dashed arrow highlight selected object responses. (a) Prior models can produce incorrect object responses, yielding false success signals that mislead downstream evaluation. (b) MoReWorld predicts interaction dynamics before generation via a motion-probability intermediate, producing object motion and a final video consistent with the action.

papers.tldr: MoReWorld improves robot video world models by guiding dynamics learning and generation toward regions that move in response to actions.

papers.abstract: We present Zing-1.0, a Playable World System built on Controllable Rendering. An executable engine resolves player actions under the world's rules and produces proxy video from the updated state. A streaming video model synthesizes the player's view from this proxy, and the runtime delivers it to inform subsequent actions. (1) Principle and system. We formulate Controllable Rendering and define the interfaces among world construction, world execution, observation synthesis, and the interaction runtime. To our knowledge, this is the first implementation-independent specification of a Playable World System. (2) AI-native engine. WorldKit provides structured authoring tools and reusable character, camera, and control components for coding agents to construct executable proxy worlds. It supports extensible interactions and precise geometric motion control while separating executable behavior from final visual appearance. (3) Streaming renderer. We adapt MiniMax-H3 for block-causal autoregressive generation and incremental decoding. Proxy video constrains structure and motion, while text and separate scene and subject references specify appearance. We train the generator on diverse tasks and distill it to generate each block in a few denoising steps. The renderer leads the compared streaming editors on OpenVE (3.90) and LongV2VBench (3.44). On StreamEval, Zing-1.0 scores 57.86 on instruction editing and 54.06 on reference editing, exceeding the published baselines on both tracks. (4) Interaction infrastructure. We build an Interaction Runtime that routes player actions to WorldKit while supporting in-play prompt and reference updates. Cross-block joint execution and sparse attention with compressed K/V reduce inference overhead. With the DiT on a single H200 and encoding and decoding on one H100 each, the serving system achieves a steady-state throughput of 23.82 FPS at $832\times480$.
authors: Wenbo Zhang, Guoli Zhang, Xuewen Yu, Xueliang Yang, Jiangqiao Yan, Teng Xia, Xinmiao Wu, Zeyang Tian, Haoze Sun, Jinghui Niu, Hongli Ning, Zhiyuan Liu, Xinna Liu, Weimin Liu, Jialin Liu, Tianpeng Li, Kejun Li, Jun Li, Jiawen Li, Yirong He, Haoyuan Guo, Bosheng Gong, Junhao Gao, Xiaoxiao Fu, Xuezhi Chen, Shengdong Chen, Mingyang Chen, Diying Chen, Yinglun Chai, Yiwen Cai
bullets: Defines interfaces connecting world construction, execution, observation synthesis, and interaction runtime.
WorldKit lets coding agents author executable proxy worlds with reusable characters, cameras, controls, and precise motion.
A block-causal streaming renderer uses proxy video for structure and motion, with text and references controlling appearance.
Reports strong benchmark results, including 3.90 on OpenVE, 3.44 on LongV2VBench, and higher-than-published-baseline scores on both StreamEval tracks.
The runtime supports in-play prompt/reference updates and reaches 23.82 FPS at 832×480 using specified H200/H100 hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Conceptual overview of Zing-1.0 as a Playable World System. World construction produces an executable WorldKit world. Player actions update its state, and proxy frames guide observation synthesis under separate scene and subject references. The interaction runtime links displayed views to their source updates and returns feedback to the player.

Figure 2. Zing-1.0 system architecture, with the control side (the coding agent and WorldKit) and the rendering side (the streaming renderer) connected by proxy frames. Offline construction produces an executable proxy world. Online, player actions update WorldKit state; proxy frames convey its visible consequences to the streaming renderer, while text and references specify appearance. Generated video returns to the browser as feedback for subsequent actions. The runtime coordinates the input-to-display path without feeding generated frames directly into world state.

Figure 4. Architecture of the Zing-1.0 streaming renderer. (a) Frozen Qwen encodes the instruction and references, while the frozen visual VAE encodes the references and live proxy video. (b) The block-causal DiT processes interleaved proxy and target blocks after a static conditioning prefix. Role-specific AdaLN modulates both self-attention and the FFN. Dashed arrows indicate initialization from H3’s video AdaLN branch. (c) The streaming decoder uses cached K/V to decode one latent at a time. (b) The decoder is adapted independently on paired latents and RGB frames with reconstruction and temporal losses.

(a) Parallel teacher forcing evaluates multiple noisy target queries against clean context. Only the two bracketed target rows contribute to the loss in this example. Each block k can attend only to x<k in this history. The blank branch replaces only the Qwen context with a blank-prompt embedding, and sg stops gradients through its prediction nθ. (b) DM compares the conditional real and fake scores, whereas CA compares conditional and blank real scores at a separately sampled noise level. The DMD loss uses rollout values, but gradients pass through the packed replay with generated history latents held fixed.

Figure 11. Interactions and locomotion with prebuilt 3C. Rows (a) and (b) show interaction sequences read from left to right. Row (c) presents independent examples of wall contact, vehicle driving, and fixed-wing takeoff. Examples were recorded in separate offline proxy sessions using two WorldKit builds.

Figure 10. Single-latent streaming decoder. (a) A phase embedding and bounded historical K/V support incremental RGB decoding. (b) H3’s inherited phase cycle yields one RGB frame at phase zero and four at each other phase.

The arm shortens to 2.50 m when the wall blocks the view. After the camera turns away at step 162, the arm returns to the desired 11.0 m by step 386.

(c) The recorded playtest path. Numbers 1–8 indicate the order of first entry into each target region, and grey squares mark pillars.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models aim to predict how visual environments evolve in response to user interventions, including physically consistent state changes induced by applied forces. Existing methods often represent forces as motion trajectories, which may introduce inappropriate motion priors, causing the model to over-rely on encoded displacement patterns. More fundamentally, the model's internal representations do not reliably localize force-induced state changes, making it difficult to associate applied forces with their resulting physical responses. Also, limited force-annotated data make it difficult to produce physically consistent and temporally stable predictions in unseen scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose PhysForce, a two-stage framework that integrates supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning through three complementary components. During supervised fine-tuning, (1) the Latent Force Intervention Encoder maps force location, direction, and magnitude into the video latent space without exposing future motion; and (2) the Physics Attribution Network associates force interventions with localized changes in the latent state, strengthening the learning of physical responses to applied forces. During reinforcement learning, (3) Physics-Aware Reinforcement Learning uses self-supervised rewards on out-of-distribution videos to improve physical consistency and generalization. Extensive experiments show that PhysForce improves force responsiveness, physical consistency, and generalization, demonstrating its effectiveness for interactive video world models.
authors: Xuancheng Xu, Xiaofeng Wang, Yue Ma, Zheng Zhu, Bing-Kun Bao
bullets: Addresses motion-prior bias, poor localization of force-induced changes, and limited force-annotated data.
Encodes force location, direction, and magnitude directly into the video latent space without revealing future motion.
Uses a Physics Attribution Network to link force interventions to localized latent-state changes.
Applies self-supervised, physics-aware reinforcement learning on out-of-distribution videos to improve consistency and generalization.
Experiments report improved force responsiveness, physical consistency, and generalization.

papers.abstract: If we optimize an image until a classifier is confident it shows a cat, we may get an adversarial example, not a cat. Planning with a latent world model is a similar search for actions whose predicted future is closest to the goal. Is the result a plan, or an adversarial example of the world model? We show that it can be either. On the released DINO-WM and LeWM, more iterations of the cross-entropy method (CEM) lower the predicted cost but lose up to half of the problems CEM had already solved. The model's own predictions do not reveal these failures. We propose a simple test that executes the plan after every iteration and counts the problems a planner solves and then loses. Unlike an image, a plan comes with its actions, which our round-trip check reads back from the predicted states with a small network, penalizing mismatches. The check reads back the sum of each block of five actions, the part that two consecutive predicted states determine. Without retraining the world model and at only 0.2% to 3.1% more planning time, it improves the widely used planners CEM and MPPI on three released world models, and gains more where planners lose more problems. Without replanning, success rises from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall with DINO-WM and from 0.56 to 0.94 for MPPI on JEPA-WM. With replanning (MPC), it rises from 0.70 to 0.81 on Cube with LeWM.
authors: Huiyuan Tian, Chih-Yung Wen, Shijian Li
bullets: More CEM iterations can reduce predicted cost while causing planners to lose up to half of previously solved problems.
The world model’s predictions alone fail to reveal these planning failures.
The proposed check executes plans after each iteration and compares predicted actions with actions read back from predicted states.
It improves CEM and MPPI across three released world models with only 0.2%–3.1% additional planning time.
Reported success increases from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall, 0.56 to 0.94 on JEPA-WM, and 0.70 to 0.81 with MPC on Cube.

figures.caption: Figure 1. A plan can be an adversarial example of the world model. The model cannot recognize it, and our round-trip check repairs the planner. (a) A mosaic of color blocks optimized against an ImageNet [13] classifier (ViT-B/16 [14]) is labeled a tabby cat with probability 0.99. (b) The standard CEM planner optimizes actions against DINO-WM [56]. Its plan reaches the goal after 10 iterations and becomes an adversarial example after 30. The model predicts that the final plan reaches the goal, but in the simulator it ends on the wrong side of the wall. (c) The same happens with LeWM [34], whose final plan drops the cube far from its target. With our round-trip check, the same planner’s final plans reach the goal, without retraining the world model and at only 0.2% and 3.1% more planning time.

Figure 3. The round-trip check. (a) The frozen predictor rolls out the candidate plans a of the planner, and the inverse-dynamics network gϕ reads the summed action of each block back from consecutive predicted states. Its residual r against the planned sums s(at) is added to the predicted cost ĉ with weight λ. (b) Decoded predicted states of the final plan of CEM and of the plan found with the check, with the residual r of each plan at the end of its row. Each circle compares the planned sum of a block with the sum that gϕ reads back, and its radius is the largest sum in the training data. The final plan of CEM asks for block sums that its own predicted states do not support, while the plan found with the check agrees with its prediction. (c) Many action sequences connect the same two predicted states, and only their sum is identifiable, so the check reads back this sum.

Figure 4. The same divergence for CEM with LeWM. We use 200 problems per task. (a, c) Success rate of the plan executed after each iteration. (b, d) Median cost of that plan, dashed as the model predicts it and solid as the simulator measures it. On both tasks the predicted cost of the plan of CEM keeps falling, while its true cost stops falling or rises, so the shaded gap between the two widens. With the round-trip check, the plan ends at a lower true cost and a higher success rate.

Figure 2. With the standard planner, planning longer makes the model more confident and the plan worse. The data are from DINO-WM on the Wall task with 148 problems. (a) With the standard CEM planner, the success rate peaks at 0.56 after 11 iterations and falls to 0.39 after 30, and with our round-trip check it rises to 0.76. (b) The median cost that the model predicts for the plan of CEM keeps falling, while the cost that the plan achieves in the simulator rises after iteration 11, and the shaded gap between the two widens. With the round-trip check, the true cost ends at less than a third of that of CEM. The dotted line marks iteration 11 in both panels.

Figure 5. The standard planners can end in adversarial plans, and the round-trip check finds plans that reach the goal. Each example shows the goal, the end of the final plan as the model predicts it and as it is executed, and the end of the plan found with the round-trip check. The predicted end is the nearest training frame, and a tick or a cross marks whether an end reaches the goal. In (a) the final plan of MPPI fails, and in (b) CEM solves the problem after 10 iterations and loses it after 30. The dotted circle marks the distance within which a problem counts as solved.

papers.abstract: We study spatio-temporal forecasting in networked systems under specified actions. The challenge is to capture the action's effects without predicting spurious changes in unaffected regions. However, direct supervision and evaluation of these effects require paired futures with and without the action, whereas observational trajectories reveal only the realized future. We introduce PairST, a benchmark comprising six datasets across traffic, power transmission and water distribution, with paired reference and intervened futures simulated from the same system state. These pairs enable separate evaluation of affected-region forecast accuracy and quiet-region response error. We further propose ActionST, which forecasts the intervened future by writing an explicit response onto an intervention-independent reference forecast. Specifically, node-time addressing constructs a query for each response position, a state-conditioned response writer computes candidate responses, and a graph-aware locality gate controls their strength. Experiments on six datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ActionST at new action targets, with the lowest mean absolute error on five datasets and the best average rank. Our source code and the PairST benchmark are available at https://github.com/yutong-xia/ActionST.
authors: Yutong Xia, Yangyou Liu, Yuxuan Liang, Yuankai Wu, See-Kiong Ng, Roger Zimmermann
bullets: PairST provides six datasets with paired reference and intervened futures across traffic, power transmission, and water distribution.
The benchmark separately evaluates accuracy in affected regions and response error in quiet regions.
ActionST writes an action response onto an intervention-independent reference forecast using node-time addressing, state-conditioned response generation, and graph-aware locality gating.
It achieves the lowest mean absolute error on five of six datasets and the best average rank, including at new action targets.

papers.abstract: The world evolves through the dynamics of its constituent entities and their interactions, with changes in one entity influencing the behavior of others. To simulate this evolution under different actions, interactive world models need to capture the resulting agent responses as part of the world's own dynamics. In autonomous driving, errors in modeling these responses can misrepresent maneuver safety and undermine the reliability of generated videos used for policy evaluation and learning. To formalize this intrinsic requirement for driving world model, we define self-reactivity as the capability to model agent responses from observed history and a specified ego action, and generate visual futures that reflect those responses without prescribed future agent trajectories. To realize this capability, we introduce ReactDrive, a driving world model that jointly learns agent dynamics and visual generation through a shared agent state representation. Within this framework, dynamics supervision grounds a reactive dynamics prior in observed agent states, while the video objective jointly optimizes the self-reactivity and visual realism. Experiments show improved agent responses, ego controllability, and video quality, a 96.0% preference for agent reactivity in human comparisons across five baselines, and better downstream planning through augmentation with generated videos. We hope this work encourages the community to recognize self-reactivityas a foundational capability for developing and evaluating interactive world models. Project page: https://reactdrive.github.io/ .
authors: Yifan Wang, Xiaoqi Wang, Cho-Ying Wu, Wenbin He, Chenyu You, Liu Ren
bullets: Motivation: Accurate modeling of other agents’ responses is essential for reliable safety evaluation and policy learning in autonomous driving.
Method: Jointly learns agent dynamics and video generation through a shared agent-state representation, using dynamics supervision and a video objective.
Contribution: Formalizes self-reactivity as a core capability for interactive driving world models without requiring future agent trajectories.
Results: Reports improved agent responses, ego controllability, video quality, and downstream planning; human evaluators preferred its agent reactivity in 96.0% of comparisons across five baselines.
Scope: Evaluations focus on generated-video quality, reactive behavior, controllability, and planning augmentation in autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are increasingly important for robot learning, yet most generate each camera view separately or tile all views in a fixed layout. Robot demonstrations, however, are captured by synchronized cameras whose number, placement, and order vary across embodiments. We present ViewDreamer, a single world model that handles variable sets of cameras by disentangling per-view generation from cross-view interaction. Each view follows the generation path of a pretrained single-view model, and views interact only through shared slot tokens. We stabilize multi-view training with a curriculum that gradually increases the number of views. Cross-View Slot Agreement uses visual foundation models to group geometrically and semantically similar regions across views into shared slots. On RoboView-Bench, which covers one to four cameras, ViewDreamer achieves the best generation quality among the models evaluated and improves cross-view consistency over independent per-view generation. These gains carry over to our world-action model (WAM) and action-conditioned world model (AC-WM). Our WAM outperforms the FastWAM-Joint baseline on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboDojo, and on a real Franka robot. Both variants improve out-of-domain generalization to various camera settings and scenes.
authors: Ye Mao, Jinhui Xiong, Egor Larionov, Shiyang Lu, Krystian Mikolajczyk, Wei Ye
bullets: Addresses the limitation of models tied to fixed camera counts, placements, or layouts.
Disentangles per-view generation from cross-view interaction using shared slot tokens.
Uses curriculum training and Cross-View Slot Agreement to align geometrically and semantically similar regions.
Achieves the best evaluated generation quality on RoboView-Bench and improves cross-view consistency over independent view generation.
Transfers gains to world-action models, robot benchmarks, and a real Franka robot, including better generalization across camera settings and scenes.

papers.abstract: Learning robotic ultrasound policies requires interactive environments for scalable data generation and repeatable evaluation, while exploration on real patients is limited by acquisition costs and safety constraints. Generative world models offer an alternative, but image history and probe actions alone do not ensure anatomical consistency across wide-range scans and changing acoustic windows. We introduce SonoAtlasWorld, an ultrasound world model built on anatomy as state. A persistent 3D anatomical asset extracted from computed tomography (CT) anchors each scan to a specific anatomy. Probe actions determine anatomical and acoustic visibility conditions for a causal ultrasound generator trained on clinical videos. Our three-stage pipeline combines anatomy-conditioned pretraining, causal conversion and long-rollout alignment. Inference optimizations achieve pose-to-ultrasound throughput of 81.2 FPS. To evaluate anatomical control beyond image similarity, we introduce the Action-Following Index (AFI), which measures normalized reconstruction gain over a static-prefix baseline. On 40 held-out 3D volumes, SonoAtlasWorld achieves liver and macro-organ AFI of 0.428 and 0.262, compared with at most 0.117 and 0.038 for the tested action- and geometry-conditioned methods. Long-rollout alignment reduces brightness drift by 3.46x at the end of 40 repeated scan cycles. SonoAtlasWorld also generates offline policy-training demonstrations and supports anatomically grounded closed-loop evaluation. Scaling the generated training data improves key-plane acquisition success from 48.2% to 81.2% on unseen anatomies in simulation, demonstrating its utility for robotic ultrasound policy learning.
authors: Zheyuan Zhang, Boris Mailhe, Hang Yu, Yikang Liu, Xiao Chen, Ankush Mukherjee, Terrence Chen, Shanhui Sun
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable, safe interactive environments for robotic ultrasound learning.
Conditions a causal ultrasound generator on CT-derived anatomy and probe-controlled anatomical and acoustic visibility.
Combines anatomy-conditioned pretraining, causal conversion, and long-rollout alignment; inference reaches 81.2 FPS.
Introduces the Action-Following Index to evaluate anatomical control beyond image similarity.
On 40 held-out volumes, it improves liver and macro-organ AFI, reduces long-rollout brightness drift, and raises simulated key-plane success from 48.2% to 81.2%.

papers.abstract: World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history. Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model. We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length. It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions. The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window. LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training. Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4,s of history matches one trained with 9.6,s, while a model with 4.8,s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points. Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.
bullets: Uses newly observed frames for label-free test-time training while preserving a short input history.
Accumulates updates within an episode and resets them between episodes, retaining information beyond the observation window.
Improves task success across four simulation benchmarks and two world-action models.
On RoboCasa GR-1, 2.4 seconds of history matches a 9.6-second model; 4.8 seconds exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points.
Adaptation improves predicted future frames and increasingly influences actions as episodes progress.

papers.abstract: Planning with learned world models amounts to finding action sequences whose predicted rollouts reach a goal. Sampling-based planners often struggle at longer horizons, while gradient-based methods can become trapped in local minima. Meanwhile, model predictive path integral control (MPPI), a complementary approach, alternates between estimating an expectation under a cost-weighted distribution from samples and updating the plan from this estimate. Its samples, however, are drawn afresh at every iteration from a Gaussian proposal and reach the target distribution only through importance weights. Moreover, a target distribution favoring goal-reaching trajectories can be difficult to define directly, motivating a sequence of intermediate distributions. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) provides a natural mechanism for evolving such a sequence through importance weighting and resampling. Motivated by this, we formulate latent-space planning as optimization guided by SMC, which moves a population of action sequences while a gradient-based optimizer updates the plan. Inspired by classical planning, we further introduce a PDE-derived cost-to-go that guides the evolution of the sample distribution using the structure of the latent state space. On navigation and manipulation tasks with visual and proprioceptive world models, our formulation outperforms gradient-based planners by $29$ and $50$, sampling-based planners by $35$ and MPPI by $7$ percentage points in average success rate, while succeeding in fewer iterations than gradient-based planners and within 4\% of MPPI.
authors: Hrishikesh Viswanath, Anindita Ghosh, Uttaran Bhattacharya, Aniket Bera
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of long-horizon planning, where sampling methods struggle and gradient methods can get trapped in local minima.
Uses Sequential Monte Carlo to evolve action-sequence populations through intermediate target distributions with importance weighting and resampling.
Combines SMC population updates with gradient-based plan optimization in learned latent world models.
Introduces a PDE-derived cost-to-go to guide sampling using latent-state-space structure.
On visual and proprioceptive navigation/manipulation tasks, improves average success rates over gradient-based, sampling-based, and MPPI planners, with competitive iteration counts.

papers.abstract: Most world models for future prediction prioritize aestetic quality of generated videos, but offer only weak physical grounding and limited geometric consistency over time, due to the lack of explicit 4D modeling. In this paper, we introduce plan4d, a possible next milestone towards building a generative plannable 4D world model that predicts future RGB videos together with dense 4D geometry, including depth, cameras, point clouds, and scene flow from an observed scene context and text-specified actions. Since training data with paired actions and dense 4D annotations is inherently scarce, plan4d leverages the complementary priors of foundational video generators and 3D reconstructors. Specifically, we propose a model-stitching architecture that couples Depth Anything 3 with LongCat-Video and augments it with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction. The resulting model allows us to plan and generate complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in a dynamic 3D scenes, while substantially improving both visual fidelity and geometric accuracy of the generated future videos. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that plan4d achieves state-of-the-art performance in generative 4D modeling of environmental reactions. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/plan4d-project
authors: Hangwei Zhang, Rujing Dang, Ruimin Lin, Jiahong Wu, Xiangxiang Chu, Chuanxia Zheng
bullets: Addresses the weak physical grounding and geometric consistency of video-focused world models.
Uses a model-stitching architecture combining Depth Anything 3 and LongCat-Video, with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction.
Predicts RGB videos, depth, camera poses, point clouds, and scene flow from observed context and text-specified actions.
Supports complex, long-horizon, fine-grained actions and reports improved visual fidelity and geometric accuracy on synthetic and real-world datasets.
The approach targets settings where paired action and dense 4D supervision is scarce by leveraging pretrained video and 3D reconstruction priors.

papers.abstract: Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorer's evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the target's latent velocity field. Verification also yields a reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. On WBench Navigation, SpecWM improves visual quality at 1.63$\times$ speedup over the target and raises NavScore from the draft's 75.99 to 85.63, achieving the best quality-speed-control trade-off. Additionally, our LongSpecBench shows sustained quality and control over long, multi-turn rollouts, while experiments on Hy-Nomas validate SpecWM across backbones and denoising budgets.
authors: Jiaming Li, Lingzhen Li, Xiaze Yang, Chenyu Zhu, Kaiqi Liu, Xiaotong Zhao, Songlian Li, Toyota Li, Alan Zhao, Haobin Zhong, Yue Ma, Zhiyuan Ma
bullets: Replaces decoded-frame reward verification with checks based on the target model’s latent velocity field.
Uses two thresholds to choose among Accept, one-step Refine, and three-step Refine or Reject.
Reuses verification signals to correct drafts, targeting perceptual quality, camera following, and trajectory consistency.
On WBench Navigation, reports 1.63× speedup and raises NavScore from 75.99 to 85.63.
LongSpecBench and Hy-Nomas experiments support sustained rollout performance and applicability across backbones and denoising budgets.

Bottom: generationloop speedup over Target-only. Longer fixed refinements improve navigation but reduce speed. papers.abstract: Controllable streaming video generation offers a promising route toward interactive game simulation, yet existing methods remain far from practical gameplay. They often fail to jointly achieve high visual fidelity, high frame rates, and low interaction latency, resulting in poor responsiveness and degraded user experience. We present Streaming-AAA, a new paradigm for controllable infinite generation of AAA-quality game videos. Our system generates 1080p gameplay videos at 43 FPS with 198 ms end-to-end latency interaction on merely NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while supporting long-horizon play without severe temporal degradation or collapse. Streaming-AAA is built upon three key designs. First, we redesign the VAE architecture for efficient high-resolution decoding, enabling real-time synthesis at 1080p. Second, we pretrain the diffusion model using diffusion forcing and significantly extend the temporal training horizon, allowing the model to capture long-term dependencies and maintain persistent memory. Third, we perform post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while retaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Experiments show that Streaming-AAA substantially improves visual fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation approaches, enabling a significantly more playable experience for interactive AAA game video generation.
authors: Zhihao Hu, Jianqi Ma, Jun Zhang, Jiayang Bai, Haifeng Shi, Yanxiang Zhuang, Zhongqian Sun, Weidong Zhang, Wei Yang
bullets: Targets the challenge of jointly achieving high visual fidelity, frame rate, responsiveness, and long-term stability in interactive game video generation.
Redesigns the VAE for efficient 1080p decoding and real-time synthesis.
Uses diffusion forcing with an extended temporal training horizon to capture long-term dependencies and persistent memory.
Applies post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while preserving visual and temporal quality.
Experiments report improved fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation methods.

papers.abstract: World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. To address this, we propose AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations. Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation. We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state. Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes. On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD. These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT-trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3%.
authors: John Won, Yonghoon Dong, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Current video-predictive world models may look realistic while misrepresenting the consequences of similar actions.
AFFECT injects temporally correlated action noise during task-agnostic teleoperation and matches the resulting visual-change distributions.
It avoids requiring repeated executions from the same initial state.
Across OGBench, DROID, and ALOHA-2, AFFECT improves correspondence between simulated and real outcomes, lowers FVD, and boosts planning success.
On DROID, success-rate correlation increases from 0.47 to 0.79, with up to 23% lower FVD and 8.3% higher planning success.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of AFFECT. Frozen encoders ϕ, ψ extract video features from both the recorded and generated futures, and perturbation features from the logged action perturbations. Pairing the centered perturbations with each set of video features gives the recorded and predicted action effects (Φ(O),Φ(Ô)), which measure how visual change moves with the perturbation across rollouts. The AFFECT loss optimizes over the distance between the two distributions, so that generated futures respond to perturbations in the same direction and with the same strength as real ones.

Figure 1: Small action perturbations lead to distinct action effects. From the same initial state, actions drawn from a narrow distribution change the gripper’s approach only slightly, yet produce qualitatively different outcomes, where the cube is grasped, missed, or pushed away. A faithful world model must reproduce how these outcomes shift as the action is perturbed, rather than only rendering a plausible video for generic actions.

Figure 3: Planning with action-faithful world models. Success rates (%) of plans selected with each world model on (a) UR5e and (b) ALOHA-2, where one long-horizon task consists of three consecutive subtasks. Candidate action chunks are proposed by an ensemble of five policy checkpoints. Uniform picks one at random, while DreamDojo and DreamDojo + AFFECT imagine each chunk and select the one whose imagined video scores highest under a learned success estimator.
Figure 4: Action-effect localization. Frozen-feature responses on UR5e relative to shuffled pairs, where brighter cells indicate stronger responses.

papers.tldr: AFFECT trains world models to faithfully reflect how small action changes alter future observations, improving rollout realism and planning utility.

papers.abstract: Robotic world models predict future video frames from the current observation and a sequence of robot actions. While recent models follow the given actions closely, manipulated objects often collapse or move inconsistently with the action. We attribute this to the conditioning: an action, or a rendering of the robot, specifies where the robot goes but not how the scene responds, leaving a single video model to infer the interaction dynamics implicitly while also rendering appearance. We therefore separate dynamics prediction from visual rendering, with 3D point dynamics as the proxy between them. Specifically, we lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate how they respond to the robot's motion with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points back into pixel-aligned videos that any video model can read. In controlled experiments on the DROID dataset with two video renderers of different architectures, this point dynamics proxy reduces object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot. Moreover, the video follows the simulation: more accurate dynamics yield more accurate object motion, and editing the points steers the video. This suggests that advances in dynamics modeling can translate into more faithful robotic world models.
authors: Dong An, Tianyu Liu, Haoran Ding, Wen Yang, Anqing Duan, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric P. Xing, Guangyi Liu
bullets: Problem: Video world models often follow robot actions but predict inconsistent or collapsed object motion because scene dynamics and appearance are inferred together.
Method: Lift the initial frame into 3D points, predict their response to robot motion with a learned dynamics model, then render the simulated points into pixel-aligned videos for a video model.
Results: Object-motion error decreases by 8.6% and 6.2% with two DROID video renderers, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot, without reducing image quality.
The rendered video tracks the simulated dynamics: better point predictions produce better object motion, while editing points can steer the generated video.
Scope: Results are demonstrated in controlled DROID experiments and on a real bimanual robot.

papers.selection_reason: Separates dynamics prediction from visual rendering in robotic world models by using 3D point dynamics as a proxy, significantly improving object motion accuracy in simulation and real-world manipulation.
papers.title: Point Dynamics as Proxy for Robotic World Models
papers.tldr: A 3D point-dynamics proxy separates robot interaction modeling from video rendering, improving manipulated-object motion while preserving visual quality.

papers.abstract: Interactive game world models separate executable world evolution from visual generation, using video models to render engine-provided scene representations into detailed observations. During sustained gameplay, however, existing generative renderers struggle to follow changing conditions while preserving visual continuity across diverse proxies and target styles. We therefore introduce ContextRenderer, an autoregressive video diffusion framework designed for both dynamic conditioning and cross-proxy generalization. It couples Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) for chunk-level interaction supervision with Recurrent History Compression (RHC) to follow condition updates while preserving visual continuity within a bounded token budget. Across proxy representations, Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects proxy reconstruction with appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction. WorldPrism, our interaction-centric dataset constructed from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos, supplies the corresponding renderings and chunk-level annotations for these learning tasks. Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality, while qualitative results demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references. Project page: https://rainzor.github.io/contextrenderer/
authors: Runze Wang, Fei Zha, Bing He, Ke Xu, Zhongyuan Wu, Yuxuan Xie, Wenzheng Wu, Zhongyuan Liu, Youcheng Cai, Ligang Liu
bullets: Targets generative renderers that lose continuity and fail to follow evolving gameplay conditions.
Uses Dynamic-Context Learning for chunk-level interaction supervision and Recurrent History Compression to maintain continuity within a bounded token budget.
Introduces Cross-Representation Flow Alignment to support generalization across diverse scene proxies and target appearances.
Provides WorldPrism, a dataset of agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos with renderings and chunk-level annotations.
Improves reconstruction and visual quality on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench; qualitative results show sustained interactive rendering under changing prompts and references.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces ContextRenderer for dynamic-context video generation in interactive game worlds, bridging video generation with interactive environment simulation.
papers.title: ContextRenderer: Dynamic-Context Video Generation for Interactive Game Worlds
papers.tldr: ContextRenderer enables visually consistent, minute-long video rendering for interactive game worlds despite changing conditions, proxies, and styles.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict future videos and actions with one backbone, and their imagined future is often seen as a safety signal. We introduce SteerTrace, a targeted universal attack on WAMs that also traces its effect inside the model. One $\ell_\infty$-bounded (4/255) perturbation per model, shared across frames, tasks, and camera views, pushes the executed action toward an attacker-chosen target. On eight WAMs from four families (FastWAM, Faster-WAM, OpenWAM and LingBot-VA) on LIBERO and RoboTwin, it drives task success close to zero and moves the attacked action toward the target. Same-budget noise and BadWAM produce little action shift in the target direction. We use the signed targeted effect to measure how much of the effect each intervention removes or reproduces. Under the standard attack, restoring future tokens removes 61-94% of the targeted effect in the five models whose action experts attend to them. When the attack is constrained to keep the predicted future close to the clean prediction, the targeted effect can become more dependent on current-frame tokens. In three of these five models, restoring current-frame tokens removes 87-99% of the effect, compared with 9-15% for future tokens. In six models, restoring just 0.36% of the FFN neurons in layers 10-29 of the video expert removes 72-96% of the targeted effect. Residual directions 2-16 hold only 11-18% of the shift energy, yet removing them cancels most of the targeted effect.
authors: Yukun Dai, Tianshi Wang, Fengling Li, Jingjing Li, Xin Li, Lei Zhu
bullets: Targets world action models with one shared ℓ∞-bounded (4/255) perturbation across frames, tasks, and camera views.
Across eight models on LIBERO and RoboTwin, the attack drives task success near zero and shifts actions toward the chosen target; control attacks cause little target-direction shift.
Restoring future tokens removes 61–94% of the targeted effect in five models, while constrained attacks can make current-frame tokens more important.
Restoring only 0.36% of FFN neurons in layers 10–29 removes 72–96% of the effect in six models.
Low-energy residual directions can still be critical: removing directions 2–16 cancels most of the targeted effect despite containing only 11–18% of shift energy.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Framework overview. Top: (a) one perturbation δ is added to every camera frame and is the only quantity optimized. The WAM is frozen. The action tokens read the K/V of the current-frame tokens C and, if the mask allows (dashed), of the future tokens F . Bottom: three analyses intervene at the sites b–d and measure the remaining targeted effect T ′. (b) For one token group, we restore clean K/V in the attacked run or inject attacked K/V into the clean run. (c) For the top-k FFN neurons ranked by SteerTrace, we restore clean activations in the attacked run or inject attacked activations into the clean run. (d) We remove or keep a band B of the residual shift ∆. State outlines and action-value circles are gray for clean and red for attacked. Green outlines mark replaced states.

Figure 3. The imagined future does not show the executed action (FastWAM-Joint, LIBERO). (a) Model input and last imagined frame for clean, standard and preserve inputs (third-person view top, wrist view bottom), with the end-effector distance from clean execution below. (b) One point per executed chunk from 200 initial states: end-effector displacement from clean execution versus the projection ratio of imagined onto real visual change. Large markers are group means.

Figure 1. Targeted universal attacks that reveal how world action models are steered. (a) Prior attacks [25] optimize a perturbation for every input and maximize the distance between each action (solid) and its clean value (dashed), with no control over where the action goes. (b) One perturbation pushes every output action toward an attacker-chosen target action a⋆, yielding a targeted effect (Target, T ). (c) Using this targeted effect as the measure: share of T removed by restoring one video layer of the future (F ) or current-frame (C) tokens in FastWAM-Joint, a few FFN neurons, or residual directions 2–16. (d) Closed-loop success rate (SR) and shift toward the target (TDS). Value axes are broken at 3.

Figure 5. Attributed neurons carry the targeted effect. Fraction of the targeted effect removed, R (Eq. (7)), under the standard attack when 1,024 FFN neurons (0.36%) of video layers 10–29 are restored to clean, selected by attribution (Eq. (10)), by the largest activation change |∆g|, or at random. “All FFN” restores every neuron in these layers. OW denotes OpenWAM. Results for other k are in the Supplementary.

Figure 4. Preserve moves the targeted effect from F to C. Percentage of the targeted effect removed in FastWAM-Joint when the action expert reads clean keys and values at a single video layer, for the current-frame tokens C (solid) or the future tokens F (dashed), under the standard (red) and preserve (blue) attacks. The standard attack peaks on F at layer 27 (23%), and the preserve attack peaks on C at layer 26 (34%). Restoring layers 25–29 together removes 34% of the targeted effect of the standard attack through C and 42% through F , against 82% and 8% of that of the preserve attack. Layers 0–9 remove less than 1.5% in every condition and are omitted.

Table 1. Attack effectiveness on LIBERO. SR is the task success rate (%) on each suite. TDS is the shift of the executed attacked action toward a⋆ relative to a paired clean query, in per cent of the half range of the normalized action. Clean TDS compares paired unperturbed rollouts that differ only in the sampling seed. For perturbed conditions, ± is the error across repeated runs. Noise is same-budget Gaussian noise clipped to ∥δ∥∞ ≤ 4/255. BadWAM is the attack of [25], restricted to the same budget ϵ as ours. Since it has no target direction, its TDS is measured along the same axis. Standard (λ = 0) and preserve (λ = 1) are the two variants of SteerTrace, with ϵ = 4/255.
Table 3. Predicted future fidelity. Lower is better. Noise is samebudget Gaussian noise. Std. and Pres. denote the standard and preserve attacks. Full results are in Supplementary.

Random: 15 random directions removed instead of u2–16. LIBERO for FastWAM, FastWAM-Joint, Faster-WAM and LingBot-VA, RoboTwin for OpenWAM.

Table 4. Pathways of successful attacks. LIBERO for FastWAMJoint, Faster-WAM and LingBot-VA, RoboTwin for OpenWAM. NF and NC are the percentages of the targeted effect removed by restoring the future or current-frame K/V to clean. ΣF is the percentage reproduced by injecting only the attacked future K/V into a clean pass. ∗For LingBot-VA, NC restores the most recent observed video tokens in the history cache.

Table 2. Attack effectiveness on RoboTwin. SR is the task success rate (%) over all tasks. TDS is the commanded end-effector shift along the target axis toward a⋆ relative to a paired clean query, in per cent of half the expert range of that axis, and ± is the error across repeated attack runs. Noise, BadWAM and standard are as in Tab. 1, and preserve uses λ = 0.1. MUT, ASV, VSA and ISO denote the four OpenWAM variants.

papers.selection_reason: Targeted attack and internal tracing for world action models; directly relevant to world-model safety and VLA action prediction.
papers.title: SteerTrace: Tracing How Target Attacks Steer World Action Models
papers.tldr: SteerTrace shows that tiny universal perturbations can reliably steer world action models toward attacker-chosen actions and identifies the internal tokens, neurons, and residual directions responsible.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) offer a foundation for predictive decision-making by modeling the consequences of actions in representation space. Yet evaluating local reachability in latent space does not by itself provide a task-level execution interface: intermediate targets must be generated, local inference has finite budgets, and execution requires spatial feedback and persistent interaction state. We introduce LeCompass, a state-indexed execution framework built around a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). A proposer supplies intermediate latent targets, while CompassFlow searches the source space of a learned trajectory prior to obtain effective action candidates under limited predictive-evaluation budgets. Patch-token readouts provide spatial feedback, while observation-based memory supports phase transitions and bounded recovery. State-indexed targets support cross-episode context-goal composition. On 1,000 official TEST full-episode Cube trials, the complete LeCompass execution system achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach. Separate matched analyses show that predictive ranking raises success from 4.7% to 44.9% on TEST PushT and from 33.8% to 77.7% on TEST TwoRoom. These results demonstrate task-level execution with task-dependent roles for latent target proposal, predictive search, and observation-grounded control.
authors: Kai Shi, Shiqi Zhao, Zimo Li, Hairong Qu, Hongyu Ma, Yongsong Yang, Jiahao Ai, Ziran Yin, Peng Yin
bullets: Addresses the gap between local latent reachability and persistent, task-level execution.
Uses a frozen LeWorldModel with a proposer for intermediate targets and CompassFlow to search trajectory-prior actions under limited evaluation budgets.
Adds patch-token spatial feedback and observation-based memory for phase transitions and bounded recovery.
State-indexed targets enable cross-episode context-goal composition.
Achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach on 1,000 TEST Cube trials; predictive ranking improves matched PushT success from 4.7% to 44.9% and TwoRoom from 33.8% to 77.7%.

Figure 2: LeCompass planning and execution interfaces. (a) History, final goal, and span κ condition the proposer; its latest inverse-normalized prediction supplies the scoring reference. (b) CompassFlow decodes 25-action candidates with eight Euler steps. Source-CEM evaluates three 64-source rounds, using frozen LeWM to score predicted outcomes. The reference enters scoring, not the trajectory prior. (c) Cube acquisition reads current patch tokens; placement also uses cached final-goal tokens to estimate displacement and block height. (d) Observation-based memory confirms phases and permits bounded recovery from contact loss in CARRY. The placement controller assigns action channels, after which grip-floor and release actuators may override the gripper command. Environment observations update the encoded history and patch tokens.

Figure 1: Three interfaces from local prediction to task-level execution. (a) Observed history and the final goal yield a local latent reference. (b) Target-independent CompassFlow generates action candidates; frozen LeWM scores them against the reference, and Source-CEM refines sources over three 64-sample rounds. (c) Cube uses patch-token readouts and observation-based memory for action realization, phase transitions, and bounded recovery.

papers.abstract: Early interactions can reveal physical properties that later observations no longer show. These properties can still gov- ern the effects of future actions. Inspired by the distinction between retention and selective readout in working mem- ory and cognitive science, we introduce LATER, an action- conditioned world model built on CF-JEPA. LATER stores completed real transitions in partitioned memories that remain fixed during candidate rollouts. A response bridge queries these memories using the current state and candidate action, while multi-cut auxiliary supervision trains the memory writ- ers. On distracted Two-Stage PushT, LATER raises terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA. In a separate comparison across six models and two scratch- training seeds, LATER achieves the lowest mean physical readout error in both clean and distracted views, reducing along-push mean absolute error (MAE) under distractors by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA. Controlled history interventions show that later predictions depend on earlier physical evi- dence even when query observations and actions are fixed, with larger effects during pushing than waiting.
authors: Zihan Zhou, Wenxi Xu, Qilin Wang, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses the problem of physical properties becoming unobservable in later frames while still affecting future actions.
Stores completed transitions in fixed, partitioned memories and uses a response bridge to retrieve evidence based on the current state and candidate action.
Trains memory writers with multi-cut auxiliary supervision within a CF-JEPA-based world model.
On distracted Two-Stage PushT, improves terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA.
Achieves the lowest mean physical readout error across six models and two seeds, reducing distractor-induced along-push MAE by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies must react while visual inference is still running. Overlapping computation and execution reduces waiting, yet leaves perceptual memory stale and successive action chunks disconnected. We present CauSyncVLA, an asynchronous dual-system controller that aligns perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction with actual robot execution. Rather than forecasting pixels or physical states, a Causal Latent World Model predicts current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history, supervised through action-sensitive distillation to retain the frozen expert's control response. Conditioned on this updated memory, Predictive Flow Warm-Starting (PFWS) aligns the unexecuted action horizon for single-step flow correction without extra training. On LIBERO-10, CauSyncVLA reaches 93.8% success at 5.04$\times$ inference throughput, improving closed-loop robustness and robot motion smoothness.
authors: Xu Pan, Chubin Zhang, Xingrui Yu, Runmin Lan, Zihao Wang, Wenkai Guo, Bofang Jia, Bo An, Ziwei Wang
bullets: Addresses stale visual memory and disconnected action chunks caused by overlapping perception and execution.
Uses a Causal Latent World Model to predict current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history.
Applies action-sensitive distillation to preserve the frozen expert’s control behavior.
Uses Predictive Flow Warm-Starting for single-step correction of the remaining action horizon without additional training.
On LIBERO-10, achieves 93.8% success with 5.04× inference throughput, alongside improved robustness and motion smoothness.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how a scene will evolve and condition their actions on this predicted future. Deploying them on a robot's onboard computer calls for 4-bit weights, activations and key-value caches (W4A4KV4). Existing 4-bit quantizers for WAMs preserve the generated action, and estimate sensitivity one denoising step at a time. However, they fail to preserve the fidelity of the predicted future: once the action pathway is protected, the remaining action error enters mostly through a degraded future that none of them deliberately protects. We propose LAQ, a latent-aware quantization framework that preserves the predicted future where it is written, stored and read. Specifically, we introduce a reader metric, which measures future error by its effect on the action, and a read count, which weights each rounding error by the number of denoising steps that read it. Together they give the allocation of precision over activations and caches a closed-form solution. We further develop gaze-guided refinement, which gives the tokens the action attends to a second 4-bit pass in the denoising loop and in the cache. All weights stay at 4 bits, with no high-precision branch and no per-task recalibration. On the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, LAQ reaches 76.4% and 83.3% average success on Fast-WAM and Cosmos-Policy, within 1.2 percentage points of the 16-bit models and all above the baselines with 16-bit KV caches. It compresses the model by 3.8x, reduces the peak GPU memory of the whole policy by 2.3x, and runs 1.66x faster than the 16-bit model. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, it reaches 47.0% average success over three tasks, against 52.0% for the 16-bit model and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.
authors: Yichen Guo, Yanlong Chen, Xinyue Zhang, Mohan Liu, Song Zhang, Yawei Li
bullets: Targets W4A4KV4 deployment of world action models on onboard robot computers.
Uses a reader metric to measure future errors by their impact on actions, and read counts to allocate activation/cache precision across denoising steps.
Adds gaze-guided refinement, giving action-relevant tokens a second 4-bit quantization pass in the denoising loop and cache.
On LIBERO-Plus, achieves 76.4% and 83.3% success—within 1.2 points of 16-bit models—while compressing 3.8×, reducing peak memory 2.3×, and running 1.66× faster.
On a real AgileX PiPER arm, reaches 47.0% success versus 52.0% for 16-bit and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.

At every control step, gaze-guided refinement (d) gives the tokens selected under the current gaze a second 4-bit code in the linear layers and in the cache, and the attention of the action tokens gives the gaze for the next step.

papers.title: Don't Lose the Future: Latent-Aware 4-Bit Quantization of World Action Models
papers.tldr: LAQ enables near-16-bit robot performance with fully 4-bit WAMs by explicitly protecting the predicted future that guides actions.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using $7.4\times$ less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.
authors: Anh Dao, Xinxin Liu, Hang Yu, Jeffrey A Chan Santiago, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: WAMs are costly because they combine video generation with action prediction using large transformers.
A shared six-block core is recurrently applied to execute 30 layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert; video and action experts use different depths.
Elastic self-distillation trains one checkpoint to support varied action-depth and sampling-step budgets.
The 0.58B-parameter model reports 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, with 7.4× lower peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched measurements.
On real hardware, it achieved 71.3% success over 80 trials; performance degrades when action depth is aggressively reduced without budget-aware training.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. (a) Each expert stores a prelude, a shared core, and a coda, and loops the core Kv times in the video expert and Ka times in the action expert (shown for Kv=4, Ka=2). The video expert encodes the current frame once per query and caches its keys and values. At every sampling step, the action expert reads them in a joint attention; late alignment lets action loop r attend to video loop σ(r), so even a single action loop sees the deepest visual features. Both experts also cross-attend to frozen text embeddings of the instruction, and future frames are predicted only during training. (b) One student learns every setting (Ka, N) in S. The target of each macro step is the frozen teacher’s fine Euler map started from the student’s own state (Llocal), and the final chunk is matched to the teacher’s chunk from the same noise (Lend).

Figure 1. LoopedWAM is small, fast, and elastic. (a) Each expert stores 12 blocks and loops its shared 6-block core K times. One checkpoint thus reaches the 30-layer depth of its dense donor with 2.4× fewer parameters, and the depth is chosen at test time. (b) RoboTwin 2.0 success against parameters, as reported by each paper. At 0.58B, LoopedWAM (91.9%) is the best model below 2B and on par with the ∼6B Fast-WAM (91.8%). (c) LIBERO success against latency on one H100 for each setting of action loops Ka and sampling steps N of LoopedWAM-E. One checkpoint spans 24.7–86.2 ms at 95.2–96.2% success, and at (2, 2) it is 3.9× faster than Fast-WAM.

Figure 3. Elastic inference (LIBERO, shorter ablation schedule; latency: one H100, batch 1). (a) Running fewer action loops than trained collapses the success of the fixed Kv/Ka=4/4 model (orange), and more loops lower it as well, whereas the elastic student keeps it at every loop count. Filled markers: loop counts used in training; hollow: not used (at Ka=4 both models score 94.9%). (b) The nine settings of one elastic checkpoint (blue, Pareto frontier as a line) against models trained separately at fixed loop counts Kv/Ka (the 4/4 model in orange; all fixed models use N=10), the 12- and 30-layer dense controls, and a specialist distilled only for (Ka, N) = (1, 2). papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video prediction lets robots anticipate the visual consequences of their actions for planning and policy evaluation. Existing predictors denoise each future from noise without using their own estimate of it, which limits the quality of the predicted future, in particular of the manipulated objects, and requires many network calls. We present TwoPass, a self-conditioned training-and-inference framework that keeps the standard flow-matching objective. Self-Generated Draft Training supplies a detached clean-video estimate from the shared network as conditioning at the same noisy state. A Refinement-Only Late Adapter applies a dedicated residual transformation when a draft is present. At inference, Draft-Reuse Iterative Refinement obtains both a solver update and the next draft from each velocity prediction, requiring as few as 4 function evaluations (NFE) per video chunk. Training samples discrete solver-query noise levels and updates the pretrained backbone. Extensive experiments on Bridge and Language Table show that TwoPass achieves state-of-the-art results with 4 NFE, far fewer than the 50-59 calls of existing predictors. Code: https://github.com/PlantPotatoOnMoon/TwoPass.
authors: Yijun Liu, Shijia Ge, Tongtong Feng, Xin Wang, Yuan Meng, Yuwei Liu, Zhi Wang, Wenwu Zhu
bullets: Targets low-quality predictions of manipulated objects and the high inference cost of existing video predictors.
Uses self-generated draft training to condition predictions on a detached clean-video estimate at the same noisy state.
Adds a refinement-only late adapter that applies a residual transformation when a draft is available.
Reuses each velocity prediction to produce both a solver update and the next draft during inference.
Evaluated on Bridge and Language Table, with 4 NFE versus 50–59 calls for existing predictors.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of TWOPASS. (1) Self-Generated Draft Training: on feedback-enabled updates (probability 0.5), two passes share weights and the noisy state. The first runs without gradients and produces a detached draft d = sg(xσ − σṽ) for the supervised second pass. (2) Refinement-Only Late Adapter: a bottleneck with a zero-initialized up-projection sits before the shared prediction head; the role flag r disables it when no draft is available (draft call) and enables it for draft-conditioned (refine) calls. (3) Draft-Reuse Iterative Refinement: inference starts without a draft, then reuses each clean estimate while the solver advances the noisy state, so each solver step costs one network call. Draft training and draft reuse are stages of the same self-conditioning mechanism.

The draft and supervised training passes share a noisy state, whereas inference advances the solver state between calls.

papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned video prediction for robotic manipulation; directly fits world models and interactive prediction.
papers.title: TwoPass: Draft-Guided Few-Step Video Prediction for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: TwoPass improves action-conditioned robotic video prediction by reusing draft predictions for iterative refinement, achieving state-of-the-art results with as few as 4 network evaluations.

papers.abstract: 3D worlds can now be captured, reconstructed, and generated at scale, yet the objects in them stay still: a pressed pillow does not compress, and a pulled door does not swing. Bringing these objects into interactive 4D world models requires a representation of how they can move, deform, and respond physically to user actions in real time. We present PRIO, a pre-trained representation for interactive objects. Given static geometry, PRIO predicts an object-specific configuration space in a single forward pass. This space provides generalized coordinates for Lagrangian mechanics, allowing physical laws and user actions to govern motion. Configurations are linear in these coordinates, allowing the quantities needed by the dynamics to be precomputed. Dynamics then run at interactive rates without further network inference. Pre-trained on diverse 4D trajectories, PRIO learns priors over object configurations that generalize to unseen shapes. It supports meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians, bringing objects in reconstructed and generated scenes into interaction. We demonstrate its use in real-to-sim workflows and robot manipulation. In addition, compared with existing 4D generation methods, PRIO generates dynamics faster and follows user actions more faithfully.
authors: Shixun Huang, Lifu Wei, Yue Chang, Chen Geng, Heng Zhang, Jinhyung Ahn, Caoliwen Wang, Siyuan Chen, Donglai Xiang, Jiajun Wu, Peter Yichen Chen
bullets: Addresses the challenge of making reconstructed or generated 3D-world objects physically interactive.
Predicts an object-specific configuration space in one forward pass from static geometry.
Uses linear generalized coordinates with Lagrangian mechanics, so dynamics quantities can be precomputed and simulated without further network inference.
Pre-trained on diverse 4D trajectories to generalize configuration priors to unseen shapes and support meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians.
Demonstrated in real-to-sim workflows and robot manipulation; reported faster dynamics and more faithful response to user actions than existing 4D generation methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PRIO. Given a mesh, point cloud or 3D Gaussians, PRIO encodes the geometry into shape tokens and predicts, at any point X , the fields ΦG(X) that span a linear configuration space. The network runs once per object; at inference, user actions drive the dynamics through the Euler–Lagrange equations in real time.

Figure 3. Qualitative inverse kinematics comparison. We evaluate how well each method’s predicted representation captures target configurations. Given an object’s rest shape, we optimize its latent coordinates to fit each target and compare the resulting reconstructions. PRIO reproduces the targets most closely.

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison of interactive 4D dynamics. We evaluate how naturally and plausibly objects move in response to user actions. PRIO deforms each object locally along the action and keeps it intact, whereas the baselines respond weakly or tear it.

Figure 10. Robot interaction. (a) Starting from the pillow’s surface mesh, PRIO models the deformation under a robot grasp at 7.6 ms per step. (b) A humanoid robot grasps eight plush toys in the same scene, all simulated together at 25 ms per step.

Figure 8. Live recordings of real-time interaction across 3D input formats. Screenshots of a user-controlled robot arm interacting with a 3D Gaussian ficus (top) and point-cloud flowers (bottom). The same pre-trained PRIO model simulates both objects’ responses directly in their respective 3D representations, at 125– 292 FPS for the ficus and 155–167 FPS for the flowers.

Figure 5. Interacting with real captured objects. PRIO enables physically driven responses to robot-arm manipulation for objects captured in Deform360 [37]. Ropes bend and plush toys deform naturally without per-object training.

Figure 4. Effect of pre-training scale. Reconstruction error on unseen shapes as the pre-training set grows from 266 to 2,142 objects under the same training budget. The error falls steadily, from 2.19 % to 1.43 %.

Figure 9. Interactive real-world objects. Objects reconstructed from photographs deform under user actions; overlaid frames show the motion. Each responds at interactive rates without perobject training.

Figure 7. Speed and accuracy against VBD. PRIO (left) and VBD [11] run to convergence (right) deform the same apple mesh on the same GPU. PRIO runs 7.1× faster, while their surfaces differ by only 0.1 % of the object size on average.

papers.title: PRIO: Pre-trained Representation for Interactive Objects in 4D Worlds
papers.tldr: PRIO predicts a compact, physics-compatible representation of how objects move and deform, enabling fast interactive 4D simulation from static geometry.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models plan from pixels with model predictive control, yet often fail on tasks their model should handle. Test-time adaptation attributes such failures to model error under distribution shift and updates the weights on the current episode, without checking this attribution against the planning loop itself. We follow the executed planning loop on pushing tasks. In most settings, with and without distribution shift, nearly all failures (at least 96%) are stalls, where the object stays in place while the model predicts progress. The warm-started gradient-descent (GD) planner then returns nearly the same plan, a fixed point where the agent mostly idles. We propose Unstick, which pairs on-policy fine-tuning before deployment with a fixed-weight loop breaker: a residual memory of the episode's prediction errors or random re-initialization at every replan. With GD, Unstick recovers most of the adaptation gain on pushing tasks with the memory, and with re-initialization most of it on shape shifts but much less on visual shifts. A large part of what limits these planners under GD is thus a fixed point of the planning loop, present with and without distribution shift, which a planner with fixed weights can break. Code is available at https://github.com/jhlee0619/unstick.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Dongheon Lee, Kyu Sung Choi
bullets: At least 96% of observed failures are stalls: the object remains stationary while the model predicts progress.
Stalls arise both with and without distribution shift, challenging the attribution of failures solely to model error.
Unstick combines on-policy fine-tuning with a fixed-weight loop breaker: prediction-error memory or random re-initialization at each replan.
Residual memory recovers most adaptation gains on pushing tasks; re-initialization works well for shape shifts but less for visual shifts.
The findings identify planning-loop fixed points as a major limitation of warm-started gradient-descent planners.
