papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and remedies planning-loop failures in JEPA world-model planners for robotic pushing, relevant to world models and embodied planning.
papers.title: Stuck in Place: Stall Diagnosis and Remedies for JEPA Planners
papers.tldr: JEPA planners on pushing tasks often fail because gradient-descent planning gets stuck in fixed-point idle plans, and Unstick mitigates this by breaking the loop with residual memory or re-initialization.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) unify world modeling and action generation for robotic control by integrating flow-matching velocities, yet suffer from high multi-step denoising latency. Recent studies have explored speculative inference to accelerate WAMs by drafting and verifying denoising steps in parallel. However, existing methods either require training task-specific draft models or overlook critical WAM denoising dynamics when reusing past velocities as drafts. We revisit the denoising dynamics of WAMs and identify a dual nonuniformity that breaks standard velocity-reuse assumptions: velocity smoothness is nonuniform as adjacent velocity residuals differ sharply at early and final steps, so reuse there yields large residuals, which nonuniform integration time steps further translate into local state errors that accumulate into the final action distribution. Accordingly, we formalize this by theoretically deriving a trajectory error tolerance bound that characterizes how velocity residuals and integration time steps affect the final action distribution. Based on this, we propose WAMotor, the first speculative inference method tailored to the dual nonuniformity in WAMs. It selects reliable anchor velocities by deferring speculation and employs time-step-aware verification that scales acceptance thresholds by integration time step size. WAMotor offers plug-and-play benefits, enabling seamless integration with prior WAMs. Extensive evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show that WAMotor achieves 2.86$\times$--4.28$\times$ end-to-end speedups while maintaining task success rates. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Overdue-Lin/WAMotor
authors: Zexun Lin, Yuan Feng, Xike Xie
bullets: WAMs incur high latency from multi-step denoising during robotic control.
The method addresses dual nonuniformity: velocity residuals vary sharply across denoising stages, and integration step sizes unevenly amplify state errors.
It derives a trajectory error tolerance bound linking velocity residuals and integration steps to final action-distribution error.
WAMotor selects reliable anchor velocities, delays speculation when needed, and uses integration-step-aware verification thresholds.
Evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show 2.86×–4.28× speedups with maintained success rates.

papers.selection_reason: Speculative inference acceleration for world action models in robotic control, relevant to embodied action models and inference efficiency.
papers.title: WAMotor: Accelerating World Action Models via Speculative Inference under Dual Nonuniform Denoising Dynamics
papers.tldr: WAMotor accelerates world action model inference by adapting speculative denoising to nonuniform velocity changes and integration steps, achieving 2.86×–4.28× end-to-end speedups while maintaining task success rates.

papers.abstract: Visual world models such as DINO-WM and JEPA-WM plan with an optimizer that searches for actions whose predicted outcome has the lowest cost, its distance to a goal image. A plan can thus fail in two ways: the optimizer never tries a good action that the cost would prefer (a search failure), or the cost, computed on predictions, ranks a bad action first (a scoring failure). The two need different remedies, more search or a better model, but a planner does not record which one occurred. We tell them apart by executing the optimizer's candidates, scoring a known solution with the planner's own cost, and comparing costs on predicted and real outcomes. An error model explains when each arises and so how to use retrieved demonstration windows (DemoProp): start the search from them (a warm start) when prediction errors are small, and average them without the model when large errors make the optimizer pick overrated actions. Across four simulated environments and three world models, on short tasks whose goals the planner can represent, PushT and Wall fail mostly by search, while Metaworld and RoboCasa fail by scoring because the cost, sound on real outcomes (AUROC 0.94 on Metaworld), is at chance on predictions (0.54). The diagnosis tells which remedy pays off: a four times larger search lowers the real-outcome cost only where failures come from search (clearly for DINO-WM), and where they come from scoring, averaging the windows without the model solves 127 of 168 new Metaworld tasks, against at most 87 when the model chooses among them. Within PushT, degrading only the model flips which use is better, and our rule, frozen in advance, follows the flip and solves 678 of 960 new episodes, against 530 for the best fixed use.
authors: Haoxuan Jia, Yang Liu, Shang Luo, Chenhao Wu, Zixiang Ni, Yingguang Yang, Feng Zhang, Chongyang Zhang, Hao Zheng, Kefu Xu, Congjing Ran, Jifeng Zhu, Bin Chong
bullets: Planner failures are separated into search failures—good actions are not tried—and scoring failures—predictions rank bad actions as best.
The diagnosis executes candidate actions, evaluates a known solution, and compares costs on predicted versus real outcomes.
DemoProp warm-starts optimization when prediction errors are small, but averages retrieved demonstrations without the model when errors are large.
Across four environments and three world models, PushT and Wall mainly exhibit search failures, while Metaworld and RoboCasa mainly exhibit scoring failures.
Adaptive remedy selection outperforms fixed demonstration use in the reported PushT evaluation, solving 678 of 960 episodes versus 530 for the best fixed strategy.

papers.abstract: A robotic world model should predict how objects evolve under robot actions and physical dynamics. While recent 3D world models have shown strong predictive capabilities, they still struggle with the heterogeneous dynamics arising from diverse object interactions. To address this in a unified framework, we decompose robotic interactions into distinct physical regimes and assign each to a specialized motion expert. We introduce MoRE, a 3D world model with a mixture of motion experts organized around rigid, deformable, and prehensile dynamics. This design enables a single model to capture diverse physical behaviors while preserving regime-specific priors. Trained on mixed simulation and real-world data, MoRE integrates with Model Predictive Control (MPC) to support diverse manipulation tasks. Experiments show that MoRE improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes, leading to stronger real-world MPC performance. Code, data, and project website are available at https://alwaysleepy.github.io/MoRE-WM-site/.
authors: Ziyu Zhu, Shaowei Liu, Albert J. Zhai, Henry Che, Wei-Chiu Ma, Shenlong Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling heterogeneous physical interactions in robotics.
Assigns distinct motion experts to rigid, deformable, and prehensile physical regimes.
Trains on mixed simulation and real-world data and integrates with Model Predictive Control.
Improves prediction accuracy across physics regimes and strengthens real-world MPC performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MoRE. Given the current and historical object states and actions, represented as point clouds, we first encode the scene and actor inputs into point tokens using two encoders. An explicit gating network then selects among specialized motion experts, each tailored to a distinct physical regime, to predict the next object state in 3D. P = prehensile, NP = non-prehensile.

Figure 4: Model Predictive Control (MPC) performance. (a) Box pushing and (b) toy manipulation results. Each section details the prediction error across planning steps (left) and success rate vs. error threshold (right). MoRE achieves lower error and higher success than the baselines.

Figure 3: Qualitative results on DROID evaluation. We compare model predictions with ground truth on challenging DROID scenes with clutter, diverse objects, and partial observations. Even for small, low-resolution manipulated objects, our model produces accurate dynamics, demonstrating robustness to occlusion and noise.

Figure 5: Real world dynamics predictions. We visualize predictions of point motion on real world data. The red points are the end-effector (action) points. The Vanilla model struggles to treat the box as rigid and the toy sloth as soft. In contrast, our model correctly handles the different cases.

Figure 6: Benchmark tasks visualization: Simulation and real-world benchmarks covering rigid and soft objects under non-prehensile and prehensile interactions, designed to evaluate generalization across diverse physical regimes.

Table 2: Dynamic model comparison across interaction types and physics. We report geometric accuracy (MSE, CD) and material structural metrics (rigidity or Laplacian). Privileged experts (gray) are domain-specific and assume known interaction types at test time, while our Mixture-of-Experts model handles diverse interactions in a unified framework with consistently strong performance.
Table 4: Comparison with Point-World on the DROID dataset. Our method performs better across all three cases, showing strong generalization to real-world object dynamics.

Table 5: Gating Network Accuracy. Expert selection accuracy (%) evaluated over 50 random interactions per task category. The gating network maintains consistently high accuracy across diverse regimes, indicating reliable expert routing for different physical dynamics.

Table 3: Ablation of MoRE under different interaction types and physical regimes. papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve vision-language-action (VLA) policies beyond imitation, but humanoid exploration is unsafe and simulator RL can exploit residual sim-to-real gaps. We present WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for post-training a whole-body humanoid VLA in an action-conditioned video world model (WM). Simulated manipulation and locomotion play data improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction. A VLA trained on synthetic demonstrations collects 20 autonomous real robot rollouts per task to align the WM with deployment observations. The VLA, whole-body controller (WBC), and video WM then form a closed-loop RL environment with dense progress rewards. Across three real robot tasks, play data improves every evaluated WM metric and downstream policy success; video WM RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, compared with 48.3% for real robot RL. We therefore leverage the complementary strengths of both environments: simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM offers a deployment-aligned environment for policy improvement. Project website: https://qianzhong-chen.github.io/wevo.github.io/.
authors: Qianzhong Chen, Muyuan Lin, Yuyin Sun, Mac Schwager, Cheng-Hao Kuo, Roberto Mart\'in-Mart\'in

Aligns the world model with deployment observations using 20 autonomous real-robot rollouts per task, without teleoperation.
Forms a closed-loop RL environment from the VLA, whole-body controller, and video world model with dense progress rewards.
Across three real-robot tasks, video-world-model RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, versus 48.3% for real-robot RL.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can propose multi-step manipulation plans, but they have no grounded model of how a scene will change, and the pixel-level world models that could check those plans are slow and drift over long horizons. We present Verify2Act, a modular verification framework that separates semantic action proposal from latent physical verification. A VLM proposes candidate plans, a latent world model (V2A-WM) imagines each of them in the DINOv2 feature space, and a dual-head critic checks the imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before anything is executed. V2A-WM extends recent flow-matching world models with cross-attention action grounding and a causal temporal history window. We deploy the full system on a low-cost robot arm, training the world model and critic only on data generated in a digital twin. Across six language-conditioned tasks, Verify2Act reaches 83.3\% task success, compared with 61.7\% for a latent world model without our architectural changes, 53.3\% for the VLM alone, and 46.7\% for a pixel-diffusion world model. It verified every plan it executed and incurred no planning-induced failures: all of its failed episodes were caused by low-level grasp or placement slips. In simulation, Verify2Act obtains the highest five-task chain success on CALVIN among the compared baselines with 30$\times$ fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification, and the highest success on cluttered nut assembly.
bullets: Addresses the lack of grounded scene-change reasoning in VLM-generated multi-step manipulation plans and the inefficiency and drift of pixel-level world models.
Imagines candidate plans in DINOv2 feature space using a flow-matching world model with action cross-attention and causal temporal history.
A dual-head critic evaluates imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before robot execution.
On six language-conditioned tasks, it achieved 83.3% success, outperforming the reported latent-world-model, VLM-only, and pixel-diffusion baselines.

All executed plans were verified successfully; remaining failures came from low-level grasp or placement slips, while simulation results showed strong CALVIN and cluttered nut-assembly performance with 30× fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Verify2Act overview. Stage 1: a VLM proposes candidate multi-step plans from the camera observation and the language instruction. Stage 2: V2A-WM rolls out each candidate in the frozen DINOv2 latent space (St → St+k), conditioned on CLIP action tokens. Stage 3: a goal head scores the terminal latent state against the goal, and a temporal consistency head checks consecutive imagined states; the best verified plan is executed.

Fig. 4. Results on the robot. (a) Task success per task and averaged over tasks. (b) Outcome of the episodes of each method: success, execution failure (the plan was correct but a skill failed), or planning failure (the executed plan could not satisfy the goal).

Fig. 2. V2A-WM training and inference. Training: the delta encoder gives the target latent zgt = fenc(∆St); we interpolate zτ = τzgt + (1− τ)z0 and the flow-matching transformer, conditioned on past frames and CLIP action tokens through cross-attention, predicts the velocity v̂. Inference: a single Euler step integrates from noise z0 to z1 = z0 + v̂, and the delta decoder reconstructs Ŝt+1 = St + fdec(z1).
Fig. 5. CALVIN. Left: SR5 against reflective VLM calls (log scale). Right: success SRk over the chain length.

papers.abstract: Visual world models enable effective short-horizon goal-conditioned planning, such as reaching nearby targets and pushing objects over short distances, by predicting candidate action outcomes and comparing their representations with a goal representation. However, extending this approach to long-horizon tasks is challenging: prediction errors accumulate over extended rollouts, while latent-space similarity to distant goals provides limited guidance for ranking candidate outcomes. Existing methods address these limitations by introducing intermediate subgoals, either generated by learned models or selected from experience memory. Generated subgoals can contain hallucinations or be inaccurate in aspects such as object positions and timing. Memory-based approaches are constrained by experience coverage and may lack precise guidance for selecting appropriate intermediate states from stored observations. We introduce GEMS, which generates temporally structured subgoals to guide action search and state selection from Latent Experience Memory (LEM). A distance gate determines whether predicted outcomes are evaluated against the generated subgoal or the selected memory state. Experiments across six tasks and task suites spanning manipulation, navigation, and reaching demonstrate the effectiveness of GEMS for long-horizon planning. GEMS outperforms state-of-the-art world-model planning baselines across different manipulation settings, achieving success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World. It improves over the strongest evaluated baseline on these tasks by 24.0, 7.3, and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate that generated subgoals and experience memory can jointly strengthen long-horizon planning with a frozen world model.
authors: Yangchen Zhao, Ali Payani, Caiwen Ding
bullets: Long-horizon planning suffers from compounding prediction errors and weak guidance from distant goal similarity.
GEMS generates structured intermediate subgoals and selects relevant states from Latent Experience Memory (LEM).
A distance gate chooses whether to evaluate predicted outcomes against the generated subgoal or a retrieved memory state.
Across manipulation, navigation, and reaching tasks, GEMS achieves success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World.
The method outperforms evaluated world-model planning baselines, while relying on a frozen world model.

papers.abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.

Ablations show cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision are important for coordination.

papers.title: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation

papers.abstract: We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Coupling a foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a mixture-of-transformers, $Z$-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.
authors: Junjie Ye, Yiqi Zhao, Muchen Xu, Celina Shiyu Wang, Hao Dong, Ruohai Ge, Rong Xue, Benjamin J Kolligs, Aditya Dutt, Sasanka Nagavalli, Nassim A. Samad, Gaurav S. Sukhatme, Jyotirmoy V. Deshmukh, Yue Wang, Yuliang Guo
bullets: Addresses the cost of video-generative world models and the feature-space disconnect in existing latent policies.
Uses a mixture-of-transformers that couples the VLM with foresight and continuous action experts.
Predicts future spatial tokens directly in the VLM’s native visual-token space.
Trained on human videos and robot trajectories, it reports 81.9% success on SIMPLE and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks at 110 ms per chunk.
Also remains competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Z-sight. A foresight expert denoises future spatial tokens against an EMA teacher (Lview). Simultaneously, an action expert generates continuous actions via flow matching (Lflow) while attending to the predicted future features.

Figure 1. Z-sight predicts the future in the policy’s native representation space. Top: Z-sight performs diverse loco-manipulation tasks in a real-world setting. Bottom: comparison of policy designs. (a) Vision-language-action models (VLAs) map the current observation to actions through a VLM and an action expert. (b) World action models (WAMs) build on a pretrained video generator to predict future video alongside actions. (c) Z-sight (ours) co-denoises future spatial tokens and actions in the co-evolving visual space of its own VLM, allowing the action expert to read the forming prediction during generation.

Values are means over three evaluation passes of one checkpoint per method, with error bars showing ± one sample standard deviation across passes (ten episodes per task and level per pass). papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet reconstruction-oriented visual representations do not explicitly emphasize the spatial relationships and object-state changes needed for manipulation. We introduce Phoenix, which learns representations of scene structure for world-action modeling. Specifically, Phoenix Encoder enriches DINOv3's general visual semantics through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. Next, CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses Phoenix Encoder features into generative latents while preserving scene information and spatial layout. Finally, Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions, linking scene evolution with action generation. To study pretraining data efficiency, we curate approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data for representation learning and use the robot demonstration subset for WAM pretraining. Following benchmark-specific post-training, Phoenix achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-robot benchmarks spanning single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous manipulation. It demonstrates strong robustness to perturbations, achieving success rates of 94.8% on LIBERO-Plus and 72.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 C2R, alongside strong cross-embodiment transfer and real-world manipulation performance on Bench2Dex and RoboDojo-RealWorld, respectively. Pretraining-scale analysis shows larger performance gains from data scaling than a video-VAE-only baseline, indicating stronger scaling benefits and more effective data utilization. Moreover, Phoenix maintains high success rates when adapted with limited downstream demonstrations, demonstrating strong few-shot adaptation. Our code, pretraining data, and models are available on the project page to help the community reproduce our results.

Jointly predicts scene-structure latents, appearance latents, and robot actions to model scene evolution and action generation.
Pretrained with approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot-manipulation data; achieves strong results across simulated and real-robot, single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous benchmarks.
Shows robustness to perturbations, improved scaling with more data than a video-VAE-only baseline, cross-embodiment transfer, and effective few-shot adaptation.

papers.abstract: Predicting the consequences of an agent's actions requires modeling both the body's motion and the environment's response. Most video world models attempt to learn both from numerical actions, even though geometry and kinematics already specify the intended motion. We introduce Doppel, an embodiment-agnostic video world model conditioned on camera-aligned renderings of future body configurations and numerical action trajectories. By explicitly providing the intended motion, Doppel can focus on predicting object motion and interaction-driven changes in the environment. Rendered motion also provides a common visual interface across different embodiments and action spaces. To train on robot datasets without camera extrinsics, we recover camera poses and align rendered trajectories with recorded observations. We jointly train a single shared video backbone and conditioning adapter on eight datasets spanning eight robot and human embodiments, from single- and bimanual robot arms to a dexterous humanoid and human hands and bodies, using about 600 hours of video without embodiment labels. Across three robot-arm datasets, Doppel improves PSNR over action-only baselines by 1.00 dB on held-out trajectories and 1.20 dB under out-of-distribution evaluation, while predicting more consistent object motion. Training on all eight embodiments (Doppel-8) improves robot predictions over the three-robot model (Doppel-3) on four of six evaluation sets. Project page: https://doppelwm.github.io/.

Results: Improves PSNR over action-only baselines by 1.00 dB on held-out robot-arm trajectories and 1.20 dB under out-of-distribution evaluation.

papers.abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.

bullets: Addresses rule-state persistence across saving and loading and rule-to-visual realization, including unseen affected objects.
Represents rules, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph linked to video generation and perceptual feedback.
Uses dynamic object binding, state-constrained generation, attribute state replacement, and counterfactual reconstruction training.
Introduces RuleVerse, a rule-driven interaction dataset built from GTA-V and Habitat with detailed state and event annotations.
Experiments show improved consistency of saved/restored rules and accurate realization of rule outcomes on specified objects and attributes.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used in autonomous driving to predict how a scene evolves under the ego vehicle's actions, supporting counterfactual reasoning and model-based planning. However, existing evaluations focus on prediction fidelity and planning performance, and rarely verify that the predictions depend on the conditioning action. In this paper, we study action dependence in action-conditioned semantic forecasting, which predicts future semantic segmentation from past segmentations and the ego action. We compare a forecaster with feature-wise and input-level action conditioning against an identical model without action input, and measure action dependence with test-time action interventions scored by standard segmentation metrics. The evaluation is validated in a synthetic environment with known action-dependent dynamics and applied to Cityscapes and BDD100K, both within each dataset and across the two vehicle platforms. Experiments show that the executed action improves mid-term mIoU by at most 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K, whereas a wrong action reduces it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, below the model without action input. On real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6 times more on the action than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy, whereas both depend on it equally in the synthetic environment, where the history does not determine the action. These results show that an accuracy gain indicates that a driving world model uses its action, but not how strongly its forecasts depend on it. Code is available at https://github.com/binayksingh/does-action-matter.
authors: Binay Kumar Singh, Niels Da Vitoria Lobo
bullets: The study evaluates whether semantic forecasts change appropriately when the ego action is altered.

Correct actions improve mid-term mIoU by up to 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K; incorrect actions reduce it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, respectively.
On real data, feature-wise conditioning is 1.6× more action-dependent than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in world models are opening new possibilities for fine-grained embodied tasks, with hand-object interaction offering a particularly demanding setting. Modeling these interactions involves capturing how hand actions change objects and how the resulting states persist over time. Yet systematic evaluation tailored to these hand-centric capabilities remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce HandWorldBench, a unified benchmark that systematically evaluates hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence. To construct the benchmark, we develop a data curation pipeline that extracts hand-object interaction clips and screens them for quality, yielding 20,500 high-quality egocentric clips from over 600 hours of footage. We then manually select 500 clips covering seven task families for evaluation. Benchmarking eleven models under a unified protocol reveals that stronger hand-pose control does not consistently translate into coherent object-state evolution and persistence or robust cross-embodiment performance, with several specialized hand-control models underperforming general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.

papers.abstract: Deployed world-action models (WAMs) can keep improving only if they make good use of their own experience. Existing methods supply retrieved rollouts or demonstrations to the policy as context, yet such experience often turns previously solved tasks into failures. What, then, makes good experience for a WAM? We show that experience is valuable only in use: its value depends not on whether the source rollout succeeded but on what is stored, when it is used, and where it enters the policy. We therefore propose F$^3$, which makes these three decisions with Form, Fit, and Fusion. Form compresses successful and failed rollouts alike into short, verified operation records; Fit teaches the policy to read a record and to predict when it helps; Fusion injects the record's images, text and actions into the policy as a prefix and an action prior. Trained once on only 200 examples and deployed with a growing experience library, the model achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab without any training on RoboLab: over native Cosmos 3 Nano, it raises success by 12.0 pp and 10.8 pp, reduces steps to success by 12.2% and 11.3%, and cuts regressions by 57%.

Fusion adds records’ images, text, and actions as a prefix and action prior.
Trained on 200 examples, F³ achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab, including gains over native Cosmos 3 Nano and 57% fewer regressions.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces F$^3$ for managing experience in World-Action Models (WAMs), focusing on Form, Fit, and Fusion to improve policy learning and reduce regressions in interactive environments.
papers.title: F$^3$: What Makes Good Experience in World-Action Models?
papers.tldr: F³ improves world-action models by deciding what experience to store, when to use it, and how to inject it into the policy.

papers.abstract: Planning with a visual world model requires deciding both which actions to execute and how long to search for them. We introduce Selective CEM Refinement (SCR), a learned rule for deciding whether to continue cross-entropy method (CEM) search with a frozen LeWorldModel. After five it- erations, the gate measures how far the mean first action chunk has moved, how much the mean terminal cost of elite plans has fallen, and how widely their first chunks vary. It returns the current plan for execution or continues the same search for ten more iterations. The gate requires no addi- tional world-model rollout. On 16 PushT scenes evaluated with two planning seeds, SCR succeeded in 25 of 32 trials, compared with 28 of 32 for fixed 15-iteration search (Fixed-15). All 25 SCR suc- cesses occurred in trials that Fixed-15 also solved, yield- ing 89.29% paired success retention. Across complete episodes, including replanning, SCR evaluated 23.81% fewer candidate plans and reduced mean controller time per eight-environment batch by 17.22%. Its observed suc- cess rate was 5.36 percentage points above an analytic mix- ture of the two fixed-depth controllers at the same expected candidate workload, although the difference changed sign across planning seeds. Compared with gating only at the initial solve under the same random-draw padding proto- col, gating again at replanning produced nine additional early exits. This reduced total candidate evaluations by 15.79%, while successes fell from 27 to 25.
bullets: SCR decides after five CEM iterations whether to execute the current plan or search for ten more.
Its gate uses first-action movement, elite-plan terminal-cost reduction, and first-chunk diversity, requiring no extra world-model rollout.
On 32 PushT trials, SCR solved 25 versus 28 for fixed 15-iteration search, retaining 89.29% of paired successes.
Across episodes, SCR evaluated 23.81% fewer candidate plans and reduced mean controller time by 17.22% per eight-environment batch.
Replanning-time gating produced more early exits and 15.79% fewer evaluations, but reduced successes from 27 to 25.

papers.abstract: Occupancy world models struggle to forecast moving objects due to motion uncertainty and shape distortion. A single trajectory can average plausible futures into an implausible path, and repeated re-voxelization can erode or inflate object shape even under correct motion. We introduce ShoWorld to address these challenges through separate motion and shape representations. The motion forecaster predicts probabilistic trajectories conditioned on scene layout, nearby agents and the future ego trajectory. Each hypothesis is rendered into occupancy and fused according to its probability to retain alternative futures. The shape component predicts sub-voxel points with occupancy probabilities and offsets from local geometry. These points move rigidly with the object, and voxel occupancy follows the probability that at least one occupied point falls within it. This representation reduces shape distortion under motion. ShoWorld achieves state-of-the-art results on Occ3D-nuScenes. With ground-truth occupancy and ego trajectory, it improves mIoU and IoU by 6.56 and 9.16 points overall and by 6.06 and 5.53 points on dynamic classes.
authors: Zhiqiang Yan, Guangfa Wang, Yuan Wu, Jian Yang, Gim Hee Lee
bullets: Addresses motion uncertainty and shape distortion in occupancy world models.
Predicts probabilistic trajectories conditioned on scene context, nearby agents, and future ego motion.
Renders and probability-fuses multiple trajectory hypotheses instead of averaging them into one path.
Models shape with moving sub-voxel points, occupancy probabilities, and geometry offsets to reduce voxelization distortion.
On Occ3D-nuScenes with ground-truth occupancy and ego trajectory, improves overall mIoU and IoU by 6.56 and 9.16 points, respectively; dynamic-class gains are 6.06 and 5.53 points.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained visual world models generate multi-step action plans from current and goal observations, yet terminal-proximity objectives fail to prevent forbidden-zone traversal or rigid-body collision sliding. Purely visual interfaces may lack analytical dynamics, structured states, or explicit collision geometry, requiring internal prediction of action-conditioned process risk. We propose Risk-Triggered Search (RTS) for frozen Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world models. Rather than relying on static state features that cannot distinguish candidate plans sharing an observation, RTS unrolls action-conditioned future latent prefixes in the frozen world model and trains a lightweight risk head with process-violation supervision. To intervene selectively while preserving safe nominal behavior, RTS uses the same predicted prefix-risk criterion as both the search trigger gate and hard feasibility gate: safe nominal plans execute directly, whereas alarms trigger local Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) search to minimize nominal deviation within the feasible set. To prevent isotropic Euclidean minimal modification from shrinking obstacle-directed actions into zero-amplitude stalling, we introduce an amplitude-preserving metric $d_{\mathrm{AP}}$ that retains tangential progression while maintaining a unique zero at the nominal plan. Under unified gating and this unique-zero condition, bypassing safe-state search yields closed-loop trajectories strictly identical to every-step same-kernel search. Evaluated under a process-safety benchmark and Safe Arrival Rate (SAR) metric across five tasks, RTS improves SAR over Direct by 12.67--41.67 percentage points on navigation and articulated control and +2.08/+4.17 pp on Cube/PushT boundary cohorts, maintaining 100% action identity with every-step search while cutting controller time by 17.71%--70.41% across 1,968 paired trajectories.
authors: Xinyu Deng, Bohao Lan, Kunpeng Li, Mingkai Yuan, Weihang Pan, Binbin Lin
bullets: Addresses forbidden-zone traversal and collision sliding in visual world-model planning when explicit dynamics or collision geometry are unavailable.
Unrolls future latent action prefixes in a frozen JEPA world model and trains a lightweight risk head using process-violation supervision.
Uses predicted prefix risk for both search triggering and feasibility gating; risky plans invoke local CEM search, while safe plans execute unchanged.
Introduces an amplitude-preserving deviation metric to retain tangential progress instead of collapsing obstacle-directed actions into stalling.
Across five tasks, improves Safe Arrival Rate by 2.08–41.67 percentage points, matches every-step search action-for-action, and reduces controller time by 17.71%–70.41%.

papers.selection_reason: Integrates a frozen JEPA world model with a risk-triggered search mechanism for safe control, bridging interactive world models and embodied navigation/safe control.
papers.title: Risk-Triggered Search: Behavior-Preserving Safe Control
papers.tldr: Risk-Triggered Search selectively invokes local safety search only when predicted action-conditioned risk is detected, preserving nominal behavior while improving safe task completion and reducing control cost.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models turn user commands into the exploration of a generated scene, which requires the scene to keep its 3D structure as the camera moves and each action to keep a stable effect. Existing benchmarks mostly evaluate these properties against references fitted to the video under test, either a scene reconstructed from its own frames or a camera trajectory aligned to the command path with a free scale. Such references can absorb gradual scene deformation and changes in pace and route length, so these errors can pass undetected. We therefore introduce StrideWorld, a benchmark whose references are fixed before the motion they judge. It evaluates scene rigidity against the ground-truth geometry of the start view, and action consistency against the stride of each action, the camera motion of one command. The stride is measured on the model's first steps and then used to test the steps that follow, so each model is judged only against its own steps. Its measurements are validated on rendered videos with known camera motion, and its scores agree with human judgments. Across \nvideos{} videos generated by \nmodels{} open models from $140$ start views, all models but one deform their scenes as the camera moves, with offsets up to $7.3$ times those of a rigid rendering along the same camera path. Most models keep a steady pace when a single action is held. Along composed routes, several models often stall, and most completed routes end away from the positions predicted by each model's own strides. Only the two models that scale commands by the estimated scene depth bring most routes close to these positions. Fine-tuning two models on a few rendered clips removes most of their mid-route stalls. Code, data, and a leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/chuangwang123/strideworld.
authors: Chuang Wang, Rui Nie, Jie Song, Junyuan Gao, Jiahe Song, Haitao Zhou, Boyu Zhu, Xing Li, Jiang Wu, Conghui He, Qian Yu, Weijia Li
bullets: Existing reference-based evaluations can hide scene deformation, pace changes, and incorrect route lengths.
The benchmark measures rigidity against the start view’s ground-truth geometry and action consistency against each model’s measured initial stride.
Validation on rendered videos and agreement with human judgments support the reliability of its metrics.
Across 140 start views and videos from open models, nearly all models deform scenes; composed routes often stall or end away from stride-predicted positions.
Depth-scaled command control improves route accuracy, while limited fine-tuning reduces mid-route stalls in two models.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for interactive video world models, directly relevant to world models and action-conditioned generation.
papers.title: StrideWorld: Benchmarking Scene Rigidity and Action Consistency in Interactive Video World Model
papers.tldr: StrideWorld benchmarks whether interactive video world models preserve scene geometry and execute actions consistently using fixed, model-specific references that expose deformation and route errors.

papers.abstract: Reliable cellular connectivity and collision-free flight are essential for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operations in low-altitude urban canyons, where dense 3D buildings obstruct flight clearance, shadow serving base stations, and create strong co-channel interference at street intersections. Existing planners either require prior 3D city meshes and channel knowledge maps unavailable onboard, or rely on model-free reinforcement learning with low sample efficiency and poor cross-city generalization. We propose CommDreamer, a mapless radio-geometric world model that fuses raw onboard 3D LiDAR scans, multicell cellular reports, and shift-invariant relative kinematics to jointly infer local obstacle clearance and directional signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) dynamics. Using a categorical recurrent state-space model, CommDreamer compresses multimodal measurement histories into a coordinate-invariant latent belief, enabling the UAV to foresee deep shadow zones and train a lightweight online policy purely via multi-step latent imagination without prior maps or antenna patterns. Zero-shot evaluations across unseen urban morphologies in our open-source ray-tracing simulator, AeroCity-RT, show that CommDreamer converges within 150 episodes where model-free reinforcement learning fails to complete flights, achieving 100.0% mission success with zero collisions while lifting median route SINR to 8.02 dB and cutting effective SINR outage by over 50% relative to radio-blind world-model and reactive LiDAR baselines.
authors: Yuqi Ping, Tianhao Liang, Tingting Zhang
bullets: Targets safe, cellular-connected flight in dense urban canyons without prior 3D maps or channel knowledge.
Fuses multimodal histories with a categorical recurrent state-space model into a coordinate-invariant latent belief.
Trains an online policy through multi-step latent imagination rather than model-free trial and error.
In zero-shot unseen urban morphologies, it achieved 100% mission success with zero collisions and a median route SINR of 8.02 dB.
Reduced effective SINR outage by over 50% versus radio-blind world-model and reactive LiDAR baselines; scope is evaluated in the AeroCity-RT ray-tracing simulator.

papers.selection_reason: Radio-geometric world model for UAV trajectory planning.
papers.title: CommDreamer: Radio-Geometric World Models for Mapless Cellular-Connected UAV Trajectory Planning
papers.tldr: CommDreamer enables mapless UAV trajectory planning by learning a latent world model from onboard LiDAR, cellular reports, and relative motion to jointly anticipate obstacles and radio shadow zones.

papers.abstract: Visual planning with a frozen joint-embedding world model supports robotic reaching and object manipulation by evaluating candidate action sequences against an image goal before execution. Standard cross-entropy method (CEM) planners roll out every candidate independently through a billion-parameter predictor, even when nearby actions induce similar scene changes. This redundant computation grows with population size and search rounds, slowing closed-loop replanning. We observe that candidates within a planning step share an observation history and thus a common action-to-feature map. Based on this insight, we propose ProbeShare, which measures local responses with a few representative probes and reconstructs each candidate's feature grid through scene-conditioned, geometry-aware weighting. When promising candidates move beyond existing probe coverage, ProbeShare evaluates a new probe to rescore nearby candidates. Across four RoboCasa tasks, ProbeShare accelerates episode planning by 43.8--128.9 times over dense RoboJEPA and at least $14.2\times$ over competitive baselines, with greater mean goal progress in a matched-time comparison.
authors: Zejian Kang, Xiantao Lin, Zekai Chen, Boyang Shen, Mingyu Ma, Shengwen Zheng, Chengtai Guo, Xiangru Huang
bullets: Targets redundant computation in CEM planning with frozen, large joint-embedding world models.
Uses a few representative action probes, then reconstructs other candidates’ feature grids with scene-conditioned, geometry-aware weighting.
Adds new probes when promising actions fall outside existing coverage.
Across four RoboCasa tasks, achieves 43.8–128.9× faster episode planning than dense RoboJEPA and at least 14.2× faster than competitive baselines.
Provides greater mean goal progress than dense planning under matched time, with scope limited to the evaluated robotic reaching and manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models let robots imagine the outcomes of their actions for planning and offline policy evaluation, but these uses need many rollouts, which multi-step diffusion makes expensive. Drifting models move the iteration from inference to training and generate samples in one network pass. DriftWorld brought this paradigm to action-conditioned world models; to strengthen action following, it repels predictions from the current frame, a construction borrowed from classifier-free guidance. We show that this accentuation has a target bias: the push persists even when a prediction matches the recorded future, in kernel, balanced, and unbalanced Wasserstein drifting fields alike. We introduce Mass-Share Accentuation (MSA) to remove this bias. MSA treats the current frame as a counterfactual destination competing with the recorded future in a semi-relaxed optimal transport problem; subtracting the closed-form share of the correct future makes the guidance vanish at the target, and the remainder is shared by all predictions. We prove that the recorded future is the unique fixed point along the motion direction for collapsed predictions, and that the guidance fades with prediction error. On Push-T, Robomimic, and BridgeV2, where trained models under-react rather than overshoot, MSA improves action ranking, response slope, and moving-region error over latent-space baselines at no inference cost, though these benchmarks do not isolate bias removal as the cause.
authors: Md Abtahi Majeed Chowdhury, Md Rifat Ur Rahman, Md Sakib Hossain Shovon, Jaesik Choi, Minhyuk Sung
bullets: Drifting world models reduce the cost of multi-step diffusion rollouts but can weaken action following.
Existing repulsive guidance remains active even when predictions match the recorded future, creating target bias.
MSA uses semi-relaxed optimal transport to subtract the correct future’s closed-form mass share, making guidance vanish at the target.
Theory shows the recorded future is the unique fixed point for collapsed predictions and that guidance decreases with prediction error.
On Push-T, Robomimic, and BridgeV2, MSA improves action ranking, response slope, and moving-region error over latent-space baselines.

papers.abstract: Video world models keep the world in the context of a generator, so a revisit is synthesized again and earlier edits can drift or disappear. We present WM^MLLM, the first interactive world model built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), for persistent, editable world generation from a single image. WM^MLLM keeps the world state outside every generator, as a panorama with a revision history, and lets the MLLMs write it: they turn each request into operations on this state, select where a local edit is written, and check every candidate before it becomes the next state. Image generators only propose views, and video only presents them. Users can walk to new places and return, edit objects through text or a box, place subjects, and change lighting, weather or season. By construction, a revisit at the same revision reproduces the earlier view exactly, a local edit leaves every panorama pixel outside its region unchanged, and each request starts from the result of the previous one. Against six world model baselines on MBench-A, WM^MLLM has the highest mean on all four environment-recovery metrics (Epipolar 91.5 versus 0.1 to 74.0) and completes the most camera round trips (85.3% versus at most 50.9%). It has the best value in all 15 CompBench columns against 15 baselines. On 112 local edits judged blind, selecting the region to write after generation raises completion from 34.8% to 83.0%. On 258 WBench and MBench-A items, all 46 revisits recover their earlier views, and all 97 local edits that pass the check leave panorama pixels outside their region unchanged.
authors: Baiang Li, Enze Xie, Jincheng Yu, Jin Wang, Haozhe Liu, Yitong Li, Juanxi Tian, Felix Heide
bullets: Maintains world state outside the generator as a panorama with revision history, preventing revisit drift and preserving prior edits.
Uses MLLMs to translate requests into state operations, select edit regions, and validate generated candidates before updating the world.
Supports navigation, text- or box-based object edits, subject placement, and changes to lighting, weather, and season.
Reports the strongest results across stated environment-recovery and editing benchmarks, including consistent revisits and region-preserving edits.
Scope is single-image initialization with generated views serving presentation rather than state storage.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) connect future scene prediction with action planning for autonomous driving. Each driving record pairs an executed ego trajectory with its observed future, providing a factual outcome for learning this connection. We present TrajWAM, a trajectory-conditioned WAM that improves vision-language driving through auxiliary bird's-eye-view (BEV) future learning. An ego-trajectory query conditions DINOv3-aligned BEV predictions from shared planner representations. Training combines factual reconstruction under the executed trajectory with one-sided feature separation under an unlabeled perturbed trajectory. Together, these objectives train the shared planner to generate driving waypoints. Native inference directly generates waypoints and bypasses the auxiliary future-prediction branch. On all 220 Bench2Drive routes, TrajWAM achieves 91.53 Driving Score and 75.45% Success Rate, exceeding a schedule-matched planning-only fine-tuning baseline by 5.31 Driving Score points and eight successful routes.
authors: Xuerui Fang, Gulimila Kezierbieke, Chen Wangxing, Hui Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting future scene prediction with action planning in autonomous driving.
Uses an ego-trajectory query to condition DINOv3-aligned BEV future predictions from shared planner representations.

At inference, directly generates waypoints without running the auxiliary future-prediction branch.
On 220 Bench2Drive routes, achieves 91.53 Driving Score and 75.45% Success Rate, outperforming a schedule-matched planning-only baseline.

papers.abstract: World models support autonomous driving by evaluating candidate trajectories through predicted future scene evolution. However, accurate future prediction does not ensure road-compliant execution; when all candidates violate road boundaries, re-ranking cannot select a feasible trajectory. We propose Physics-Guided Search Distillation (PGSD), a single-view planning framework that combines future representations and execution feedback for verified beyond-pool repair through three components: (1) Execution-Aware Selection checks ego-vehicle road compliance under simulated execution and selects the highest-scoring feasible trajectory; (2) a Clearance-Aware Search Teacher generates beyond-pool corrections and selects demonstrations with larger minimum road-boundary clearance during execution to buffer imitation errors; and (3) a Future-Conditioned Repair Student predicts one correction from rewarder features and execution feedback for single-rollout verification. The pretrained planner and rewarder remain frozen; no future scenes are generated online. On NAVSIM v1, single-view PGSD achieves 90.97 PDMS, exceeding all compared prior single-view planners and retaining 73.2% of the search teacher's PDMS gain over execution-aware selection. On NAVSIM v2 navhard, it reaches 38.96 EPDMS, improving on WorldDrive by 11.24 points (40.5%). The student replaces up to ten search rollouts with a single verification rollout per repair trigger. HUGSIM Hard examples provide qualitative evidence of zero-shot transfer.

Achieves 90.97 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 38.96 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navhard, with reported gains over prior methods.
Replaces up to ten search rollouts with one verification rollout per repair trigger; qualitative HUGSIM Hard results suggest zero-shot transfer.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon tasks in embodied and web environments involve extended decision sequences and delayed feedback, making accurate planning crucial for success. World models tackle this by learning latent dynamics for imagination-based planning. However, existing approaches merely rely on dense pixel-level observations, which forces the model to absorb redundant information while overlooking relations among task-relevant entities. Consequently, small errors may accumulate over long imagined rollouts and gradually corrupt the predictions. In this paper, we explore world models that imagine over sparse state abstractions, which poses two key challenges: 1) how to remove redundant information and form a compact state abstraction; 2) how to incorporate the relational structure to learn reliable long-horizon dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose Embodied Graph, a relational state abstraction that supports structured dynamics modeling and long-horizon imagination, and the Relational World Model (RWM), which performs imagination directly over graph states. RWM consists of (i) a Task-Aware Embodied Graph Constructor that filters redundant details and maintains graph memory through online updates, and (ii) an Embodied Graph Recurrent State Space Model that learns node-wise latent dynamics while capturing inter-node dependencies. The imagined graph states provide predictions of action consequences to guide decision-making. Experiments on Minecraft and Crafter demonstrate the effectiveness of RWM in embodied environments. Notably, in Minecraft, RWM is the only method that obtains diamonds within the given budget. Experiments on web interaction further illustrate the applicability of relational state prediction to the decision making process of web agents.
authors: Zongyuan Wu, Xin Wang, Tongtong Feng, Yuan Meng, Zeyang Zhang, Ling Feng, Wenwu Zhu
bullets: Addresses redundant visual information and error accumulation in long-horizon world-model rollouts.
Builds compact, task-aware graph abstractions with online graph-memory updates.
Uses a recurrent state-space model to learn node-wise dynamics and inter-node dependencies.
Experiments on Minecraft, Crafter, and web interaction demonstrate effective relational imagination; in Minecraft, it is the only evaluated method reported to obtain diamonds within the budget.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall framework of RWM. papers.title: Embodied Graph: A Relational World Model for Long-Horizon Tasks
papers.tldr: Embodied Graph improves long-horizon planning by modeling task-relevant entities and their relations as graph states rather than dense pixels.

papers.abstract: In human-robot collaboration, natural language lets people direct a humanoid's whole-body movements without programming joint trajectories. A common approach generates a kinematic reference from an instruction and relies on a tracking controller to execute it. However, as the controller maintains balance under contact constraints, the executed motion can depart from the reference in ways that change the action it conveys. Our central insight is that semantic alignment must be evaluated directly on the complete motion the robot physically executes. Building on this insight, we introduce \textbf{SemPhys}, a framework that trains motion generators using semantic feedback from simulated executions. A differentiable world model and a fixed tracking controller predict a short segment of a recorded execution. SemPhys inserts this prediction at its original position, scores the complete trajectory against the instruction, and backpropagates through the predicted segment. A paired anchoring loss stabilizes adaptation by keeping each generated reference close to its counterpart from the initial generator. On BONES-SEED, SemPhys largely preserves instruction retrieval accuracy from reference to execution and achieves the highest retrieval accuracy on executed motions among the evaluated methods.
authors: Zejian Kang, Yeqiang Wang, Zekai Chen, Boyang Shen, Mingyu Ma, Bingqian Wu, Fan Zhou, Jianjie Zhang, Chentao Shen, Wentao Yang, Rui Qian, Xiangru Huang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between language-conditioned reference motions and controller-executed motions under balance and contact constraints.
Uses a differentiable world model with a fixed tracking controller to predict execution segments and assess the complete resulting trajectory against the instruction.
Backpropagates semantic feedback through inserted predicted segments to adapt the motion generator.
Adds an anchoring loss to keep adapted references close to those from the initial generator.
On BONES-SEED, it largely preserves reference-to-execution instruction retrieval accuracy and achieves the highest executed-motion retrieval accuracy among evaluated methods.

papers.tldr: SemPhys trains humanoid motion generators against the semantics of physically executed motions, not just planned references, using differentiable simulated feedback.

papers.abstract: Predictive world models for language-guided robot control face a fundamental conditioning challenge: instructions should influence action selection without altering the predicted consequences of fixed actions under identical observations. To address this challenge, we introduce JEPA Dots (Dynamics-Oriented Task Separation), a compact dual-latent framework that jointly learns visual dynamics and language-guided control through separate dynamics and task representations. Language-conditioned task features guide a flow-matching policy, while masked attention restricts world prediction to instruction-independent dynamics history and supplied actions. In closed-loop evaluation on 40 trained LIBERO tasks, JEPA Dots achieves 84.9% overall success with approximately 39.1M parameters, compared with the published 78.7% of NanoVLA-S with 161.0M parameters under a different evaluation protocol. In the reference experiment, JEPA Dots also improves overall success from 76.0% for our task-ID-conditioned adaptation baseline to 84.9%, with LIBERO-Goal success increasing from 67.1% to 88.5%. Instruction-switching experiments further confirm that task representations and policy outputs respond to language changes, while dynamics representations and world predictions remain invariant under fixed observations and supplied actions.
authors: Xianhao Pan, Chi Li, Hanchao Li, Yunxin Liu, Jiankai Sun, Luhui Hu
bullets: Addresses the conflict between language-conditioned control and instruction-independent world dynamics.
Uses dual latent representations: language-conditioned task features guide a flow-matching policy, while masked attention predicts dynamics from observation history and actions.
On 40 trained LIBERO tasks, achieves 84.9% overall success with approximately 39.1M parameters.
Outperforms the authors’ task-ID-conditioned baseline, improving overall success from 76.0% to 84.9% and LIBERO-Goal success from 67.1% to 88.5%.
Instruction-switching tests show task and policy outputs change with language, while dynamics representations and predictions remain invariant under fixed observations and actions.

papers.abstract: Driving scenes keep changing during model computation, making both observation freshness and action-delivery time central to world-action planning. To retain rich generative world priors in autonomous driving without stalling real-time control, we present SWIFT (Slow World, Instant Freshness, and Timely action), a deployment-oriented asynchronous world-action system that moves world updates off the observation-to-action critical path. On a background GPU, a slow Video DiT streams surround-view history into read-only predictive world context, trained with a predictive span that covers both the update interval and background world computation. On a foreground GPU, a lightweight freshness carrier encodes current surround-view images into a gated key/value bank at every step, letting a fast Action DiT combine live visual feedback with the latest completed world context without waiting. On open-loop NAVSIM, SWIFT reaches 94.2 PDMS at 198.4 ms per decision with a trajectory scorer; on closed-loop Bench2Drive, it achieves an 80.30 Driving Score at 109.9 ms foreground latency. SWIFT further transfers to the Waymo E2E hidden test (8.0050 Rater Feedback Score) and nuScenes (0.54 m mean endpoint error, 0.03% mean collision rate). Across all four benchmarks, SWIFT achieves the best results among compared world-action methods, establishing a favorable accuracy-latency trade-off.
authors: Jiazhe Wang, Tianyi Yang, Ruihang Li, Fan Lu, Xianming Zeng, Jianyun Xu, Xingliang Liu, Lei Yang
bullets: Addresses stale observations and action delays caused by changing driving scenes during model computation.
Runs a Video DiT world model asynchronously on a background GPU to stream predictive surround-view context.
Uses a lightweight freshness carrier and gated key/value bank on a foreground GPU for current visual feedback.
A fast Action DiT combines fresh observations with the latest completed world context without waiting for updates.
Reports strong accuracy-latency results across NAVSIM, Bench2Drive, Waymo E2E, and nuScenes benchmarks.

papers.abstract: General robot manipulation requires both semantic competence and physical foresight. World action models (WAMs) acquire an understanding of and predictive capability over the physical world by jointly modeling visual foresight and action distributions. However, existing WAMs still lack semantic competence: they have limited ability to perform open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. Although vision-language models (VLMs) provide these capabilities, effectively integrating their semantic priors into WAM prediction and control remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose CoT-WAM, a jointly trained WAM-VLM framework. CoT-WAM uses a learnable embedding to exchange information between the VLM and the WAM, which is supervised by textual and goal-image signals during training to encode rich intent information. A tailored two-stage training strategy enables joint optimization and more effective collaboration between the VLM and WAM. We evaluate CoT-WAM on six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. CoT-WAM achieves SOTA performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, and demonstrates stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning. On RoboCasa365, it further improves long-horizon planning over baselines with and without external planners. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in practical deployments.
authors: Jinhao Zhang, Yushen Zuo, Ke Rui, Weitao Zhou, Haibao Yu, Honglong Tian, Xiaoheng Ma, Jie Mei, Jiawei Wang, Minglei Li
bullets: Addresses WAMs’ limited open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning.
Uses a learnable embedding to exchange intent information between the VLM and WAM, supervised by text and goal images.
Introduces a two-stage training strategy for effective joint optimization and collaboration.
Reports leading performance across LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro, and improved long-horizon planning on RoboCasa365.
Real-world experiments support the method’s practical effectiveness.

papers.abstract: A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model's own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramer-Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. Self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the harder Cube task, levels with an oracle that is told the true shift at the same block, better than five common test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92-94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift. The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.
authors: Siqing Li, Luming Yang, Yijia Jiao, Junze Deng, Alper Yilmaz
bullets: Addresses the inability of frozen planners to notice when executed actions differ from commands.
Runs the world model in reverse to score hypothesized actuation shifts against actual observations.
The shift-specific score separates actuator shifts from the model’s intrinsic prediction error and supports locally optimal detection, estimation, and source identification.
Self-correction improves success on PushT and Cube tasks and reduces real-robot reach error from 36 mm to 3–5 mm.
Scope: evaluation covers simulated manipulation tasks and a real robotic arm with sealed or unknown action shifts.

papers.title: How Uncertain Is My Action? Self-Correcting Visual Planning with Frozen World Models
papers.tldr: A frozen visual world model can detect, estimate, and correct action-execution errors by comparing observed outcomes with shift-conditioned predictions.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.
bullets: Pixel-level future generation contains many visually plausible but planning-irrelevant details.
The model represents each surrounding agent with discrete tokens encoding identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context.
Agent tokens are learned through geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning.
Open- and closed-loop experiments across diverse driving scenarios show stronger planning, better use of visual and dynamic information, and interpretable world states.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of AgentWorld. Given multi-view observations, ego-status, navigation goals, and language prompts, AgentWorld constructs an agent-centric world state by grounding discrete agent tokens with 4D geometry and 2D visual features through multimodal routed anchoring. The grounded agent tokens are then used by the policy model for reasoning, action, and planning through grounding, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning stages.
Figure 4: The pipeline of the multimodal routed anchoring. Agent queries are routed to geometry and vision branches, and fused through cross-attention to produce grounded agent tokens.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison between VLA-World [30] and AgentWorld. For each scene, the left panels visualize the future ego trajectories of VLA-World (top) and AgentWorld (bottom), with AgentWorld additionally showing the traffic participants aligned with the special tokens ⟨agent_i⟩. The right panels present the corresponding perception, reasoning, and planning results.

Figure 1: (a) VLA models output actions from observations and prompts, lacking explicit spatiotemporal modeling and interaction awareness. (b) World models learn predictive latent futures, yet their imagined states fail to align with causal reasoning. (c) VLA World models integrate imagination and language reasoning, but reason over generated frames rather than interactive agents for driving decisions. (d) By contrast, AgentWorld models futures via discrete latent agent states, enabling VLA reasoning over physically grounded 3D geometry, motion dynamics and agent interactions.
Figure 2: Visual grounding results (UniAD metric) and token efficiency of VLA models.
Figure 8: Prompt design for reasoning with agent data generation.
Figure 6: Ablation studies on agent-centric world states. (a) Perception and (b) planning performance with varying numbers of agent tokens. (c) Performance comparisons of w/ and w/o ego-status.

Figure 11: Visualization of trajectories across VLA-World and our AgentWorld on the nuScenes validation dataset. The predicted and ground-truth trajectories are depicted in red and green, respectively.

Figure 7: Example of the Stage-1 agent grounding QA template. Given multi-view driving observations and a grounding instruction, AgentWorld outputs a fixed set of <agent_i> tokens inside the <perception> field. These tokens act as latent agent slots: active slots are supervised to align with physical traffic participants through 3D box and future trajectory targets, while unused slots are trained as no-object.

Figure 9: Example of the Stage-2 reasoning-oriented SFT template. Given multi-view driving observations, ego-state instructions, and the fixed <agent_i> slots in the <perception> field, AgentWorld learns to generate a structured response consisting of concise agent-grounded reasoning in <think>, a high-level driving command in <action>, and future ego waypoints in <answer>. The rationale explicitly references decision-relevant agent tokens, encouraging the policy to plan based on surrounding-agent interactions rather than shortcut cues.

papers.abstract: Goal-conditioned planning with image observations and goals requires predictions that distinguish visual states and action consequences. Spiking neural networks offer sparse computation, but single-step spikes can obscure motion cues and merge actions with different physical outcomes. We propose the Spiking Latent World Model (SpikWM), an end-to-end joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) with one simulation step per image and one neural update per latent position. Spiking Regional Encoding retains spatial cues through regional pooling. Bi-Spike Action Encoding combines positive and negative binary responses, while Causal Membrane Prediction carries subthreshold evidence across the latent history with learned group-wise time constants. The encoder and predictor are trained jointly on reward-free image--action trajectories using next-embedding prediction and SIGReg. With a common planner, SpikWM achieves mean success rates of $88.67\%$, $97.33\%$, $99.33\%$, and $86.67\%$ on Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube, respectively, outperforming two spiking baselines. Push-T ablations support each module, and controlled replays examine responses to appearance and physical state changes. Under a matched planning budget, SpikWM reduces estimated arithmetic energy by $75.6\%$ relative to LeWM. Code will be released at https://github.com/ShawnYE618/SpikWM.
authors: Shuhan Ye, Hongbin Yu, Chong Wang, Hui Lu, Jiaming He, Yi Yu, Jiangbo Qian, Xudong Jiang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting visually distinct states and differing physical outcomes from image–action sequences.
Uses a joint-embedding predictive architecture with regional spatial encoding, bidirectional spike action encoding, and causal membrane memory.
Trains end-to-end on reward-free image–action trajectories using next-embedding prediction and SIGReg.
With a common planner, reports 86.67%–99.33% mean success across four benchmarks and outperforms two spiking baselines.
Reduces estimated arithmetic energy by 75.6% versus LeWM under a matched planning budget.

papers.abstract: Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned approximately 200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). ProForcing first trains a causal predictor and distills it into a four-step renderer using histories derived from training videos. Training then shifts to continuous self-generated rollouts. A pipelined serving stack supports efficient streaming inference. Experiments show versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts that preserve scene and subject appearance.
