papers.abstract: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both the worlds agents interact with and the tasks they must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a scalable benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation. World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, interaction constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components, which are composed into interactive worlds with explicit states, actions, and temporal dynamics. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis, allowing new capabilities to enter evaluation through a shared construction pipeline. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone domains with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. The stateful design enables task validation and agent evaluation through state correctness and tool-call traces. We evaluate seven models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 68.2% Pass@1. Error analysis reveals challenges in answer delivery, feasibility diagnosis, and temporal coordination. Construction experiments demonstrate scalability across domains and token efficiency: world distillation reduces token consumption by 0.9-66.0% and 46.2-92.5% relative to Codex with low and xhigh reasoning effort, respectively, while achieving broader capability coverage. SynthDCB makes executable world construction the basis of scalable device-control benchmarking, connecting an expanding space of capabilities and interactions to verifiable agent evaluation.

papers.abstract: Plan-conditioned driving world models are used to compare candidate plans, so their forecast should change with the plan as the real scene would, yet widely used control metrics check only whether the camera follows the command. Recorded drives already contain real outcomes of plans that were never driven: retiming a log gives pose-matched images and LiDAR for other speeds, and a stereo rig records a laterally shifted view. Against these references, released world models move their camera but barely move the scene: their scene response, the share of the real change in distance that the forecast reproduces, reaches at most about a third of real video's, and the trajectory score cannot tell an executed speed command from an ignored one. Interventions inside the generator trace the failure to the plan's channel. The forecast geometry follows the context frames; once they carry the planned geometry, plan tokens add little. ReTime-Compose therefore delivers the plan as geometry, without training. It transports the frames of one logged-speed rollout to the planned cameras, and the frozen model completes only what no frame covers. Frozen generators then follow a 0.54 m lateral shift nearly as the real scene does on KITTI, nuScenes and Argoverse 2, and respond more than re-sampling to slow-down plans in three generators and to speed-up plans in two.
bullets: Existing control metrics can miss whether a forecast reflects the planned scene dynamics.
Retimed driving logs and laterally shifted stereo views provide pose-matched references for evaluating scene changes.
Released models reproduce at most about one-third of the real video’s scene response, and trajectory scores may not distinguish obeyed from ignored speed commands.
ReTime-Compose transports logged frames to the planned camera geometry and lets a frozen model generate only uncovered content.
It closely matches real responses to a 0.54 m lateral shift across KITTI, nuScenes, and Argoverse 2, and improves speed-plan responses across multiple generators.

papers.abstract: Direct image-to-video diffusion models entangle pixel synthesis with implicit latent motion, precluding persistent 3D mechanical equilibrium, mid-rollout intervention, and counterfactual force control. Conversely, single-pass programmatic 3D reconstruction from an uncalibrated photograph leaves monocular depth and support clearance underconstrained, causing reconstructed scenes to interpenetrate or collapse under gravity. We present TelePhysica, a closed-loop framework that reconstructs an executable, multi-regime physical world from a single photograph to drive stateful 3D interaction and trajectory-grounded video synthesis. A vision-language coding agent synthesizes separable visual meshes and declarative physical models within a two-stage verification loop that pairs pixel-aligned silhouette critique with a zero-force gravitational equilibrium preflight. The verified world compiles into a unified solver coupling rigid bodies, articulated chains, co-dimensional cloth shells, and 3D tetrahedral elastodynamics, whose simulated rollouts condition pretrained video diffusion models through pixel-aligned structural streams. On a 100-scene single-image benchmark, closed-loop execution raises equilibrium-verified world recovery from $0\%$ in single-pass synthesis to $81\%$. Controlled constitutive ablations show over an order-of-magnitude larger localized corner displacement and out-of-plane pleating in finite-element cloth than in matched rigid-plate proxies. Conditioning video diffusion on simulated trajectories increases dynamic motion-mask overlap by $2{\times}\text{--}5{\times}$ and preserves motion direction under counterfactual force reversals where direct image-to-video models fail.
authors: Ruiqi Shu, Xufeng Zhan, Yuanzhi Liang, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses image-to-video models’ lack of persistent 3D mechanics and single-pass reconstruction failures such as interpenetration or collapse.
Uses a vision-language coding agent with silhouette critique and zero-force gravitational preflight to build verified visual meshes and physical models.
Compiles scenes into a solver supporting rigid bodies, articulated chains, cloth shells, and tetrahedral elastodynamics.
On a 100-scene benchmark, equilibrium-verified recovery improves from 0% with single-pass synthesis to 81% with closed-loop execution.

Simulated trajectory conditioning improves dynamic motion-mask overlap by 2–5× and preserves motion direction under reversed forces; finite-element cloth exhibits stronger deformation than rigid proxies.

papers.abstract: Joint world action models (WAMs) generate future actions and states together, modeling world-action trajectories rather than actions alone. However, trajectory imitation does not ensure that these trajectories are task-effective or consistent with dynamics. We present \textbf{world action trajectory optimization (WATO)}, which optimizes generated actions and future states jointly for control. WATO uses both as references in a dynamics-constrained trajectory optimization problem and differentiates the task loss through the optimized trajectory to train the generator. This makes generated trajectories task-aware and dynamics-consistent while using trajectory optimization only during training. At deployment, WATO directly generates candidate trajectories and ranks them with a world model, without iterative trajectory optimization. Across $7$ visual control environments, WATO improves average success from $79.9\%$ for the imitation joint WAM to $91.7\%$, outperforming strong model-based, goal-conditioned RL, and generative control baselines. Compared with cross-entropy method (CEM), WATO is on average $11.5\times$ faster and uses $600.5\times$ fewer world model evaluations at deployment.
bullets: Joint world-action models generate future actions and states, but imitation alone may yield ineffective or dynamically inconsistent trajectories.
WATO jointly optimizes generated actions and states using task loss and dynamics constraints during training.

At deployment, it directly generates candidate trajectories and ranks them with a world model, without iterative optimization.
Across 7 visual control environments, WATO raises average success from 79.9% to 91.7% and is faster and more evaluation-efficient than CEM.

papers.abstract: Imitation policies can perform complex manipulation, yet small execution errors can accumulate and cause failure. Refinement can correct these errors, but existing approaches often require additional on-policy learning or costly online planning. Our key insight is that a pretrained policy already supplies a useful nominal behavior: refinement can focus on predicting how small action corrections change its outcome. We therefore learn this local response in a form that is cheap to optimize. Our \textit{action-affine world model} (A\textsuperscript{2}WM) learns local action sensitivities offline from action-perturbed policy rollouts. Given interaction history and a policy proposal, it predicts task-relevant geometry as a nominal trajectory plus a linear response to corrections. It predicts the full planning horizon directly, avoiding the propagation of intermediate errors through recursive model evaluations. Quadratic penalties on predicted task errors and linear correction constraints then yield a cheap convex quadratic program (QP). Online refinement requires one model evaluation and one QP solve, while both policy and model weights remain frozen. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, our framework achieves the highest success rate among evaluated baselines, adding only 3.8 ms of mean refinement overhead per control step, excluding base-policy sampling.
bullets: Addresses execution errors that accumulate in imitation-based manipulation.
Learns local action sensitivities offline from action-perturbed policy rollouts.
Predicts full-horizon task geometry as nominal behavior plus linear action corrections.
Performs refinement with one model evaluation and one QP solve while keeping policy and model weights frozen.
Achieves the highest success rate among evaluated baselines across four simulated tasks, with 3.8 ms mean overhead per control step excluding policy sampling.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of fast inference-time policy refinement. A frozen base policy generates action proposals every K control steps. At each control step, the action-affine world model uses interaction history and the current proposal to predict a nominal trajectory Z̄ and a causal action-response matrix F , yielding the direct multi-step prediction Ẑ = F∆A+ Z̄. With F and Z̄ fixed, quadratic task costs and linear correction bounds define a convex QP over ∆A. The first optimized correction is applied to the base action, and refinement repeats after the next observation. Both the base policy and world model remain frozen during deployment.

Fig. 1. (a) Success rate comparison across four simulated manipulation tasks. Our method achieves the highest observed success rate on each task among the evaluated refinement methods, tying GPC-OPT on PushT. (b) Success–latency trade-off. Our method achieves the highest taskaveraged success rate with only a modest increase in mean per-control-step inference time over the frozen diffusion policy (DP). Inference time includes both policy sampling and online refinement. GPC-QP is our baseline that linearizes the GPC world model around the action proposal via its Jacobian and solves a quadratic program for refinement.

Fig. 5. Breakdown of online refinement latency. Times are amortized per control step and averaged equally across the four tasks, excluding simulation and each method’s base-policy sampling time. For GPC-RANK, we instead subtract our method’s single-proposal sampling time, retaining excess candidate-sampling cost as Extra DP. Model Computation includes Jacobian evaluation for GPC-QP; Optimization includes scoring, gradientbased refinement, and QP processing; Other covers remaining overhead.

papers.abstract: Recent video world models have witnessed the paradigm shift from single-agent to multi-agent involvements, which can reveal more complicated dynamics and cross-agent interaction in the real world. However, existing approaches commonly adopt implicit inter-agent communications via cross attention, which lack explicit geometry constraints and unified 3D state, thereby leading to poor multi-view consistency and struggling with recovering out-of-sight agents. In addition, most of them assume a static background, failing to represent uncontrolled background dynamics. To address these problems, we propose Artemis: a geometry-grounded multi-agent world model with explicit memory sharing. An explicit 3D world map is reconstructed from multi-agent observations to enforce a unified 3D state across agents, offering high cross-view consistency. Specifically, an action-guided geometric injection module is developed to simultaneously render decomposed foreground-background control maps, which are then injected into a diffusion transformer through a designed GeoAdapter block. Compared to previous methods assuming static-only background, our GeoAdapter can also distinguish uncontrolled non-agent dynamics, which are conditioned on their own multi-frame history positions to provide consistent motion cues. Keyframes selected from progressive video rollouts are used to progressively update the reconstructed 3D world maps. To effectively capture complex dynamic patterns, we curate a novel dataset sampled from the CARLA simulator called MA-CARLA. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method in terms of visual fidelity and cross-view consistency in the generated videos. In addition, our Artemis can support simultaneous multi-modal rollouts with both 2D video and 3D point map maintenance, scale to scenarios beyond two agents and multi-camera setting.
bullets: Addresses poor cross-view consistency, out-of-sight agent recovery, and static-background assumptions in prior multi-agent world models.
Reconstructs an explicit 3D world map from multi-agent observations to enforce a unified geometric state.
Uses an action-guided GeoAdapter to inject decomposed foreground–background control maps into a diffusion transformer.
Models uncontrolled background dynamics using their own multi-frame position histories, while keyframes progressively update the 3D map.
Introduces the MA-CARLA dataset; experiments report improved visual fidelity and cross-view consistency, with support for multi-modal 2D video/3D point-map rollouts and more than two agents.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based world models can generate and predict trajectories in high-dimensional dynamical systems, but predictive accuracy does not imply that their latent coordinates recover the underlying state variables or causal interactions. We ask whether a frozen pretrained diffusion model can be equipped with identifiable coordinates without retraining its generative backbone. We show that auxiliary-variable nonlinear ICA guarantees can be transferred to Contrastive Diffusion Alignment (ConDA), which learns only a lightweight alignment map on top of frozen diffusion latents. Under standard TCL/GCL assumptions, the aligned representation identifies latent dynamical states up to permutation and componentwise invertible transformations, preserves the latent dynamic structural causal model, and reduces lagged graph recovery to transition-Jacobian sparsity. We evaluate TCL-, GCL-, and CEBRA-based ConDA against TDRL, CaRiNG, IDOL, temporal SuaVE, and iVAE across physical and robotic video systems. TCL and GCL achieve near-perfect blockwise state recovery and competitive lagged graph recovery, including exact recovery in a simulated falling-body system. In a simulated bipedal robot, learned dynamics recover the sign and temporal structure of responses to held-out control perturbations. These results show that a frozen generative diffusion model can be equipped with coordinates that are identifiable, structurally interpretable, and useful for analyzing intervention-relevant dynamics.
bullets: Addresses the gap between accurate trajectory prediction and recovery of true latent state variables or causal structure.
Applies auxiliary-variable nonlinear ICA guarantees to Contrastive Diffusion Alignment (ConDA) without retraining the diffusion backbone.
Under TCL/GCL assumptions, states are identified up to permutation and componentwise invertible transformations, while latent structural dynamics are preserved.
Experiments on physical and robotic video systems show near-perfect blockwise state recovery, competitive lagged graph recovery, and exact recovery in a simulated falling-body system.
Control-perturbation tests in a simulated bipedal robot recover the sign and temporal structure of held-out responses.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed framework. (a) A frozen pretrained diffusion model serves as a generative world model: it embeds video frames yt into diffusion latents xt by inversion (solid arrows) and decodes latents back into frames (dashed arrows). The latents are in turn generated by a lagged dynamic SCM over the latent state st, driven by inputs ut and independent noise, through xt = g(st). (b) TCL- or GCL-based ConDA trains only a lightweight map h, using temporal or auxiliary information, to obtain zt = h(xt). Under nonlinear ICA assumptions, zt identifies st up to permutation and componentwise invertible transformations, and can be lifted back to xt for generation. (c) Lagged causal structure is characterized theoretically by inverse transition-noise Jacobian sparsity and estimated empirically from states aligned from zt. Dynamics learned in these coordinates are validated by predicting responses to held-out control perturbations.

Figure 2: Recovered lag-1 dynamics graphs across datasets and methods. Binary adjacency matrices are shown for IDOL, CaRiNG, TDRL, temporal SuaVE, iVAE, ConDA-CEBRA, ConDATCL, ConDA-GCL, and the true-state reference. Blue entries indicate recovered edges and gray entries indicate absent edges. Rows correspond to the different dynamical systems considered in the study. The ConDA variants more closely reproduce the sparsity structure of the true-state dynamics, with TCL and GCL showing particularly strong agreement across settings.

papers.abstract: Model-based planners that roll out imagined futures assume the transition model faithfully propagates task-relevant signals---a property rarely measured directly. In a single-seed case study of a Recurrent State Space Model world model with active-inference planning in the CARLA driving simulator, we identify a \textbf{posterior-prior gap}---posterior (observation-filtered) states retain obstacle information that imagined rollout states progressively lose: a supervised obstacle probe achieves AUC 0.85 on posterior states, but the same probe applied to imagined prior states shows monotonic decay (AUC 0.85$\rightarrow$0.71 over 15 steps; logit separation drops 57\%). Because the probe is identical, the decay isolates the transition model---not the representation---as the information bottleneck. Obstacle avoidance drops to 0\% without privileged runtime coordinates, and the planner's own ensemble-based epistemic term does not flag the loss---ensemble disagreement yields AUC 0.52 as an obstacle classifier (chance level), making the failure an unflagged imagination failure---an unknown unknown at planning time. As a secondary contribution, we show that \textbf{task-conditioned weighting of Effective Free Energy components} over the same world model yields lane keeping ($81.2 \pm 1.8$\% route completion) and obstacle avoidance (28/28 avoided, \emph{using privileged coordinates}) in the CARLA simulator, with runtime weight modulation enabling post-evasion centering.
bullets: Posterior states preserve obstacle signals (probe AUC 0.85), while imagined priors decline from AUC 0.85 to 0.71 over 15 steps.
Using the same probe isolates the transition model—not the state representation—as the information bottleneck.
Obstacle avoidance falls to 0% without privileged runtime coordinates, and ensemble disagreement fails to detect the loss (AUC 0.52).
Task-conditioned Effective Free Energy weighting supports 81.2 ± 1.8% route completion and avoids 28/28 obstacles when privileged coordinates are available.
Findings come from a single-seed CARLA case study and may not generalize beyond this setting.

papers.abstract: Endovascular catheter navigation relies on continuous fluoroscopy, exposing patients and clinical staff to ionizing radiation throughout the procedure. We investigate whether a physics-based world model can sustain the navigation task between deliberately sparse X-ray acquisitions, and whether the model can signal when its internal state estimate is no longer reliable. We formulate sparse-fluoroscopy navigation as a partially observable Markov decision process where a Cosserat rod simulator supplies transition dynamics, sparse noisy projections provide observations, and a particle filter maintains a belief over the device state, reduced in this implementation to a tip state with a geometric contact proxy. We evaluate this formulation in a deliberately simplified setting: a synthetic planar vessel phantom with a quasi-static rod model and simulated projections, without clinical or animal data. In this setting, the belief-state model tracks the simulated tip with a root mean square error of 1.30 mm while acquiring observations at one fifteenth of the continuous rate (0.97 mm at every frame, 1.51 mm at one thirtieth), reported 90 percent credible intervals achieve 0.92 empirical coverage, and the belief-derived contact risk estimate discriminates unsafe contact events with an AUROC of 0.68. These results constitute a proof of concept on a simplified simulation rather than a demonstration of clinical readiness; their purpose is to establish that calibrated belief, rather than point-estimate accuracy alone, is the essential property a sparse-imaging world model must deliver.
bullets: Frames sparse-fluoroscopy navigation as a partially observable Markov decision process.
Uses a Cosserat rod simulator for dynamics, simulated projections for observations, and a particle filter over catheter-tip state.
At one-fifteenth of the continuous imaging rate, tip tracking reached 1.30 mm RMSE; 90% credible intervals achieved 0.92 empirical coverage.
Belief-derived contact risk detected unsafe events with AUROC 0.68.
Results are limited to a synthetic planar phantom and do not establish clinical readiness.

papers.abstract: Within the CG animation production pipeline, the challenges artists tackle in Lighting can be immense. Even minor adjustments require re-rendering massive scenes with slow offline renderers; global illumination has to be sampled and complex shaders have to be evaluated, leading to iteration times of minutes to hours per frame. To accelerate this process, we introduce a novel neural render proxy (NRP) that enables differentiable relighting of static scenes with fixed camera and materials at interactive rates. Our main insight is the decoupling of traditional rendering into path sampling and emission computation. From a single, light-agnostic render pass, we collect light transport data in the form of path samples. This enables rapidly sampling lighting conditions on the fly, and training a scene-specific lightweight neural network that learns how light is transported from any scene location to any image pixel. This approach is compatible with non-differentiable production renderers, induces minimal memory requirements during inference, and scales only with resolution and the number of light sources and parameters, but independently of scene and appearance complexity. Our evaluation demonstrates interactive frame rates for relighting (~30-60 Hz) while closely approximating the visual fidelity of ground-truth path tracing. In addition, the differentiable NRP enables fast, gradient-based inverse workflows, allowing artists to efficiently solve for lighting parameters from intuitive image-space edits or generative targets.
authors: Sergio Sancho, Alexander Rath, Marco Manzi, Pascal Chang, Amit H. Bermano, Derek Nowrouzezahrai, Markus Gross, Marios Papas
bullets: Targets slow lighting iteration caused by global-illumination sampling and complex shader evaluation.
Decouples rendering into path sampling and emission computation using a light-agnostic render pass.
Trains a scene-specific neural network to predict light transport from scene locations to image pixels.
Supports relighting at approximately 30–60 Hz with inference cost tied to resolution and lighting parameters, not scene complexity.
Enables gradient-based inverse lighting workflows from image edits or generative targets.

figures.caption: Figure 12: Controllable relighting using our optimization pipeline. Left two columns (Art-directed edits): Lighting parameters are optimized to adhere to hand-drawn scribbles depicting desired illumination phenomena. Right two columns (Generative edits): We leverage generative image models (Qwen-Image-Edit) to create relighting targets. In both cases, given an initial image and a target, we optimize through our NRP to extract physically plausible lighting parameters that accurately reconstruct the prompted appearance. © Disney

Figure 2: Our Pipeline. Training (left): We collect lighting agnostic paths from path tracing the scene before generating denoised image with random lighting conditions to serve as training data. Our neural render proxy (NRP; middle) is a lightweight MLP with hashgrid positional encoding that predicts light transport to a sensor pixel from an input light. To reduce training time and avoid spectral bias, we condition the NRP on auxiliary features (albedo, depth and normals) at sensor image coordinates. At inference time (top right), we can relight the scene at interactive rates by inserting virtual light sources into the scene. Since the NRP is also differentiable, we can optimize for lighting parameters (bottom right) using gradient descent, driven by any number of image-space guidance approaches.

Figure 5: Qualitative image-based relighting comparison. Our relighting setting matches that of image-based relighting using generative networks. Two leading approaches with similar input settings (image, auxiliary features, and lighting condition) are presented. Generative models do not preserve scene geometry, do not adhere to material appearance behavior, and produce lighting that is plausible, but is not physically reasonable. Our method produces high-quality and high-fidelity appearance in real-time. Note that the aspect ratio is different since the generative models used consider squared images.

Figure 4: Production scenes. Interactive relighting results created by artists using our neural render proxy on large-scale production scenes. Each row shows three different light configurations for the same scene. Our method faithfully captures complex light transport effects including fur (top), translucency (middle), and volumetric lighting (bottom). © Disney

Right: Bigger models improve prediction quality. We use 256 neurons with 8 layers by default.

Figure 6: Path-based training. PSNR (dB) in tonemapped space, averaged across three scenes. Each bar is a network trained on N images at S spp with NEE (N×S). Blue: increasing dataset size at 1 spp. Orange: fixed budget of 1024 total samples per pixel, redistributed across images. Dashed red line: our method, trained on light-agnostic path data from a 64 spp render. Despite 16× fewer sampled paths, our approach outperforms all image-based configurations.

Figure 9: Inverse optimization comparison. A light source is optimized from a random initial position to match a target appearance. Error maps (middle) show the relative squared error of path-traced re-renders against the target. This comparison serves as validation: Baselines operate at low spp for tractable runtimes, and their accuracy could improve with higher sample counts at proportionally longer optimization times.

Higher spp improves both reconstruction and prediction quality. Notably, at low spp the learned model can outperform the reconstruction it was trained on. Unless stated otherwise, we use 512 spp for training.

papers.abstract: Actions in expert demonstrations exhibit temporal structure. An ordered-versus-shuffled analysis across five environments confirms this dependence. We ask whether action proposals that better reflect expert continuity can improve visual world-model planning. Rather than imposing generic smoothness, we learn continuations from the temporal structure of demonstrated actions. Our locality-gated deep-kernel Gaussian-process prior, LG-DKGP, combines recent and longer-range executed action history, predicts a neural continuation, and learns a temporal Gaussian-process (GP) residual. A training-derived exploration scale initializes search around the corrected mean; a frozen world model evaluates progress toward the goal. Training first fits the neural mean, then jointly optimizes the prior with the GP residual using expert future actions. The resulting planner achieves 87.07\% macro success across five simulated tasks spanning native and fragment-level goal attainment, compared with 71.03\% for INTACT, 61.66\% for PRISM, and 58.66\% for LeWM. Component interventions and expert-relative action-structure comparisons support demonstration-informed continuations and reveal task-dependent effects of visual conditioning, history length, and planning horizon.
authors: Shaobo Yang, Zichen Ai, Ziyang Ma, Qian Yang, Bin Fang
bullets: Expert actions show meaningful temporal dependence: ordered demonstrations outperform shuffled ones.
LG-DKGP combines recent and long-range action history with a neural continuation and temporal Gaussian-process residual.
A training-derived exploration scale initializes planning, while a frozen world model evaluates goal progress.
The planner reaches 87.07% macro success, compared with 71.03% for INTACT, 61.66% for PRISM, and 58.66% for LeWM.
Component studies indicate task-dependent effects from visual conditioning, history length, and planning horizon.

papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) enable future prediction in latent space without pixel reconstruction. However, latent predictive consistency alone does not establish the relative driving quality of candidate plans. We present ActWorld-JEPA, a joint-embedding formulation for candidate-based driving. Where Plan-Conditioned JEPA (PC-JEPA) uses global and step-wise trajectory intentions to guide recurrent latent prediction, then combines the predicted future with the current scene through gated cross-attention; Relational Residual Reranking ($R^3$) models agreement and discrepancy between plan and future representations under planning supervision, yielding bounded, gated residual corrections to the base planning scores. This formulation connects latent prediction to candidate selection using only observed context and proposed trajectories at inference. Benchmark-specific implementations report 94.1 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, with the final selector calibrated using aggregate NAVTEST feedback, and 91.6 and 42.7 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and navhard, respectively. The nuScenes evaluation reports a mean $L_2$ error of 1.20 m and a predicted collision rate of 0.76% over 1--6 s. This work provides an effective path from JEPA's predictive representations to driving decisions informed by anticipated consequences.
authors: Ziying Song, Shengkai Zhang, Caiyan Jia, Lei Yang, Lin Liu, Yuchen Liu, Ziyang Liu, Zirui Li, Gang Wang, Peiliang Wu, Li Wang, Yadan Luo, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses the gap between latent future-prediction consistency and the relative quality of candidate driving plans.
Uses Plan-Conditioned JEPA to predict future latent states from scene context and global/step-wise trajectory intentions.
Applies Relational Residual Reranking to model plan–future agreement and discrepancy, producing gated corrections to base planning scores.
Reports 94.1 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 91.6/42.7 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest/navhard, and 1.20 m mean L2 error with 0.76% predicted collision rate on nuScenes.
Inference uses only observed context and proposed trajectories; the reported selector is calibrated using aggregate NAVTEST feedback.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The overall architecture of ActWorld-JEPA. The driving encoder extracts the current representation, and the planner produces candidate trajectories. PC-JEPA encodes global and step-wise plan conditions, initializes plan-modulated latents, and rolls out candidatespecific futures. Cross-attention and gated residual interaction fuse predicted future evidence with the current scene. R3 combines plan and fused-future features to rank the original candidates. The rightmost trajectory panel illustrates future-guided selection.
Figure 4. Qualitative comparison of trajectory selection by Drive-JEPA (top) and ActWorld-JEPA (bottom) across five challenging driving scenarios. Selected trajectories are shown in red.

Figure 1. From predictive representations to candidate-conditioned planning. (a) JEPA-style representation learning predicts target features from observed context, as in V-JEPA [3]. (b) Drive-JEPA [50] combines video-JEPA representations with multimodal trajectory distillation and momentum-aware selection. (c) ActWorld-JEPA conditions latent prediction on candidate plans and relates the predicted futures to trajectory ranking through PC-JEPA and R3. Both observed scene context and candidate intention contribute to the decision. (d) Planning performance. PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest [10], comparing ActWorld-JEPA with Epona [65], DiffusionDrive [30], DIVER [43], GraphWorld [45], GoalFlow [57], DriveFuture [16], and Drive-JEPA [50].

(a) Plan-future compatibility modeling combines projected features and their agreement and discrepancy to predict a score correction ∆skt and confidence logit ρkt . (b) Future-consistent candidate ranking gates the bounded correction, adds the baseline score bkt , and selects an original trajectory. (c) JEPA rollout predicts latent futures conditioned on step-wise trajectory intentions over the planning horizon.

papers.abstract: Generating diverse robot videos requires control over scene geometry, robot motion, and viewpoints. End-to-end video generation offers limited direct access to these variables, making targeted edits and reuse across tasks difficult. We present BWM-Forge, a code-driven framework for controllable video generation in robotics. Given robot assets and a task description, the framework accepts an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video. A coding agent constructs editable Blender scene programs that specify objects, robot motion, and cameras. The resulting proxy videos provide structural and motion references for a video generation model, which adds visual detail. A multi-agent harness coordinates input processing, scene construction, review, and rendering. Automated evaluation and user feedback support iterative refinement, while an experience repository stores and retrieves reusable modeling and rendering rules. This design supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, and appearance variation from a shared scene program. We evaluate the framework on 15 tasks covering five robot types. Compared with LingBot-World Base Cam on these tasks, BWM-Forge achieves higher aesthetic quality, imaging quality, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, and RoboJudge-9B physical adherence and instruction alignment scores. The baseline scores higher in dynamic degree. Qualitative cases illustrate viewpoint control, scene variation, feedback-driven edits, and experience reuse across scenes. These results demonstrate a practical approach to generating controllable robot videos through editable, executable scene representations.

Supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, appearance variation, and reusable modeling rules.
Across 15 tasks and five robot types, it outperformed the compared baseline on most quality, consistency, smoothness, and physical-adherence measures, but had lower dynamic degree.

papers.abstract: Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of $432$ strictly paired test cases across $48$ executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a $3 \times 3$ factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across $12$ representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to $64\%$), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.

papers.abstract: Turbulence modeling relies on human choices of closure form, physical inputs, and tunable parameters. Training closures a posteriori is efficient only with gradients through long chaotic rollouts, which few solvers provide. Most a posteriori approaches therefore resort to gradient-free optimization, and nearly all fix the closure form in advance, learning only its parameters. In this work, we introduce a gradient-aware agentic framework that poses closure discovery as a bilevel problem: a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system searches over closure forms, while a GPU-native differentiable computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver supplies gradients, making differentiable a posteriori learning an action of the autonomous AI agent. For each proposal, the agents construct a differentiable training program by embedding the analytical, neural, or hybrid closure in the solver, implementing a differentiable objective, and validating the gradient path. They then decide whether to evaluate the closure, compute its parameter sensitivities, or train it a posteriori, select the optimization settings, and revise subsequent proposals using the simulation outcomes and returned gradients. Truncated-horizon gradients make this training usable under chaotic dynamics for closures with tens of thousands of parameters. Demonstrations include dissipation-law and subgrid-scale closure discovery in two-dimensional turbulence and wall-model discovery for large-eddy simulation of three-dimensional channel flow. With gradient-based training, the agent recovers reference coefficients that forward evaluation alone does not reach within the same budget, and autonomously discovers and trains analytical and neural closures that improve agreement with the targeted reference statistics. These results demonstrate the feasibility of end-to-end autonomous turbulence model development in time-resolved flows.
authors: Yi Liu, Xiantao Fan, Mingqi Xu, Jian-Xun Wang

papers.abstract: In active object search, a robot must decide where to look and when to stop. Imperfect detection complicates both decisions: a non-detection may indicate occlusion, an out-of-view target, or a false negative, while a detection may be a false positive. This raises the question of which representations a world model needs to support reliable search under imperfect detection. We introduce Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS) to investigate how target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors affect search decisions. Through comprehensive ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses, we examine the roles of these representations and their update mechanisms across different detector configurations. Notably, target belief and its update mechanisms are critical to search performance, with their contribution generally increasing as detection errors become more prevalent. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining and updating target beliefs to support reliable active search under uncertain detector observations, providing insights into the design of world models for embodied agents. Code is available in https://github.com/gokyeongryeol/BAMOS.
bullets: Imperfect detections make both search-location and stopping decisions uncertain.
The method models target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors in a Bayesian active-search framework.
Ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses evaluate these representations and their update mechanisms across detector configurations.
Target belief and its updates are critical, especially as false detections and missed detections become more prevalent.
The work informs world-model design for embodied agents operating under uncertain observations.

papers.abstract: Multiplayer generative world models must produce observations that agree on shared entities despite different camera motions and occlusions. Explicit world representations provide spatial control, but precise modeling of individual game maps limits scene diversity, while shared geometry alone cannot ensure consistent appearance across views. We present CoCode-World, a shared 3D proxy framework that separates structural control from visual synthesis for two-player video generation. Programmable proxies specify scene layout, motion, and occlusion, while RGB references guide character and scene appearance. To coordinate visual details across players, we concatenate paired proxy videos, appearance references, and target views in a consistent spatial layout and generate both views jointly with a pretrained video model. This formulation uses the model's native attention for cross-view communication within a single generation branch, with LoRA adaptation learning proxy adherence and appearance correspondence from paired observations. We construct a two-player GTA~V dataset that pairs synchronized RGB observations with proxy videos derived from shared map geometry and game-engine state. Experiments demonstrate appearance transfer to characters and scene styles unseen during training, with improvements in video quality and cross-view player identity over the evaluated baseline. Ablations further examine how proxy construction and cross-view communication affect generation. Project page: https://iapple233.github.io/CCW/.

On a two-player GTA V dataset, transfers unseen character and scene styles and improves video quality and cross-view player identity over the evaluated baseline; ablations study proxy design and communication.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) can improve robot learning by jointly predicting future visual states and actions, but generating a visual future at every replanning step is expensive and sometimes unnecessary. This raises a critical question: when should a robot policy imagine the future? In this paper, we propose Bind-WAM, a binding-uncertainty-guided WAM for selective future imagination. Bind-WAM introduces language-object binding uncertainty, selectively invoking joint future-action generation when the current observation does not support stable task-relevant action generation. An offline labeling pipeline uses complete demonstrations and action context to identify task-relevant objects and detect reference mismatch, invisibility, and identity drift. The resulting pseudo-labels supervise a lightweight router that predicts binding uncertainty from the current observation and language instruction. At inference, a shared WAM policy invokes selective future imagination according to the predicted uncertainty and its change between consecutive replanning steps. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that Bind-WAM can establish binding uncertainty as a strong, interpretable signal for selective future imagination.

papers.abstract: In this report, we introduce the Reciprocal World Model (RWM) and present Duo v1, a full-duplex world model that continuously perceives audiovisual inputs while responding to users in real time. The RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental to what constitutes a world. Existing world models largely focus on simulating the latter, leaving reasoning and decision-making as external controls rather than intrinsic parts of the world itself. In RWM, we identify two equally fundamental capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audio-visual behavior. To realize this formulation, Duo v1 introduces three key technical designs: (1) Leveraging autoregressive modeling for continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions, rather than restricting it to instruction understanding for diffusion models. (2) Constructing chunk-specific conditions and synchronize tokens across Intent and Realization on a unified timeline. Module-specific attention masks enforce causal dependencies both within and across chunks, preventing access to future inputs. (3) Mitigating distribution shift in both modules through dual rollout distillation, training on autoregressively generated Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories from Realization. Both modules continuously perceive real-time audio, video, and text, enabling full-duplex interaction with spontaneous conversations and interruptions. Beyond conversation, users can share real objects, reshape virtual scenes, guide assistants, or play audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls. The release of Duo v1 makes our first step, with the next version coming soon. We look forward to broader exploration of this emerging field.
authors: Hengyuan Cao, Biao Gong, Guoshan Lu, Qiyuan Zhang, Lin Liu, Yiding Tian, Yilei Jiang, Yuxin Ma, Chengzhang Wu, Kun Chen, Yiqian Xie, Ting Liu, Xin Zheng, Xijun Gu, Tianren Ma, Jiancheng Pan, Chi Zhang, Xuzhe Zheng, Siyi Li, Zhenzhong Lan
bullets: The Reciprocal World Model treats cognition and physical reality as equally fundamental components of an interactive world.
Its Intent module handles interaction reasoning and participation decisions, while Realization produces coherent audio-visual responses.
Chunk-specific conditions, synchronization tokens, and causal attention masks coordinate both modules without access to future inputs.
Dual rollout distillation reduces distribution shift by training on generated intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories.
Duo supports spontaneous conversation, interruptions, object sharing, virtual-scene manipulation, and audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls.

papers.abstract: Embodied world models (WMs) are implicit learning systems that predict the next future latent state directly from observations and actions. Unique from other end-to-end learning systems, the dynamics predictor of WMs can simulate the environment's response to alternative actions without physical deployment nor pre-specifying states of the dynamical system. Current metrics focus on the quality of model outputs, e.g., clarity of reconstructions or task success, but fail to assess the fidelity of modeling consequences of counterfactual actions. Inspecting the forced response to action perturbations through sensitivity analysis is one way to audit how well WMs can predict the consequences of counterfactual actions. Deploying WMs on hardware will require new evaluation frameworks to analyze the tradeoffs between state error and accurate sensitivity prediction.
authors: Ayush Gaggar, Jared Berry, Todd D. Murphey
bullets: Existing metrics overlook fidelity to counterfactual action consequences.
Sensitivity analysis can audit model responses to perturbed actions.
Evaluation should assess the tradeoff between state-prediction error and sensitivity accuracy.
The framework is motivated by reliable deployment of world models on physical hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Designing world models will often involve a tradeoff between low state error and low error in predicted action sensitivity. For four example scenarios: a) Structured environments, like open-loop pick and place, only require low state error. b) High accuracy in both action sensitivity and state prediction is only possible when robot motion can be modeled and is repeatable. c) Poor performance in both dimensions is acceptable with effectively unlimited time and compute for non-critical tasks. d) Action sensitivity is more relevant than state error in unstructured, unknown environments, where environmental uncertainty dominates error.

papers.abstract: Autonomous cyber defense is widely studied with deep reinforcement learning, but most work trains policies inside simulators because learning requires many trial-and-error interactions. Simulator-based training carries a fidelity gap: trained policies face authentication delays, partial action failures, service dependencies, and user traffic patterns that the simulator did not represent, and degrade on transfer. Training directly in the network being defended removes the gap but makes every interaction slow and costly, so sample efficiency becomes the binding constraint. Model-based reinforcement learning has reduced sample requirements on games and physical robots by orders of magnitude by planning inside a learned world model, but it has not been applied to defenders trained in operational networks. We present FOE-Dreamer (Factored Opponent-Enhanced Dreamer), a model-based reinforcement learning framework that trains a defender online and directly in a network on cloud infrastructure, without a simulator stage. FOE-Dreamer separates three sources of variation in the latent state: a controllable component driven by defender actions, an exogenous component driven by benign user activity, and an opponent embedding inferred from defender-observable signals alone. Separating the components reduces the variance in policy gradients during planning in imagination. Against two scripted attacker profiles with user activity emulated by the GHOSTS framework on an 8-host OpenStack testbed, FOE-Dreamer trains within a 3-day budget on a single GPU and achieves about 2$\times$ better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN baselines under matched compute. Both the factoring and the opponent model contribute to the gain, and the learned latents are consistent with the intended separation.
bullets: Addresses the simulator-to-network fidelity gap while avoiding the high interaction cost of online training.
Separates latent state variation into defender-controllable, benign-user, and opponent-related components.
Infers the opponent component only from signals observable to the defender and uses the model for imagined planning.
On an 8-host OpenStack testbed with two scripted attackers, it trained within a 3-day single-GPU budget.
Achieved about 2× better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN under matched compute; both factoring and opponent modeling contributed.

papers.abstract: Driving world models aim to simulate how a scene unfolds under different ego actions. This requires plausible motion of surrounding vehicles as well as precise ego-trajectory control. Learning vehicle motion from perspective video alone is challenging because motion is entangled with appearance and vehicles can be occluded. Prior work therefore conditions video generation on layouts that specify vehicle motion, providing control over surrounding vehicles but requiring their future trajectories as inputs. We introduce BirdDreams, an autoregressive driving world model that jointly generates perspective video and a schematic bird's-eye-view (BEV) video, making scene layout part of the predicted future. The BEV, rendered from scene annotations for training, depicts roads and vehicles as simple shapes at a fixed metric scale, providing a top-down view of their positions and motion with reduced occlusion between vehicles. Perspective video, by contrast, retains scene details that the BEV omits, such as traffic signals and object appearance. Joint attention between two video diffusion transformers, one per stream, lets each stream inform the other during generation. The predicted BEV also provides a geometric interface for ego control: we translate and rotate its latest frame along an input ego trajectory and use the resulting frames as a soft condition that shows how the scene would appear to move if only the ego vehicle moved. At inference, BirdDreams generates both videos from a single camera image without requiring an HD map or vehicle-state inputs. On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, BirdDreams follows input ego trajectories more faithfully than prior driving world models and generates more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning. Human evaluation shows that BirdDreams outperforms a perspective-only baseline in generating realistic surrounding-vehicle behavior.
authors: Junyoung Seo, Jaewoo Seo, Seungryong Kim, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Xiuming Zhang, Seung Wook Kim
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling surrounding-vehicle motion and precise ego control from perspective video, where appearance and occlusion confound motion learning.
Uses two autoregressive video diffusion transformers with joint attention: one generates detailed perspective video, while the other generates a metric-scale schematic BEV video.
Uses the predicted BEV as a geometric interface for ego control by transforming its latest frame along a requested ego trajectory as a soft condition.
At inference, requires neither an HD map nor vehicle-state inputs.

On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, it follows ego trajectories more faithfully, produces more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning, and improves surrounding-vehicle realism in human evaluation versus a perspective-only baseline.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) offer a powerful foundation for World Action Models (WAMs), which jointly predict robot actions and future observations. Building such models requires injecting low-dimensional robot signals (e.g. proprioception, actions, and values) into a latent space shaped by natural videos, and a key design choice is the interface through which these signals enter: existing schemes treat it as a formatting detail, spending a separate latent frame on each signal or bolting on dedicated encoders and decoders. We argue that signal injection is instead a distribution-alignment problem: how well a representation matches the prior of the pretrained VDMs during denoising. Using the relative reconstruction error of a frozen VDM denoiser as a probe, we find that conventional spatial encodings sit far off this prior, whereas frequency-domain packing yields latents that the denoiser corrects far less. Motivated by this diagnostic result, we propose MetaWAM, which folds all robot signals into a single unified meta-frame: each signal is assigned to a disjoint frequency-domain channel band and lifted to the spatial latent by an inverse DCT, yielding a decodable interface aligned with the pretrained VDM prior without any added module or architectural change. A fixed band layout together with slot-aware routing lets the same meta-frame support policy, world-model, and value prediction over a shared set of robot variables. On RoboCasa, MetaWAM reaches 68.9% success while collapsing the per-signal frames into one and cutting inference latency by 39%, and attains 85.0% success on three real-world Franka tasks. Code and models are available at https://github.com/showlab/MetaWAM
authors: Guoqiang Liang, Yiqi Lin, Yanzhe Chen, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Frames signal injection as a distribution-alignment problem rather than a formatting choice.
Uses frozen-denoiser reconstruction error to show frequency-domain encodings better match the pretrained video latent prior than conventional spatial encodings.
Packs proprioception, actions, and values into disjoint frequency bands, lifted by inverse DCT without adding modules or changing architecture.
Supports policy, world-model, and value prediction through a fixed band layout and slot-aware routing.
Reports 68.9% success on RoboCasa with 39% lower inference latency, and 85.0% success across three real-world Franka tasks.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation, endowing policies with strong capabilities for modeling temporal and physical dynamics. Existing WAMs, encompassing both video-first action prediction and joint video-action modeling, directly transfer global physical representations from world models to action generation. However, global scene representations may underemphasize local robot-object interactions, creating a mismatch between representations optimized for world evolution and those required for manipulation. To bridge this gap, we propose LaST0.5, a novel WAM that introduces an interaction-centric physical representation between world modeling and action generation. Specifically, LaST0.5 learns a compact interaction-centric latent space under the supervision of visual interaction cues between the robot and the environment. This reasoning space is instantiated as a latent expert that bridges the world expert and the action expert within a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture. Furthermore, LaST0.5 performs adaptive world-to-action transfer by jointly predicting future representations and progress values, using progress consistency to adjust action execution and trigger future resampling. Finally, we pretrain LaST0.5 on a large-scale robotic data corpus comprising over 14k hours of data, establishing interaction-centric physical reasoning as a scalable and effective paradigm. LaST0.5 achieves 99.5% on LIBERO, surpasses the previous state of the art on ten evaluated RLBench tasks, and demonstrates robust long-horizon execution and precise dexterous manipulation in real-world experiments.
authors: Xuheng Zhang, Yiming Zhang, Jialin Gao, Hao Chen, Jiaming Liu, Ji Li, Runzhong Huang, Yinxi Wang, Chenyang Gu, Zihan Yang, Yaowei Liu, Zhonghao Yan, Ziyu Guo, Renrui Zhang, Peng Jia, Pheng-Ann Heng, Shanghang Zhang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between global world representations and the local robot–object interactions needed for manipulation.
Uses a latent expert within a Mixture-of-Transformers to connect world and action experts through interaction-focused physical reasoning.
Adaptively transfers world predictions to actions by jointly predicting future representations and progress values, enabling execution adjustment and future resampling.

Pretrained on over 14k hours of robotic data; achieves 99.5% on LIBERO, exceeds prior state of the art on ten RLBench tasks, and performs robustly in real-world long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.
Scope: evaluated across benchmark and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, with the abstract not specifying broader domains.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The LaST0.5 Framework. (a) LaST0.5 unifies a World Expert, Latent Expert, and Action Expert within a Mixtureof-Transformers (MoT) architecture. To bridge global scene dynamics and precise local control, the Latent Expert distills future frames into compact, interaction-centric representations. (b) The Adaptive World-to-Action Transfer (AWAT) mechanism predicts progress values to assess task-progress consistency in imagined futures. Action execution is dynamically truncated when progress value drops, adapting the execution horizon to the predicted progress sequence. (c) Attention mask of LaST0.5.

Figure 1: Overview. Existing WAMs directly transfer representations of global scene dynamics to action prediction, potentially overlooking the localized robot–environment interactions required for manipulation. LaST0.5 bridges this gap through Interaction-Centric Latent Reasoning (ICLR), which learns a compact latent space supervised by visual motion and objectaffordance cues, establishing a hierarchical reasoning paradigm that progressively transforms global world representations into interaction-centric abstractions and ultimately into robot actions. LaST0.5 achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO and RLBench simulation benchmarks and demonstrates robust long-horizon and precise manipulation in real-world tasks.

papers.abstract: This work presents the 2nd-place solution (Team IF1001) to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge, which evaluates mobile manipulation across 100 household tasks. Our method is built on a powerful world action model (WAM), Cosmos 3. We improve Cosmos 3 by using richer visual history, task-progress conditioning, and task-group and skill-specific LoRA adapters. During inference, we apply a separate progress estimator to supply task-progress context, and use task- and progress-conditioned routing to select a task-group or skill-specific policy, complemented by action-candidate aggregation, rolling inpainting, and task-specific temporal and gripper control. To meet the minimum inference requirement of 1 FPS, we use neither recursive self-improvement (RSI) nor agentic harness methods and rely on no closed-source models; during official private-test evaluation, our system handled concurrent requests across 100 evaluation ports with limited hardware resources, sustaining an average end-to-end inference rate above 2 FPS per port. Our method achieves a mean Q-score of 0.613 and a full-task success rate of 40.9%, averaged over 3 self-evaluation rounds across all 100 tasks. On the official private test set, with 20 instances per task, our system achieves a mean Q-score of 0.615 and a full-task success rate of 41.2%.
authors: Yelin He, Jiaquan Ye, Xinming Wei, Wenjie Xiao, Gengming Zhang, Guoting Wei, Xianbiao Qi, Rong Xiao
bullets: Targets mobile manipulation across 100 household tasks in the BEHAVIOR Challenge.
Enhances Cosmos 3 with richer visual history, task-progress conditioning, and task-group/skill-specific LoRA adapters.
Uses a separate progress estimator, conditioned policy routing, action-candidate aggregation, rolling inpainting, and specialized temporal and gripper control.
Avoids recursive self-improvement, agentic harnesses, and closed-source models while sustaining over 2 FPS per evaluation port on limited hardware.
Achieves a 0.615 mean Q-score and 41.2% full-task success on the official private test set.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems increasingly rely on generating multiple trajectory candidates and selecting one for execution. In this setting, a central challenge is no longer only candidate generation, but how to evaluate candidates according to their long-horizon consequences under uncertainty. Existing methods still mainly use deterministic point scores, heuristic subscores, or single-outcome evaluations, which makes it difficult to capture delayed failures, tail risk, and ranking instability under plausible future perturbations. We present RiSE-Drive, a framework for risk-sensitive long-horizon candidate evaluation in end-to-end autonomous driving. RiSE-Drive first performs candidate-conditioned latent future rollout, then estimates long-horizon outcome distributions instead of single scalar scores, and finally ranks candidates using a tail-risk-aware and perturbation-robust decision criterion. This reformulates candidate scoring from deterministic oracle-style evaluation into distributional outcome assessment with explicit risk control. As a result, the evaluator is encouraged to prefer candidates that are not only strong under nominal conditions, but also reliable under long-horizon rollout and safety-critical deviations. Experiments on the NAVSIM-v1 and NAVSIM-v2 benchmarks, as well as the closed-loop HUGSIM benchmark, show that RiSE-Drive achieves state-of-the-art performance and significantly improves the robustness of candidate selection.
authors: Yu Zhao, Hongyi Duan, Ming Yin, Hongyuan Zhang, Fan Yang, Hongzhi Wang, Xiubo Liang
bullets: Addresses delayed failures, tail risk, and unstable candidate rankings in end-to-end autonomous driving.
Uses candidate-conditioned latent future rollouts to estimate distributions of long-horizon outcomes.
Ranks candidates with a tail-risk-aware, perturbation-robust decision criterion rather than deterministic point scores.
Evaluated on NAVSIM-v1, NAVSIM-v2, and closed-loop HUGSIM, where it reports state-of-the-art performance and more robust candidate selection.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the RiSE-Drive pipeline. Multi-view observations are encoded, and the proposal generator produces 𝐾 ego-trajectory candidates. A future-condition generator predicts 𝐿 branch-specific condition codes that parameterize plausible downstream evolutions. For each candidate–condition pair, RiSE-Drive initializes a latent consequence state, propagates it along the trajectory, and decodes one branch-level long-horizon outcome sample. The resulting branchwise consequence traces are pooled over time and across branches and mapped to ordered outcome quantiles by a distribution head. The final ranking score combines the mean estimate, lower-tail CVaR, and cross-condition instability, thereby favoring candidates that remain reliable under plausible future deviations rather than merely optimal under a single nominal forecast.

Figure 3: Qualitative results of RiSE-Drive on representative NavSafe safety-critical scenarios. From left to right, columns (a)–(d) correspond to UNPL (unprotected left turn), EXR (exit ramp), YLD (yielding), and RDBT (roundabout). Each column shows two temporal snapshots of one representative case. Magenta denotes the RiSE-Drive plan, green the human future trajectory, orange dashed the ego history, and blue the future trajectories of surrounding vehicles. Across all four cases, RiSE-Drive produces smooth, route-consistent, and interaction-aware behaviors while remaining close to safe human driving in conflict-prone regions.

papers.abstract: Learning representations from multimodal observations is difficult in reinforcement learning with limited interaction data. Multimodal Joint Predictive Representation combines multimodal latent prediction with contrastive learning across modalities, but its recursive rollout depends on earlier predictions and its pairwise alignment focuses on correspondence between modalities. We propose Improved Predictive Representation, which combines prediction from action prefixes with alignment at the observed anchor based on Contrastive Multimodal learning. At each horizon, it predicts future representations directly from the observed anchor and the corresponding sequence of actions. We evaluate two crop configurations: IPR-S with a minimum retained crop area of 10%, and IPR-H with 50%. Across five DeepMind Control Suite tasks, IPR-H achieves an average return across tasks that is 10.0% higher than the baseline with visual and depth images and 3.4% higher with visual images and position vectors. The relative performance of the two configurations varies across tasks. In Webots, both IPR configurations achieve higher mean final returns than the baseline without LiDAR, but not when LiDAR is available.
bullets: Addresses recursive prediction errors and limited pairwise modality alignment in multimodal representation learning.
Predicts future representations directly from the observed anchor using action sequences, while aligning modalities at that anchor.
Evaluates two crop configurations: IPR-S (10% minimum retained area) and IPR-H (50%).
Across five DeepMind Control Suite tasks, IPR-H improves average return by 10.0% with visual/depth inputs and 3.4% with visual/position inputs.
In Webots, both variants outperform the baseline without LiDAR, but not when LiDAR is available; performance varies by task and crop configuration.

papers.abstract: Pretrained latent world models can support visual planning and control, but their predictions may fail when physical dynamics change at deployment. We study whether such models can adapt from only a few interactions without modifying their pretrained weights or identifying the changed physical parameters. We introduce a few-shot residual adaptation approach that learns self-supervised corrections from latent prediction errors. The corrections are applied both inside the latent predictor and directly to its predicted latent state, while the pretrained world model remains frozen. We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts. These changes reduce the success of the frozen model to near zero. Using three interaction episodes for adaptation, our dual-site approach recovers 90\% success under the center-of-mass shift and 100\% under the modified friction on the real robot. Ablations show that correcting both locations outperforms single-site adaptation. Our diagnostics further suggest that much of the learned correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while successful control also depends on shift-specific information captured during adaptation.
authors: Jakub Suliga, Pankhuri Vanjani, Nisarga Nilavadi, Wolfram Burgard, Rudolf Lioutikov
bullets: Addresses deployment failures caused by shifts in physical dynamics without retraining or identifying changed parameters.
Learns residual corrections from latent prediction errors and applies them both within the latent predictor and to its predicted latent state.
Evaluated in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts.
With three adaptation episodes, real-robot success reached 90% for the center-of-mass shift and 100% for the friction shift.
Dual-site correction outperformed single-site adaptation; learned corrections captured both general prediction mismatch and shift-specific information.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Dual-site latent correction in a frozen world model. The frozen predictor rolls out sampled actions, corrected inside every block and once more on its output. The CEM controller ranks the corrected predictions by latent distance to the encoded goal and executes the best action. The next observation supplies the target of the self-supervised loss that trains both residuals.
Figure 2: The pushing task in simulation and on the real robot, each shown at the start of an episode and after a successful push.

papers.abstract: Protein engineering requires navigating rugged fitness landscapes, where small sequence changes can produce large functional differences, but experimental screening can only sample a small fraction of sequence space. Thus, a central challenge is to efficiently traverse the large combinatorial space of mutations in silico. We introduce ProTEUS, a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution. Pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays, ProTEUS learns a joint representation of sequence, evolutionary, and structural information using MutationFormer, a mutation-biased attention architecture. Variants are represented as states in this joint latent space, and mutations define actions whose functional consequences are predicted. To support exploration of many mutants, we developed a fast, physics-constrained all-atom predictor that utilizes explicit geometric constraint enforcement to achieve >10 fold increase in speed than AlphaFold3 with guaranteed physical validity. Lastly, ProTEUS refines its prediction and understanding of protein activity through closed loop experimental feedback to guide evolution toward a desired phenotype. ProTEUS surpasses established models in both zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning mutation prediction tasks. We experimentally demonstrate its utility in two closed-loop multi-objective engineering campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase, yielding variants with >10 fold higher activity than wild type. ProTEUS provides a world-model framework that connects virtual evaluation of mutational outcomes with experimental learning for efficient protein evolution.
authors: Yikun Zhang, Minghao Guo, Guangxue Xu, Peter Yichen Chen, Wojciech Matusik, Wengong Jin, Jingjing Chai, Kaiyi Jiang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of exploring vast, rugged protein fitness landscapes when experiments can test only a small fraction of variants.
Uses MutationFormer to jointly represent sequence, evolutionary, and structural information from deep mutational scanning data.
Models variants as latent-space states and mutations as actions with predicted functional consequences.
Includes a physics-constrained all-atom structure predictor reported as over 10× faster than AlphaFold3 while maintaining physical validity.
Outperformed established mutation-prediction models and produced variants with over 10× wild-type activity in two closed-loop campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase.
papers.selection_reason: ProTEUS is a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution, using a physics-constrained predictor and feedback loops. This fits World Models (Latent Action Models, Interactive World Models).
papers.title: ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution
papers.tldr: ProTEUS is a closed-loop protein evolution framework that predicts mutation effects, rapidly evaluates structures, and uses experimental feedback to guide engineering toward desired phenotypes.

papers.abstract: Synthetic data augmentation promises to scale offline reinforcement learning beyond fixed logged datasets, but leading diffusion-based generators model the transition tuple (state, action, next state, reward, terminal) as a monolith: no single factor can be natively redrawn in isolation. We present FaST (Factored Synthesis of Transitions), which factors transitions via the chain rule into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, fitting each with an estimator matched to its statistical properties. Across twelve D4RL locomotion and maze benchmarks, TD3+BC and IQL agents trained on FaST transitions match the SynthER diffusion baseline while generating transitions over 90x faster. The explicit action-given-state conditional can also be re-queried for a fixed state, enabling targeted action synthesis: drawing N candidate actions per generated state and keeping the highest-advantage one under a value function fit to the same data, thereby synthesizing improved behavior during generation rather than filtering for it post-hoc. Best-of-10 synthesis beats training on real data on 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings (+8.9 D4RL points on average, up to +28.4), and is competitive with advantage-filtered SynthER at a fraction of its generation cost. On expert mixtures both mechanisms degrade identically, tracing the failure to the advantage estimate itself rather than to either targeting mechanism.
authors: Daniel Campa, Spandan Das, Srinjoy Das
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency and inflexibility of monolithic diffusion models for offline RL transition synthesis.
Uses a chain-rule factorization into state, action, dynamics, reward, and terminal stages, with estimators suited to each factor.
Matches the SynthER baseline across 12 D4RL locomotion and maze benchmarks while substantially reducing generation cost.
Best-of-10 targeted action synthesis improves over real-data training on 11 of 12 medium and medium-replay settings, averaging +8.9 D4RL points.
Performance degrades on expert mixtures because of inaccurate advantage estimates, not the synthesis mechanisms themselves.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon urban navigation requires sequential local decisions whose errors can compound over time. Imitation learning (IL) rarely learns from failures, while physical trial-and-error reinforcement learning (RL) is costly. Action-conditioned world models can provide imagined feedback by predicting visual consequences for candidate actions. However, a frozen world model may become less reliable as the policy evolves. In this paper, we introduce RIWANAV, a post-training framework that casts the coupled adaptation of a world model and an action model (policy) as task-specific recursive self-improvement (RSI). Each cycle alternates two updates. The world model evaluates policy actions through imagined outcomes, providing comparative feedback for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). The improved policy then constructs a grounded self-curriculum, selecting expert-consistent action-video pairs by behavioral novelty and prediction error. The refined world model supplies feedback for the next policy update, closing the recursive self-improvement loop. Experiments show that RIWANAV outperforms training baselines and prior methods, validating the proposed recursive self-improvement loop between the policy and world model. Real-world trials further demonstrate its practical applicability.
bullets: Addresses compounding errors in long-horizon navigation and the limitations of failure-insensitive imitation learning and costly physical RL.
Alternates world-model refinement and policy improvement in a recursive self-improvement loop.
Uses imagined action outcomes for group-relative policy optimization and behavioral novelty/prediction error to build a grounded self-curriculum.
Experiments report gains over training baselines and prior methods, with real-world trials supporting practical applicability.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Recursive self-improvement loop in RIWANAV. (1) The current world model imagines action consequences that improve the policy. (2) The improved policy constructs a grounded self-curriculum that improves the next world model. Repeating these updates recursively changes both components and the feedback exchanged between them. The flame marks the component optimized in each phase.

Fig. 4. Qualitative evidence for recursive world-model improvement on actions generated by the improved policy. All three models receive the same observation, language goal, and action; the aligned recorded future is shown as reference. The rows depict night traffic, a bicycle-lined sidewalk, and a rainy sidewalk. In these cases, the RIWANAV world model after recursive updates better preserves traversable corridors and scene layout, with fewer long-horizon artifacts.

Fig. 1. From imitation learning to recursive world–action models selfimprovement. (a) Imitation learning trains the policy from expert trajectories but provides limited supervision for policy-induced failures. (b) A frozen world model enables learning from imagined outcomes, but its predictions become misaligned with the evolving policy. (c) RIWANAV closes the training loop: imagined outcomes improve the policy, while grounded policyinduced samples refine the world model for subsequent policy learning.

Points are means over 128 samples and error bars denote standard error. Round 0 uses the initial world model, whereas the final round K = 19 uses the final RIWANAV world model. Lower is better.
