papers.selection_reason: Couples action-conditioned world models with policy self-improvement for urban navigation.
papers.title: RIWANav: Recursive World-Action Models with Self-Improvement for Urban Navigation
papers.tldr: RIWANav jointly self-improves an action-conditioned world model and navigation policy through iterative imagined feedback and self-curated training data for long-horizon urban navigation.

papers.abstract: Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions in large-scale physical environments. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of the consequences of actions and future conditions, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, an agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with anticipatory reasoning for robust urban navigation. Our central idea is to anchor local decisions in persistent medium-horizon subgoals, assess the consequences of predicted actions before execution, and continually update the reasoning context using actual outcomes. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. We further introduce a predictive world sandbox that uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to forecast world dynamics conditioned on candidate movements. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions under the current subgoal to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.
bullets: Targets the difficulty of translating distant navigation goals into coherent local decisions in large, complex environments.
Maintains persistent medium-horizon subgoals and relevant experience through a navigation memory module.
Uses an action-conditioned world model to predict candidate movement outcomes in a visual sandbox.
A vision-language reasoner evaluates predictions, while real observations update memory and revise actions or subgoals.
Evaluations report stronger gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.

papers.title: PreAct-Nav: Agentic Reasoning Before Action for Urban Navigation

papers.abstract: We introduce DreamFormer, a model-based agent that acquires language-conditioned, multi-task skills by imitating expert demonstrations within the latent imagination of a learned world model. DreamFormer first learns a task-agnostic Transformer world model from unstructured play data, then acquires task-specific behaviors by optimizing an intrinsic reward that aligns agent-generated rollouts with expert demonstrations in latent space. Since the policy is trained on-policy inside imagination, it is exposed to its own errors during training, mitigating the covariate shift inherent to offline behavioral cloning. To make long-horizon imagination affordable, DreamFormer encodes a high-resolution multi-view robotic observation into a single input token, avoiding both spatial downsampling and the multi-token representations used by prior Transformer world models. On the long-horizon CALVIN benchmark, DreamFormer outperforms LUMOS, the comparable model-based agent, on single-environment evaluation (2.52 vs 2.34 average tasks completed per chain of five) while keeping imagination rollouts tractable. Against HULC, the behavior cloning baseline, it nearly doubles performance on zero-shot transfer to an unseen environment (1.30 vs 0.67), indicating that dynamics learned by the world model transfer more readily than a directly cloned policy. This is consistent with the role attributed to internal models in biological agents, where a model of environment dynamics supports behavior in situations not previously encountered.
bullets: Learns a task-agnostic world model from unstructured play data, then optimizes task behavior in imagined rollouts aligned with expert demonstrations.
On-policy training within imagination exposes the policy to its own errors, reducing offline behavioral-cloning covariate shift.
Compresses high-resolution multi-view observations into a single token to keep long-horizon Transformer imagination tractable.
On CALVIN, completes more tasks than LUMOS in single-environment evaluation (2.52 vs. 2.34) and nearly doubles HULC’s zero-shot transfer performance (1.30 vs. 0.67).

papers.title: DreamFormer: Dream Imitation with a Transformer World Model for Language-Conditioned Robotic Manipulation

papers.abstract: Soft powered descent landings are becoming evermore important in the field of space exploration and scientific advancement, because of their ability to deliver mission critical payloads, both highly accurately and safely. The high efficiency restriction on planetary landings due to the severely limited fuel supply results in the need for optimal guidance trajectories and control. Model based reinforcement learning is proving to be an important tool in simplifying the highly complex process of generating optimal guidance trajectories and control. In this work, we present DreamLander, a state of the art model based reinforcement learning algorithm based on DreamerV3, to generate optimal guidance and control for a realistic 6 degree of freedom entry descent landing problem. The model based approach creates a sample efficient and highly generalizable model that can be applied to a variety of scenarios whilst maintaining a high degree of accuracy, landing within 2 meters of the designated landing zone, and with velocity norm less than 0.3 meters per second. DreamLander makes use of state sensor observations, making progress toward End-to-End solutions of the Entry Descent Landing problem.
bullets: Targets soft powered descent, where limited fuel demands efficient guidance trajectories and control.
Uses model-based reinforcement learning built on DreamerV3 for the entry-descent-landing problem.
Operates from state sensor observations, advancing toward end-to-end landing solutions.
Reportedly lands within 2 m of the designated zone with velocity norm below 0.3 m/s.
Designed to be sample-efficient and generalizable across landing scenarios.

papers.abstract: World models have increasingly been applied as a model-based control method for robotics tasks such as manipulation and locomotion. While early world model architectures relied on decoders to prevent mode collapse and learn a predictable latent space, recent works on world models, such as Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture or LeWorldModel, increasingly aim to learn embeddings without a grounding decoder, utilising only a latent forward dynamics predictor and a stabilising entropy term. In this paper, we set out to demonstrate that the further introduction of two additional latent losses to LeWorldModel, a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor, enforces further structure on the latent embedding, leading to further gains in both performance and planning efficiency. These are critical properties for improving the applicability of such methods to real-time model-based control of real-world robots. We demonstrate these gains on standard world model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.
bullets: Targets more effective, real-time model-based control for robotics.
Extends LeWorldModel with a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor.
Uses these auxiliary latent losses to impose additional structure on learned embeddings.
Evaluated on standard world-model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.
The abstract does not report specific quantitative gains or limitations.

papers.title: $Σ$-LeWM: Learning World Models via S-Information for Robot Control
papers.tldr: Σ-LeWM improves decoder-free world models for robot control by adding backward and inverse-dynamics losses that structure latent representations and enhance performance and planning efficiency.

papers.abstract: A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.
bullets: Problem: Camera or controller changes can make a planner’s commands produce different motions, sharply reducing performance.
Method: Infer the current command-to-action mapping—or “hand”—from image changes using the frozen world model, without extra sensors or training data.
LoH stores identified hands so previously seen setups can be recognized instead of relearned.
In closed-loop tests, success increased from 28.6% to 62.3% across three simulated tasks, while unchanged setups lost only 0.6 percentage points.
The method also transferred unchanged to other world models and most tested models pretrained on real-robot data; performance depended on reading quality.

papers.title: Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model
papers.tldr: Library of Hands (LoH) adapts a frozen world model to changing robot command mappings without retraining by identifying and reusing the current action-to-motion mapping.

papers.abstract: Video world models conditioned on an input video make it possible to explore real, recorded dynamic scenes, enabling re-shooting of footage, free-viewpoint replay, and real-to-sim environments for embodied agents. Such uses require the generated rollout to stay faithful to the recorded world, yet existing benchmarks start from a single image or a text prompt, and video-conditioned generation is evaluated mainly on perceptual quality and camera following. These evaluations do not directly assess whether exploration preserves subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency upon revisiting a location. We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos of real and AI-generated content in three difficulty tiers (3-25 s), paired with camera routes given as keyboard actions, and evaluates six dimensions with 24 human-validated sub-metrics. Benchmarking eight models, we find that as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics, and that none keeps revisited places consistent. We further propose WanderLand, a training-free framework that conditions each frame of a frozen model on the same-instant source and, on revisits, on its own earlier static content. WanderLand improves five models on every dimension, by up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 745 real and AI-generated single-shot videos across three difficulty tiers, paired with keyboard-action camera routes.
Evaluates six dimensions through 24 human-validated sub-metrics, including identity, event progression, camera control, and consistency when revisiting locations.
Across eight models, longer rollouts preserve static appearance and visual quality but degrade camera control and source dynamics.
No evaluated model maintains consistency when revisiting previously seen places.
Proposes WanderLand, a training-free conditioning framework that improves all dimensions across five models, with up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.

All geometry comes from the model’s own front-end. The frozen model then generates the output rollout.

papers.title: WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?
papers.tldr: WanderBench evaluates whether video-conditioned world models can explore dynamic scenes while preserving their content, motion, and consistency over time.

papers.abstract: A key challenge in action-conditioned world modeling is to construct macro-states from high-dimensional observations that support recursive prediction under actions, while keeping their predicted evolution consistent with visual changes in generated observations. We propose QCC-WM, a visual world model based on Quotient-based Causal Construction. QCC-WM uses action responses to guide macro-variable construction for recursive action-conditioned prediction. A shared reference quotient measurement constrains the consistency between predicted states and observed changes, allowing macro-level predictions to provide structured constraints for future visual generation. Using translational and rotational actions and their predicted responses, the model aggregates local visual features into macro-nodes with spatial correspondence through causal abstraction, and recursively predicts node content and motion under a shared reference measurement. Macro-level predictions guide future observation generation, while predicted motion transports historical appearance information. Node-level errors between generated observations and macro-level targets are then mapped back to the corresponding spatial regions for correction, improving consistency between visual generation and macro-level predictions. On the US-VLA dataset, QCC-WM achieves an ROI-MSE of 0.01861 for four-step prediction. Compared with the best baseline at each prediction horizon, it reduces LPIPS by 48.59%, 41.68%, and 30.23% for four-step prediction and eight- and sixteen-step recursive extrapolation, respectively. Ablation studies and mechanism analyses show that motion-guided reference transport mainly improves pixel reconstruction, while node-level error feedback further improves perceptual quality and consistency between generated observations and macro-level predictions.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of linking high-dimensional visual observations, action-conditioned macro-state prediction, and future image generation.
Uses action responses and causal abstraction to aggregate local visual features into spatially corresponding macro-nodes.
A shared reference quotient measurement and motion-based appearance transport constrain recursive state and visual prediction.
Node-level visual errors are mapped back to spatial regions to correct generated observations and improve consistency.
On US-VLA, it reports 0.01861 ROI-MSE for four-step prediction and reduced LPIPS versus the best horizon-specific baseline for four-, eight-, and sixteen-step prediction.

papers.abstract: World models enable agents to plan and learn from imagined experience, but in an unfamiliar environment they must learn its mechanics from limited interaction. A mechanic is a rule for how an action or an interaction changes part of the environment. Each occurrence of a mechanic that the model observes is one exposure. We ask how many exposures a world model needs to predict the effects of a new environment's mechanics. We address this question on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark of interactive games defined by their programs. We introduce MechEval, which labels 69 recurring mechanics across 20 games from these programs. It scores each prediction on the cells the mechanic changes at each exposure. As a test bed, we build WARC (World model for ARC-AGI-3), a 35M-parameter vision transformer that is pretrained on other games and updates all of its parameters after each transition. On held-out games, WARC learns to predict four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy on the cells they change and keeps that accuracy to the end of the recordings. Half of them reach that accuracy within about 80 exposures, in a single play of the game, and without updates only one in seven does at all. In closed-loop play on the public games, WARC-Agent, which pairs WARC with a fixed graph explorer, triples the explorer's official efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, mostly through test-time training. On the hidden games of the Kaggle leaderboard, our entry scores 0.20.
bullets: Studies how many observations are needed to predict mechanics—rules governing how actions alter an environment—in unfamiliar games.
Introduces MechEval, covering 69 recurring mechanics across 20 ARC-AGI-3 games and scoring predictions on changed cells.
Builds WARC, a 35M-parameter vision transformer that updates all parameters after each observed transition.
On held-out games, WARC predicts four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy; about half reach that level within roughly 80 exposures.
Pairing WARC with a fixed graph explorer triples the public-game efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, while the hidden-game leaderboard score is 0.20.

papers.abstract: World models are widely considered to be a potential key component of model-based reinforcement learning and robot planning, but typically require task-specific training on substantial interaction data. We investigate whether a pretrained tabular foundation model (TabFM) can serve as a training-free dynamics model for world modeling by framing next-state prediction as in-context regression over transition pairs, and where such a model helps and where it breaks. Across synthetic dynamical systems and robot locomotion benchmarks, TabFM is more accurate than LSTM and MLP models trained from scratch on the same limited transitions in almost all settings, and among regressors fitted to the same data it is the most accurate on locomotion, while a Gaussian process is more accurate on smooth low-dimensional systems. However, models trained on the full dataset remain substantially better on most systems. When rolled out autoregressively over multiple steps, TabFM's accuracy depends strongly on how much context it is given. With a short context, its rollouts quickly degrade to the level of a trivial baseline, whereas with a long context they improve substantially and, on one locomotion task, exceed a trained LSTM. Inference is also about three orders of magnitude slower than an LSTM. Overall, in their current state, we find that training-free priors are useful as predictors when data are scarce and enough context is available, but they are not yet a substitute for trained world models in planning.
bullets: Frames next-state prediction as in-context regression over transition pairs using a pretrained TabFM.
Outperforms from-scratch LSTM and MLP models in almost all limited-data settings; performs best among same-data regressors on locomotion.
Gaussian processes are more accurate on smooth, low-dimensional systems, while models trained on full data remain substantially better overall.
Autoregressive rollout quality depends strongly on context length: short contexts degrade quickly, whereas long contexts can outperform a trained LSTM on one locomotion task.
Inference is about three orders of magnitude slower than an LSTM, limiting current use in planning.

papers.abstract: One-step stochastic world models avoid the mode averaging of deterministic feature predictors without the tens of network evaluations per step that diffusion and flow matching require. The simplest such objective is nearest-of-m matching (conditional implicit maximum likelihood estimation, IMLE): draw m candidate futures and pull only the one closest to the observed outcome. Recent work conjectures that a small m suffices for feature-space world models and that a strictly proper energy score should replace the hard minimum. We test both claims with one-step world models on frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens, using benchmarks whose futures can be enumerated. Under mode-like uncertainty, nearest-of-m with m=16 covers the enumerated futures better than 50-step flow matching (at about 1/30 of its latency), one-step flow generators and an energy-score generator at matched parameter counts, and its rollouts stay on the token manifold where flow rollouts drift. One quantity governs the choice of m: the nearest-of-m objective is the expected distortion of a random codebook of m draws from the generator. This view yields three predictions, recorded before the corresponding runs: (i) memorization of the realized outcome in contexts that never repeat, whose strength is governed by the codebook's miss distortion I(m) rather than its miss probability, and which an energy-score generator does not escape by raising m; (ii) a flattening of mode probabilities with m, matching a known optimum within 0.01; and (iii) under-dispersion on continuous high-dimensional outcomes, which bounds the method on real robot video. Per-step matching on self-rollouts cuts long-horizon error by a third on a stochastic Push-T variant; an ablation separates its manifold and coverage benefits. Planning success does not improve despite accurate risk estimates, a negative result we report with its diagnosis.
bullets: Nearest-of-m training selects the closest of m sampled futures, avoiding deterministic mode averaging with one network evaluation.
For frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens and enumerable futures, m=16 outperformed 50-step flow matching, one-step flow generators, and energy-score generators at matched parameter counts.
The method keeps rollouts on the token manifold and improves long-horizon stochastic Push-T error by one third with per-step self-rollout matching.
Increasing m flattens mode probabilities and can cause memorization in nonrepeating contexts; the key factor is expected codebook miss distortion, not merely miss probability.
Continuous high-dimensional outcomes remain under-dispersed, and better risk estimates did not improve planning success.

papers.abstract: Spatial generalization in robot world models depends on whether action representations capture the physical relationships that remain valid across changing spatial configurations. Yet different coordinates can describe the same interaction, whereas similar motions can produce different outcomes when local physical conditions change. How these distinctions affect learned prediction remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluates matched action representations defined in world, object, and surface coordinate frames using a controlled robotic peeling benchmark. Global pose and contact relocation experiments reveal a cost associated with limited training data when equivalent interactions receive different spatial descriptions. Removing information about peel thickness creates an irreducible ambiguity because identical predictive inputs can correspond to different material removal outcomes. Coordinates defined relative to the surface improve consequence prediction and counterfactual action selection under accurate local observations, but learned predictors remain vulnerable to uncertainty in the coordinate frame. Joint centering of the surface and tool removes sensitivity to translation of their common origin, whereas incorrect contact geometry and actual execution deviations introduce different failure mechanisms. These results show that effective spatial generalization depends on preserving the relationships between actions and states that determine physical consequences, rather than simply minimizing coordinate variation. This perspective provides a principled basis for designing robot world models that reuse physical knowledge across spatial configurations while retaining the distinctions essential to prediction and planning.
bullets: The study compares matched action representations in world, object, and surface coordinate frames using a controlled robotic peeling benchmark.
Equivalent interactions described differently can increase data requirements, while omitting peel thickness creates irreducible ambiguity in material-removal predictions.
Surface-relative coordinates improve consequence prediction and counterfactual action selection when local observations are accurate.

Jointly centering the surface and tool removes sensitivity to their shared translation, but uncertainty in coordinate frames, incorrect contact geometry, and execution deviations cause distinct failures.
The findings support designing representations that preserve outcome-relevant action–state relationships for reuse across spatial configurations.

papers.abstract: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.
bullets: Round-to-nearest activation quantization can severely degrade planning despite one-step prediction error comparable to stochastic rounding.
The key issue is error persistence and sharing across planner candidates, not simply rounding-error magnitude.
Redrawing common dither each planner iteration removes most of the degradation without retraining across tested TD-MPC2 and DINO-WM settings.
An W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model speeds planning rollouts by 1.9–3.3× and full planning steps by 1.3–1.5× versus FP32; dither adds at most 2.3% latency.
Block-scaled NVFP4 largely avoids the problem, while fixed dither within a step or episode restores planner drift.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) requires large amounts of interaction data or a reliable simulator, both hard to obtain for nonlinear soft robotic hardware. Recent work shows that a time-scale separation inherent to soft robot dynamics justifies their reduction to low-dimensional invariant manifolds, known as adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs). We demonstrate that an aSSM-reduced model, a simple polynomial ordinary differential equation learned purely from pre-collected data, can serve as an RL training environment. On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, we train a trajectory-tracking policy in 3 hours on a six-dimensional aSSM-reduced model and deploy it without fine-tuning, whereas reproducing this policy training extrapolates to 3 years of hardware interaction. Our policy tracks dynamic targets with 40% lower error than otherwise identical policies trained on a 4.8-million-parameter recurrent neural network (RNN) or a 1.7-million-parameter transformer, which take 13 and 100 hours to identify, against 5 minutes for our mathematically justified 6,924-parameter model.
bullets: Soft-robot RL is hindered by costly hardware interactions and unreliable or unavailable simulators.
A time-scale separation reduces the robot dynamics to a low-dimensional adiabatic spectral submanifold (aSSM).
A 6,924-parameter polynomial ODE learned from pre-collected data provides the RL training environment.
On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, the policy trained in 3 hours deployed without fine-tuning and achieved 40% lower tracking error than comparable RNN- and transformer-based approaches.
The approach remains demonstrated on one soft-arm trajectory-tracking task and depends on the validity of the aSSM reduction.

papers.abstract: A purely data-driven method grounded in the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) was recently used to model and control nonlinear soft robotic simulators. Here, we extend the methodology to learn aSSM-reduced models from data collected from hardware soft robotic platforms. Specifically, we learn a five dimensional (5D) aSSM-reduced nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE) that accurately models the dynamics of a soft-helicoid trunk robot. We then use this ODE in a model predictive control scheme to demonstrate real-time precision control across various challenging closed-loop trajectory-tracking tasks, ranging from 2D to 3D trajectories with static and dynamic constraints. We find that our methodology enhances accuracy and precision across all control tasks compared to available data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning. While we focus here on a soft-helicoid trunk robot, our methodology relies solely on hardware data and is therefore applicable to a broader class of soft robotic systems.
bullets: Learns a nonlinear reduced-order ODE directly from hardware data.
Integrates the learned model into a model predictive control scheme.
Demonstrates closed-loop tracking with static and dynamic constraints.
Reports improved accuracy and precision over data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning.
The hardware-data-based approach is intended to generalize to other soft robotic systems.

papers.abstract: Quadrotors inspecting buildings and tunnels must navigate unknown clutter with a forward-facing depth camera whose limited field of view constrains scene understanding and collision-avoiding navigation. Recent world-model agents learn navigation through imagined experience (e.g., AirDreamer), but remain data-intensive and often lack explicit geometric memory and awareness of what the camera can observe. We propose ScanDreamer, a map-grounded world model that constructs an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose. Our world model, actor, and critic are conditioned on this map, which also defines a geodesic progress reward. Moreover, a forward-cone penalty discourages horizontal motion outside the camera's viewing direction. During imagination, ScanDreamer propagates the quadrotor pose over a frozen map and derives progress and wall-contact signals from the mapped geometry. We train ScanDreamer for 0.8 million environment steps (5.5 h on one GPU) and evaluate it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim over 1560 episodes spanning unseen layouts and parameter ranges. Across three seeds (mean $\pm$ SD), ScanDreamer achieves 96.3 $\pm$ 0.3% success with 3.6 $\pm$ 0.3% collision, compared with 59.6 $\pm$ 3.0% success and 28.8 $\pm$ 2.8% collision for AirDreamer at the same online-interaction budget. Removing the forward-cone penalty increases collisions to 9.9 $\pm$ 3.1%. These results show that combining explicit map memory, map-grounded imagination, and perception-aware motion substantially improves navigation performance and data efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/WANGSHUAIzzzz/ScanDreamer.
bullets: Builds an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose to provide explicit geometric memory.
Conditions the world model, actor, and critic on the map and uses mapped geometry for geodesic progress and wall-contact signals.
Adds a forward-cone penalty to discourage motion outside the forward-facing camera’s view.
In Isaac Sim, it achieves 96.3% success and 3.6% collision across 1,560 episodes, outperforming AirDreamer under the same interaction budget.
Removing the forward-cone penalty raises collisions to 9.9%, highlighting its role in perception-aware navigation.

papers.abstract: A driving foundation model must learn reusable decision knowledge from rare critical events and apply it under strict runtime constraints. We introduce DriveFoundry, a closed-loop framework improving iteration efficiency under data and computation budgets by coupling structured causal data refinement with adaptive inference. The Data Engine builds traceable scene-candidate records linking scene evidence and factor-decision relations to candidate trajectories and outcome assessments. Candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations clarify how scene factors affect behavioral feasibility and preference. Verified model failures guide VLM-assisted annotation and expert correction, refining training data and annotation systems. The model engine, Xiaomi-Drive-o1, unifies Perception, Causation, Action, World, and Value within a shared vision-language backbone to enable cross-task knowledge transfer. Block-wise latent refill passes candidate-specific evidence and predicted visual consequences between task blocks, connecting scene understanding, planning, and evaluation. A learned value-of-computation head selects tasks and allocates latent tokens based on expected benefit and cost, adapting inference to each decision. On PhysicalAI, the 9B model achieves the lowest ADE@1 across evaluated splits and horizons among tested models. In AlpaSim, it outperforms Alpamayo 1.5 across all metrics and achieves lower close-encounter and off-road rates than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, while trailing in progress and AlpaSim scores. For the 0.8B variant, joint training reduces 5 s minADE@6 by about 54% without altering the inference path or token budget. Adaptive inference matches full reasoning performance using only 28% of tokens. Real-vehicle tests confirm runtime feasibility, supporting a unified paradigm for learning from critical experience and dynamically allocating computation.
bullets: Builds traceable scene–factor–decision records with candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations to refine training data from critical events and verified failures.
Uses Xiaomi-Drive-o1, a shared vision-language model integrating perception, causation, action, world modeling, and value estimation.
Connects task blocks through candidate-specific latent evidence and predicted visual consequences, while a value-of-computation head allocates inference effort adaptively.
Reports strong benchmark results, including the lowest ADE@1 among tested models on PhysicalAI and broad metric improvements over Alpamayo 1.5 in AlpaSim.
Joint training improves 5 s minADE@6 for the 0.8B model by about 54%, and adaptive inference reaches full-reasoning performance with 28% of the tokens; real-vehicle tests support runtime feasibility.

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation requires rich spatial foresight over both the surrounding scene and the robot hand. Existing world-action models often acquire such predictive knowledge through explicit future prediction. We introduce DexForesight, a framework that learns spatial foresight implicitly by injecting dynamics-aware world representations into the latent space of a dexterous policy. During training, DexForesight learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from offline scene depth, kinematic hand geometry, and demonstration trajectories. The world model predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, capturing both articulated hand dynamics and scene changes under demonstrated actions, including the motion of fingers occluded from the cameras. We then freeze the world model and align policy queries with its predictive world queries, transferring the learned spatial dynamics into policy latents and using them to condition action generation. At deployment, only the policy is retained, operating on RGB observations, language, and robot state without depth input or explicit future prediction. On 11 DexJoCo simulation tasks, DexForesight improves the overall success rate of the base policy from 49.4% to 60.5%. On three real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks, DexForesight achieves 58.3% success, compared with 50.0% for the strongest baseline. Project page https://dexforesight.github.io/
bullets: Learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from depth, hand geometry, and demonstrations.
Predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, including occluded finger dynamics and scene changes.
Aligns policy queries with world-model predictions, then freezes the world model and transfers its dynamics into policy latents.
At deployment, the policy uses only RGB observations, language, and robot state.
Improves success from 49.4% to 60.5% on 11 DexJoCo tasks and achieves 58.3% versus 50.0% for the strongest baseline on three real-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: In offline reinforcement learning, diffusion models fill two roles with complementary strengths. Typically guided by a critic, a diffusion policy is value-aware and favors high-return, behavior-supported actions, but it is short-sighted: it never lays out the states it intends to visit. A diffusion planner is far-sighted, synthesizing such a long-horizon trajectory, but it is only behavior-driven at execution, realizing each planned transition using only offline behavior.Each is strong exactly where the other is weak. We introduce DPDP to bring them together at the planner's execution step, where a planned transition becomes an action. Reading the planner's inverse-dynamics executor as a posterior over actions: the environment's transition likelihood relates an action to the planned next state, while the behavioral prior determines its weight under the offline data. Replacing this prior with a value-optimized diffusion policy preserves the planned transition likelihood and favors valuable actions that can serve the plan. We target the resulting clean-action distribution in two ways. A training-free sampler composes policy and inverse-dynamics scores at matched action noise levels and applies Langevin correction; this route uses a shared action noise schedule and an approximately common terminal prior. A preference objective instead amortizes the transfer into a single diffusion executor. Across D4RL, DPDP improves the planner it builds on, staying competitive with reactive diffusion policies on locomotion and leading on long-horizon navigation.
bullets: Addresses the short-horizon nature of critic-guided diffusion policies and the behavior-only execution of diffusion planners.
Reinterprets the planner’s inverse-dynamics executor as an action posterior and replaces its behavioral prior with a value-optimized diffusion policy.
Provides a training-free score-composition sampler with Langevin correction and a preference-based objective for a single amortized executor.
Across D4RL, improves its underlying planner, remains competitive with reactive diffusion policies on locomotion, and leads on long-horizon navigation.

On both suites, the policy and the planner are individually comparable, and unifying them exceeds both on the suite average.

Table 2: Gym-MuJoCo locomotion on D4RL. Normalized return averaged over five seeds; columns as in Table 1. The blue DQL+ (value policy) and DV+ (planner) are our reimplemented schedulematched base models. These are dense-reward, reactive tasks with no goal to reach: every step is scored on the spot, so they reward immediate control rather than foresight. The value policy DQL+ therefore leads and planning is unnecessary, yet the transfer still improves the base planner DV+ on nearly every task, narrowing the gap to the reactive frontier.

papers.selection_reason: Combines a diffusion policy and a diffusion planner for offline RL, creating an interactive world model for long-horizon planning and robot control.
papers.title: DPDP: Diffusion Policy-Steered Diffusion Planner for Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: DPDP combines long-horizon diffusion planning with value-aware diffusion policies to select high-value actions that still realize planned transitions in offline RL.

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation with world action models (WAMs) relies on hand configuration and contact information, yet joint-state and whole-hand tactile observations may be partially or entirely missing. RGB images provide scene context and hand-object geometry but are insufficient to reliably recover these missing modalities. We further observe a correlation between hand state and tactile information. Motivated by this observation, we introduce BAT-WAM, a framework that bridges visual, joint-state, and tactile representations for WAMs. BAT-WAM learns separate codebooks and decoders for the tactile and action streams. An RGB-conditioned continuous latent bridge connects the two streams for bidirectional learning, while visual information serves as continuous context. Under the HTBench evaluation protocol, BAT-WAM reduces the root mean squared error (RMSE) of tactile reconstruction by 34.73% under fully masked conditions and 38.84% under partially masked conditions, relative to an image-conditioned HandTouch checkpoint. For future tactile prediction conditioned on target-time RGB and historical actions, it reduces mean RMSE by 85.56% relative to OpenWAM with HandTouch. Real-robot experiments further show that BAT-WAM consistently outperforms related WAM baselines in dexterous manipulation. Generalization experiments on unseen objects and scenes also demonstrate substantial improvements over baseline models. These findings support joint modeling of visual context, hand state, and touch as a representation approach for multimodal WAMs.
bullets: Addresses missing or incomplete hand-state and whole-hand tactile observations, which RGB alone cannot reliably reconstruct.
Uses separate tactile and action codebooks/decoders connected by an RGB-conditioned continuous latent bridge for bidirectional learning.
Reduces tactile reconstruction RMSE by 34.73% under fully masked and 38.84% under partially masked conditions versus an image-conditioned HandTouch checkpoint.
Improves future tactile prediction mean RMSE by 85.56% versus OpenWAM with HandTouch.
Outperforms related baselines in real-robot manipulation and generalizes better to unseen objects and scenes.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (H-JEPA) enable long-horizon visual control but rely on costly test-time gradient descent for planning. Our analysis reveals that iterative optimization consumes up to 97.7% of episode runtime and that low predicted rollout costs do not necessarily translate into successful control. We further identify a planning-horizon asymmetry between long-horizon top-level composition and short two-step subordinate planning. To address these challenges, we propose WARP-JEPA, a hierarchical amortized planning framework that replaces online gradient optimization with learned multi-candidate trajectory proposers while keeping the world models frozen. WARP-JEPA combines a lightweight world-model-in-the-loop causal Transformer at the top level with parallel residual MLPs at subordinate levels. The proposers are trained using model-based rollout costs and best-of-K behavior cloning, enabling efficient candidate selection without test-time gradient optimization. Across 30 frozen H-JEPA models on four benchmarks, WARP-JEPA achieves 9.6-18.8x faster episode inference on long-horizon tasks (2.9-3.0x on Cube) and improves task success by up to 33.3 percentage points. These results demonstrate that amortized planning can substantially improve both inference efficiency and control performance without retraining the world models. Code is available at https://github.com/hideinsewer/WARP-JEPA.
bullets: H-JEPA planning can spend up to 97.7% of episode runtime on iterative optimization, and low predicted rollout costs may not ensure successful control.
The method uses a hierarchical planner: a causal Transformer for top-level composition and parallel residual MLPs for short-horizon subordinate planning.
Proposers are trained with model-based rollout costs and best-of-K behavior cloning, while the underlying world models remain frozen.
Across 30 frozen H-JEPA models and four benchmarks, inference is 9.6–18.8× faster on long-horizon tasks and 2.9–3.0× faster on Cube.
Task success improves by up to 33.3 percentage points, demonstrating gains in both efficiency and control without world-model retraining.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robot teams deployed in remote, unstructured environments may face changes in the environment, hardware, and team composition that degrade previously effective policies. Shifting mission objectives can be handled by selecting a different solution from an existing Pareto set, but shifting deployment conditions can reorder the set itself, making previously dominated policies competitive or new policies necessary. However, evaluating these policies in new contexts while minimizing risk to the hardware remains an open problem. We argue that, although largely untested in this domain, world models merit investigation for post-deployment multi-objective adaptation. By predicting policy outcomes under updated estimates of current conditions, world models could enable teams to re-evaluate existing policies without physically executing each candidate, provided predicted performance changes reflect those realized on deployed systems. We identify research priorities for model-based policy re-evaluation, validation of predicted against realized performance, and incorporating shared information into world models to support coordinated team adaptation.
bullets: Environmental, hardware, or team changes can reorder the Pareto set, making previously dominated or new policies viable.
Selecting among existing Pareto-optimal policies may address objective shifts but not changing deployment conditions.
World models could predict policy outcomes under updated conditions, reducing the need to physically test every candidate.
Safe adoption requires validating predicted performance against outcomes on deployed systems.
Shared information should be incorporated to support coordinated adaptation across robot teams.

figures.caption: Figure 1: This is a proposed pipeline for maintaining a shared, current representation of the world using world models after deployment. Distributed agents collect local observations, model predictions are tracked against realized performance, and if the context is out of distribution, the model can be updated. The model is used to evaluate policies when objectives change, or possibly even learn new policies with the updated world models.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes using world models for post-deployment multi-objective adaptation in remote robot teams, directly addressing world models for robotics.
papers.title: Multi-Objective Adaptation After Deployment: A Position on World Models for Remote Robot Teams
papers.tldr: World models could help remote robot teams safely reassess and adapt policies after deployment as conditions and objectives change.

papers.abstract: World models enable planning through internal simulation, while natural language provides intuitive task specification. Yet, language-conditioned world modeling remains fragmented across domains with disparate action spaces, datasets, and evaluation protocols. We introduce LCWM, a shared task that maps an initial agent-view observation and a language instruction to an action sequence that fulfills the instruction. Its accompanying benchmark, LCWM-Bench, integrates 15 datasets across navigation, robotics, 3D gaming, and driving under a shared action interface and evaluation protocol, pairing 142,987 episodes with 428,961 instructions in three styles. We further propose Tiresias, an agent that plans via selective imagination: a language-conditioned diffusion policy generates candidate trajectories, a trajectory ranker shortlists them, and a video-pretrained world model imagines their visual consequences. A visual ranker evaluates these rollouts, complementing trajectory scores to select the final plan. Tiresias achieves competitive planning and imagination performance on LCWM-Bench. Ablations demonstrate the complementary benefits of trajectory ranking and visual verification, while experiments with alternative proposal methods show that the trained rankers remain effective beyond our diffusion policy. Together, LCWM-Bench and Tiresias provide a unified evaluation setting and an effective starting point for studying language-guided planning through world models.
bullets: LCWM-Bench unifies 15 datasets spanning navigation, robotics, 3D gaming, and driving under shared actions and evaluation.
The benchmark contains 142,987 episodes and 428,961 instructions in three language styles.
Tiresias uses a language-conditioned diffusion policy to propose trajectories, then combines trajectory ranking with video-based visual verification.
A video-pretrained world model imagines the visual outcomes of shortlisted plans before final selection.
Ablations support the complementary value of trajectory ranking and visual verification; performance is reported as competitive on LCWM-Bench.

papers.abstract: Embedded AI is moving from perception to prediction. Robots now use world models$\unicode{x2014}$learned simulators that predict the outcome of candidate actions in a compressed latent space before any is executed. Every predicted step must be computed on board within a tight power and thermal budget, yet the energy these steps fundamentally require, and how far real hardware sits from it, have not been characterized. We derive lower bounds on the arithmetic operations and the CMOS dynamic energy of a latent state transition from information theory and Boolean circuit complexity. Profiling a DreamerV3-style Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) shows that every rollout operation is memory-bandwidth bound and that a GPU consumes at least $5.9\times10^{10}$ times the CMOS energy floor. Transient 3D thermal simulations show that this inefficiency is also a thermal one, since sustained back-to-back planning heats a millimeter-scale silicon tile to 556 K even behind an ideal copper heat spreader. Guided by this chain from bound to bottleneck, we propose the World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA), a chip architecture for embedded world model planning that combines near-memory computation, real-time entropy estimation, variable-precision rollout units, and copy-on-write latent scratchpads. With a design target of 40x lower power, the same tile stays near ambient at 306 K in simulation, pointing toward practical planning on thermally constrained robots.
bullets: Derives information-theoretic and Boolean-circuit lower bounds for latent state-transition operations and their CMOS dynamic energy.
Finds that DreamerV3-style RSSM rollouts are memory-bandwidth bound, while GPU energy is reported as far above the CMOS energy floor.
Thermal simulations show sustained planning can overheat a millimeter-scale silicon tile, even with ideal copper heat spreading.
Proposes WMPA with near-memory computation, entropy-aware precision, variable-precision rollout units, and copy-on-write latent scratchpads.
A 40× lower-power design target is simulated to keep the tile near ambient temperature, suggesting feasibility for thermally constrained robots.

papers.tldr: WMPA is a hardware–algorithm co-design that targets the severe energy, bandwidth, and thermal costs of embedded world-model planning in robots.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have continuous deficiency in spatial reasoning tasks that require \emph{mental spatial transformation}, such as reasoning under hypothetical changes in viewpoint or position, known as perspective-taking tasks. Existing approaches either scale linguistic reasoning or augment VLMs with static geometric representations, but neither directly enables active transformation of the represented scene. World models offer this capability, yet existing systems typically communicate through synthesized RGB images, introducing a latent-to-pixel-to-latent bottleneck. We introduce \emph{WorldMind}, a framework for test-time scaling of spatial reasoning through latent world simulation. Given a query and observation, the VLM selects useful spatial transformations, while a world model executes them and exposes aligned intermediate latent features directly to the VLM. The resulting latent evidence is incorporated into subsequent reasoning steps, enabling iterative spatial simulation without repeatedly decoding imagined states into pixels. To optimize this interaction, WorldMind further employs process-verifiable reinforcement learning that rewards reasoning progress only when the associated action and latent transition are valid. WorldMind thus scales spatial reasoning by allocating additional inference-time computation to active world simulation rather than generating more language or pixels. Across VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench, and MindCube-Tiny, WorldMind achieves an average improvement of 16.0% over the base VLM and 8.3% over the strongest RGB-based world simulation.
bullets: Targets VLM deficiencies in mental spatial transformations, including hypothetical viewpoint and position changes.
The VLM selects useful transformations, while a world model executes them and returns aligned latent features directly for iterative reasoning.
Uses process-verifiable reinforcement learning to reward only valid actions and latent transitions that make reasoning progress.
Achieves average gains of 16.0% over the base VLM and 8.3% over the strongest RGB-based world simulation across three benchmarks.
Scope: focused on visual spatial reasoning and perspective-taking tasks evaluated on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench, and MindCube-Tiny.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of WorldMind design. Given the currently observed RGB frames and a spatial query, WorldMind augments standard VLM visual tokens with the selected latent features from a pre-trained world model, and performs iterative reasoning through camera actions and latent world simulation. To ensure proper latent world simulation, WorldMind first trains an adapter that selects latent features from the world model and aligns them with a frozen VLM. Then, it fine-tunes the VLM in two stages: (1) supervised fine-tuning with simulated reasoning trajectories; and (2) process-verifiable reinforcement learning, which further optimizes action selection and reasoning using intermediate and final rewards.

papers.title: WorldMind: Test-Time Scaling for Visual Spatial Reasoning through Latent World Simulation

papers.abstract: Learning control from action-free recordings is challenging because intervention effects are unobserved and policies may exploit errors in reconstructed dynamics. We present a hierarchical model-based reinforcement learning framework that uses shared structure across related systems to learn system-specific control policies from action-free recordings. A hierarchical dynamical system reconstruction model captures shared dynamics and individual variation through low-dimensional embeddings. These embeddings are then reused to parameterize shared policy and value networks, linking differences in reconstructed dynamics to differences in control. Policies are trained entirely via simulation under an explicit intervention model with additive latent perturbations. Piecewise-linear recurrent neural networks enable mechanistic analyses of the controlled dynamics, while decoder-based constraints make the immediate effects of interventions interpretable in observation space and permit interventions on one modality while protecting another from direct manipulation. On Lorenz-63 and double-pendulum systems, hierarchical policies improve transfer over independently trained policies. On Lorenz-63, they also achieve a higher mean reward than repeated planning with the same reconstructed models, perform comparably to methods trained with controlled interactions, and generalize to systems absent from policy training after embedding inference alone. Applications to neural-behavioral recordings demonstrate suppression of predicted movement under constrained neural perturbations. Together, these findings show how shared dynamical representations support transferable control and mechanistic hypothesis generation from action-free recordings.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning intervention effects when recordings contain no observed actions.
Reconstructs related dynamical systems with low-dimensional embeddings capturing shared structure and individual variation.
Reuses embeddings to parameterize shared policy and value networks, connecting inferred dynamics to control.
Uses simulated interventions, interpretable decoder constraints, and piecewise-linear recurrent networks for mechanistic analysis.
Improves transfer on Lorenz-63 and double-pendulum systems, and can generalize to unseen systems after embedding inference.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Framework overview. a: A hierarchical DSR model is trained on multiple related dynamical systems (“subjects”) and used as world model for MBRL. Subject-specific parameters φ(j) are obtained by projecting shared parameters Pφ onto low-dimensional subject embeddings S(j). These embeddings are reused to condition the policy πψ and value networks Qθ by modulating group-level parameters Pψ and Pθ. b: For unseen subjects, learning only a new embedding via DSR fine-tuning enables insertion into the control model. c: The high-dimensional dynamics are controlled only in the directions that are decoded (z̃t). To underactuate the problem and for application-specific constraints, actions are constrained to be orthogonal to the target modalities and target dimensions. d: In the Lorenz-63 benchmark, the actions only affect the y− and z−directions.

Figure 5: Behavioral control through neural stimulation. a, left: Predicted trajectories without control. The model receives the goal position cue (black dashed) and go cue (cyan) as external inputs and generates trajectories (solid) that reproduce the empirical test data (dashed). Hand (green) and eye (blue) positions are shown separately. In successful trials, the hand follows the instructed target, whereas eye position is not consistently target-aligned in either the model or the data. center: Two-dimensional trajectories without (top) and with (bottom) control. The policy suppresses hand movement and, to a lesser extent, eye movement despite external inputs driving both toward the target. Color gradients indicate time. right: Neural stimulation remains sparse and selective, with no statistically significant changes in mean firing rate (t = −1.33, p = 0.18) or Fano factor (t = 1.04, p = 0.30). b: Value function, control energy, and latent states for a representative trial. Actions become effective once the goal-position cue is presented and steer the system into a high-value region of latent space associated with trajectories that remain insensitive to the subsequent go cue.

Figure 10: Generalization through fine-tuned subject vectors. On unseen subjects, fine-tuned subject vectors achieved a reward of = −0.036 ± 0.002, compared with −0.046 ± 0.005 for the unchanged vectors of the nearest training subjects. a: Fine-tuned subject vectors inserted into the fixed SAC model control the true, unseen systems without further optimization (cf. figure 2c). b: PCA projection of the subject vectors of the fine-tuned (colored) and original Lorenz-63 systems. Shifted parameter regimes produce corresponding shifts in the PCA embedding (cf. figure 6).

Figure 4: Reconstruction and model-based control of the LINK data. a: The first principal component of the subject vectors shows a linear relationship with recording days, indicating that the learned subject representations capture structure across sessions. b: Finger positions of the index and middle, ring and small (MRS) finger groups, neural activity, and control energy for one representative session. Each new goal position, presented to the monkey and provided to the model as external input, triggers a movement in the recorded (red) and simulated (blue) trajectories. Under the learned policy (orange), the simulated finger positions stay at rest. Neural activity follows a quasi-periodic dynamics in the uncontrolled model and changes under control. Control energy is the squared norm of the decoded action. Controlled trajectories are reinitialized from the recorded state every 200 time steps, which produces the visible jumps. c: Action magnitude over time for 0 to 12 excluded channels (color, top) and median reward as a function of the number of excluded channels (bottom). Actions are forced to zero on randomly selected channels. Action magnitude first increases to compensate and is then suppressed entirely once 8 channels are excluded, causing a drop in reward.

Figure 3: Reconstruction and stabilization of the double-pendulum. a: Colors indicate mass ratios m1/m2 and length ratios l1/l2, respectively. Analogous to the Lorenz-63 System, subject vectors cluster according to system parameters. b: Example trajectory of the true double-pendulum under control, with the target position indicated by the dashed red line. The 6 variables are sine and cosine of the joint angles as well as the angular velocities. Despite its inherent instability the controlled system converges to the target.

Figure 2: Controlling the Lorenz-63 benchmark. a: Reward histograms for randomly initialized trajectories across all subjects for the simulated system (left) and the true system (right) using hierarchically (top) and independently trained models (bottom). Black line denotes uncontrolled baseline. b: Representative Lorenz–63 trajectories with reward = −0.020 generated by the world model under SAC control during uncontrolled and controlled phases (gray shading), with the value function and occupied LSRs shown below. While x2 and x3 are directly controlled and rapidly approach the target (dashed red line), x1 converges to a nearby FP. c: Corresponding trajectories of the true system, demonstrating sim-to-real transfer, with a reward of −0.03. d, e: For the same subject, the most frequently occupied subregions (indices 3 and 5) are those admitting non-virtual FPs (red crosses) close to the target. f : During extended control, the trajectory approaches the target while action-dependent FPs are progressively shifted toward it.

Figure 7: Limited controllability under single dimension actuation. Example trajectory of the true Lorenz-63 system with actions applied exclusively to the third state dimension. The dashed line indicates the target state.

Figure 8: Mechanisms underlying Lorenz-63 control. a: Number of LSRs required to cover 90% of time steps for uncontrolled (blue) and controlled (red) trajectories of each subject. Control strongly reduces region occupancy. Subject 54 (cf. figure 2) is highlighted. b: Minimal distance to the target of the nonvirtual FPs computed from sampled actions in each occupied LSR (cf. figure 2e). c: Eigenvalues of the Jacobian at the FPs, which depends only on the LSR, indicate stability along most directions. The unit circle is shown in gray.

Figure 15: Reconstruction of neural spike rates. Empirical (left) and reconstructed (right) spike rates for a representative trial. Across all test trials, the world model achieves a variance-normalized mean squared error of 0.17 ± 0.06.

Figure 11: Control mechanisms in multimodal neural data. a: Occupancy of LSRs during control. b: Minimal distance of non-virtual FPs to the target in each occupied LSR. papers.title: Learning Transferable Policies from Action-free Time Series Through Dynamical Embeddings
papers.tldr: A hierarchical model-based RL framework learns transferable control policies from action-free time series by embedding shared and system-specific dynamics, then simulating interventions to train policies.

papers.abstract: Low latent prediction error does not establish that a world model distinguishes the consequences of its actions. We introduce an evaluation protocol that traces the same intervention through simulator state, raster observations, target embeddings, and predictor outputs. Exact simulator-state forks in a controlled deformable-physics testbed reveal distinct bottlenecks. Changed commands alter particle motion, yet 41.5% of one-step raster pairs are identical. Observation loss is not the whole explanation: among 579 high-visibility counterfactuals, median predictor-to-target response is 0.0051 and 0.0217 across two seeds, falling to 0.0027 and 0.0116 after variance normalization. An isotropic state perturbation matched to the target counterfactual embedding shift produces 190x and 53x larger predictor changes on the same visible pairs, isolating action-path under-use rather than a dead or globally shrunk predictor. MSE-only training gives 8.36x lower 10-step latent error in matched seeds, but in spectrally concentrated spaces; one VICReg target encoder is also strongly concentrated, so neither error nor rank alone certifies physical state. Finally, stiffness remains near chance even from full-resolution rasters and mechanical state while privileged material parameters decode perfectly, indicating weak identifiability under this excitation rather than encoder discard. These results motivate auditing physical effect, observation visibility, representation geometry, and action dependence separately.
bullets: A counterfactual protocol traces interventions from simulator state through raster observations, target embeddings, and predictor outputs.
In the testbed, 41.5% of one-step raster counterfactual pairs are identical despite changed particle motion, revealing an observation bottleneck.

Among visible counterfactuals, predictor responses are very small; matched isotropic embedding perturbations cause 53–190× larger changes, indicating action-path under-use rather than a globally inactive predictor.
MSE-only training achieves lower 10-step latent error, but concentrated representations show that prediction error and rank do not guarantee physical-state encoding.
Material stiffness remains near chance from images and mechanical state while privileged parameters decode perfectly, indicating weak identifiability under the tested excitation.

papers.abstract: Video generation models can produce highly realistic videos while generating physically inconsistent object motion. This limitation suggests that visual modeling alone may not provide a transferable representation of physical dynamics. We introduce MotionCore, a framework for learning physical dynamics via a learnable partial differential equation solver and focuses on rigid-body motion. We introduce a latent neural simulator learning to predict the evolution of object-level physical states from observed motion. Its predictions are then converted into spatially aligned latent controls for a controllable video diffusion model. The generator serves as a visual interface: it provides appearance and scene detail, while the learned dynamics model specifies the physical trajectory. To preserve this trajectory through the interface, MotionCore combines a diffusion-matching objective with a low-capacity decodability constraint on object identity and position. We evaluate MotionCore on public physical-consistency benchmarks and on paired data with known trajectories. Results indicate that MotionCore improves physical consistency and trajectory obedience in the evaluated rigid-body settings, while maintaining comparable visual quality. A controlled ablation protocol compares learned dynamics with an analytic prior and studies the choice of latent evolution processor.
authors: Zheng Wang, Zhengwei Gong, Yuanzhi Liang, Chi Zhang
bullets: Targets physically inconsistent object motion in otherwise realistic video generation.
Learns object-level state evolution with a neural PDE solver focused on rigid-body dynamics.
Converts predicted trajectories into spatially aligned latent controls for a controllable video diffusion model.
Uses diffusion matching plus a low-capacity decodability constraint to preserve object identity and position.
Improves physical consistency and trajectory obedience on evaluated benchmarks while maintaining comparable visual quality; scope is limited to rigid-body settings.

papers.abstract: Reliable relative tracking is fundamental to cooperative autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), yet remains challenging under nonlinear vehicle dynamics and degraded underwater visual conditions. Active light markers improve robustness to appearance variation, but provide deliberately sparse observations that can become incomplete or corrupted by occlusion, reflections, and detection noise during dynamic motion. To address the resulting partial-observation control problem, this paper proposes FATHOM, a world-model-guided diffusion action-trajectory selection framework for sparse-marker AUV tracking. FATHOM first integrates structured marker observations, inertial measurements, action history, and temporal dynamics into a predictive tracking belief using a multimodal task-supervised recurrent state-space model. A diffusion action prior then generates multiple expert-like multi-thruster trajectories, whose future tracking consequences are predicted through the learned latent dynamics. Rather than directly executing a generated trajectory, FATHOM selects the most favorable candidate under an explicit receding-horizon objective and continually updates the decision from onboard observations. Extensive offline analyses verify the learned predictive belief, multi-step world-model prediction, diffusion trajectory generation, and predictive selection. More importantly, comprehensive real-AUV experiments, including strong pose-based comparisons and component ablations, demonstrate robust autonomous tracking across nominal and challenging motions with naturally occurring partial marker visibility, while maintaining real-time onboard operation without motion-capture feedback.
authors: Xiaorui Wang, Zeyu Sha, Mingyang Yang, David Chen Wang, Feitian Zhang
bullets: Addresses partial-observation tracking caused by occlusion, reflections, detection noise, nonlinear dynamics, and degraded underwater vision.
Builds a predictive tracking belief from marker observations, inertial measurements, action history, and temporal dynamics using a multimodal recurrent state-space model.
Generates multiple multi-thruster action trajectories with a diffusion prior, predicts their consequences in latent dynamics, and chooses among them using a receding-horizon objective.
Offline analyses validate belief modeling, world-model prediction, trajectory generation, and predictive selection.

Real-AUV experiments and component ablations show robust autonomous tracking under nominal and challenging motions with partial marker visibility and real-time onboard execution without motion-capture feedback.

papers.title: FATHOM: World-Model-Guided Diffusion Action-Trajectory Selection for Sparse-Marker AUV Tracking

papers.abstract: Personalized health coaching requires moving beyond retrospective wearable summaries toward quantitative, actionable behavioral prescriptions. We introduce Coachable Health Age (CHA), an interpretable health-age metric built from modifiable physiological and behavioral signals passively captured by consumer wearables. Across the WEAR-ME (N=2,780), All of Us (N=22,748), and longitudinal Fitbit (N=1,464) cohorts, CHA aligns with established cardiometabolic health constructs and improves prognostic discrimination for incident cardiovascular and metabolic disease beyond age, sex, and body mass index. To enable prospective behavioral optimization, we developed Sensor World Model (SensorWM), an action-conditioned wearable world model pretrained on over 2.2 million person-weeks of longitudinal sensor data from approximately 100,000 participants. SensorWM accurately forecasts multi-week physiological responses to candidate lifestyle changes ($R^2=0.664$), outperforming generic time-series foundation models while preserving downstream clinical signal for diabetes, hypertension, and other health outcomes. Finally, we integrate CHA and SensorWM into an agentic counterfactual coaching system to synthesize personalized 12-week coaching plans. In blinded paired reviews, certified lifestyle coaches preferred counterfactual-grounded plans over plans grounded in wearable history alone for overall quality (71.4%, P < 0.001) and anticipated adherence (71.0%, P < 0.001), and board-certified clinicians judged 99.2% of counterfactual-grounded plans to meet clinical safety criteria (vs. 97.6% of comparison plans). Automated evaluations across the full cohort (N=2,780) also favored counterfactual-grounded plans. By closing the loop between longitudinal tracking, trajectory prediction, and counterfactual coaching, our framework provides a scalable path to systematically improve cardiometabolic health.
authors: Simon A. Lee, Zeinab Esmaeilpour, Menglian Zhou, Marius Guerard, Sohrab Sidhu, Alexandru Solot, Hamid Palangi, Pramod Rudrapatna, Ming-Zher Poh, Max A. Xu, Daniel McDuff, Dimitrios Antos, Yuzhe Yang, Jeffrey N. Chiang, Anthony Z. Faranesh, Lindsey Sunden, Mark Malhotra, Shwetak Patel, A. Ali Heydari, Ahmed A. Metwally
bullets: Introduces Coachable Health Age (CHA), which summarizes modifiable physiological and behavioral signals from consumer wearables.
Develops SensorWM, an action-conditioned model that forecasts multi-week physiological responses to lifestyle changes.
Integrates CHA and SensorWM into an agentic system that creates personalized 12-week counterfactual coaching plans.
Across three cohorts, CHA aligned with cardiometabolic health constructs and improved prediction of incident cardiovascular and metabolic disease beyond basic demographics and BMI.

Lifestyle coaches preferred counterfactual-grounded plans, while clinicians rated 99.2% as meeting clinical safety criteria; the framework’s scope is primarily cardiometabolic health and wearable-observable behaviors.

papers.abstract: We introduce GPWM, a Generative Particle World Model that predicts how 3D scenes evolve by generating the motion of particles and rigid bodies over time. Unlike video world models that generate scene appearance, GPWM operates directly in 3D physical space. A single representation and architecture cover rigid, deformable, cloth, and granular materials, in both passive physics and robotic interaction. GPWM is an object-aware multi-resolution transformer that combines flow matching with diffusion forcing to generate coherent physical trajectories far beyond its training horizon. We train and evaluate GPWM on ParticleWorlds, a 25.5-million-frame corpus spanning diverse geometries, materials, interactions, and robot embodiments. GPWM outperforms the best prior learned-dynamics baseline in each of six physical domains, reducing prediction error by 31% on average. Breaking from the domain-specific setting of prior methods, a single Unified GPWM models these heterogeneous regimes with one set of weights, largely outperforming per-domain baselines and even surpassing our own specialist models in two domains. GPWM further generalizes to unseen geometries, physical properties, object counts, and rollout horizons. Beyond prediction, GPWM enables contact-rich planning by learning a generative prior over joint actuator-object motion. Instead of searching over unconstrained actions, planning searches the model's latent noise for interactions that achieve a desired object-space goal. With the same world model, noise-space planning substantially outperforms action-space search on pushing and picking, where complex contact sequences are hard to discover. Executed open-loop in simulation, the resulting plans achieve goal-directed manipulation without reference action trajectories or goal-specific policies.
bullets: Models rigid, deformable, cloth, and granular materials in passive and robotic-interaction settings with one representation and architecture.
Uses an object-aware multi-resolution transformer with flow matching and diffusion forcing to generate coherent long-horizon trajectories.
Trained and evaluated on the 25.5-million-frame ParticleWorlds corpus spanning varied geometries, materials, interactions, and robot embodiments.
Reduces prediction error by 31% on average across six physical domains versus the strongest prior learned-dynamics baseline, while generalizing beyond training conditions.
Enables noise-space planning for pushing and picking, outperforming action-space search without reference trajectories or goal-specific policies.

Each block (right) applies temporal attention, 3D relative spatial attention, and pointwise feed-forward layers, modulated by AdaLN-Zero from the per-frame noise level τ , and the network outputs clean future displacements.
