papers.abstract: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.5, completes only 53.5% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.
bullets: Addresses the gap between offline replay benchmarks and real-world interaction, where assistant responses affect user behavior and task outcomes.
Provides simulators for cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface tasks, plus persona-conditioned users with execution errors and out-of-plan behavior.
Introduces IVG-Bench with 315 interaction scenarios for evaluating visual grounding, actionable guidance, latency, and task completion.
The best evaluated model completed 53.5% of tasks within the time limit; the interaction-quality metric achieved 78.5% agreement with human preferences.
A proof-of-concept GRPO experiment improved task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B in the cooking environment.

papers.abstract: Current 4D occupancy world models use heavy cross-attention or deep recurrence to disentangle ego-motion from scene dynamics. This requires significant computational capacity. However, this effort is largely redundant since the ego-vehicle's intended future motion is provided by the downstream motion planner. We present FreeOcc, a lightweight continuous-time world model that introduces explicit $SE(2)$ geometric decoupling into a conditional flow-matching framework. By mathematically factoring out self-motion, we create a purely dynamic feature space. This space supports attention-free temporal fusion and allows physics-constrained ODEs to operate strictly on residual agent kinematics. To maximize deployment efficiency, FreeOcc introduces an uncertainty-aware blending mechanism. This routes well-observed voxels to a single-pass decoder, reserving the ODE solver exclusively for ambiguous, high-uncertainty regions. Requiring only 28.3M parameters-roughly 40% of comparable models-our optimal ensemble mode (FreeOcc-E) runs at 27 FPS. On nuScenes, FreeOcc achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance with a 0.47 m Near Field Chamfer Distance (NFCD) and 32.1% mIoU. Furthermore, the model transfers zero-shot to SemanticKITTI. It also proves highly robust, retaining 92.8% of its ideal mIoU under significant sensor packet loss and timestamp jitter.
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of disentangling ego-motion from scene dynamics in 4D occupancy world models.
Uses explicit SE(2) geometric decoupling to create a purely dynamic feature space with attention-free temporal fusion.
Applies physics-constrained ODEs only to residual agent motion and ambiguous, high-uncertainty voxels.
The 28.3M-parameter FreeOcc-E runs at 27 FPS and reports 0.47 m NFCD and 32.1% mIoU on nuScenes.
Transfers zero-shot to SemanticKITTI and retains 92.8% of ideal mIoU under sensor packet loss and timestamp jitter.

figures.caption: Figure 16: Rain scene overview (nuScenes scene-0441). Left: front camera image showing wet road, reflections, and rain droplets. Right: LiDAR BEV coloured by height; the intersection geometry and parked vehicles are clearly visible despite rain-induced noise in the point cloud.

Figure 1: Overview of FreeOcc. Previous sweeps are encoded into BEV, fused by a continuoustime temporal aggregator, propagated to future ego frames by SE(2) warping, and decoded by the Discriminative Occupancy Decoder plus the Physics-Aware Continuous Flow Matching. The final prediction blends both paths using decoder uncertainty.

Figure 3: 4D occupancy forecasting on nuScenes(sample 1720) in BEV and 3D views across six horizons. FreeOcc-E is compared against OccWorld and ViDAR; more qualitative examples are given in Section D.

Figure 2: Ego-aware future propagator. At each horizon, the warped BEV—obtained via SE(2) ego-motion alignment—is explicitly added to the residual scene dynamics predicted by a ConvGRU and a residual projector.

Figure 10: Zero-shot SemanticKITTI predictions (sample 2070). BEV and 3D occupancy predictions from a nuScenes-trained model evaluated on SemanticKITTI, comparing FreeOcc-E against OccWorld and ViDAR. Despite domain differences (64-beam LiDAR, different driving context, no fine-tuning), FreeOcc-E preserves road-level structure and major obstacles. The denser 64-beam input provides richer geometric detail than nuScenes’s 32-beam data, and FreeOcc adapts without retraining, an advantage of operating on raw 3D geometry rather than appearance-dependent features.

Figure 6: Long-horizon comparison at τ=6 (3.0 s, nuScenes sample 3380). Ground Truth, OccWorld, FreeOcc-D, and FreeOcc-E are shown in paired BEV and 3D views. At 3.0 s, OccWorld exhibits boundary blur and noise around moving objects. FreeOcc-D slightly over-predicts occupancy, whereas FreeOcc-E preserves sharper boundaries and cleaner free space.

Figure 5: Temporal evolution of GT vs. FreeOcc-E (nuScenes sample 1730). Top row: groundtruth occupancy at τ=2 (1.0 s), τ=4 (2.0 s), and τ=6 (3.0 s), each shown as BEV (left) and 3D voxel rendering (right). Bottom row: corresponding FreeOcc-E predictions. Agreement is strongest at short horizons. By τ=6, the main discrepancies appear in the far field and around dynamic actors, while large static structures remain well preserved.

Figure 11: Additional zero-shot SemanticKITTI scene (sample 1080) and noise suppression analysis. Top: 3D occupancy predictions at the maximum forecasting horizon (τ = 6, 3.0s), comparing our model variants (FreeOcc-D, -G, -E) against Ground Truth. Bottom: BEV temporal evolution at τ = 3 and τ = 6. Road geometry, vegetation boundaries, and building walls are consistently captured, reinforcing the cross-domain robustness reported in Table 4.

Figure 7: 3D voxel-level uncertainty across prediction horizons (scene-0274, τ=1 to τ=6). Each panel renders occupied voxels coloured by the decoder’s predicted aleatoric uncertainty ŝv; cool tones indicate low uncertainty and warm tones indicate high. At short horizons, uncertainty is concentrated near dynamic actors and occupancy boundaries. As the horizon increases, uncertainty expands into the far field and intensifies around moving objects. By τ=6 (3.0 s), most remaining structures are assigned substantially higher uncertainty. This behaviour is consistent with the ensemble design in Section 3.7, which assigns more weight to the ODE path where decoder confidence weakens.

Figure 4: BEV visualization of 4D occupancy forecasting (additional scene, sample 0970). Columns span τ=1 to τ=6, comparing FreeOcc against OccWorld and ViDAR on a dense urban scene with multiple interacting vehicles. FreeOcc-E preserves scene layout and object extent more faithfully over the full 3.0 s horizon, whereas OccWorld and ViDAR drift more noticeably after τ=3.

Figure 8: Noise suppression analysis (nuScenes sample 1290). Paired BEV and 3D views highlighting hallucinated occupancy at long prediction horizons between FreeOcc-D and FreeOcc-E. FreeOcc-E clears vacated space more effectively while preserving plausible future object positions.

Figure 12: Robustness on nuScenes (τ = 4, 2.0s, sample 2500). Occupancy predictions under ideal and imperfect sensor conditions. FreeOcc-E retains its predictions under severe temporal perturbations, while OccWorld and ViDAR break into fragments and hallucinated clusters when temporal input is degraded.

Figure 13: Cross-domain robustness on SemanticKITTI (τ = 4, 2.0s, sample 2090). Zero-shot predictions under ideal (top two rows) and imperfect (bottom two rows) sensor conditions. The cross-domain robustness gap compounds both the sensor-domain shift (nuScenes→SemanticKITTI) and the temporal perturbation, yet FreeOcc-E retains recognisable road and object geometry in both cases, while OccWorld and ViDAR suffer severe structural collapse.

Figure 14: Robustness on nuScenes at τ=6 (3.0 s, sample 1600). Long-horizon predictions under ideal (top) and imperfect (bottom) sensor conditions. At the maximum forecasting horizon, OccWorld and ViDAR dissolve into discontiguous fragments, whereas FreeOcc-E preserves the road layout and principal object silhouettes. The gap between ideal and imperfect rows is noticeably smaller for FreeOcc-E than for OccWorld or ViDAR, consistent with the quantitative retention rate in Table 5.

Figure 15: Cross-domain robustness on SemanticKITTI at τ=6 (3.0 s, sample 2090). The most challenging evaluation setting: simultaneous cross-domain transfer, long-horizon prediction, and degraded sensor input. FreeOcc-E still recovers the overall road layout and major object boundaries, whereas OccWorld and ViDAR suffer near-complete structural collapse.

Figure 9: BEV uncertainty evolution (nuScenes scene-0220, τ=1 to τ=6). Each panel shows the BEV occupancy coloured by the predicted aleatoric uncertainty ŝv at horizon τ . Cool colours (cyan/green) indicate low uncertainty; warm colours (orange/red) indicate high uncertainty. Uncertainty increases with horizon and concentrates on dynamic objects and far-field voxels. papers.abstract: Autoregressive driving world models systematically suffer from structural drift, identity drift, and quality decay over long rollout horizons due to transient conditioning signals that lack persistent state. We present WAM-Sim, a driving world model anchored by a persistent hierarchical memory and optimized via online flow-matching RL. WAM-Sim structures persistent context across three temporal and semantic scales: pose-aligned structural tokens encoding persistent road topology, read-only scene tokens supplying geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens preserving individual traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. To restore visual sharpness and physical plausibility degraded by multi-scale conditioning, we introduce an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge. The invariant memory empirically confines policy optimization within the anchored context, helping suppress semantic collapse and reward hacking, while online RL systematically enforces physical commonsense and fine-grained visual fidelity. On the nuScenes benchmark, WAM-Sim achieves a superior generation fidelity (FID=3.47, FVD=25.72) and strong downstream perception performance (24.16 mAP, 71.23 road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, WAM-Sim substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, preserving high scene similarity and subject identity coherence across extended horizons. papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) for autonomous driving couple the driving policy and the visual world model in a single generative network whose objectives are fixed post-training. Conditioning on a new driving objective requires retraining. We study energy guidance as a general mechanism and present GuidedWAM, a model-agnostic framework for injecting driving objectives into frozen WAMs at sampling time. Our framework constructs each objective as differentiable energies on the sampler's intermediate clean-action estimate, which needs only forward access to the frozen model, and is stabilized by sampling-time guidance scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity-bounded correction. On the NAVSIM v2 hard-split, guidance improves all three frozen, publicly released WAMs by 1.8 to 3.6 EPDMS, averaged over three sampler seeds, and adds less than 10% to the sampling time per step. These results position energy guidance as a practical post-training control channel for WAMs.
bullets: Addresses the need to condition fixed-objective WAMs on new driving goals without retraining.
Applies model-agnostic energy guidance to intermediate clean-action estimates using only forward access to the frozen model.
Stabilizes guidance with scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity-bounded corrections.
Improves three frozen WAMs by 1.8–3.6 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 hard-split across three sampler seeds.
Adds less than 10% sampling time per step, supporting practical post-training control.

papers.abstract: Building a playable world requires more than generating plausible video: it demands responsive control, persistent spatial structure, and coherent interactions with dynamic entities. Using generated frames as the sole recurrent world representation ties these requirements to view-dependent appearance synthesis, making it difficult to maintain long-term spatial and temporal consistency in generation and interaction. We present PlayGen2, a real-time interactive world model that separates learned 3D state evolution from neural rendering. PlayGen2 maintains a persistent world memory comprising static geometry represented by a volumetric occupancy grid and identity-indexed 3D states for the player and other entities. Within a fixed-size local region, its world-state model jointly learns action-conditioned entity dynamics, geometry completion, and entity discovery, committing updates to a persistent world memory. A separate neural renderer synthesizes first-person observations from depth and semantic projections of the world state, without feeding generated images back into state prediction. Using Doom as a testbed, we demonstrate that the model successfully learns world dynamics including geometry-aware player motion and player--NPC interactions. The framework is computationally efficient, enabling the complete simulation and rendering pipeline to achieve approximately 160ms backend latency on a MacBook Pro with an M4 Pro chip. Beyond single-player interaction, we demonstrate zero-shot deployment on unseen Doom maps, multiplayer interaction through the composition of single-player models, and programmable gameplay through rule-based state interventions. These capabilities demonstrate the transferability and extensibility of the learned game-world model. Code and pretrained model weights are publicly available.
bullets: Targets the challenge of combining responsive control, persistent spatial structure, and coherent interactions in generated playable worlds.
Uses a persistent memory with a volumetric occupancy grid for static geometry and identity-indexed 3D states for players and other entities.
Jointly learns action-conditioned dynamics, geometry completion, and entity discovery within a local region, while a separate renderer generates first-person views.
In Doom, it models geometry-aware movement and player–NPC interactions, with an end-to-end backend latency of about 160 ms on an M4 Pro MacBook Pro.
Demonstrates zero-shot use on unseen maps, multiplayer via composition of single-player models, and programmable gameplay through rule-based state interventions.

papers.abstract: Robot world models predict action-conditioned future visual states to support robotic planning and decision making. However, visual reconstruction does not fully capture task progress, semantic evaluation alone provides limited constraints on fine-grained visual errors, and homogeneous predictions limit comparative feedback. We present RoboImagine, a framework for post-training autoregressive robotic world models through candidate-future comparisons with semantic and visual feedback. Diverse search promotes diversity among candidate trajectories under shared visual observations, action sequences, and task instructions. A frozen multimodal evaluator provides task-relevant semantic preferences through pairwise video comparisons in both presentation orders, complemented by pixel- and perceptual-level visual consistency feedback that constrains local structural and appearance errors. These signals drive policy optimization through group-relative advantages. Fixed initial context and branch-specific rolling histories support long-sequence generation with bounded context and consistent conditioning between candidate generation and policy optimization. Experiments with separately trained models on RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa cover real-world and simulated manipulation. On RT-1, under matched initialization, update counts, and evaluation protocols, RoboImagine improves PSNR by 1.26 dB and reduces LPIPS by 11.93% relative to continued supervised fine-tuning. Ablations show that diverse search improves prediction quality and that combined semantic and visual feedback yields higher external multimodal evaluation scores than visual feedback alone while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. Rolling histories further improve long-horizon prediction. These results support improving visual fidelity, task relevance, and long-horizon prediction through candidate comparison and complementary feedback.
bullets: Addresses the limits of relying on visual reconstruction or semantic feedback alone for evaluating robotic futures.
Uses diverse candidate trajectory search, pairwise multimodal semantic comparisons, and pixel/perceptual consistency signals.
Optimizes the model with group-relative advantages using fixed context and branch-specific rolling histories for long sequences.
Across RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa, experiments report improved visual fidelity on RT-1 over continued supervised fine-tuning under matched protocols.
Ablations indicate benefits from diverse search, combined feedback, and rolling histories; scope covers real-world and simulated manipulation.

papers.abstract: Selecting a next motion in a populated scene is not just a matter of avoiding what is currently in the way: an action can be locally feasible yet drift onto the road instead of the crosswalk, cut into a stream of crossing pedestrians, or bottleneck a narrow passage. These failure modes are invisible from the current state alone, and acting on them requires reasoning about what each candidate action will cause. World models offer exactly this, namely action-conditioned predictions of the future, but rolling them out at every decision step is a cost deployable navigation systems cannot pay, and the field has largely traded foresight for speed. We argue this is a false dichotomy. The natural place for a world model in human-aware navigation is at training time, as a preference oracle that distills foresight into a fast policy, rather than at inference time, as an online planner. We pair a discrete visual action prior with two task-aligned world models, one for nearby social dynamics and one for future scene semantics, that score candidate actions by their predicted consequences and refine the policy through group-relative preference distillation. At deployment, both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass. Across five held-out evaluation scenarios, this yields navigation that is simultaneously safer, more socially and group-coherent, and more goal-directed than strong reactive and learned baselines, with naive observers rating the resulting motion as more human-like. Taken together, our findings point to a different approach for bringing world-model foresight into deployable agents: not accelerating rollouts, but amortizing them into the policy so that the cost of looking ahead is confined to training. Project page: https://seoneun.github.io/-NeurIPS-2026-Seeing-Beyond-the-Next-Step/
bullets: Reactive navigation may choose locally feasible actions that cause unsafe, socially disruptive, or semantically inappropriate futures.
The method uses a discrete visual action prior and two task-aligned world models: one predicts nearby social dynamics, while the other predicts future scene semantics.
World models score candidate actions during training and guide group-relative preference distillation; they are removed at deployment for single-pass inference.
Across five held-out scenarios, the resulting policy is reported as safer, more socially and group-coherent, more goal-directed, and more human-like than reactive and learned baselines.
The approach confines the computational cost of foresight to training rather than performing online world-model rollouts.

In Stage 2, we further refine the policy with dual world models, which teaches the agent action–outcome knowledge by comparing plausible candidate actions according to their predicted social, semantic, and goal-directed consequences.
Figure 2: Overview of the training and evaluation scenes. We use six scenes in our experiments: Students003, ETH_Hotel, Zara01, ETH, ETH_Hallway, and ETH_Intersection.

We randomly sample 20 trajectory clips and visualize each real trajectory against its nearest anchor reconstruction from the K = 100 vocabulary. Blue solid lines denote real trajectory clips, and red dashed lines denote anchor reconstructions. The examples show that the 100-anchor vocabulary preserves the main direction, scale, and endpoint tendency of short-horizon pedestrian motion, supporting its use as a compact discrete action space.

Figure 12: Narrow-alley interaction with an approaching vehicle. Blue highlights indicate collision-prone trajectories produced by existing methods and the ablated variant, while green highlights show the collision-free trajectory produced by our method.

Figure 10: Additional qualitative comparison on group-coherent navigation. We compare CCP, CEDRL, GBM, and our method in a representative group-navigation scene. Each row shows a later timestep in the same rollout, and trajectory traces indicate recent motion over the previous 60 frames. The highlighted regions show representative failure modes of the baseline methods, including group separation, collision with a vehicle, and excessive group spread that causes group members to move into road regions. By contrast, our method maintains a more compact and coherent relation among group members while avoiding vehicles and road regions, producing trajectories that better preserve group-level motion and scene compliance.

Figure 3: Crosswalk navigation comparison. We compare CCP, CEDRL, GBM, and our method in a road-crossing scene with a marked pedestrian crosswalk. Red curves show each agent’s trajectory over the previous 60 frames. Blue boxes mark frames where the baselines leave the crosswalk and traverse road regions directly, indicating limited use of semantic scene cues. Our method, by contrast, remains on the crosswalk throughout the crossing, producing semantically compliant and pedestrian-like behavior. All trajectories are generated by the respective policies. In the second frame of ours, the agent moves along the crosswalk edge to avoid an oncoming pedestrian while staying on the crosswalk.

Figure 11: Qualitative ablation on the dual world models. We compare our full method with the variant without the dual world models in a representative closed-loop navigation scene; time runs from left to right. Without the dual world models, the agent shows typical failure cases such as less anticipatory interaction behavior, unstable trajectory adjustment, or reduced compliance with scene semantics. In contrast, the full model, refined with world-model-predicted consequences, produces more stable, safe, and scene-aware trajectories.

papers.abstract: Replay attacks are difficult to detect in vision-based control systems because previously recorded observations can remain plausible while the physical system follows a different trajectory. This paper develops an adaptive dynamic-watermarking framework for detecting replay attacks against vision-based controllers. A private Gaussian watermark is added to the nominal control input, and a control input-conditioned latent dynamics network (LDN) predicts the corresponding evolution in a compact latent space learned from image observations. Attack evidence is obtained from the discrepancy between the predicted latent response and the latent representation of the received image observation. A reinforcement learning policy adjusts the watermark covariance using the latent state and detector confidence, thereby balancing attack detectability, watermark energy, and control distortion. A Lagrangian penalty on task-specific safety costs is included during training to limit the adverse effect of the excitation. The framework is evaluated on a vision-guided UR5 manipulation task in which the robot reaches a target while avoiding a moving human arm under nominal and replay-attacked observations.
bullets: Addresses replay attacks where recorded camera observations remain plausible despite changed physical trajectories.
Adds private Gaussian noise to control inputs and predicts image-derived latent dynamics conditioned on those inputs.
Detects attacks through discrepancies between predicted latent responses and received-image latent representations.
Uses reinforcement learning to adapt watermark covariance based on latent state and detector confidence.
Evaluated on a vision-guided UR5 reaching-and-avoidance task under nominal and replay-attacked observations.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed framework. (a) The live observation xt−H is provided to the vision-based controller policy F , which predicts the control input ut−H . In parallel, an encoder maps xt−H to the latent state zt−H . The latent state, together with the detector confidence cj , is provided to the DWM policy to select the covariance Σt−H , from which the private watermark ϕt−H is sampled. The watermark and control input are combined to form the watermarked control input ūt−H , which is applied to the plant. (b) When a replay attack occurs, the encoder maps the received replayed observations to latent states [z′t−H+1, . . . , z ′ t]. These are compared with the predicted latent states [z̃t−H+1|t−H , . . . , z̃t|t−H ] to obtain the residual window rj , defined in (8). The MCUSUM detector processes this window, and the resulting evidence updates the attack confidence cj through (18). When attack evidence persists, the supervisor switches to the damped-stop controller and applies uds t as specified in (7).

papers.abstract: Video generation models (VGMs) offer strong spatiotemporal priors for embodied observation--action modeling. However, joint-space action vectors lack explicit image-space structure and vary in dimensionality and semantics across embodiments, making it challenging to directly leverage the rich spatiotemporal priors of VGMs. End-effector visualizations provide an alternative but do not specify the full articulated configuration needed for robot execution. We present Dream4ACT, a world model built for joint video-action modeling across embodiments. To unify action representations across embodiments, we introduce a shared visual action interface, called action views, which render target joint configurations from four prescribed virtual cameras using URDF-based forward kinematics. This shared visual representation preserves embodiment-specific articulated geometry while allowing observation and action sequences to share a video autoencoder and diffusion transformer. Through masked flow-matching, our model supports forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, and joint observation--action generation within a single jointly trained model by varying which future sequences are corrupted. To recover executable action sequences from predicted action views, we propose a training-free, URDF-constrained multiview recovery mechanism, without a learned embodiment-specific decoder. Dream4ACT achieves an average success rate of 88.98\% on RoboTwin~2.0 and an overall score of 65.66 on TriWorldBench, supporting effective closed-loop manipulation and competitive action-conditioned multiview prediction through the visual action interface.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between embodiment-specific joint-space actions and video models’ image-space representations.

Recovers executable actions with a training-free, URDF-constrained multiview procedure.
Reports an 88.98% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 65.66 overall score on TriWorldBench.

papers.abstract: Generative video models are increasingly used as visual world simulators, yet their primary strength lies in rendering plausible pixels rather than reasoning about how a world should evolve. Coherent world evolution requires more than visual fidelity: when an event occurs, a model must infer its consequences for the entities in the world and then render the resulting state. For example, after a wild beast appears, the model should not only depict the wild beast, but also infer whether a nearby person should flee, take cover, or fight back based on the realized scene. Existing diffusion-based video models lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining world state and reasoning over such event-conditioned consequences, often producing visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent outputs. To make this reasoning gap concrete and measurable, we propose a new problem, Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, which requires a model to render an event, reason about its consequences for the evolving world state, and reveal a causally plausible outcome as the world continues to evolve, even out of sight. As a baseline reference solution, we introduce EvoWorld, a brain-renderer collaboration framework in which a vision-language model serves as the world brain: it observes generated segments, maintains an evolving account of the world, and reasons about plausible state transitions, while a segment-autoregressive video renderer realizes them visually. We further introduce EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for training and evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency. Experiments show that EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency, establishing a reference point for reasoning-guided, autonomous world evolution beyond the current field of view.
authors: Yequan Bie, Dengyang Jiang, Zhixuan Chen, Xiaozhuan Liang, Haoxuan Che, Quande Liu, Xi Chen, Hao Chen

Provides EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency.

papers.abstract: We present a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation in Physical AI. By streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls, the framework enables users and embodied agents to interact with evolving virtual environments. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator. We demonstrate this approach across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. These examples provide a shared foundation for developing interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation. Our code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/nvidia/cosmos and https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/cosmos3-examples. The project website is available at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/cosmos-lab/cosmos-simulation.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a framework for real-time interactive world simulation using Cosmos foundation models, directly applicable to Physical AI, robot manipulation, and interactive world modeling.
papers.title: Interactive World Simulation with Cosmos for Physical AI
papers.tldr: A Cosmos-based framework enables real-time, action- and state-conditioned interactive world simulation for Physical AI training and evaluation.

papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents can improve decision-making with world-model foresight, provided that predicted states accurately reflect post-action interfaces. Existing state representations fail to jointly capture interface layout, UI semantics, and explicit locations. We introduce Typed Spatial Markdown (TSM), a Markdown-style textual state representation for desktop web interfaces. TSM serializes block-level and atomic-level UI elements according to their spatial relationships, jointly encoding their types, visual semantics, explicit locations, optional control states, and hierarchical membership. To train a screenshot-to-TSM renderer, we construct AtomBlock-WebUI, a dataset with precise annotations at both granularities. By injecting element-type labels into HTML and directly extracting bounding boxes after rendering, we avoid annotation errors caused by post-hoc inference from webpage structures. Building on TSM, we propose MKD2World, a desktop web world model trained in two stages for current-state description and action-conditioned next-state prediction. During inference, the web agent queries MKD2World as needed and performs a ``digest'' step, in which it interprets each predicted state and extracts task-relevant evidence for selecting the best action. Experiments show that MKD2World-9B achieves an EleF1 score of 26.50 on the out-of-domain test set, outperforming GPT-5.6-Sol(14.98) by 11.52 points. Across Online-Mind2Web tasks, MKD2World-9B improves the success rate of the Qwen3.5-35B web agent from 22.94% to 37.61%, achieving competitive performance among leading open-source GUI world models. Code is available at https://github.com/OmniAI-Lab-CUHKSZ/MKD2World.
authors: Zhihao Nan, Sifan Zhou, Yiming Cheng, Jinkai Zheng, Zheng Zhu, Si Shi, Ming Li, Fei Yu
bullets: TSM jointly represents UI layout, element types, visual semantics, locations, control states, and hierarchy.
AtomBlock-WebUI provides block- and atomic-level screenshot annotations for training screenshot-to-TSM rendering.
MKD2World predicts current and action-conditioned future web states, then digests them for task-relevant evidence.
MKD2World-9B achieves 26.50 EleF1 out of domain and raises Qwen3.5-35B agent success from 22.94% to 37.61% on Online-Mind2Web.
The approach targets desktop web interfaces and relies on spatially structured textual state predictions.

papers.abstract: Embodied video world models predict scene changes caused by robot actions, yet generated object responses may remain inconsistent with task intent and contact dynamics. Critical responses in embodied scenes often concentrate in local regions and specific time intervals. Inspired by chain-of-thought reasoning, we introduce ReactWorld, an embodied video generation model guided by structured interaction anticipation. In the generation backbone's feature space, an interaction response field predictor anticipates how the interaction will unfold, explicitly describing participant roles, future motion response intensity, and local motion changes. A response feedback adapter forms increments to object features from the difference between the object branch's outputs with predicted and zeroed local dynamics inputs. It also converts predicted displacements into positional biases for temporal attention. These two mechanisms guide object feature updates and information retrieval across frames, respectively. Through interaction anticipation and generative feedback, ReactWorld achieves an average score of 77.51 on RBench, outperforming PhysisForcing by 3.29 points with improvements in all nine categories. On EZS-Bench, it achieves a Domain score of 86.98 and an average score of 81.87.
authors: Hanwei Liu, Huijia Zhang, Hanzhang Wang, Guangyu Liu, Hanbei Zhan, Linjie Hu, Bin Xiao, Xuan Zhou, Dong Zhang
bullets: Targets inconsistent object responses to robot actions, especially in localized regions and time intervals.
Predicts participant roles, motion-response intensity, and local motion changes in a structured interaction response field.
Uses response feedback to update object features and convert predicted displacements into temporal-attention positional biases.
Scores 77.51 on RBench, 3.29 points above PhysisForcing, with gains across all nine categories.
Achieves an 86.98 Domain score and 81.87 average score on EZS-Bench.

papers.abstract: Recent video world models allow users to explore generated environments through camera navigation. Continuous hand motion provides a fine-grained action channel for interacting with the people and objects encountered during exploration. We present Touch\'{e}World, a framework that integrates gesture-driven interaction into a camera-controlled video world model. Given an initial image and a scene-description prompt, the model generates video conditioned on temporally aligned camera and hand controls. We construct joint camera--hand training data from heterogeneous egocentric videos through annotation completion, consistency-based filtering, and temporal alignment. Building on a pretrained camera-controlled world model, we combine spatial hand-skeleton conditioning with numerical hand-motion features through parameter-efficient adaptation. Causal adaptation and few-step distillation support chunk-level online generation, allowing users to update their controls based on generated visual feedback. We further introduce Touch\'{e}Bench to evaluate hand-motion following, camera--hand coordination, online interaction, and object response. Together, these components establish a framework for studying continuous exploration and hand-driven interaction within generative worlds.

bullets: Addresses the need for fine-grained hand interaction beyond camera-only navigation in video world models.

Builds joint training data from heterogeneous egocentric videos using annotation completion, consistency filtering, and temporal alignment.
Adapts a pretrained camera-controlled world model with hand-skeleton and numerical motion features using parameter-efficient methods.
Introduces chunk-level online generation and TouchéBench for evaluating hand following, camera–hand coordination, online interaction, and object response.

papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) support planning by comparing predicted latent states with an encoded goal. For this comparison to guide temporal progress, states closer in time to the goal should receive lower costs. However, training representations for prediction and distribution regularization does not directly enforce this ordering. We examine this mismatch in flat LeWorldModel (LeWM) by analyzing how its Euclidean goal cost changes with temporal separation. Our analysis identifies conditions under which states at different long offsets receive similar average costs, weakening their temporal distinction. To learn the missing ordering explicitly, we introduce Time-to-Goal (T2G), a lightweight metric trained on latent triples from offline trajectories. A margin ranking loss encourages smaller distances for temporally nearer states, requiring no rewards or policy labels. The learned metric then replaces the Euclidean planning cost while the JEPA encoder and predictor remain frozen. Diagnostics on AntMaze and FourRoom show that T2G preserves stronger temporal contrast and improves near--far ranking at long offsets. Across four navigation and manipulation benchmarks, T2G improves the average planning success rate from 32.7\% (flat LeWM) to 63.0\% and approaches or even surpasses the performance of the hierarchical H-JEPA baselines. These results show that learning temporal ordering for the goal cost can substantially improve latent planning even with a flat world model.
bullets: Flat JEPA Euclidean goal costs may fail to distinguish states by temporal proximity, especially at long offsets.
T2G trains a lightweight metric on offline trajectory latent triples using a margin-ranking loss, without rewards or policy labels.
The metric replaces Euclidean planning costs while keeping the JEPA encoder and predictor frozen.
Diagnostics show stronger temporal contrast and improved near–far ranking on AntMaze and FourRoom.
Across four benchmarks, average success rises from 32.7% to 63.0%, matching or surpassing hierarchical H-JEPA baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of T2G metric training. A latent triple (zt, zt+k, zt+k+∆) is sampled from an offline trajectory, where the near and far states are separated from the anchor by k and k+∆ steps, respectively. The three encoder blocks denote the same frozen JEPA encoder applied to the corresponding observations. T2G evaluates the learned temporal distances from the anchor to the near and far latents and optimizes the metric with a margin ranking objective, so that the near state is closer to the anchor than the far state by at least a margin m. Only the metric network and its scale are updated, and the world model remains frozen.

Figure 6: Temporal guidance of Euclidean squared and T2G costs on recorded AntMaze (top) and FourRoom (bottom) executions. Right: the fraction of comparisons in which the temporally nearer state receives a lower cost, with ties receiving half credit; the dashed line marks 50%. Horizontal axes report temporal separation in environment steps. At long offsets, T2G maintains a larger positive contrast and higher ranking accuracy in both environments.

Figure 4: Overview of T2G planning. The current observation o1 and goal observation og are encoded into latents z1 and zg by the frozen JEPA encoder. A solver optimizes an action sequence a1:H , and the frozen predictor rolls out the resulting latent trajectory z1→z2→· · ·→zH . Each predicted latent is scored by its learned temporal distance to the goal, dθ(zt, zg), and the solver updates the actions to minimize the aggregated cost. The updated actions are executed and planning is repeated from new observations in a receding-horizon loop, while the encoder, predictor, and solver remain unchanged.

papers.abstract: Large language models understand passengers' driving commands, but as driving agents they reason in generated text for seconds and must infer each action's consequences implicitly from the scene. We present Jev-AD, which pairs Jev, a typed decision model that answers predefined questions with probabilities, not generated text, with a language world model that predicts for every candidate action how nearby vehicles move over the next two seconds. Code turns these predictions into foreseen consequences, which Jev compares instead of inferring them from coordinates. In simulated highway merging (500 car-episodes), this foresight lowers the same decision model's collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% at 0.25 seconds per decision, and Jev-AD achieves the passenger's intent in 93% of free-form command trials. In 500 replayed real-world NGSIM episodes, foresight lowers the collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%, and the world model, learned from this traffic, foresees 93% of dangerous actions. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/jev-ad-website.
authors: Yansong Qu, Jiancong Chen, Samuel Labi
bullets: Addresses the risk that language-based driving agents reason too slowly and infer action consequences implicitly.
Combines Jev, a typed probabilistic decision model, with a language world model forecasting two seconds of surrounding-vehicle motion.
Uses code to convert forecasts into explicit consequences that Jev compares across candidate actions.
In simulated highway merging, foresight reduced collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% while maintaining 0.25-second decision latency.
Across free-form commands and replayed NGSIM episodes, the system achieved 93% intent fulfillment and reduced replay collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%.

papers.abstract: Cascade world-action models (WAMs) use predicted visual futures to condition robot actions, but inherit costly iterative inference from diffusion-pretrained experts. We ask what a single-step predicted future must preserve to support accurate single-step action prediction. In the evaluated WAM, resampling video noise has little effect on downstream actions, yet naively truncating both streams to one step substantially reduces task success. Video-space supervision only partially closes this gap, and a local sensitivity analysis shows that vision prediction errors have highly unequal consequences for action accuracy. These findings motivate DirectWAM, which converts pretrained video and action experts into single-step predictors without stochastic sampling through action-sufficient distillation, while retaining the explicit future-to-action cascade. After learning a one-step action model, we train the future predictor by decoding actions from its own predicted futures and backpropagating demonstration action error through the expert, with an optional future-latent reconstruction loss. The resulting objective evaluates the student-generated future through its downstream control consequences rather than relying on representation matching alone. DirectWAM achieves 97.1% average success across four LIBERO suites and 85.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming Flash-WAM at the same one-evaluation-per-stream budget. This advantage has also extended to three real-world tasks that we designed. Compared with the full iterative teacher, it reduces inference latency by $28.0\times$.
bullets: WAMs can lose task success when diffusion inference is naively reduced to one step, even though video-noise resampling has little effect on actions.
Vision prediction errors have unequal impacts on action accuracy, motivating action-sufficient rather than purely representation-matching distillation.
DirectWAM retains the future-to-action cascade and trains the future predictor through downstream demonstration-action error, with optional future-latent reconstruction.
It achieves 97.1% average success on four LIBERO suites and 85.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming Flash-WAM at the same inference budget.
The method also extends to three designed real-world tasks and reduces latency 28.0× versus the full iterative teacher.

papers.abstract: Although existing candidate trajectory evaluators have substantially improved end-to-end planning accuracy, their underlying mechanism remains suboptimal. Model-based evaluators typically make scoring future-aware by explicitly predicting candidate-conditioned future states over the planning horizon, which we term rollout. However, rollout incurs high inference cost and accumulates prediction errors. We argue that planning does not require reconstructing a full future scene for each candidate, but only future-relevant information for reliable comparison. We therefore propose RFWorld, a Rollout-Free World model for end-to-end trajectory evaluation. RFWorld constructs a shared scene memory and shapes it into a future-readable representation via lightweight training-time temporal readout with semantic supervision, keeping training overhead low. At inference time, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory via sparse spatial readout for scoring, reducing computation by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidate trajectories, while avoiding recursive rollout errors. Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive show that RFWorld learns a more planning-aligned world representation and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Junzhe Wang, Jinqing Zhang, Qingjie Liu
bullets: Existing rollout-based evaluators are costly and accumulate prediction errors over the planning horizon.
RFWorld builds a shared scene memory and trains it with lightweight temporally supervised readout to encode future-relevant information.
At inference, candidate trajectories sparsely query the shared memory instead of generating candidate-specific future states.
This reduces computation by roughly the planning horizon multiplied by the number of candidates.
Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive report state-of-the-art performance and more planning-aligned representations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall framework of RFWorld. The current BEV representation is transformed into a shared memory. During inference, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory for reward prediction, and the trajectory with highest score is selected as the final planning output.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video generation models distill internet-scale motion priors into robot policies, but full video is a redundant signal for action prediction. We argue that dense 3D motion is the medium through which video pretraining best transfers to robot actions, and that predicting motion rather than video affords better sample-efficiency for action prediction. FloMo is a 5B video-generation model fine-tuned to predict 3D scene-flow and action tokens. Rendering scene flow as RGB and encoding it into the same latent space as video enables a pretrained video generation backbone to efficiently adapt to predict 3D scene flow. Co-trained on action-free human video and action-labeled robot teleoperation data, our model benefits from human-video pretraining and generalizes to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks. Replacing motion prediction with a video prediction objective degrades out-of-distribution generalization, while adding a video prediction target alongside motion lowers policy success rather than improving it. When motion, video, and action are predicted jointly, action tokens attend far more to motion than to video, suggesting that predicting video wastes model capacity. Together, these results indicate that motion effectively mediates the transfer from video pretraining to action. More information can be found at flomo-wam.github.io.
authors: Jeremy Collins, Namra Patel, Ayush Agarwal, Shitij Govil, Animesh Garg
bullets: Motivation: Full video is redundant for action prediction; dense 3D motion may transfer video-learned priors more effectively.
Method: A 5B video-generation model is fine-tuned to predict 3D scene flow and action tokens, using rendered flow encoded in the video model’s latent space.
Training: The model combines action-free human video with action-labeled robot teleoperation data.

Findings: Motion prediction supports generalization to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks; replacing or augmenting it with video prediction harms policy success and out-of-distribution generalization.
Interpretation: Action tokens attend substantially more to motion than video, indicating that video prediction can waste model capacity.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by jointly modeling visual dynamics and robot actions. However, most existing WAMs model dense short-horizon visual dynamics, capturing local interactions but providing limited long-range task context. Extending prediction horizons increases uncertainty and computation while entangling task-level evolution with fine-grained local dynamics, obscuring their dependencies and distinct roles in action generation. We propose HiLo-WAM, which decouples long-horizon task evolution from local visual dynamics while jointly modeling their interaction with robot actions. A sparse long-horizon visual stream captures historical task context and future evolution, while a dense local dynamics visual stream models short-horizon robot-object interactions. The two streams operate at different temporal scales within a unified dual-DiT architecture and guide actions through structured cross-stream attention. Progressive inference further reduces unnecessary computation through stream-wise partial denoising, joint denoising, and dynamic skipping. Experiments demonstrate strong long-horizon manipulation performance: HiLo-WAM achieves a 93.70% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with robust in-domain and OOD performance on the Fourier GR-3 robot. Ablations confirm the complementary contributions of long-horizon task evolution and local interaction dynamics, while temporal-scale analyses highlight the importance of balancing temporal coverage and resolution. Progressive inference further achieves a 2.93x speedup while improving performance.
authors: Xingyu Wang, Yanjiang Guo, Zhijing Ding, Jiaxin Fang, Zeyu Lai, Jiayu Dong, Weikang Wan, Jianyu Chen, Yuxiang Gao, Mengdi Xu
bullets: Addresses the limited long-range context and high computational cost of dense short-horizon WAM prediction.
Uses sparse long-horizon and dense local-dynamics visual streams at different temporal scales.
A unified dual-DiT architecture connects the streams with structured cross-stream attention to guide actions.
Progressive inference with partial, joint, and dynamically skipped denoising achieves a reported 2.93× speedup.
Reports 93.70% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with in-domain and OOD performance on Fourier GR-3.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of HiLo-WAM. HiLo-WAM builds on a dual-DiT World Action Model consisting of a shared Video DiT and an Action DiT. The visual world is modeled at two complementary temporal scales: a sparse long-horizon visual stream captures historical context and coarse future evolution, while a dense local visual dynamics stream captures fine-grained local interactions. Both visual streams are jointly modeled with robot actions. During inference, the visual streams progressively terminate and are cached, while the action stream continues denoising to completion.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison between Fast-WAM and HiLo-WAM in simulation and realworld tasks. papers.abstract: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body motion and hand interaction over time, and a plausible-looking command sequence can still drop a held object or leave an interaction incomplete. We present action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world-action model (WAM) that evaluates proposed command sequences before execution. An action generator proposes joint motion-hand command sequences from vision, language, and the robot state. An action-conditioned endpoint predictor estimates the visual features each sequence prefix reaches and measures progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, while a joint temporal prior scores temporal consistency given the robot state and preceding commands. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation. During training, action consistency regularization reconstructs the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predictor to retain action-relevant information. On ten tasks in the humanoid loco-manipulation simulation benchmark SIMPLE, our method achieves 89.7% average success, compared with 73.7% for Psi-Zero and 82.0% for DiT4DiT. On seven real-robot tasks, it achieves 85.7% under standard conditions and 65.7% under unseen object configurations, while GR00T N1.7 achieves 70.0% and 48.6%, respectively. Project page: https://ju6276.github.io/Action-Grounded-Foresight/
authors: Ju Dong, Xinyu Xiao, Yiming Zhou, Tianshuo Yang, Xuerong Liu, Lei Zhang, Jian Chen, Haocheng Zhao, Yu Fu, Yujie Wei, Diwen Zheng, Alois Christian Knoll, Angela P. Schoellig, Ping Luo, Jianwei Zhang

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video modeling have driven substantial progress in world action models (WAMs). Existing approaches exploit pretrained video priors by decoding actions from latent representations or inferring them from generated videos. The underlying link is causal: robot actions produce changes in the scene, and video observations of these changes provide evidence for inferring the actions that produced them. However, existing training formulations do not by themselves ensure that actions and their predicted visual consequences are consistent, potentially limiting the use of pretrained capabilities. We treat video and action as paired modalities linked by this causal relationship and learn their correspondence through a unified training framework designed to better exploit pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM first augments video-action co-training with bidirectional conversion to reinforce cross-modal correspondence and recover forward and inverse dynamics. It then introduces a differentiable cycle-reconstruction objective to further couple the two mappings. The resulting model supports both forward and inverse dynamics, with the potential to improve performance through more effective use of pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance among comparable methods on LIBERO-Pro and substantially improves DreamZero on DROID. Comparisons with UWM characterize its inverse-dynamics performance and show sharper visual detail in the displayed forward-dynamics predictions.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use the predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models for robot control through future video prediction. However, iterative video denoising is costly, and inaccurate visual predictions can compromise action prediction. Our key idea is to make this predictive knowledge available through visual representations computed from the current observation, enabling action prediction without generating future videos. We introduce DreamFree, a WAM that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a predictive visual encoder through representation distillation. The visual encoder learns to predict a frozen video diffusion model's representation using only the current observation. An action module is then trained to predict actions by extracting action-relevant information from the visual encoder. Across real-world and simulated tasks, DreamFree achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs, while performing real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz with a 14B video diffusion backbone. Experiments show that DreamFree can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control and enable learning new robot tasks from video demonstrations, including videos from a different embodiment, without action annotation for the new tasks.

papers.abstract: Predicting how the world evolves in response to robot actions is central to policy learning, evaluation, and planning. However, many action-conditioned world models predict future observations in 2D image or video space without explicitly modeling the underlying 3D scene, making spatial consistency across viewpoints and over long-horizon interactions challenging. We introduce 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework that jointly predicts appearance, geometry, and tactile observations from a unified 3D representation. Our approach combines a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents with an action-conditioned latent dynamics model that predicts their evolution. The shared 3D representation supports geometrically consistent rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and flexible integration of spatially aligned tactile signals. Our experiments demonstrate interactive, long-horizon, multimodal prediction at 50 Hz. We then show how our model enables scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation using tactile and multi-view visual observations, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views. Furthermore, we scale our method to large datasets containing diverse objects and demonstrate model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations. Together, these results highlight the potential of hybrid particle-voxel dynamics as a foundation for multimodal 3D world simulation.
authors: Jimmy Wang, Yifan Chou, Kaifeng Zhang, Yixuan Wang, Binghao Huang, Tao Yu, Saleh Nabi, Yunzhu Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining 3D spatial consistency across viewpoints and extended interactions.

Supports interactive multimodal prediction at 50 Hz, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views.
Enables scalable policy data generation, evaluation, and planning with unseen objects and robot configurations.

This voxel latent is progressively upsampled into finer voxels, which are then upsampled into dense visual particles and optional tactile particles. Each visual particle is attached to Gaussian parameters that can be rendered at novel viewpoints. (b) Our 3D latent dynamics model then directly operates on voxel latents produced by the autoencoder. Given robot actions, history latents, and a current latent observation, the dynamics model uses 3D convolutions and spatiotemporal attention to autoregressively predict future voxel latents during open-loop rollouts. These latents can then be decoded into point clouds, multi-view renders, and tactile observations.

papers.abstract: Scientific agents can find interventions that work without understanding why they do. We study this failure mode in controlled synthetic regulatory systems, where agents must experimentally identify a hidden fault and rescue the resulting phenotype. Across seven LLMs, every model restores the healthy phenotypes more often than it identifies the fault. Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 rescue every organism while diagnosing only 55% and 35% of them. This failure is not simply due to insufficient exploration or unavailable evidence. In most cases, the cause is experimentally identifiable, and agents encounter evidence that distinguishes competing causes in 91% of relevant sessions, and still frequently misdiagnose the system. Targeted probes reveal where experimental reasoning breaks down. Models reliably interpret decisive evidence and revise hypotheses when the causal comparison is explicit, and can locate that evidence within a full experimental record. However, they struggle to predict the outcome of the experiment under each competing cause, a necessary step in using the observed result to distinguish between them. Agents can therefore gather the right evidence and still infer the wrong cause. As AI systems take on a growing role in synthesising scientific evidence, these findings highlight the need to evaluate how they use evidence to reach causal conclusions, alongside whether their interventions succeed.
authors: Anna Gogleva, Thomas Charman, Martin Balla, Karl Gemayel
bullets: In controlled synthetic regulatory systems, all seven evaluated LLMs restored healthy phenotypes more often than they diagnosed the hidden fault.
The strongest agents rescued every organism but diagnosed only 55% and 35% of cases, respectively.
Misdiagnosis persisted despite agents encountering evidence distinguishing competing causes in 91% of relevant sessions.
Models could interpret decisive evidence and revise hypotheses when causal comparisons were explicit, but struggled to predict outcomes under each competing cause.
Evaluations of scientific AI should assess causal inference and evidence use, not only intervention success.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Tracing the diagnosis–rescue gap through the investigation. Successive analyses rule out insufficient exploration and, for most systems, missing evidence, while bidirectional testing (dashed box) marks a correlate of successful diagnosis. Probes localise the remaining failure: models interpret and revise on isolated evidence, and still locate it inside a full record, but cannot derive what each competing cause predicts.

Figure 1: Controlled experimental environment. (a) A synthetic organism maps environmental inputs through an unknown gene regulatory network to three observable phenotypes; one example hidden fault is highlighted. Agents cannot observe the network directly and must learn about the system through perturbations. (b) Each session proceeds under a fixed experimental budget. All sessions include exploration and prediction; disease sessions additionally require diagnosis of a hidden fault followed by an intervention to rescue the phenotypes.

Figure 7: Evidence use breaks in context. (a) Each probe shows more of the investigation and gives less help with it: the two competing causes, the readout each one predicts, both, or neither. (b) Accuracy on decisive evidence, each gray line represents a model; per-model values are in Tables 5 and 6. Accuracy stays close to 1.00 for as long as the predicted readouts are given (Probes 1–2 and 3a), falls once the models must work them out (3b–c), and falls further in live sessions.

Figure 3: Exploration does not simply explain diagnostic success. (a) Models differ substantially in both the number of experiments they run and the ratio of genes they probe. (b) Within each model, sessions above versus below its median experiment count show no consistent advantage from greater exploration.

Figure 4: Alternative hypotheses and discriminating experiments. (a) Two different faults can produce the same abnormal readout, leaving both as plausible causes. (b) An experiment is discriminating if its outcome differs depending on which fault is present. Values in (a) and (b) are illustrative. (c) We classify the 60 organisms by whether an alternative fault fits the initial observation and, if so, whether an available experiment can distinguish it from the true fault.

Figure 2: The diagnosis–rescue gap. (a) A downstream gene can provide a plausible diagnosis and rescue target, restoring the phenotype without correcting the true fault. The shaded band marks the three G008 probes of Figure 6; the dashed line marks the commit; the red segment at experiment 22 is the post-commit refutation.

Figure 5: Agents usually encounter discriminating evidence, but barely use it. Each point shows, for one organism with a resolvable alternative (n = 43), how often agents choose discriminating experiments relative to random choice. Agents show only a small preference above chance (24.1% vs. 19.2%). Nevertheless, 91% of sessions encounter discriminating evidence before diagnosis, yet diagnosis accuracy in those sessions is only 0.30.

Figure 6: One agent holds the evidence and commits against it. Experiments 5–7 probe the agent’s eventual diagnosis, G008, in three directions. papers.abstract: Recent work has improved computer-use agents (CUAs) by combining retrieved task-relevant tutorials and look-ahead planning using world models with MLLM judges. However, the contribution of each component -- tutorials, the judge, and the world model -- to overall improvement has not been evaluated in isolation. To fill this gap, we first construct OSWorld-Tutorial and ScienceBoard-Tutorial: two datasets for CUAs with curated multimodal tutorials, covering everyday and scientific domains. We then propose RAG-PolicyJudge (RAG-PJ), a policy-judge framework for CUAs conditioned on task-specific tutorials: the policy proposes candidate actions, and the judge selects among them. To isolate the effect of world models given tutorials, we compare RAG-PJ with and without common world models: using either zero-shot text-based descriptions of next states or an oracle that returns ground-truth visual observations. We find that RAG-PJ gains little benefit from these rollouts when tutorials are present, even with perfect visual futures. This suggests prior world-model gains in tutorial-conditioned methods come mainly from tutorial understanding and the judge's ability to select the proposed actions, rather than from predicted rollouts. Error analysis reveals that the bottleneck is not rollout fidelity, but the judge's ability to reason over future states and recognize task completion. This highlights the need to improve not just next-state prediction in world models, but also reasoning over their predicted rollouts. Datasets and code are available at https://github.com/realjoenguyen/RAGPJ-official.
authors: Anh Nguyen, Tianyi Xu, Phat Tran, Harry Yu, Huazheng Wang, Stefan Lee
bullets: Introduces OSWorld-Tutorial and ScienceBoard-Tutorial, covering everyday and scientific computer-use tasks with curated multimodal tutorials.
Proposes RAG-PolicyJudge, where a policy generates candidate actions and a judge selects among them.
Compares tutorial-conditioned agents with and without text-based or oracle visual world-model rollouts.
Finds little benefit from rollouts even with perfect visual futures, suggesting gains mainly come from tutorial understanding and action selection.
Error analysis identifies future-state reasoning and task-completion recognition as key bottlenecks.

papers.abstract: Learned temporal models are moving beyond offline forecasting toward interactive environments for decision making, yet logged-trajectory accuracy need not predict closed-loop behavior under policies optimized in the learned model. This forecasting-control gap matters in tokamak magnetic control, where coupled plasma-circuit dynamics and actuator constraints can amplify errors through feedback. Using a calibrated free-boundary Grad-Shafranov solver, we collect four datasets in a 2x2 design over physics-parameter and current-reference coverage. At matched budgets of 500, 1k, 3k, and 5k rollouts, we train 16 action-conditioned Transformers; PPO policies optimized in the 5k surrogates are then evaluated without adaptation on six reference-solver conditions. Only joint-coverage D4 shows monotonically decreasing cross-condition mean error, whereas D1 improves in distribution but degrades out of distribution. Binary completion masks substantial closed-loop differences: D2-D4 each complete 83.3% of conditions, but reach on average 99.0%, 94.7%, and 90.5% of the evaluation horizon, while their worst conditions reach 94.2%, 68.2%, and 43.2%. Policies trained with action noise complete 5/24 matched conditions, compared with 19/24 under nominal training, and have a lower mean horizon-capped episode length. Based on one trained policy per configuration and one evaluation realization per condition, the results support combining prediction error, episode completion, condition-level duration, and tracking quality.
authors: Guoyang Shi, Siqi Ding, Xuanhe Wang, Pei Guo, Changquan Yu, Jiale Hu, Jiayi Zhi, Zhengyuan Chen, Jianguo Chen, Tianyuan Liu
bullets: Forecasting accuracy on logged trajectories does not necessarily predict feedback-control performance.

papers.abstract: Evaluating end-to-end autonomous driving under rare, safety-critical vehicle-pedestrian interactions requires photorealistic, sensor-level scenarios. However, trajectory-based scenario generators cannot synthesize raw visual observations, whereas video-based approaches lack controllability. To bridge this gap, we present ControlPed, a novel framework that combines trajectory-level conflict synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to generate photorealistic, motion-controllable safety-critical scenarios. Built upon HazardPed, a dataset derived from 10,352 traffic videos comprising 422 conflict trajectories, HD maps, and 857 annotated 3D human motions, ControlPed first generates conflict trajectories, lifts them into 3D human motion sequences via text-conditioned motion diffusion, and finally renders multi-view sensor observations using animatable 3DGS avatars. Safety evaluation in 88 rendered photorealistic scenarios reveals that seven leading end-to-end driving models suffer a severe performance drop, with their mean HDScore plunging from 88.8 to 47.4, exposing major failure modes under dangerous pedestrian behaviors. The dataset and testing benchmarks will be released to facilitate safety assessment of vehicle-pedestrian interactions.
bullets: Addresses the gap between controllable trajectory generators and video-based methods that cannot synthesize raw sensor observations.
Combines conflict-trajectory synthesis, text-conditioned motion diffusion, and animatable 3D Gaussian Splatting avatars.
Built on HazardPed, which includes traffic videos, conflict trajectories, HD maps, and annotated 3D human motions.
In 88 rendered scenarios, seven end-to-end driving models’ mean HDScore fell from 88.8 to 47.4, revealing failures under risky pedestrian behavior.
The dataset and evaluation benchmarks are planned for release to support vehicle–pedestrian safety assessment.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly generate actions and imagined futures, but a plausible prediction need not be realized by its co-generated action. We introduce WISE (\emph{World Action Inference Scaling through Evaluation}), a pre-execution selector that scores each sampled rollout on action validity and temporal regularity, inverse-dynamics consistency between the proposed action and the imagined motion, and instruction-conditioned task progress, and executes the highest-scoring candidate while keeping the WAM frozen. With four candidates per decision, WISE raises closed-loop success from 6.0\% to 24.0\% on RoboLab with Cosmos~3 Edge and from 75.1\% to 78.3\% mean success on LIBERO with DreamZero, and exceeds the best existing selector in aggregate by 4.0 and 0.9 points. Component ablations and agreement analyses show that the three scores rank candidates differently and that task progress carries the largest weight in the fused decision.
bullets: Addresses the gap between plausible imagined futures and actions that actually succeed.
Scores sampled rollouts using action validity and temporal regularity, inverse-dynamics consistency, and instruction-conditioned task progress.
Executes the highest-scoring candidate without updating the underlying world action model.
With four candidates, success increases from 6.0% to 24.0% on RoboLab and from 75.1% to 78.3% on LIBERO.
Task progress contributes the largest weight, while the three scoring components rank candidates differently.

The IDM maps imagined frames back to actions for comparison with the candidate’s proposed controls; the task evaluator scores progress at the final imagined frame. WISE sums the scores, executes the selected action chunk, and observes the resulting state before replanning.

papers.abstract: In the prediction and control of physical systems, combining records from different experiments and operations is expected to supply information that no single experiment provides on its own. Time-series foundation models, which learn a shared predictor from diverse time series, offer a framework for treating such records as a common training resource. Moreover, query-based prediction models, which switch between known and target signals within the same time series, make it possible to handle response prediction and control-input generation in a unified manner. However, in control-experiment data, the connections between signals change with the experimental stage, such as system identification, filtering, and feedback control, which calls for a formulation that handles signal values and connection structures dynamically and in a unified way. We formulate a control foundation model that defines a data space of dynamic graphs containing connections, signal values, and missing values, together with an operation on this space that specifies the known signals and the prediction targets. This allows response prediction and control-input generation to be described as a common masked prediction problem, even for experimental data with different connections and recorded signals. The Block Diagram Transformer (BDT), which implements this formulation, combines attention along the time axis with a graph neural network that follows the block-diagram connections, and can be initialized with the pretrained parameters of existing time-series foundation models. Trained on control-experiment data that mix multiple experimental settings, the proposed model stabilized an unstable system through feedback control, which is difficult to achieve by fine-tuning existing time-series foundation models. Ongoing work applying this approach to a wide range of target systems is also yielding promising results.
bullets: Addresses control data whose signal connections change across stages such as identification, filtering, and feedback.
Formulates response prediction and control-input generation as one masked prediction problem over dynamic graphs with missing values.
Introduces the Block Diagram Transformer (BDT), combining temporal attention with a graph neural network guided by block-diagram connections.
BDT can be initialized from pretrained time-series foundation models and trained on mixed control-experiment settings.
The model stabilized an unstable system through feedback control, an outcome reported as difficult for fine-tuned existing time-series foundation models.
