papers.abstract: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.
authors: Zhifei Hu, Alexandra I. Cristea, Adel Bibi, Jialin Yu
bullets: A human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models found 86.1% semantically plausible, but several models overused BLOCK and missed clarifiable ASK cases.
The paper defines safety sufficiency as preserving and exposing evidence needed for policy-conditioned authorisation decisions.
SafeWebWorld benchmarks safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains using action-conditioned futures, decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions.
Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning improved evidence preservation but could worsen authorisation-sensitive decisions.
Latent Authorisation Recovery recovered some performance through score recalibration, but fine-grained and matched-authorisation behaviour remained poor.

papers.abstract: Vehicle-infrastructure cooperation can complement onboard sensing with broader and more informative observations of the traffic environment, providing valuable support for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing cooperative driving methods mainly exploit roadside information to enhance the representation of the current scene, while the future consequences of prospective driving actions are rarely modeled explicitly. This limits the ability of the planner to anticipate how its decisions may interact with the evolving traffic environment. To address this issue, we propose V2X-WAM, a cooperative world action model that tightly couples cooperative scene understanding, action generation, and future-world reasoning. V2X-WAM constructs a reliability-aware spatiotemporal representation from vehicle- and infrastructure-side observations, while compressing infrastructure information into a compact quantized message for efficient communication. Based on the resulting cooperative representation, a multimodal planner generates prospective trajectories, which explicitly condition future occupancy and dynamic-flow prediction. The predicted world consequences are then fed back to refine the planned trajectory, forming a closed interaction between action and future-world evolution. Experiments on a large-scale real-world cooperative driving dataset demonstrate that V2X-WAM consistently improves planning accuracy and safety over representative end-to-end cooperative driving methods, while achieving stronger future-world prediction and substantially lower communication overhead. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the proposed design.
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing V2X methods mainly represent the current scene without explicitly modeling action consequences.
Builds a reliability-aware spatiotemporal representation from vehicle and infrastructure observations, with infrastructure data compressed into a quantized message.
Uses a multimodal planner whose candidate trajectories condition future occupancy and dynamic-flow predictions.
Feeds predicted future-world consequences back into trajectory planning, creating a closed action–world interaction loop.
Experiments show improved planning accuracy and safety, stronger future-world prediction, and substantially lower communication overhead; ablations support the design.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at instruction following, yet most remain feed-forward: they condition actions only on the current observation and discard both long-horizon temporal context and the hierarchical structure of VLM representations. We present PRIME W0, a hierarchical conditional flow-matching framework that closes this gap through three synergistic designs: (1)per-layer KV injection from a pretrained VLM into an Adaptive MoE action expert; (2)dynamics-aware conditioning via asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and a DINOv2 historical-frame semantic bridge; and (3)Action Dynamic Manifold (ADM) flow matching with covariance-structured noise that respects robot kinematic coupling. PRIME W0 is trained in four stages---VLM pre-training, DAT/NTP visuomotor pre-training, DiT flow-matching decoder assembly with WM injection, and end-to-end SFT---and achieves state-of-the-art results on LIBERO and real-robot benchmarks, with systematic ablations validating each architectural component.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of feed-forward VLA models, which ignore long-horizon context and hierarchical visual-language representations.
Injects pretrained VLM key-value features into an adaptive mixture-of-experts action module.
Uses asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and DINOv2 historical-frame features for dynamics-aware temporal conditioning.
Applies covariance-structured flow matching on an Action Dynamic Manifold to model coupled robot actions.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO and real-robot benchmarks, with ablations supporting the proposed components.

figures.caption: Figure 1: PRIME W0 architecture.

Figure 2: Four-stage training pipeline. (1) VLM Pretrain: the vision–language backbone is trained on general multimodal supervision (e.g. captioning / VQA). (2) NTP / task-specific pre-training: with DAT action tokens, the VLM learns visuomotor next-token prediction over instruction–observation–action sequences. (3) DiT Pretrain: the VLM is frozen while the MoT / Adaptive MoE flow-matching action expert is trained with world-model conditioning to denoise continuous actions (and associated state tokens). (4) SFT: both the VLM and the action expert are jointly fine-tuned end-to-end, optionally with action-prefix tokens that shorten the denoising trajectory at inference. Flame / snowflake icons indicate trainable vs. frozen modules.

papers.abstract: World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery.
authors: Tobias Schmidt, Rodrigo Gonzalez Laiz, Kriszti\'an Szuppinger, Steffen Schneider
bullets: Targets world models that control effectively but may not faithfully represent environment dynamics.
Learns latent dynamics without reward information and maintains accurate predictions over long horizons.
Uses at least an order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2, and LeWM.
Achieves state-of-the-art pixel-based control in continuous environments.
Accurately identifies systems across a benchmark of 71 attractors, illustrating potential for scientific discovery.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models generate visual content conditioned on user actions, yet maintaining spatial consistency over long-horizon exploration in real time remains challenging. Existing approaches rely on either temporal context or explicit 3D memory, both of which scale poorly because memory grows with the length of the generated stream. Moreover, explicit 3D memories condition latent video generators by re-encoding RGB renderings, which precludes real-time generation. In this paper, we introduce a Latent 3D Gaussian Memory (L3G) that combines the efficiency of feed-forward reconstruction with a compact, rapidly renderable scene representation. Building on this memory, we propose L3G-World, in which a memory updater and a video diffusion transformer (DiT) alternate autoregressively to generate spatially consistent worlds. The memory updater spawns Gaussians in newly observed regions and refines existing ones, so that the memory grows with scene extent rather than stream length. Each Gaussian further stores a VAE latent feature, allowing the memory to be rendered directly into the DiT's latent space without VAE re-encoding. Experiments show that L3G-World achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and long-horizon spatial consistency, with up to $38.6\times$ fewer 3D primitives, $3.2\times$ faster memory updates, and $359\times$ faster memory rendering relative to the most efficient prior 3D-memory baseline for each metric, enabling real-time world generation at 9 FPS.
authors: Jinhyeok Choi, JoungBin Lee, Jongmin Lee, Minkyeong Jeon, Jiyoung Kim, Kaeun Han, Yoonjin Yoon, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses the poor scalability and slow rendering of temporal-context and explicit-3D-memory world models during long-horizon exploration.
Alternates a memory updater with a video diffusion transformer to autoregressively generate observations and maintain scene consistency.
Stores VAE latent features in Gaussians, avoiding RGB rendering and VAE re-encoding during conditioning.
Grows memory with newly explored scene extent rather than generated stream length, while refining previously observed regions.
Reports state-of-the-art quality and long-horizon consistency, reaching 9 FPS with substantially fewer primitives and faster memory updates and rendering than prior 3D-memory baselines.

papers.abstract: A playable, programmable game world must maintain persistent state, enforce executable rules, and support extensible gameplay mechanics. Existing video world models can generate plausible combat, yet struggle to keep hit reactions and health updates consistent with game rules. We introduce Fight World Model (FWM), which separates rule-governed combat execution from video rendering. An executable engine maintains state and resolves interactions. A deterministic compiler encodes these outcomes and attempted actions in a spatially and temporally aligned interaction proxy. The proxy aligns action and skill windows, brief hit reactions, and persistent health by fighter identity and timing. These cues can be controlled separately to render interactions under modified rules. Identity-bound references preserve character appearance across side switches. We train FWM on FightWorld Corpus, spanning 52 skill effects, 187 character-appearance variants, and 15 arenas. Without retraining the renderer, FWM supports damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal, and multi-stage skill mechanisms beyond the native game. It also allows character and arena customization. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FWM, which outperforms existing game world models in action fidelity, hit reactions, health-state consistency, and character appearance preservation. Our project is available at https://fight-world-model.github.io.
authors: Jiahua Li, Zixu John, Tom Zhong, Fuping Wu, Tianhao Xu, Ruicheng Zhang, Jun Zhou, Zunnan Xu
bullets: Addresses inconsistent hit reactions and health updates in existing video world models.
Uses an executable engine for persistent state and interaction resolution, then encodes outcomes into aligned interaction proxies.
The proxy controls action and skill timing, hit reactions, persistent health, and identity-bound character references.
Supports modified combat rules—including damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal, and multi-stage skills—without retraining the renderer.
Experiments report stronger action fidelity, hit-reaction quality, health consistency, and appearance preservation than existing game world models.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of FWM. The Proxy Engine executes gameplay rules, and the resulting state trajectories, action windows, and events are compiled into a visual interaction proxy. The proxy and appearance references are encoded with a shared VAE and concatenated with video tokens. Matching spatiotemporal rotary positions align the proxy with the video, while shared identity embeddings bind character references to the corresponding regions in the first video latent and proxy sequence. papers.abstract: Mobile robots must open doors and drawers, yet their scene maps record what each object is and whether it has moved, not how it will respond to a pull. This paper proposes PhysVLMM, a method that maintains a physical belief for every articulated part of a Vision-Language-Motion Map and answers a planner's queries about it, with two algorithms: a map update and a query. Watching a part move provably cannot identify its dynamics, and a measured pull identifies only the pulled part, up to one direction. PhysVLMM therefore (i) keeps that direction as a posterior instead of a point estimate, (ii) passes the evidence of each pull in closed form to the untouched look-alike parts of the map, and (iii) answers whether an action will succeed at a stated risk, or abstains. On real doors and drawers in 18 homes, it identifies the joint type in 86% of held-out pulls (48% for a learned single-view method) and predicts the response to a pull with 41% lower error than differentiable simulation (CRPS 0.323 vs. 0.544), four orders of magnitude faster (13 ms vs. 230 s per case). The posterior lowers the final-position error from 0.460 to 0.270, sharing lowers the force error of untouched parts from 56% to 42%, and at every stated risk from 0.02 to 0.30 the false-safe answers stay within it. Pooling all measured parts of a home does as well as the look-alike groups, and simpler variants predict where a pulled part stops at least as well.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled the generation of increasingly realistic and interactive virtual environments, opening new possibilities for player-customizable gameplay. Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured representations. We leverage these representations as intermediate proxies to condition a video generation model, together with an adaptive masking mechanism that improves alignment between the conditioning signals and generated video rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce an agentic framework that explicitly maintains and updates game states, allowing players to freely configure their virtual worlds and exercise fine-grained control over character motions while preserving visual quality and gameplay consistency. By combining agentic control with structured proxy-based generation, our framework unlocks new possibilities for player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.
authors: Yuzhe Wu, Zijun Lin, Yeying Jin
bullets: Addresses limited generalization, motion control, and interactivity in existing video world models.

papers.abstract: Video generation is shifting from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, where planning, tool use, and feedback enable coherent, controllable multi-shot videos. In parallel, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures, serving as interactive environments for agents. We study their intersection through the agent harness: an executable runtime that constructs context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and manages budgets around video models. This report examines three directions. First, agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate scripting, shot planning, asset management, production, and editing, alongside the evaluation challenges of these systems. Second, agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state. We discuss hybrid designs in which game engines or agent-written programs maintain world state while video models render observations, and how agents and world models can mutually evaluate and improve one another. Third, recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video model development, distinguishing output revisions, updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and changes to the improvement procedure itself. We identify how these improvements feed back into subsequent development. Across these directions, we analyze essential agent capabilities, including audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, memory, code-based interaction, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent coordination. We conclude with challenges in autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance, cost accounting, and evaluation linking video quality and task performance to sustained improvements in models and harnesses.
authors: Liaoyuan Fan, Yuhao Zheng, Dongxing Mao, Hangyu Ran, Siyuan Hu, Weijia Mao, Rui Zhao, Weijia Wu, Guian Fang, Yanzhe Chen, Zeyu Zhu, Yuxin Jiang, Yiren Song, Yuchao Gu, Junchao Yi, Qi Hu, Dan Kong, Alex Jinpeng Wang, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Mike Zheng Shou, Wei Liu

papers.abstract: Choosing a robot action model requires evidence about task capability, adaptation cost, deployment requirements, and the reliability of reported conclusions. Success rates alone offer limited guidance to researchers with different computing budgets and goals. We propose RoboSeed, a multidimensional evaluation framework for vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAM), within a continuing program to train, evaluate, and openly release robot models with verifiable evidence for model selection. The framework defines five dimensions: capability, downstream training affordability, deployment affordability, locally verified research value, and reproduction evidence. It maps empirical measurements and audit criteria to 0-100 profiles using fixed normalization anchors, with balanced, training-constrained, and deployment-constrained preference settings. Interface and protocol checks establish when comparisons are appropriate. Missing measurements remain explicit, incomplete aggregate scores are withheld, and weighted input coverage identifies evidence gaps. We apply the framework to representative VLA and WAM models, drawing on local training, released-weight evaluation, task-level audits, and an evaluation-system study. The results reveal budget-dependent backbone choices, sensitivity to adaptation recipes, and differences between language and visual task interfaces. Reproducible scoring code and machine-readable evidence support extension to additional models. The study provides dimension-level assessments and priorities for further measurement, while incomplete serving traces and heterogeneous protocols preclude overall numerical rankings.

papers.selection_reason: Multidimensional evaluation framework for vision-language-action and world-action models, directly relevant to embodied model selection.
papers.title: RoboSeed: Multidimensional Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action and World-Action Models: Capability, Resource Affordability, and Research Evidence
papers.tldr: RoboSeed evaluates robot action models across capability, cost, research evidence, and reproducibility rather than relying on success rates alone.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) increasingly couple internal visual or world representations with action generation, making their world-to-action pathways a critical yet poorly understood source of robustness. We investigate when perturbations to these internal representations actually become behaviorally consequential, and uncover a pronounced mismatch between representation perturbability and closed-loop vulnerability: attack effectiveness varies sharply across visual K/V routes, while larger representation displacement does not reliably imply stronger control failure. Our analysis attributes this mismatch to the action-conditioned readout, where keys determine where action queries read and values determine what content they receive. This motivates an action-facing view of vulnerability, in which the effect of a perturbation depends on how it is routed into action generation rather than on representation-space magnitude alone. We instantiate this view with Tail-AV, a short-probe signal for identifying vulnerable routes, and operationalize it in PASA-KV, which selects action-facing K/V targets before training a fresh task-shared attack. Experiments across multiple WAM systems and a physical robot validate readout-informed target selection, demonstrate strong closed-loop attacks, and reveal substantial system-level differences in resistance.
authors: Zhongbo Wu, Jiakai Huang, Zheng Zhang, Siyu Xu, Kaixiang Chen, Xiaohong Liu, Shan You, Chang Xu, Tao Huang
bullets: WAM robustness can differ sharply across visual K/V routes, even when representation perturbations are similarly large.
Keys control where action queries read, while values control the content delivered to action generation.
Tail-AV provides a short probe for identifying vulnerable action-facing routes.
PASA-KV selects these targets before training a fresh task-shared attack.
Experiments on multiple WAMs and a physical robot show strong closed-loop attacks and substantial differences in system resistance.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes action-facing visual routes in world action models, revealing readout-informed vulnerabilities relevant to action-conditioned world models.
papers.title: PASA-KV: Attacking Action-Facing Visual Routes in World Action Models
papers.tldr: PASA-KV finds and attacks the visual key/value routes that most directly influence action generation, showing that perturbation impact depends on action-facing readout rather than representation displacement alone.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models aim to follow user actions while maintaining scene consistency over extended interactions. History-based methods reuse generated latents to preserve scene content, but three limitations of this reuse contribute to error recirculation. 1) The latent generated at each interaction is retained as history, potentially containing blurred details, geometric distortions, or semantic drift. 2) Although retrieved historical content matches the current scene, it can still contain errors that are carried into the next chunk. 3) New outputs then become history for later interactions, potentially reinforcing the same errors through repeated reuse. To limit this cycle, we aim to predict the future scene state from the current generated latent and the next action before generating the next interaction's video chunk. This future-state prior provides guidance for the next chunk, with the aim of reducing the errors carried forward from history. To this end, we propose a plug-and-play Causal Next-Chunk Predictor (C-NCP) with cross-model adaptability and prediction-guided modulation. We integrate C-NCP into four base generators and evaluate the augmented models across three benchmarks for interactive long-video generation and action-conditioned world modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate reduced error accumulation and improved long-horizon consistency across diverse generation settings. The project page is at https://GuangYuanKK.github.io/futureworld.
authors: Guangyuan Li, Kelu Yao, Shuolin Xu, Xinlei Yu, Wei Xing, Lei Zhao, Peng-Tao Jiang, Xiaogang Xu, Xiaobin Hu
bullets: History-based interactive video models can recycle blur, distortions, semantic drift, and prior errors across interactions.
The proposed plug-and-play Causal Next-Chunk Predictor forecasts a future scene state from the current latent and next action.
This prediction guides generation of the next video chunk through prediction-guided modulation.
C-NCP adapts across models and is integrated into four base generators.
Experiments on three interactive video and action-conditioned world-modeling benchmarks report reduced error accumulation and improved long-horizon consistency.

papers.title: FutureWorld: A Plug-and-Play Causal Next-State Predictor for Interactive Video World Exploration

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) can condition robot actions on generated visual futures, but this additional context is neither cost-free nor uniformly beneficial. We examine what a predicted future actually changes: the action delta $\Delta a$ between the future-conditioned and future-free execution paths of the same model. Under a shared WAM checkpoint, this delta barely shifts average benchmark success ($+0.8$ points on LIBERO, $-0.8$ on RoboTwin~2.0), while generating visual futures increases inference latency by 1.7--1.9$\times$. These aggregate metrics conceal a concentrated failure mode that we term \emph{future-induced negative transfer}: while predictive deltas benefit long-horizon tasks ($+2.4$ points on LIBERO-Long) and remain negligible on most routine manipulations, they induce severe degradation on precision tasks---with \emph{Press Stapler} and \emph{Place Can Basket} losing 54.0 and 34.0 points, recurring as top failure modes across independently trained WAM variants. We introduce \textbf{Utility-WAM} for in-place correction of future-conditioned control. Its primary learning component is a residual adapter that repairs future-induced velocity deltas under a frozen shared WAM by aligning them with ground-truth dynamic guidance and penalizing excess error beyond the future-free baseline. The adapter selectively eliminates the majority of severe task drops (reducing losses to 6.0 and 14.0 points) while preserving long-horizon foresight. To eliminate superfluous video computation, a lightweight pre-generation gate reuses counterfactual action outcomes to selectively bypass video generation on 75.5\% of RoboTwin queries, cutting latency by 38\% while improving average success to 93.3\% on RoboTwin~2.0 and 98.9\% on LIBERO. On physical bimanual manipulation across three real-world tasks, Utility-WAM succeeds in 53 of 60 trials, compared to 43 for FAST-WAM.
authors: Feihong Zhang, Xi Lin, Yulong Shi, Zuxing Lu, Yanghong Mei, Zhaopeng Gu, Tingyu Yuan, Zihao Liang, Yinuo Wang, Zhaowen Li

A lightweight gate bypasses video generation for 75.5% of RoboTwin queries, reducing latency by 38%.
Utility-WAM reduces major task losses, reaches 93.3% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.9% on LIBERO, and succeeds in 53/60 real-world trials versus 43/60 for FAST-WAM.

These two stages establish the core correction method. Stage 3 reuses the adapter’s paired final-action outcomes to train a gate. At inference, the gate runs before video generation: it either executes the future-free path and skips that compute, or invokes future generation and the corrected future-conditioned path. papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and corrects future-conditioned world-action control, with a selective video-generation gate for efficiency; spans world models, efficiency, and manipulation policy learning.
papers.title: Utility-WAM: Correcting Future-Induced Action Changes
papers.tldr: Utility-WAM corrects harmful future-conditioned actions and skips unnecessary video generation, improving efficiency and robustness in robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Learning from offline datasets is limited in scalability, as collecting new experience is often costly or unsafe in the real world. World models offer an alternative way to generate new experience through a learned dynamics model, yet learning policies in latent space is limited due to compounding errors in imagined rollouts. To this end, we propose using the world model as a local transition generator, leveraging critic guidance to choose actions inside that model to generate synthetic experiences. We study action refinement methodologies, introducing Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience (CGSE) generation in world models. Specifically, CGSE augments an existing offline dataset by sampling candidate actions using an offline policy and refining each to maximize a first-order approximation of the $Q$-function within a trust region. We then use a frozen latent world model to imagine the future state given each updated action, and use the critic to choose the best one, appending this synthetic transition to the replay buffer. Our method requires no additional real-environment interaction or test-time planner, as it generates synthetic experience offline using the world model. On three OGBench manipulation tasks, CGSE improves an offline policy by a relative improvement of $7.1\%$ on the average success rate.
authors: Jorge de Freitas, Christos Ziakas, Alessandra Russo
bullets: Addresses limited scalability and safety of collecting new offline experience, while reducing errors from long imagined rollouts.
Refines candidate actions from an offline policy to maximize a first-order Q-function approximation within a trust region.
Uses a frozen latent world model to predict each updated action’s transition and a critic to select the best synthetic experience.
Augments the replay buffer offline, requiring neither further environment interaction nor a test-time planner.
Improves average success rate by 7.1% relatively across three OGBench manipulation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CGSE transition generation in world model. Starting from an offline latent z0, the fixed BC-flow actor samples N candidate first actions and FMQ-style guidance applies a one-step trustregion critic-gradient refinement to each candidate. The refined candidates are rolled out under fψ, scored with Qϕ, and the best branch supplies only its first action a∗ and first model successor z′ψ = fψ(z0, a ∗). The resulting synthetic transition (z0, a ∗, z′ψ) is appended to the replay buffer.

papers.abstract: Pneumonia changes across respiration, inflammation, and organ function, while the measurements that describe it arrive at different times and are often incomplete. We introduce PULMOWORLD, a world model for longitudinal pneumonia dynamics that connects asynchronous state estimation, recursive simulation, and evidence-constrained planning. History-aware filtering separates state propagation from observation-driven correction, so a measurement updates the shared belief only when it is observed. That belief supports recursive forecasts of clinical values and modality representations, and summaries of future prognosis. Cap-MBRL searches imagined continuations inside an authorized action set and replaces a frozen fallback only when a candidate meets the risk budget and a predicted-cost margin. On the pneumonia cohort MASS, recursive forecasts are competitive with task-trained sequence models, and simulated future states retain prognostic information. Trained separately on public MIMIC-IV-CXR chest radiographs and clinical trajectories, this model improves prognostic discrimination over latest-value fusion in development and is competitive on long-horizon error on the locked pneumonia panel. In five known-mechanism MASS-Syn environments, Cap-MBRL lowers selection regret relative to direct fallback execution.

On MASS and related pneumonia evaluations, forecasts were competitive with sequence models, improved prognostic discrimination over latest-value fusion, and reduced selection regret in five synthetic environments.

papers.abstract: Controllable human motion generation has largely focused on specifying what action should occur or where the body should move. We study a complementary question: can full-body motion be controlled by specifying only when each foot contacts the ground? We introduce StepControl, an autoregressive diffusion model conditioned on a future binary left/right foot-contact schedule, without requiring target root and body poses, or semantic prompts. StepControl represents contact as explicit temporal events and injects them through dedicated cross-attention with classifier-free guidance. We further introduce a stochastic mixture noise schedule and warmup strategy for stable long-horizon autoregressive generation. Experiments show that StepControl follows prescribed contact timing more accurately than adapting existing spatially guided motion generators to contact constraints. It maintains effective contact control over long continuous rollouts and responds to edited schedules such as cadence changes, stop-and-go pauses, limping gaits, and bilateral jumping. Our results show that minimal foot-contact schedules provide an effective and intuitive temporal interface for controllable motion generation.
authors: Hojun Jang, Jinseok Bae, Donggeun Lim, Taesun Kim, Seungbin Jeong, Younghwan Lee, Yong Seok Kim, Young Min Kim

Scope: control is specified temporally through foot contacts rather than detailed spatial or semantic constraints.

papers.abstract: Embodied world models predict the visual consequences of candidate actions before execution. However, existing action-conditioned world models often adopt uniformly weighted visual generation objectives that can be misaligned with embodied prediction needs. Even with explicit motion conditioning, these objectives can underemphasize spatially sparse changes that are critical to interaction. We propose KineWorld, a transport-aware world-modeling framework that extends robot kinematics from motion conditioning to the spatial allocation of generative supervision. Kinematic Transport Lifting (KTL) constructs renderer-derived, camera-aligned transport fields from commanded robot motion. Transport-Aware World Diffusion (TAWD) calibrates their motion support on the video-latent grid and reweights future-RGB flow matching through a normalized mixture of uniform and transport-focused distributions. We train KineWorld using ALOHA-AgileX bimanual manipulation data from RoboTwin 2.0. KineWorld achieves an EWMScore-P of 68.95 in single-view evaluation and a TWB-Score of 54.82 in multi-view evaluation. These results support a shift from appearance fitting toward action-consequence modeling for embodied decision-making.
bullets: Existing action-conditioned world models may underemphasize sparse but important interaction changes under uniform visual-generation objectives.
Kinematic Transport Lifting builds camera-aligned transport fields from commanded robot motion.
Transport-Aware World Diffusion calibrates these fields on the video-latent grid and mixes uniform with transport-focused supervision.
Trained on ALOHA-AgileX bimanual manipulation data from RoboTwin 2.0, KineWorld reports an EWMScore-P of 68.95 for single-view and a TWB-Score of 54.82 for multi-view evaluation.
The framework targets action-consequence modeling, with scope demonstrated on bimanual manipulation data.

The weighting branch is used only during training, while the inherited action expert remains unchanged.

(b) Auxiliary-cue WAMs incorporate motion-focused auxiliary cues, such as masks (Chen et al., 2026c), action images (Zhen et al., 2026), optical flow (Chen et al., 2026b), or projected kinematic fields (Yang et al., 2026), to improve motion localization. These cues alone do not directly change the spatial weighting of the primary RGB objective, potentially leaving motion localization and supervision priorities misaligned. (c) KineWorld introduces action-guided RGB supervision by lifting camera-aligned kinematic transport onto the video latent grid and reweighting flow matching, enabling actionconsequence-oriented supervision while preserving the total token weight.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) are becoming increasingly important and useful for embodied intelligence, as they enable robots to anticipate the consequences of candidate actions before interacting with the physical environment. However, underwater robots are usually subject to passive dynamics, such as inertia, buoyancy, hydrodynamic drag, and persistent drift, which can continue to affect the vehicle even after an action is completed. Existing WAMs, which primarily predict action-conditioned visual observations, are not explicitly designed to capture such passive motion dynamics. In this paper, we present AquaWAM, the first World Action Model designed for underwater embodied agents. Instead of predicting future images, AquaWAM models both action-conditioned and passive physical dynamics, including the thruster dead band, the inertial glide that outlasts each command, and ambient currents. Specifically, it senses through the DVL, IMU, pressure sensor and joint encoders, while cameras supply only semantics for understanding goals and target pose. By modeling compact navigation states rather than high-dimensional visual observations, AquaWAM substantially reduces the model size and computational cost compared with conventional WAMs. Experimentally, AquaWAM achieves a 72.6% task success rate across 20 underwater tasks on the USIM benchmark, outperforming existing methods while making action decisions 2.7x faster than U0 on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Our model also remains effective when some onboard sensor measurements are unavailable. For example, without DVL velocity measurements, our method still achieves a 61.6% success rate, compared with 39.4% for U0.
bullets: Addresses inertia, buoyancy, drag, thruster dead bands, drift, and currents that conventional visual WAMs do not explicitly capture.
Uses DVL, IMU, pressure, and joint-encoder data for compact navigation-state prediction, while cameras provide semantic and target-pose information.
Achieves 72.6% success across 20 USIM underwater tasks and makes decisions 2.7× faster than U0 on a Jetson AGX Orin.
Maintains robustness under missing DVL velocity measurements, achieving 61.6% success versus 39.4% for U0.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of AquaWAM. Cameras supply the goal and the object pose; the predictor imagines each candidate two seconds ahead and executes the first 0.5 s of the best.

Figure 1: Motivation for a dynamics-aware World Action Model. Many existing World Action Models primarily predict future observations in video space, without explicitly modeling underwater vehicle dynamics. However, underwater motion is often strongly affected by passive physical factors such as buoyancy, drag, currents, and residual momentum, causing the vehicle state to continue evolving even after a control command is issued. Ignoring these dynamics can lead to inaccurate predictions of where and how the vehicle will move.
Figure 4: Execution traces of AquaWAM. Grasping and transporting run with full sensing; navigation and tracking lose the DVL where marked and finish on the estimate.
Figure 7: Computation cost on Jetson AGX Orin 32 GB. We show the number of parameters (left) and the running time (right).

papers.selection_reason: World action model for underwater robots modeling action-conditioned and passive dynamics; directly relevant to embodied navigation and interactive world models.
papers.title: AquaWAM: A Dynamics-aware World Action Model for Underwater Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: AquaWAM models both commanded actions and persistent underwater dynamics to enable faster, robust world-action planning for underwater robots.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models offer a scalable alternative to costly real-world interaction for improving robot policies. However, existing world-model-based methods largely treat world models as forward-only surrogates of the physical environment, leaving untapped a capability no physical environment affords: rewinding to past decision points to explore counterfactual futures. We introduce Rollback, a policy improvement paradigm that turns world models from passive simulators into counterfactual engines: it rolls back to critical decision points, branches into alternative actions, and contrasts their outcomes to attribute success to individual decisions. This concentrates imagination where it matters most and distills counterfactual outcomes into fine-grained, action-level supervision without a separately learned value model. We build a scalable training system that unifies distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution, forming a self-reinforcing cycle: real-world experience continually sharpens the world model, and a sharper world model in turn drives further policy improvement. We term the world-model side of this cycle test-time physics grounding, a capability that hand-built physics simulators lack: while the world model serves as the training environment, real transitions from the policy it trains correct its dynamics through a lightweight LoRA pipeline. Experiments on three challenging real-world tasks show that Rollback improves success rates over the strongest baseline by an absolute 10.67%, 11.11%, and 11.85% on block extraction, ball tossing, and tabletop curling, respectively, while achieving more stable improvement throughout training. Although initialized from teleoperated demonstrations far below human level, Rollback surpasses the average success rate of human players on both ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours of training.
authors: Jiayi Luo, Yang Zhang, Liliang Chen, Nan Wang, Chen Gao, Boxiang Qiu, Zhuoxuan Li, Baorui Peng, Chuankang Li, Yuxiang Yan, Si Liu, Qingyun Sun, Shuicheng Yan, Maoqing Yao, Jianxin Li, Guanghui Ren
bullets: Addresses the limitation of forward-only world models, which cannot identify which decisions caused success or failure.
Rolls back to critical points, branches over alternative actions, and converts outcome comparisons into fine-grained action-level supervision without a separate value model.
Combines distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution in a self-reinforcing training cycle.
On three real-world tasks, it improves success rates over the strongest baseline by 10.67%, 11.11%, and 11.85% absolute.
Surpasses average human success on ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours, despite starting from below-human teleoperated demonstrations.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'Rollback', a method for world models to perform counterfactual backtracking and policy improvement using real-world experience, directly applicable to robot learning and interactive world models.
papers.title: Rollback: Experience Backtracking in World Models for Policy Improvement
papers.tldr: Rollback improves robot policies by rewinding world models to key decisions, exploring counterfactual actions, and using real-world feedback to refine the model.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
authors: Chaehyun Kim, Chi-Pin Huang, Jisoo Kim, Min-Hung Chen, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Seungryong Kim, Fu-En Yang
bullets: Addresses limited diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations.
Represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) linking the current state to a future state through discrete motion tokens.
Initializes CoD from labeled demonstrations, then reinforces chains whose predicted futures match observed outcomes.
Uses unlabeled human videos as supervision through observed state transitions, aligning human and robot experience in one reasoning space.
Simulation and real-robot experiments show human-to-robot transfer and generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a VLA framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and uses world imagination, strongly fitting 'Vision-Language-Action' and 'Interactive World Models'.
papers.title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
papers.tldr: ThinkWorld improves VLA robot generalization by representing actions as dynamics-aware motion-token chains and refining them with imagined-world reinforcement from both robot demonstrations and unlabeled human videos.

papers.abstract: World models are widely proposed as core components for enabling agents to reason over long temporal and spatial horizons. Yet current evaluations often emphasize task performance while providing limited insight into whether learned world models acquire predictive latent dynamics that reflect the underlying structure of the environment. Here we introduce the concept of faithful latent world models as an equivariance condition between the environment's transition map and the learned latent dynamics. We propose latent rollout consistency (LRC) as a metric to evaluate action-conditioned latent prediction. Strikingly, we find that across the studied state of the art latent world models, none solves the task by actually faithfully modeling the dynamics of the environment.
bullets: Motivates evaluating latent dynamics beyond task performance, especially for long-horizon reasoning.
Defines faithful latent world models through an equivariance condition linking environmental transitions to learned latent dynamics.
Introduces latent rollout consistency (LRC) to measure action-conditioned latent prediction.
Finds that none of the studied state-of-the-art latent world models faithfully models the environment’s dynamics.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes latent rollout consistency as a faithfulness metric for action-conditioned latent world models, directly addressing world model evaluation.
papers.title: Understanding the limits of latent world models
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a principled test for whether latent world models faithfully capture environmental dynamics and finds that none of the evaluated models does so.

papers.abstract: We present a survey of approaches to Bayesian inference with simulator forward models, focusing on settings with prohibitively expensive simulators. In this domain, Bayesian optimization-based methods have emerged as the most promising approach. We unify existing methods into a general framework, enabling consistent reasoning about shared algorithmic structure across the fragmented literature. Within this framework, we identify the primary design choices and perform a systematic empirical comparison of their effects on inference efficiency in terms of required simulation budget. A key result of our study is that inference efficiency is often dominated by the choice of surrogate-model response variable, as it directly governs the complexity of the modeled function. Specifically, we demonstrate that the prevalent scalar log-likelihood is a poor response variable, as it discards crucial information. Based on this insight, we introduce the concept of custom \emph{proxy variables}: transformations of simulator outputs engineered to retain more information and provide smoother response surfaces, substantially improving inference efficiency over standard response variables. We provide actionable guidance and a numerically robust Julia package to facilitate practical adoption of Bayesian optimization for simulator inverse problems.
bullets: Bayesian optimization is identified as a promising approach for simulator-based Bayesian inference under tight simulation budgets.
The paper unifies fragmented methods into a common framework and systematically compares their design choices.
Surrogate-model response variables often dominate inference efficiency because they determine the modeled function’s complexity.
Scalar log-likelihoods are criticized for discarding information; custom proxy variables can preserve information and yield smoother response surfaces.
The work offers practical guidance and a numerically robust Julia package for simulator inverse problems.
papers.selection_reason: Surveys and compares design choices for Bayesian inference with expensive simulators. Simulators are a key component of interactive world models, and the survey provides a unifying framework for their use.
papers.title: Bayesian Inference of Expensive Simulators: Survey and Comparison of Design Choices
papers.tldr: A unified survey shows that choosing informative proxy variables for surrogate models can substantially improve Bayesian inference efficiency with expensive simulators.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in interactive world models have made it possible to generate controllable, dynamic environments from action inputs. Yet current models struggle to maintain coherence beyond roughly one minute of rollout, a limitation rooted not in model capacity but in the scarcity of long-horizon training data. Existing gameplay video datasets typically consist of clips under ten seconds, with captions that describe whole clips in coarse and undifferentiated text, which is insufficient for controllable long-horizon generation. We address this with GameVerse, a minute-scale gameplay video dataset purpose-built for long-horizon interactive world modeling. GameVerse contains 69.7K clips spanning 1,655 hours and 349.6 million frames across diverse first- and third-person gameplay, including 1,358 hours of continuous two-minute sequences, an order of magnitude longer than prior datasets. Clips pass through a unified pipeline of scene-consistent segmentation, quality filtering, camera pose estimation, and event-based caption annotation. Each clip is paired with a temporally stable camera trajectory that remains coherent across minutes, together with captions that separate static scene context from dynamic foreground events and align to event boundaries rather than fixed time windows. Comprehensive analysis shows that GameVerse surpasses existing public datasets in scale, diversity, and annotation quality. Experiments further demonstrate that training on GameVerse substantially extends the temporal horizon of interactive world models.
authors: Kang He, Wenshuo Peng, Chuanhao Li, Zihui Gao, Xiaojie Xu, Zhengyuan Lin, Yuzhe Ding, Donghong Ji, Kaipeng Zhang, Yongtao Ge
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of long-horizon gameplay data, which limits rollout coherence beyond roughly one minute.
Contains 69.7K clips covering 1,655 hours and 349.6 million frames across diverse first- and third-person games.
Includes 1,358 hours of continuous two-minute sequences—about an order of magnitude longer than prior datasets.
Uses scene-consistent segmentation, quality filtering, camera-pose estimation, and event-aligned captions separating static context from dynamic events.
Experiments show that training on GameVerse substantially extends the temporal horizon of interactive world models.
papers.selection_reason: Minute-scale curated gameplay dataset explicitly for long-horizon interactive world modeling and action-conditioned future prediction.
papers.title: GameVerse: A Minute-Scale Gameplay Dataset for Long-Horizon Interactive World Modeling
papers.tldr: GameVerse is a large, minute-scale gameplay dataset designed to help interactive world models generate coherent environments over long horizons.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict the visual consequences of the actions they generate, which makes test-time selection a natural way to improve a fixed policy: imagine the futures of candidate actions and execute the best one. The benefit of selection is bounded by the selectable headroom, how much better the best candidate truly is, but the standard estimate, which executes each candidate once and keeps the best outcome, conflates candidate quality with the randomness of everything that follows. We introduce a denoised counterfactual protocol, based on bitwise-reproducible branching, repeated continuations, held-out oracles, and common random numbers, that measures the headroom a selector can realize, and use its measurements to build a fail-gated selector. Across four WAMs, two benchmarks, over 100,000 branched rollouts, and pre-registered tests, we find that (i) the standard estimate overstates the selectable headroom of native samples: bounds from 17 continuations per candidate place its selectable share between 24% and 66% for three WAMs; (ii) structured action perturbations create up to 16 points of selectable headroom; and (iii) in both WAMs with action-conditioned imagination, imagined futures carry candidate-outcome information with no detectable loss relative to real futures, information that the value head of Cosmos Policy leaves unused. Deviating from the policy chunk only when a readout of the WAM predicts failure, the selector raises closed-loop task success from 76.9% to 81.6% on held-out episodes of training tasks, with the largest gain where the policy fails most often, and from 62.6% to 69.8% on unseen tasks.
authors: Haojia Gao, Yue Cao, Yumin Liu, Haohua Que, Mingkai Liu, Guanqiu Guo, Zhuo Zou, Bokui Chen, Xueqian Wang
bullets: Standard one-shot estimates overstate selectable headroom because they mix candidate quality with downstream randomness.
A counterfactual protocol uses reproducible branching, repeated continuations, held-out oracles, and common random numbers to measure realizable headroom.
Structured action perturbations add up to 16 points of selectable headroom; native-sample selectable share is estimated at 24–66% for three WAMs.
Action-conditioned imagined futures retain candidate-outcome information comparable to real futures, but Cosmos Policy’s value head does not exploit it.
A fail-gated selector improves success from 76.9% to 81.6% on held-out training tasks and from 62.6% to 69.8% on unseen tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Measures and exploits selectable headroom in world action models through closed-loop test-time selection, core interactive world-model research.
papers.title: How Much Can Best-of-N Help a World Action Model? Measuring Selectable Headroom and Realizing It in Closed Loop
papers.tldr: A denoised evaluation protocol shows that best-of-N selection can provide meaningful but limited gains for world action models, enabling a fail-gated selector that improves closed-loop success.

papers.abstract: We present a variational control framework that connects sampling-time guidance and reward-based model adaptation through a shared Jacobian pullback. Starting from terminal reward maximization with a path-space KL penalty, the Gibbs variational principle and Doob transform yield a correction to the generative dynamics. A local denoising approximation exposes the pullback that transports output preferences to the controlled variable. This construction gives Variational Optimal Guidance (VOG) in state space and extends to Distilled Variational Optimal Control (DVOC) by amortizing locally improved endpoints into model parameters. The resulting controls share a local variational rule: VOG acts through the denoising Jacobian, while DVOC realizes the parameter pullback by endpoint distillation. Under a linear MMSE model, VOG's exact correction lies in the data subspace. On ImageNet, VOG reduces DiT-XL/2 FID from 2.27 to 2.04 at 250 sampling steps and from 7.58 to 4.44 at 25 steps. After 20 updates on Z-Image-Turbo, DVOC improves HPSv3++ and four held-out evaluator scores over the untrained model, with the highest corresponding means among the trained methods compared. These results connect inference-time control and reward adaptation through a common geometric principle.
authors: Ruoyu Wang, Xinyi Ye, Yunshuo Shi, Liangyu Yuan, Beier Zhu, Chi Zhang
bullets: Formulates guidance from terminal reward maximization with a path-space KL penalty using the Gibbs variational principle and Doob transform.
Introduces Variational Optimal Guidance (VOG), which transports output preferences to diffusion states through the denoising Jacobian.
Introduces Distilled Variational Optimal Control (DVOC), which amortizes locally improved endpoints into model parameters.
VOG reduces DiT-XL/2 FID from 2.27 to 2.04 at 250 steps and from 7.58 to 4.44 at 25 steps on ImageNet.
DVOC improves HPSv3++ and four held-out evaluator scores on Z-Image-Turbo after 20 updates; the abstract does not specify limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Variational Optimal Control for Diffusion Guidance, connecting sampling-time guidance and reward-based adaptation through a shared Jacobian pullback. This advances Interactive World Models by providing a control framework for diffusion models.
papers.title: Variational Optimal Control for Diffusion Guidance
papers.tldr: A variational-control framework unifies diffusion sampling guidance and reward-based adaptation through Jacobian pullbacks, improving image-generation quality in both inference-time and distilled settings.

papers.abstract: Learning from experience is essential for building the next generation of agents that continually expand their capabilities. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already internalize rich world knowledge, yet this knowledge is rarely leveraged to drive policy improvement through online interaction. Realizing this potential efficiently remains challenging, as policy updates shift the agent's interaction distribution, requiring the world model to adapt accordingly, while continually updating large pretrained models is computationally expensive. To address this challenge, we introduce Dwell, a model-based reinforcement learning (RL) framework that reframes a VLM as a recurrent latent transition operator, endowing it with the ability to predict, adjust, and act in latent space. Leveraging the VLM's own representations and its dual role as both world model and policy, the agent continually learns from real interactions to anticipate and evaluate action outcomes, and from latent imagination to improve its behavior. Across five interactive visual environments, Dwell achieves the strongest overall performance among trainable methods while substantially reducing the compute required for imagination, showing that effective world models for VLM agents need not reconstruct the future; they need to predict futures that are useful for action. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Tom111-lhx/Dwell
authors: Haoxi Li, Sikai Bai, Jianfei Ma, Qinglin Hou, Xiaocheng Lu, Tao Han, Jie Zhang, Song Guo
bullets: Addresses the challenge of efficiently adapting pretrained VLM agents through online experience without continually updating large models.
Recasts a VLM as a recurrent latent transition operator serving as both world model and policy.
Combines real-interaction learning with latent imagination to anticipate action outcomes and improve behavior.
Achieves the strongest overall performance among trainable methods across five interactive visual environments.
Substantially reduces imagination compute and suggests useful world models need not reconstruct full futures.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a VLM-based recurrent latent world-model/policy for online interactive learning, directly fitting latent-action and interactive world-model research.
papers.title: Vision-Language Agents Can Learn in Their Own Latent Worlds
papers.tldr: Dwell enables vision-language agents to learn from interaction by predicting and improving actions entirely in their own latent space.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) learn representations for robot control by coupling future visual prediction with action generation. Successful manipulation depends primarily on how the robot and task-relevant objects evolve, whereas future-video prediction must also reconstruct the appearance and background of the entire scene. We therefore propose Trace-WAM, which augments video-action learning with future 3D motion prediction as an auxiliary objective. This objective supervises temporal point correspondence together with image-plane displacement and depth change, directly describing the interaction dynamics and spatial changes involved in manipulation. To this end, we adopt a three-branch Mixture-of-Transformer (Tri-MoT) architecture to jointly learn video prediction, motion prediction, and action generation. The motion expert predicts future trajectories from current visual features, allowing motion supervision to shape the representations used for action generation. Because the action expert does not consume predicted trajectories, inference retains the current-observation policy path: a single visual forward pass followed by action denoising. Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate strong in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, with particularly clear gains over Fast-WAM under limited demonstrations and distribution shifts.
authors: Xu Hu, Changjie Wu, Linzhe Shi, Hang Zhang, Chen Yang, Lingjun Zhang, Guowen Zhang, Mu Xu, Junran Peng, Qing Li, Zhaoxiang Zhang
bullets: Targets a key mismatch in WAMs: whole-scene video prediction may underemphasize robot-object interaction dynamics.
Adds auxiliary supervision for temporal point correspondence, image-plane displacement, and depth change.
Uses a three-branch Mixture-of-Transformer architecture for video prediction, motion prediction, and action generation.
Keeps the action policy conditioned only on current visual observations, requiring one visual pass followed by action denoising.
Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus show strong in-distribution performance and improved generalization, especially with limited demonstrations and distribution shifts.
papers.selection_reason: Robot manipulation policy learning augmented with future 3D motion prediction; directly fits embodied robot learning and world-action models.
papers.title: Trace-WAM: Learning to Act via 3D Motion Prediction for World Action Models
papers.tldr: Trace-WAM improves robot manipulation policies by adding future 3D motion prediction to video-action learning while preserving efficient action inference.

papers.abstract: Learning controllable world dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos is challenging because robot embodiments use incompatible action spaces, while human videos lack native control labels. We present RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model that uses the 3D-grounded latent actions introduced by RynnLAM as a shared conditioning interface. This representation enables joint pretraining on human interaction videos, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without requiring a common native action space. Built on a pretrained video transformer, RynnWorld-Latent combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway that aligns actions with future video latents. We pretrain on 23 datasets comprising approximately 553.5M frames and adapt the model to target robots through post-training. The framework supports two data-generation routes: digital teleoperation uses target robot commands to generate action-video demonstrations, while latent-action synthesis transfers source motion to an edited initial frame and pairs the resulting rollout with retargeted pseudo robot actions. Experiments show improved video prediction metrics on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, alongside qualitative action following when different action sequences share the same initial observation. Synthetic mid-training improves policy success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and both generation routes improve real-world policy success rates over real-demonstration-only training in the evaluated settings. These results support universal latent actions as a scalable interface for learning controllable visual dynamics across heterogeneous embodiments.
authors: Haoyu Zhao, Yinzhou Tang, Zixuan Wang, Minghao Zhu, Dongchi Huang, Xingyue Zhao, Qin Zhao, Kehan Li, Siteng Huang, Xin Li, Zhenyu Zeng, Mingxiu Chen, Deli Zhao, Zhongyu Li
bullets: Addresses incompatible robot action spaces and missing control labels in human videos.
Uses RynnLAM latent actions as a universal interface for joint cross-embodiment pretraining.
Combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway to align actions with future video latents.
Supports digital teleoperation and latent-action synthesis for generating robot-targeted training data.
Reports improved video prediction and policy success across benchmarks and evaluated real-robot settings; scope is limited to the described platforms and tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-embodiment video world model conditioned on universal latent actions, directly fitting world model subtopics.
papers.title: RynnWorld-Latent: A Cross-Embodiment World Model Conditioned on Universal Latent Actions
papers.tldr: RynnWorld-Latent learns controllable visual dynamics across humans, robots, and simulations by conditioning a video world model on shared 3D-grounded latent actions.

papers.abstract: Interactive world generation requires models to follow successive commands while preserving relevant history and action consequences. We present Hy-Nomas, a video world model with an 8B diffusion backbone that supports free-form text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns. It generates variable-length segments conditioned on current inputs and cached history. Our central design aligns structured video captions with action-aware causal attention: descriptive context remains accessible across segments, while action instructions are restricted to their intended temporal windows. A vision-language Prompt Enhancer (PE) translates user requests and multimodal interaction histories into structured conditions for the next segment. A multi-stage curriculum progressively introduces causal generation, text interaction, camera control, and training on model-generated histories, followed by diffusion distillation. In human evaluation, Hy-Nomas shows superior performance over existing world models. We release model weights, code and benchmarks, together with a lightweight adaptation workflow, to support reproducible research on interactive world generation.
authors: Qiaoling Chen, Jiaxiang Cheng, Xueqing Deng, Tiankai Hang, Ji Hou, Jiaqi Li, Yifan Liu, Tao Lu, Junshu Tang, Yu Tang, Yao Teng, Yu Tian, Heng Wang, Weizhi Wang, Xiyao Wang, Xilun Wu, Mingyu Yang, Yangbin Yu, Rui Zhao, Longjun Cao, Linghao Chen, Haoyi Duan, Jiaming Han, Mingji Han, Enhua Jiang, Shunkai Li, Yanzhe Liang, Qinwei Ma, Cong Wang, Lei Wang, Bing Wu, Ke Xing, Ray Ying, Zhentao Yu, Key Zhang, Yuan Zhou, Zhengguang Zhou, Kai Zou
bullets: Supports successive text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns.
Generates variable-length video segments conditioned on current inputs and cached interaction history.
Uses action-aware causal attention to preserve descriptive context while limiting actions to their intended time windows.
A vision-language Prompt Enhancer converts user requests and multimodal histories into structured next-segment conditions.
Human evaluations report better performance than existing world models; weights, code, benchmarks, and an adaptation workflow are released.
papers.selection_reason: Interactive video world model with free-form instruction and camera control, directly fitting world-model and diffusion-based video generation interests.
papers.title: Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation
papers.tldr: Hy-Nomas is an 8B video world model that generates free-form, multi-turn interactive worlds while maintaining history and responding to text and camera controls.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) enable world models to plan from images by predicting future embeddings. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly incorporate task-relevant state information, so the physical state that determines task progress may not be reliably captured in the latent space. Supervising world models with simulator state can make planning more informative, but it requires deciding which state features matter. Features are typically selected by hand or weighted uniformly, and a uniform weighting gives every standardized state feature equal influence, so redundant coordinates can overcount the same variation, while irrelevant ones can obscure task-relevant differences. To address this limitation, we propose SWIM (State Weighting with Inverse-Dynamics Model), which learns state weights from offline trajectories by predicting recorded actions from current states and observed future displacements. The learned weights quantify each feature's contribution to action prediction and define a weighted state metric for state-supervised training, which we demonstrate by aligning latent and state distances. The inverse-dynamics model is used only during training, so the resulting world model plans from images with no additional planning-time computation. Across five simulated robotic manipulation tasks, SWIM consistently improves planning success over uniform state weighting.

papers.title: SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models
papers.tldr: SWIM learns task-relevant state-feature weights from offline behavior to improve image-based JEPA world-model planning.

papers.abstract: We tackle the challenge of building real-time interactive video worlds with user-defined behaviors. Such worlds must track object states, apply interaction rules, and render the resulting consequences as users act. Yet existing end-to-end video world models typically learn interaction dynamics within the generator, making it difficult to specify object-level rules and reason about their consequences. In this work, we introduce BoxWorld, which separates interaction reasoning from generative rendering. Given user-specified rules, a coding agent creates a Box World Engine that determines interaction outcomes and exposes the resulting object states through a lightweight interface of layout boxes, persistent object attributes, and dynamic status variables, leaving appearance and physical effects to generative rendering. A Box-State Generative Renderer then renders this evolving state stream into video autoregressively, enabling online control over object motion, state switches, and conditional events. Rendering this state stream is non-trivial: the renderer must respond to object-level state updates in real time while remaining coherent with the generated history. To this end, we introduce a three-stage training strategy that learns object grounding from open-domain videos and state transitions from gameplay videos, both annotated automatically, and finally performs rollout distillation on self-generated histories. We further propose PairedStateBench, a paired benchmark for fine-grained interaction control. BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models and remains competitive across multiple public benchmarks. Project page: https://boxworld-web.github.io.
authors: Zike Wu, Ahmed Hatem, Chintan Trivedi, Wallace Michel Pinto Lira, Xuebin Qin, Lele Wang, Renjie Liao
bullets: A coding agent converts user-defined rules into a Box World Engine that tracks object states and determines interaction outcomes.
A Box-State Generative Renderer turns state updates into coherent autoregressive video while supporting online control of motion, switches, and conditional events.
The system uses a three-stage training strategy covering object grounding, state transitions, and rollout distillation.
PairedStateBench is introduced to evaluate fine-grained interaction control.
BoxWorld substantially outperforms end-to-end world models and remains competitive on multiple public benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Separates interaction reasoning (Box World Engine) from autoregressive video rendering for controllable interactive video worlds; directly an interactive world model.
papers.title: BoxWorld: Let World Engines Control and Video Generators Render
papers.tldr: BoxWorld separates rule-based interaction reasoning from generative video rendering to enable controllable, real-time interactive worlds.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) offer a promising framework for embodied intelligence, yet mainstream approaches remain centered on video foundation models or vision-language models. Even when geometric features extracted by 3D models such as VGGT are incorporated, they are typically passed into a video model or VLM that serves as the primary backbone, leaving 3D geometry as an auxiliary input or prediction target rather than the native foundation for world modeling. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. E0.5 introduces two key innovations. First, it adopts a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone, making 3D geometry the native representation for both world modeling and action prediction. Second, it explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions, enabling the model to capture geometric world dynamics beyond action-only modeling or future video prediction. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 first demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5 without embodied-data pretraining, achieving success rates of 89.90\% and 50.09\% under clean and randomized settings, respectively. Building on these results, we further pretrain E0.5 on more than 160k robot trajectories from AgiBotWorld-Beta, jointly learning robot actions and future geometry within the pretrained 3D foundation. This embodied pretraining improves mean real-world manipulation success rates by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of geometry-native foundations to acquire robot interaction knowledge and transfer it to physical manipulation. E0.5 embodies this geometry-native approach as a member of the VWA family of world-action models.

papers.title: E0.5: From Reconstructive to Future-Predictive 3D Foundations for Robotic World-Action Modeling
papers.tldr: E0.5 makes 3D geometry the native foundation for world-action modeling and jointly predicts robot actions with future 3D states, improving simulated and real-world manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Force-sensitive manipulation requires contact and load information that is not provided explicitly by visual observations. We present CW-WAM, a world action model that jointly predicts video, motion, and contact wrench. Inspired by hybrid motion-force control, it contains a unified interaction module that treats both motion and contact wrench as modeling targets and predicts time-aligned motion-wrench chunks as control references. A pair-causal attention mechanism structures the motion-wrench dependencies, while a long fixed-length wrench memory retains past interaction information. The predicted wrench chunk acts as a force reference for a 20-Hz outer-loop admittance controller within a slow-fast control system that maintains force feedback and smooth motion between model queries. CW-WAM improves contact prediction and increases the insertion success rate from 25% to 70% for square pegs with 1-mm clearance per side and from 40% to 95% for power adapters, compared with WAM without wrench input. It also improves lifting-height accuracy across different loads. Our framework with an admittance controller reduces force-reference RMSE from 4.8 to 2.7 N for peg insertion and from 2.0 to 1.3 N for wiping, respectively, with smaller force fluctuations during successful execution. Project website: https://cw-wam-project.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit contact and load information in visual observations.
Jointly predicts video, motion, and time-aligned contact-wrench chunks using pair-causal attention and long wrench memory.
Uses predicted wrench as a force reference for a 20-Hz outer-loop admittance controller in a slow-fast control system.
Compared with WAM without wrench input, insertion success rises from 25% to 70% for square pegs and from 40% to 95% for power adapters.
Reduces force-reference RMSE from 4.8 to 2.7 N for peg insertion and from 2.0 to 1.3 N for wiping, while improving lifting-height accuracy across loads.
papers.selection_reason: Force-sensitive manipulation with a world action model predicting motion and contact wrench directly fits robot learning and interactive world modeling.
papers.title: CW-WAM: A Structured Contact-Wrench World Action Model for Force-Sensitive Manipulation
papers.tldr: CW-WAM augments visual world-action modeling with contact-wrench prediction and admittance control to improve force-sensitive manipulation.

papers.abstract: The microphysics of dark matter (DM) is imprinted on cosmological structure across an enormous dynamic range. Nonlinear cosmological observables are most reliably modeled with N-body and hydrodynamic simulations. However, systematic N-body scans over DM theory space are prohibitively expensive. Machine learning emulators provide a possible solution, but are currently limited by either low resolution or only the ability to emulate specific observables. We introduce Astrolabe, a flow-matching-based generative emulator designed to be free of both constraints. Astrolabe acts directly on the 6N phase-space coordinates of N individual particles.
