With no voxel grid in the output, there is no voxel-resolution ceiling, and in principle any observable can be measured from inference. Astrolabe is computationally tractable via a field-particle hybrid transformer in which every particle cross-attends to multiscale field tokens, so compute and memory are linear in N. Astrolabe incorporates physical flow matching by taking the prior distribution for the flow to be approximate COmoving Lagrangian Acceleration (COLA)-based coordinates rather than unphysical noise, with momentum and mass conservation enforced at all points along flow time. In the Lambda-CDM cases we test, Astrolabe produces realistic fields with accurate power spectra, halo mass functions, velocity profiles, and halo density profiles. We also observe out-of-distribution generalization, with accurate emulation of dark-acoustic oscillation initial conditions. Astrolabe is also capable of being fine-tuned to simulate very large N and we demonstrate this by emulating a TNG50-3-dark simulation at a fraction of the cost. This method represents a first step toward a general and powerful cosmology simulation surrogate, which may eventually permit the inclusion of baryonic physics and a systematic exploration of richer dark sector interactions.
authors: Ibrahim Elsharkawy, David Curtin, Yonatan Kahn, Neal Weiner
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of scanning dark-matter theory space with N-body and hydrodynamic simulations.
Generates all 6N particle phase-space coordinates directly, avoiding voxel-resolution limits and restricting inference to predefined observables.
Uses a field-particle hybrid transformer with linear-in-particle compute and memory, plus COLA-based priors and enforced momentum and mass conservation.
Produces realistic power spectra, halo mass functions, velocity profiles, and density profiles in tested ΛCDM cases, and generalizes to dark-acoustic oscillation initial conditions.
Can be fine-tuned for very large particle counts, demonstrated on a TNG50-3-dark simulation at lower cost; broader baryonic and dark-sector applications remain future scope.
papers.selection_reason: A generative emulator for cosmology simulations using flow matching, which predicts future environments and acts as a world model for physical dynamics.
papers.title: ASTROLABE: A 3D Particle-Level Surrogate for Cosmology Simulation with Physical Flow Matching
papers.tldr: Astrolabe is a particle-level flow-matching emulator that efficiently generates cosmological simulations while preserving physical constraints and supporting flexible observable measurements.

papers.abstract: Deterministic dynamics modeling of tendon-driven continuum robots remains challenging owing to uncertainties in material behavior, tendon transmission, friction, and contact. Measured joint configurations and nominal tendon commands do not fully characterize these internal mechanical factors, leaving uncertainty in the subsequent motion. We therefore develop a history-conditioned, physics-informed flow-matching framework for probabilistic dynamics prediction, using motion and actuation histories to predict the distribution of the next complete joint configuration. By recursively sampling next-step configurations under prescribed commands, the model predicts distributions of future whole-body motions. In simulation, scenario-specific models achieve five-second trajectory Energy Scores (lower is better) of 12.05 mm under internal friction variation and 9.29 mm under unobserved actuation disturbances. Relative to the conditional variational autoencoder and diffusion baselines, Flow attains lower Energy Scores and coverage closer to the nominal level in both scenarios. Ablations support history and structural conditioning in both scenarios. On the physical robot, predictions under two tendon-command profiles excluded from training capture the principal motion sequences, with five-second Energy Scores of 11.91 and 11.42 mm, lower than the compared baselines. The predicted-to-measured spread ratios are 1.65 and 1.22 (closer to 1 is better). These results support history-conditioned probabilistic dynamics prediction under incomplete mechanical observations.
bullets: Addresses uncertainty from material behavior, tendon transmission, friction, and contact that is not captured by current configurations and nominal commands.
Uses motion and actuation histories with structural conditioning to predict distributions of the next complete joint configuration.
Recursive sampling produces distributions of future trajectories under prescribed tendon commands.
In simulation and physical-robot tests, the method achieved lower Energy Scores than variational and diffusion baselines, while capturing principal motion sequences.
Results support probabilistic dynamics prediction under incomplete mechanical observations, with evaluation focused on tested friction, actuation-disturbance, and command-profile scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: History-conditioned probabilistic dynamics prediction for continuum robots under actuation commands; fits action-conditioned interactive world modeling.
papers.title: History-Conditioned Flow Matching for Probabilistic Dynamics of Tendon-Driven Continuum Robots
papers.tldr: A history-conditioned, physics-informed flow-matching model predicts probabilistic whole-body motion of tendon-driven continuum robots under unobserved mechanical uncertainties.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models keep the KV of past chunks as retrieval memory so that revisited places stay consistent. On a single consumer machine (one RTX 4090, 32 GiB of host memory, one NVMe SSD), long sessions with such memory hit two walls. The first is capacity: the KV of Matrix-Game 2.0 exhausts host memory after 45 seconds of video in bf16 and after 2.8 minutes in int4. The second is the model's positional horizon of 4.3 minutes. We show that this memory is capacity-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and that its access set is known before compute, because the camera pose is an input. An analytical model built on these observations predicts spill points to within one chunk and classifies zero versus non-zero stalls correctly on held-out configurations. Guided by it, WorldPager stores int4 KV in a GPU/DRAM/NVMe hierarchy instead of recomputing it, prefetches each chunk's memory from the extrapolated pose, never waits on a miss, and writes back in the background; to our knowledge, it is the first to place the KV memory of an interactive world model on an NVMe tier with zero-stall prefetching. With training-free position handling, it generates 37.5 minutes of video continuously with zero stalls and constant host memory, at about 9.5 frames per second. On a sealed test set, int4 storage shows no measurable quality loss; on long-gap revisits it lowers image quality by about one MUSIQ point.
bullets: Addresses host-memory exhaustion and the model’s limited positional horizon during long interactive sessions.
Uses an analytical access model based on known camera poses to predict spill points and classify potential stalls.
Stores KV memory in a GPU/DRAM/NVMe hierarchy, prefetches before computation, avoids waiting on misses, and writes back asynchronously.
Generates 37.5 minutes of continuous video at about 9.5 FPS with zero stalls and constant host memory on a single RTX 4090 system.
Reports no measurable quality loss with int4 storage on a sealed test set, but about a one-point MUSIQ drop for long-gap revisits.
papers.selection_reason: Presents tiered memory and zero-stall prefetching for interactive world model KV caches, relevant to efficient inference and world model deployment.
papers.title: WorldPager: Zero-Stall Tiered Memory for Long-Horizon World Models on a Single Consumer GPU
papers.tldr: WorldPager enables continuous, zero-stall long-horizon world-model video by paging int4 KV memory across GPU, DRAM, and NVMe with pose-guided prefetching.

papers.abstract: World models are emerging as a fundamental component of policy learning for real-world agents, enabling agents to predict future world states and plan actions within a learned representation of the dynamic environment. Existing approaches, however, often model appearance, metric geometry represented by projected LiDAR depth, and ego motion either partially or independently, overlooking the fact that these modalities are different projections of a shared underlying world state. This separation can lead to information loss and cross-modal inconsistency, ultimately limiting downstream performance. Motivated by this unified view of the world, we propose DriveUniTok, a unified multimodal tokenizer for driving world-action models (WAMs) that encodes these modalities in a single decodable continuous latent. We freeze DriveUniTok and adapt a pretrained diffusion model, DriveUniWAM, to predict future unified latents; the tokenizer then decodes them into future appearance, projected LiDAR depth, and ego trajectories. Experiments on NAVSIM demonstrate that our unified design achieves better future prediction and planning performance at lower downstream computational cost than separate-stream alternatives. With reinforcement learning post-training, DriveUniWAM achieves a PDMS of 91.54, reaching state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated WAM-based planners.
authors: Jingbo Xu, Hanchao Leng, JiaHui Huang, Hanbing Li, Jingwei Zhao, Kuiyuan Yang, Chen Gao, Guang Chen, Hangjun Ye, Yong Li
bullets: Addresses information loss and cross-modal inconsistency caused by modeling driving modalities separately.
Encodes appearance, projected LiDAR depth, and ego trajectories into a shared continuous latent.
Uses a frozen tokenizer with a pretrained diffusion model, DriveUniWAM, to predict future unified latents.
On NAVSIM, the unified design improves future prediction and planning while reducing downstream computational cost.
With reinforcement-learning post-training, DriveUniWAM reaches a PDMS of 91.54 and state-of-the-art performance among evaluated WAM planners.
papers.selection_reason: Unified multimodal tokenizer for driving world-action models; directly relevant to interactive world models and learned planning.
papers.title: DriveUniTok: A Unified Multimodal Tokenizer for Driving World-Action Models
papers.tldr: DriveUniTok unifies visual appearance, LiDAR depth, and ego motion into one decodable latent, improving driving world-model prediction and planning efficiency.

papers.abstract: Assistive agents in shared-control settings face a dual challenge: acting proactively to align with the human's intentions while remaining legible enough for the human to comprehend and fluently respond in real time. We present Dream2Assist, a model-based reinforcement learning framework for tightly-coupled shared decision making that addresses both sides of this challenge. Our approach extends a recurrent state-space world model with intent inference, enabling an assistive policy trained via fictitious co-play to anticipate and support discrete human objectives without overriding human agency. Beyond the computational framework, we describe the full deployment pipeline needed to translate a world-model-based policy into a safe, human-centered system in a resource-efficient way. Crucially, we address the sim-to-real-human gap via policy down-selection and reward restructuring within an iterative human-machine interface design. We validate the framework through three human-subjects studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment spanning two qualitatively distinct domains: high-speed racing (N=30) and urban driving with richer intent structure (N=10). Our results demonstrate that intent conditioning yields measurable improvements in torque alignment and collision rate. We surface key design insights and practices for deploying learning-based assistive agents in safety-critical, real-time human-robot teaming.
authors: Jonathan DeCastro, Thomas Balch, Emily Sumner, Deepak Gopinath, Laporsha Dees, Patricio Reyes Gomez, Elliot Weiss, Megan Applegate-Kenton, Todd Rowell, John Leonard, Avinash Balachandran, Guy Rosman
bullets: Targets the challenge of proactive yet understandable assistance in tightly coupled human–vehicle control.
Extends a recurrent state-space world model with human-intent inference and trains the assistive policy through fictitious co-play.
Includes a deployment pipeline with policy down-selection, reward restructuring, and iterative human–machine interface design to address the sim-to-real-human gap.
Validated in three human-subject studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment covering high-speed racing and urban driving.
Intent conditioning improved torque alignment and collision rate; the work also reports deployment insights for safety-critical human–robot teaming.
papers.selection_reason: Intent-conditioned world model for shared vehicle control; fits interactive world models and model-based robot control.
papers.title: Dream to Assist: Intent-Conditioned World Models for Shared Vehicle Control
papers.tldr: Dream2Assist uses intent-conditioned world models to help shared-control vehicles anticipate human goals while preserving human agency and real-time legibility.

papers.abstract: Most action-conditioned video world models remain limited to a single player, while existing multiplayer models support only small, fixed groups of agents. We introduce FlockWorld, an artificial-life environment built on Reynolds's Boids algorithm for studying population-scale multi-agent video world models. Specifically, FlockWorld renders synchronized egocentric crops, assigns distinct colors to preserve camera-agent identity across views, exposes rule-derived accelerations as actions, and lets the number of camera agents be configured independently of the size of the surrounding population. We further introduce FlockDiT, an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer trained with flow matching on FlockWorld data to jointly generate synchronized egocentric videos for multiple agents. Our results suggest that joint generation benefits agent detection at density-matched settings and that diffusion forcing improves rollout fidelity. Together, FlockWorld and FlockDiT provide a controlled testbed for multi-agent video generation.
authors: Meryem Koksal, Yunzhe Wang, Volkan Ustun
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing action-conditioned video world models, which typically support one agent or small fixed groups.
Builds an environment from Reynolds’s Boids algorithm with synchronized egocentric views, color-based agent identities, and configurable camera-agent and population sizes.
Introduces FlockDiT, an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer trained with flow matching for joint multi-agent video generation.
The abstract reports improved agent detection in density-matched settings and better rollout fidelity with diffusion forcing.
Provides a controlled testbed rather than a claim of broad real-world performance; its scope is artificial-life simulation.
papers.selection_reason: Population-scale multi-agent action-conditioned video world model; fits world models and video diffusion.
papers.title: FlockWorld: Toward Population-Scale Multi-Agent Video World Models through Artificial Life Simulation
papers.tldr: FlockWorld is a controlled artificial-life benchmark and FlockDiT model for generating synchronized egocentric videos across population-scale multi-agent scenes.

papers.abstract: World action models have demonstrated promising performance in robot policy learning, yet their high inference latency remains a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment. Recent approaches have sought to improve inference efficiency by reducing test-time future-frame imagination or accelerating action prediction. However, these methods often leverage representations from all video world model layers without explicitly considering their varying relevance to action prediction, leading to redundant computation and suboptimal representation utilization. In this work, we propose TurboWAM, a fast world action model that efficiently aggregates structured world representations conditioned on action predictions. Specifically, TurboWAM introduces a structured world representation aggregation module that adaptively fuses representations from different world model layers according to their relevance to the evolving action denoising state. Furthermore, TurboWAM employs a structured action supervision mechanism that adaptively modulates gradients from action supervision across different world model layers during backward propagation, facilitating world representation learning. During inference, by reducing the number of world model layers executed and caching relevant representations across action denoising steps, TurboWAM substantially reduces computational overhead. Extensive experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that TurboWAM achieves low inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates compared with state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Guile Wu, Shuangzhi Li, Xingxin Chen, Chengjie Huang, Sam Hosseini, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang, Dongfeng Bai
bullets: Addresses high inference latency that limits real-world deployment of world action models.
Adaptively aggregates representations from different world-model layers based on the evolving action-denoising state.
Uses structured action supervision to modulate layer-wise gradients and improve representation learning.
Reduces inference cost by executing fewer world-model layers and caching relevant representations across denoising steps.
Experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks show low latency with competitive task success rates.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes TurboWAM, a fast world action model that reduces inference latency for robot policy learning by aggregating relevant world model representations.
papers.title: TurboWAM: Learning What Matters for Fast World Action Models
papers.tldr: TurboWAM accelerates robot world action models by using only action-relevant world representations while preserving competitive task success.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models hold immense potential for high-stakes applications in robotics, game engines, and immersive digital twins, yet existing benchmarks primarily focus on perceptual similarity rather than the physical-causal coherence essential for real-world utility. We introduce WMEval, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates interactive world models against Unity-based physical simulations. By leveraging Unity as a high-fidelity ground-truth oracle, we shift evaluation beyond perceptual visual assessment toward the objective state-based verification required for downstream applications. Spanning 9 diverse scenes, WMEval assesses action controllability, scene and character consistency, prompt adherence, kinematics, fluid mechanics, physical causality, and lighting. By executing matched action sequences in both the simulator and the world model, WMEval enables evaluation at both the perceptual level and the physical-causal level, using simulator-derived states as reference. Experiments on state-of-the-art models reveal significant room for improvement in dimensions that remain hidden by standard perceptual metrics but are vital for real-world deployments. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/WMEval.
authors: Lanxiang Hu, Yixin Huang, Abhilash Shankarampeta, Zilin Dai, Yuyuan Wu, Kun Qian, Junze Liu, Arvind Srinivasan, Mingjia Huo, Will Lin, Kai Zhong, Weiqi Zhang, Tian Wang, Qingjun Cui, Tajana Rosing, Hao Zhang
bullets: Evaluates world models across 9 diverse scenes using Unity as a high-fidelity ground-truth oracle.
Tests controllability, scene and character consistency, prompt adherence, kinematics, fluid mechanics, physical causality, and lighting.
Runs matched action sequences in both the simulator and world model, comparing perceptual and simulator-derived states.
Finds substantial weaknesses in state-of-the-art models that standard perceptual metrics fail to reveal.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces WMEval, a benchmark for evaluating interactive world models against physical simulations, focusing on physical-causal coherence essential for real-world utility.
papers.title: WMEval: Evaluating Interactive World Models Grounded on Physical Simulations
papers.tldr: WMEval benchmarks interactive world models against Unity physics simulations to measure physical-causal correctness beyond visual similarity.

papers.abstract: While interactive video world models require autoregressive generation, directly adapting pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into autoregressive ones with teacher forcing can disrupt their visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality. In this paper, we introduce Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (MoBA) attention. Mix Forcing jointly trains a video diffusion model with both teacher forcing and bidirectional training, yielding a strong causal initialization for few-step post-training. In self-attention, Mix Forcing leverages teacher forcing to learn causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while using bidirectional attention to preserve pretrained visual priors. To support online text interaction, Mix Forcing further adopts a chunk-wise cross-attention design that conditions each video chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, without exposing future instructions to the current chunk. Following causal pre-training on a 14B image-to-video model, we apply consistency and distribution matching distillation to obtain a four-step autoregressive generator. Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks, including WBench and SANA-WM-Bench, show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control. Notably, our model supports high-fidelity long-horizon generation without quality degradation even over one-hour rollouts. Project page is here: https://zelingao98.github.io/mixforcing
authors: Zelin Gao, Hao Ouyang, Jiapeng Zhu, Qiuyu Wang, Jingye Chen, Zichen Liu, Xing Zhu, Yujun Shen, Yinghao Xu
bullets: Addresses the degradation of visual priors when adapting bidirectional video diffusion models to causal, autoregressive generation.
Introduces MoBA attention, jointly combining teacher-forced causal prediction with bidirectional training for causal initialization.
Uses chunk-wise cross-attention to condition video on shared environment context and local instructions without revealing future prompts.
Applies consistency and distribution-matching distillation to produce a four-step autoregressive generator.
Reports state-of-the-art visual quality, event following, and camera control, with high-fidelity rollouts lasting up to one hour on reported benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Causal pre-training with mixture attention for interactive video world models, enabling long-horizon autoregressive rollout.
papers.title: Mix Forcing: Causal Pre-Training via Mixture Attention for Interactive World Models
papers.tldr: Mix Forcing converts bidirectional video diffusion models into efficient autoregressive world models while preserving visual quality and enabling long-horizon interactive generation.

papers.abstract: Robot policy evaluation informs deployment decisions and policy improvement, but physical testing and simulator preparation require substantial effort. World models offer a complementary route through closed-loop interaction in generated environments. Recent benchmarks have demonstrated their potential as policy evaluators through outcome-based evaluation (i.e., assessing task success or failure). However, such evaluation does not establish whether world models faithfully simulate how policies fail. Misrepresenting failures can lead to incorrect diagnoses of policy weaknesses and make policies appear ready for deployment even when small scene changes cause them to fail. We therefore ask: do world models faithfully simulate how and at which stages policies fail, and under what conditions they transition from success to failure? To answer this question, we introduce WorldFailBench with three evaluation tasks. Failure reason tests whether models reproduce the observable errors policies make. Failure stage assesses whether failures concentrate at the same stages of full-task execution. Failure boundary examines whether models reproduce the conditions under which policies transition from success to failure under controlled scene changes in simulation. The benchmark covers manipulation tasks in the LIBERO and RoboTwin simulation environments and real-world manipulation tasks performed by the G1 humanoid robot. Experiments across seven world models reveal substantial gaps in their understanding of policy failures, providing guidance for developing more reliable world models for policy evaluation.
authors: Zheng Zhang, Xiaoyang Tang, Shuaiqi Cheng, Jiakai Huang, Zhongbo Wu, Ziyi Zhang, Yuan Si, Zeyu Liu, Weibo Gao, Shunyu Liu, Shan You, Fei Wang, Xiaogang Wang, Dacheng Tao
bullets: Introduces three failure-focused evaluation tasks: failure reason, failure stage, and failure boundary.
Tests manipulation policies in LIBERO, RoboTwin, and real-world G1 humanoid robot tasks.
Evaluates seven world models for closed-loop policy evaluation.
Finds substantial gaps in world models’ ability to understand and simulate policy failures.
Highlights the need for more reliable world models before using them to guide deployment decisions.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating whether world models faithfully simulate policy failures in closed-loop interaction.
papers.title: WorldFailBench: Do World Models Understand Policy Failures?
papers.tldr: WorldFailBench evaluates whether world models faithfully reproduce not just policy outcomes, but also the reasons, stages, and conditions of robot policy failures.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models require coordinated control over viewing perspectives, character actions, and camera motion. Existing methods typically leave view modes implicit in text captions, conflate action with camera motion, and inject controls through fragmented architectural pathways that capture interdependencies only indirectly. In this work, we present World-in-Context, an interactive world modeling framework powered by In-Context Conditioning (ICC). Rather than relying on specialized conditioning pathways, World-in-Context unifies view, action, and camera controls into explicit tokens contextualized directly within a shared self-attention space. Our formulation reveals that (i) explicit view tokens disentangle conflicting dynamics and unlock emergent view switching from single-view data, while (ii) action and camera inputs play complementary roles in governing local responsiveness and global stability. To preserve temporal continuity across execution intervals, we further introduce Interaction-Transport RoPE (IT-RoPE), parameterizing temporal attention with accumulated control transitions. On WBench, World-in-Context-5B achieves navigation performance on par with 22B EchoWM ($81.5$ vs. $81.6$) and attains a $93.8\%$ perspective-switching success rate, substantially outperforming existing 5B baselines ($18.8\%$). Controlled analyses further demonstrate compounding advantages of World-in-Context under richer conditioning mixtures, favorable data efficiency, and natural applicability to causal rollouts.
authors: Harold Haodong Chen, Rui Peng, Rongjin Guo, Lingteng Qiu, Kejie Qiu, Chao Xu, Zilong Dong
bullets: Addresses implicit view control, entangled action–camera effects, and fragmented conditioning in existing world models.
Uses In-Context Conditioning to unify view, action, and camera inputs within shared self-attention.
Introduces Interaction-Transport RoPE to maintain temporal continuity across control execution intervals.
On WBench, the 5B model matches the navigation performance of 22B EchoWM and achieves 93.8% perspective-switching success.
Analyses indicate benefits from richer conditioning, improved data efficiency, and compatibility with causal rollouts.
papers.selection_reason: Presents World-in-Context, an interactive video world modeling framework using In-Context Conditioning to unify view, action, and camera controls, fitting the interactive world models subtopic.
papers.title: World-in-Context: Interactive Video World Modeling with In-Context Conditioning
papers.tldr: World-in-Context enables controllable interactive video world modeling by representing view, action, and camera controls as explicit in-context tokens with temporally aware attention.

papers.abstract: Latent world models are routinely selected, checkpointed and ablated on one-step prediction loss, on the assumption that a model which predicts the next latent better is a better model. In model-based RL this assumption is known to be unreliable; we ask whether it also fails for latent world models, where the training target is the model's own embedding and the loss is not expressed in interpretable units. We introduce a frozen-decoder protocol reporting one-step error in physical units, decomposed into the part already present in the encoder's representation and the part the predictor adds. Applying it to a recent end-to-end JEPA world model across three continuous-control environments, we move the metric by fine-tuning and measure goal-conditioned planning on the same checkpoints, with three training seeds and paired planning seeds throughout. Within one environment, a per-epoch ladder shows the relationship saturating after a single epoch: the first epoch improves fidelity by 32% and planning by 4.4 pp, but across the fifteen checkpoints that follow -- a further 15% fidelity improvement, monotone in every training seed -- the correlation between one-step error and planning success is r = -0.010. This is not a task-ceiling artifact: stratifying by a model-independent measure of training-data support, planning in the lowest-support stratum starts at 80%, leaving ample headroom, and is nonetheless flat from epoch 1 onward. Across environments the exchange rate is equally unstable: a 93% fidelity reduction on TwoRoom yields -0.7 pp of planning, while a 40% reduction on PushT yields +4.9 pp [+1.1, +8.9]. All results replicate under a decoder-free measure, latent drift. We also show that a matched continued-training control absorbs the entire fidelity gain we had attributed to an auxiliary objective.
bullets: The study tests whether lower one-step latent prediction error reliably indicates better goal-conditioned planning.
A frozen-decoder protocol measures prediction error in physical units and separates encoder representation error from predictor-added error.
Across three continuous-control environments, fidelity improvements often produced little, no, or inconsistent planning improvement.
Within one environment, later checkpoints improved fidelity by 15% while planning-error correlation was effectively zero (r = -0.010).
The findings replicated with a decoder-free latent-drift metric, and a continued-training control explained away gains attributed to an auxiliary objective.
papers.selection_reason: Shows one-step JEPA prediction loss is a poor proxy for planning performance; directly relevant to world-model evaluation.
papers.title: One-Step Prediction Fidelity Is a Poor Proxy for Planning Performance in JEPA World Models
papers.tldr: One-step prediction fidelity is a poor and unstable proxy for planning performance in JEPA world models.

papers.abstract: Accurate neural world models are central to model-based robotics, where they enable robots to predict future states from previously observed trajectories. Multi-step autoregressive training improves long-horizon prediction, but fixed rollout horizons also increase computational cost and can amplify early training errors when the model is still inaccurate. Existing training schemes typically use the same rollout length throughout optimization, independent of the model's current predictive reliability. We propose an epistemic uncertainty-driven adaptive rollout strategy for offline world model training following an auto-curriculum training scheme. Instead of always unrolling to a fixed horizon, the model terminates autoregressive rollouts once epistemic uncertainty exceeds a threshold calibrated from a warm-up phase. We study two uncertainty estimators: a five-head ensemble with a shared recurrent backbone and Monte Carlo Dropout. A two-stage warm-up procedure stabilizes uncertainty estimates before we enable adaptive truncation. Experiments on ANYmal-D and ANT show that ensemble-based adaptive truncation matches or improves the prediction accuracy of fixed-horizon training and the RWM-U baseline while requiring substantially fewer cumulative rollout steps. Training a world model on ANYmal-D following the presented approach reaches comparable final performance with the baselines with roughly 72% less rollout computation. These results indicate that epistemic uncertainty is useful not only for downstream policy regularization, but also for making world model training itself more compute-efficient.
bullets: Fixed rollout horizons can waste computation and amplify early autoregressive prediction errors.
The method adaptively stops rollouts when epistemic uncertainty exceeds a warm-up-calibrated threshold.
It evaluates a five-head ensemble and Monte Carlo Dropout as uncertainty estimators within an auto-curriculum.
On ANYmal-D and ANT, ensemble-based truncation matches or improves fixed-horizon and RWM-U prediction accuracy.
ANYmal-D training achieves comparable final performance with roughly 72% fewer cumulative rollout steps.
papers.selection_reason: Epistemic-uncertainty-driven adaptive rollout truncation for offline robot world model training, directly relevant to world models.
papers.title: Adaptive Rollout Truncation Based on Epistemic Uncertainty for Efficient Offline World Model Training
papers.tldr: Epistemic-uncertainty-based rollout truncation makes offline world-model training substantially more compute-efficient while preserving prediction accuracy.

papers.abstract: Actions that condition world models are highly heterogeneous, and thus existing action-conditioned world models are typically built for individual action types, fragmenting already limited action-annotated data across separate models. We introduce UniAction, a unified action-conditioning framework that represents any action as a sparse set of action elements, each with a discrete semantic identity and a continuous spatiotemporal grounding coordinate. By mapping these coordinates directly into the pretrained video model's native positional space, UniAction allows heterogeneous actions to condition a shared world model within the same spatiotemporal structure. We further introduce cardinality-calibrated attention to address the bias from differing action representation granularities. We evaluate UniAction on four representative action forms: force, camera control, hand pose, and robot pose. UniAction outperforms conditioning alternatives in action following, and a single jointly trained model surpasses the action-specific experts, showing that heterogeneous action data benefit from unified model and joint training.
authors: Bowen Xue, Zizhang Li, Hong-Xing Yu, Jiajun Wu
bullets: Addresses fragmented action-labeled data caused by action-specific world models.
Maps discrete action identities and continuous spatiotemporal coordinates into a pretrained video model’s positional space.
Uses cardinality-calibrated attention to reduce bias from different action representation granularities.
Evaluated on force, camera control, hand pose, and robot pose conditioning.
The jointly trained unified model improves action following and surpasses action-specific experts.
papers.selection_reason: Unifies heterogeneous action conditioning for action-conditioned video world models, directly addressing interactive world-model learning.
papers.title: UniAction: Unified Action Conditioning for World Models
papers.tldr: UniAction unifies heterogeneous action conditioning in one world model by encoding actions as sparse semantic elements with spatiotemporal coordinates.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has gained attention for improving action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), as it enables reward-driven optimization of visual quality (VQ) and action-following fidelity (AF) beyond flow-matching optimization. Realizing this potential requires reward signals that reliably rank videos by both VQ and AF. However, existing rewards capture only one dimension: metric-based rewards assess VQ but require ground-truth videos and do not directly assess AF, while inverse dynamics model (IDM) rewards assess AF without references but do not guarantee VQ. Moreover, IDMs, typically trained on real videos, may provide unreliable rewards for generated videos containing visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies. In this work, we introduce the Action and Video Mismatch Benchmark (AVM-Eval), comprising 67.2k pairs that evaluate how reliably IDMs assess AF on real and generated videos. We then propose ACWM-RM, a reward model that jointly assesses VQ and AF without ground-truth videos during reward computation. To train it, we first construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) with 506.3k pairs providing complementary supervision: action-mismatch pairs supervise AF, while video-mismatch pairs supervise VQ and expose the model to generated videos. We then pretrain an action-conditioned predictor on real videos to learn forward dynamics before jointly training it with a patch-weighted score head on AVM-Pref to transfer these dynamics to AF assessment on generated videos. Evaluation on AVM-Eval reveals the limited reliability of IDMs on generated videos, while downstream RL experiments show that ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines in both criteria.
authors: Shibo Hong, Siyu Ren, FengJiao Chen, Zhongyuan Peng, Wei Shi, Yixin Cao
bullets: Existing rewards assess either visual quality with ground-truth videos or action fidelity without reliably handling visual artifacts.
AVM-Eval benchmarks inverse dynamics model reliability on real and generated videos using 67.2k pairs.
AVM-Pref provides complementary action-mismatch and video-mismatch preferences across 506.3k pairs.
The model transfers forward dynamics learned from real videos to generated-video assessment via joint training with a patch-weighted score head.
Experiments show IDMs are unreliable on generated videos, while ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines on both criteria in downstream reinforcement learning.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a reward model for action-conditioned world models, directly targeting visual quality and action-following fidelity in ACWMs.
papers.title: ACWM-RM: A Reference-Free Reward Model from Complementary Mismatch Preferences
papers.tldr: ACWM-RM is a reference-free reward model that jointly evaluates visual quality and action-following fidelity for action-conditioned world models.

papers.abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $\Psi$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $\Psi$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $\Psi$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.
authors: Khai Loong Aw, Klemen Kotar, Baihan Zhang, Yifan Liu, Lilian Chen, Atlas Kazemian, Rahul Venkatesh, Daniel Yamins
bullets: Interleaves images, text, geometry, and motion representations as composable “streams of thought” through a shared token interface.
Performs zero-shot multi-view spatial reasoning and benefits from explicit geometric intermediate reasoning.
Supports counterfactual simulation, such as predicting whether moving an object would block a path.
Reinforcement learning from task feedback improves intermediate-representation selection and visual question answering, with gains transferring to unseen benchmarks.
The abstract focuses on adaptive physical reasoning; specific limitations and quantitative results are not reported.
papers.selection_reason: Unified vision-language world model with geometric/spatial reasoning and counterfactual simulation directly fits world models, spatial intelligence, and 3D reasoning.
papers.title: $\Psi$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model
papers.tldr: Ψ-0.6 is a unified vision-language world model that adaptively combines visual, linguistic, geometric, and simulated reasoning for flexible physical-world inference.

papers.abstract: Existing approaches for robot learning in simulation often require substantial manual effort to construct scenes and specify tasks, limiting training scalability and data diversity. Meanwhile, in-the-wild robot demonstrations naturally provide diverse and realistic observations of real-world interactions. Leveraging these demonstrations for simulation requires both high-fidelity visual reconstruction and physically consistent interactions. General-purpose agents offer flexible adaptation to diverse scenarios and strong reasoning about 3D spatial relationships, while specialized generative models provide high-fidelity reconstruction of scene appearance and geometry. We introduce WorldMirror, an agentic real-to-sim framework that constructs interactive digital twins from in-the-wild robot demonstrations. Our central idea is to formulate real-to-sim construction as the iterative refinement of an executable world program. A coding agent decomposes the observed scene, plans reconstruction steps, and orchestrates specialized image and 3D generation tools, refining the program through verification feedback. A camera-pose-anchored scene representation organizes the world into static visual context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets while preserving spatial relationships among the scene, objects, and robot. The agent uses this representation to diagnose and correct reconstruction errors, enabling physically consistent interaction and trajectory replay. Experiments on DROID demonstrate that WorldMirror can reconstruct visually faithful and geometrically consistent interactive worlds while preserving the physical validity of recorded robot trajectories.
authors: Tianling Xu, Weijie Wan, Honghao Su, Kailun Su, Junyuan Tang, Huichi Zhou, Haozheng Zhang, Qi Xiong, Ping Luo, Wenbo Ding, Tianxing Chen, Yue Chen
bullets: Addresses the manual effort and limited scalability of constructing robot-learning scenes and tasks in simulation.
Uses a coding agent to decompose demonstrations, orchestrate specialized image and 3D generation tools, and refine an executable world program with verification feedback.
Employs a camera-pose-anchored representation separating static context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets while preserving spatial relationships.
Supports error diagnosis, correction, physically consistent interactions, and replay of recorded robot trajectories.
Experiments on DROID show visually faithful and geometrically consistent reconstructed worlds that preserve trajectory validity.
papers.selection_reason: Constructs interactive digital twins from in-the-wild robot demonstrations, directly fitting interactive world models for robot learning in simulation.
papers.title: WorldMirror: Agentic Real-to-Sim Generation of Interactive Worlds from In-the-Wild Robot Demonstrations
papers.tldr: WorldMirror turns in-the-wild robot demonstrations into visually faithful, physically interactive simulation worlds through agent-guided iterative reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.
authors: Shengqiong Wu, Meng Luo, Bobo Li, Ziwei Liu, Shuicheng Yan, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Philip Torr, Hao Fei
bullets: Frames video as a partial, lossy, time-ordered projection of a latent temporal world.
Organizes research into reading world properties, writing videos, sharing understanding and generation, and interacting through actions and observations.
Distinguishes sequence-level temporal coherence from consistency of the underlying world state.
Highlights a shift from clip recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and decision-oriented evaluation.
Identifies open challenges in representations, models, datasets, benchmarks, and interaction-based assessment.
papers.selection_reason: Survey unifying video foundation models and world models directly fits world modeling and video understanding.
papers.title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video
papers.tldr: This survey unifies video foundation and world models through four operations—reading, writing, sharing, and interacting—to study how videos represent and support reasoning about evolving worlds.

papers.abstract: Tasks such as quadrotor dynamic-gate racing require agents to anticipate external motion while maintaining precise high-frequency control. World-model-based reinforcement learning provides a natural solution by learning latent dynamics for future imagination, yet it often entangles environmental evolution and the robot's own dynamics in a single learned rollout, where model bias can affect policy optimization efficiency. We propose DiffDreamer, a differentiable reinforcement learning framework that tightly couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation for actor optimization. In one optimization step, the learned world model propagates latent states that capture external dynamics and history-dependent features, while the differentiable simulator propagates the robot's explicit physical state. We further decompose the actor objective into a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards and a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards. Experiments on aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing show that DiffDreamer improves training convergence over the model-free, model-based, and differentiable-RL baselines, and final performance over these baselines and classical planning and control methods. Additional experiments assess reward decomposition and the odometry-conditioned relative-state representation through ablations. We also provide proof-of-concept real-world flight experiments for validation.
authors: Fanxing Li, Yuxiang Huang, Shengyang Wang, Fangyu Sun, Shuyu Wu, Tianbao Zhang, Dexin Zuo, Yan Yufei, Danping Zou, Wenxian Yu
bullets: Targets aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing, where agents must anticipate moving obstacles while controlling quadrotors at high frequency.
Uses a world model for external dynamics and history-dependent latent features, while a differentiable simulator handles the robot’s explicit physical state.
Splits actor optimization between critic-based non-differentiable task rewards and simulator-based differentiable motion rewards.
Experiments report faster training convergence and better final performance than multiple learning, planning, and control baselines.
Ablations and proof-of-concept real-world flights evaluate reward decomposition and odometry-conditioned relative-state representations.
papers.selection_reason: Couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation for agile quadrotor RL control, directly relevant to embodied robot learning and world-model-based policy optimization.
papers.title: DiffDreamer: Coupling World Models with Differentiable Simulation for Agile Quadrotor Control
papers.tldr: DiffDreamer combines learned world-model predictions with differentiable quadrotor simulation to improve agile control in dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: World Models (WMs) can support Multimodal Agents (MAs) through simulated experience, while Agent trajectories can inform World Model refinement. Evaluating this interaction requires separate evidence about action selection and state evolution. We introduce Dual Exam, which tests Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The Agent track compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories. The World Model track contains 400 cases across eight scenarios; 15 configurations have full coverage and one covers six scenarios. GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index at 31.3, and GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall at 21.7. These scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. A 150-case pilot of one coupled pairing records zero task successes and motivates component-level diagnosis. Results reveal uneven task performance and failures to preserve task-relevant state. Their value for predicting coupled success or sustained reciprocal learning remains to be established.
authors: Zhefan Rao, Meng Chu, Xuan Zhang, Jingfan Chen, Guohao Cai, Runyi Li, Shiyi Du, Ning Lu, Xu Huang, Zhixuan Chen, Feng Nie, Harold Haodong Chen, Hanwen Wang, Wen-Jie Shu, Yajing Bai, Xianfeng Wu, Xuanhua He, Shuhan Guo, Ziyue Ma, Ruichuan An, Long Bai, Miaosen Chai, Wenhao Chai, Jingye Chen, Qi Chen, Xuhang Chen, Wei Chow, Minghao Fu, Yunhao Gou, Haokun Gui, Dong Huang, Wei Huang, Zi Cheng Huang, Haibo Jin, Lingdong Kong, Leung Chun Ho, Tianqin Li, Yanheng Li, Jiayuan Liu, Jiyang Liu, Mingyu Liu, Shaoteng Liu, Xiaocheng Lu, Yawen Luo, Zeyu Qin, Tiancheng Shen, Yueqi Song, Zhaolong Su, Hengkai Tan, Tianhao Tang, Yiran Tao, Juncheng Wang, Qinghe Wang, Shangshang Wang, Yingying Wang, Fang Wu, Tiange Xiang, Qiushi Yang, Weicai Ye, Weichen Yu, Jiarui Zhang, Jize Zhang, Liuzhou Zhang, Renrui Zhang, Sheng Zhang, Wenhu Zhang, Junru Zhao, Lingting Zhu, Yuxin Zuo, Yutong Bai, Long Chen, Yang Deng, Ziqi Huang, Yeying Jin, Weijia Li, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Quande Liu, See-Kiong Ng, Hongliang Ren, Hongru Wang, Shujun Wang, Qifeng Chen, Haoxuan Che
bullets: Tests agents with fixed environment responses and world models with fixed action interventions.
Covers physical, digital, social, and scientific domains using distinct tasks and metrics.
Evaluates 10 agent configurations on 1,088 items and 16 world-model configurations across 400 cases.
Reports leading scores of 31.3 for GPT 6 Astra on the Agent Index and 21.7 for GPT-Image-2 on the full-coverage WM Overall; these are not directly comparable.
A 150-case coupled pilot achieved zero task successes, highlighting failures in task-relevant state preservation and the need for component-level diagnosis.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates world models under fixed action interventions, fitting interactive world models.
papers.title: Dual Exam: Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models
papers.tldr: Dual Exam separately evaluates multimodal agents’ action selection and world models’ state evolution, revealing uneven performance and limited evidence that either predicts successful agent–world-model coupling.

papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations record what the robot saw and what it did. They do not specify how the 3D world changed in between. Scene-level 3D flow describes it by tracking 3D scene points, providing the world representation with 4D geometry. Prior work has used flow to improve robot policies. Flow served as an intermediate prediction that a separate model converts into actions, as a prior injected at inference time, or as an extra output learned together with the action. In all of these designs, flow stays outside the policy, as a separate module or as an extra prediction head. We introduce UniFlowWAM, a Unified World-Action Model that makes 3D scene flow a third modality on par with vision and action. Its world representation therefore covers both visual semantics, through future visual features, and 4D geometry, through 3D flow, and flow receives its own supervision. UniFlowWAM is a diffusion transformer with one expert per modality, and the three experts exchange information through joint attention. We train UniFlowWAM under a ten-objective role grid, where each objective assigns every modality exactly one of three roles, namely target, condition, or absent. The same model thus serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a predictor of future visual features or 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks. On RoboCasa-GR1, UniFlowWAM raises the success rate of its base model without flow from 52.1% to 56.4%. It preserves in-distribution success on LIBERO at 98.1% and reaches 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus. On the real robot, it achieves 87.0% average success, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.
authors: Jialin Tian, Zhuofan Li, Xinkai Wang, Bokai Lin, Chenyi Wang, Xinyu Zhan, Cewu Lu, Lixin Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitation that 3D flow is typically handled outside the robot policy as a separate module or output.
Uses a diffusion transformer with one expert each for vision, action, and 3D flow, connected through joint attention.
Trains across ten objectives that assign each modality as a target, condition, or absent, enabling policy, dynamics, and future-feature prediction tasks.
Improves RoboCasa-GR1 success from 52.1% to 56.4%, while achieving 98.1% on LIBERO and 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus.
Reaches 87.0% average success on four real-world bimanual tasks, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Unified action-world model treating 3D flow as a co-equal modality for manipulation policies and dynamics prediction.
papers.title: UniFlowWAM: A Unified World-Action Model with Visual Semantics and 4D Geometry
papers.tldr: UniFlowWAM unifies vision, actions, and 3D scene flow in one multimodal model, improving simulated and real-world robot manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Robust manipulation of soft objects, such as garments, is a critical skill for service and household robots to adopt, but remains challenging due to its high-dimensional state space, and material-dependent deformations. Humans address this challenge by using mental world models that "imagine" the shape and material properties from partial observations, which enables them to predict how actions affect future states. As such, embedding such world models in robots allows for better generalization in manipulating a wide variety of garments in the real world. However, learned world models typically require large amounts of real world data that is strenuous to collect, and a mechanism to infer latent properties that govern dynamics. We present a Soft-Object World Model that performs generative full-state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction using a transformer backbone trained on large-scale simulated soft object interactions, with measures to mitigate the sim-to-real gap. By learning to infer latent shape and material cues through in-context learning over a variable-length partial point-cloud history, the model generalizes across robot embodiments, material parameters, garment types and shapes, and manipulation coordination modes without weight updates. The world model is then integrated with a Goal-Conditioned action planner for motion synthesis. We validate the approach in simulation and real world for bimanual garment folding, reporting improvements in reconstruction fidelity, prediction accuracy, and task success.
authors: Hengyi Sim, Quentin Rouxel, Dennis Hong, Darwin Caldwell, Fei Chen
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of garment manipulation under high-dimensional, material-dependent dynamics and partial observations.
Uses a transformer trained on large-scale simulated soft-object interactions for generative full-state estimation and action-conditioned prediction.
Infers latent garment shape and material properties from variable-length partial point-cloud histories through in-context learning.
Integrates the world model with a goal-conditioned planner for bimanual motion synthesis.
Simulation and real-world folding experiments show improved reconstruction fidelity, prediction accuracy, and task success.
papers.selection_reason: In-context world model for action-conditioned soft-garment dynamics prediction and bimanual manipulation.
papers.title: In-Context Learning World Models for Robot Dual-Arm Manipulation of Soft Garment with Partial Observations
papers.tldr: An in-context transformer world model enables dual-arm robots to infer and manipulate partially observed garments across varied materials, shapes, and embodiments without model updates.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to reduce environment interaction when post-training vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning. Yet they are typically trained to predict pixels one step ahead, even though their role here is not merely to render visually faithful videos but to produce learning signals from imagined rollouts that improve the policy. We show that this mismatch is substantial: lower pixel MSE can produce worse policy gradients, and a world model trained for policy utility can yield better downstream policies despite 17% higher pixel MSE on the next frame. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that updates the world model to maximize the policy's return after an inner GRPO update on imagined rollouts. DRILL has two instantiations. DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Tailong Luo, Lei Wei, Guangyuan Dong, Sihan Liu, Yingjie He, Siheng Wang, Shuaibo Li, Rongchao Zhang, Zhen Tian, Richeng Xuan, Zhichao Hu
bullets: Pixel prediction quality can misalign with policy utility: lower next-frame MSE may yield worse policy gradients.
DRILL uses bilevel optimization to update the world model based on returns after an inner GRPO update from imagined rollouts.
DRILL-VWI is a rollout-free surrogate that weights errors by policy visitation, GRPO advantage, and model confidence.
DRILL-IMG differentiates through the inner update with truncated Hessian-vector products; DRILL-VWI approximates its local one-step gradient under stated assumptions.
Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG improves mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World.
papers.selection_reason: Trains action-conditioned world models to improve VLA policies via imagined rollouts, directly relevant to world models and embodied policy learning.
papers.title: DRILL: Training World Models to Improve Policies, Not Predict Pixels
papers.tldr: DRILL trains world models to produce useful policy-learning signals rather than merely predict pixels, improving downstream VLA policy performance.

papers.abstract: Before acting on an object, a robot needs to anticipate how its hand motion will change the physical world and what the resulting scene will look like. Existing approaches typically entangle action-conditioned dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis within a video generation model, or represent dynamics as point trajectories without explicit object structure. We introduce DeXplicit, a dexterous manipulation world model that instead predicts how the world evolves explicitly in metric 3D before rendering its visual consequences. Given an initial scene and a future hand trajectory, a lightweight 3D dynamics network predicts object-centric motion and deformation, providing structured and geometrically grounded future world states. These predictions then serve as a strong scaffold for video generation: appearance is transported through the predicted 3D motion and projected into future views, allowing the renderer to focus on completing uncertain and newly visible content rather than implicitly learning world dynamics from pixels. This explicit-3D-first decomposition also enables efficient causal generation, requiring only two denoising steps per block while conditioning on generated history. Across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, DeXplicit reduces moved-point error by 27-40% relative to PointWorld and improves object fidelity IoU+ by 47% on HOT3D under a shared renderer. Our design with two-step causal generation achieves a 57x speedup from our 14B bi-directional configuration in video synthesis.
authors: Adam Lee, Mutian Xu, Yukang Cao, Shulin Tian, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis in existing video-based world models.
Uses a lightweight 3D dynamics network to predict object-centric motion and deformation from an initial scene and future hand trajectory.
Transports appearance through predicted 3D motion, letting video generation focus on uncertain or newly visible content.
Reports 27–40% lower moved-point error than PointWorld across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, plus 47% higher object-fidelity IoU+ on HOT3D under a shared renderer.
Two-step causal generation provides a reported 57× speedup relative to the authors’ 14B bidirectional configuration.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned dexterous manipulation world model with explicit 3D dynamics, fitting interactive world models and robot manipulation.
papers.title: DeXplicit: Making Physical State Explicit in Dexterous Manipulation World Models
papers.tldr: DeXplicit improves dexterous-manipulation world modeling by predicting explicit metric-3D object motion before rendering future video.

papers.abstract: We propose AgentDreamer, an agent-guided optimization framework that aligns text instructions with simulated motion through explicit 3D motion planning. Given a text instruction and scene geometry, an off-the-shelf agent translates the instruction into a structured semantic motion prior, specifying what should move, in which direction, and in what temporal order. The agent represents this prior using parametric functions over a series of temporal chunks, yielding dense 3D trajectories. We then optimize the parameters of a differentiable MPM simulator such that its rollout best matches the prior while remaining constrained by the scene dynamics. This allows the agent to provide semantic guidance from language, while the simulator grounds it in physically feasible motion. We further introduce Motion-IG, an information-theoretic metric for text-motion alignment based on masked text recovery. By comparing the likelihood of recovering masked motion-related content with and without the simulated motion, Motion-IG measures the information contributed by the motion beyond that available from the remaining text and scene context. Experiments show that AgentDreamer improves text alignment over video-based guidance, producing simulations that more closely follow the requested physical behavior.
authors: Mijeong Kim, Suho Park, Junha Park, Bohyung Han
bullets: Converts language into structured semantic motion priors describing objects, directions, and temporal order.
Represents priors as parametric dense 3D trajectories across temporal chunks.
Optimizes a differentiable MPM simulator to match the priors while respecting scene dynamics.
Introduces Motion-IG, an information-theoretic metric for measuring text–motion alignment.
Improves text alignment over video-based guidance in experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Text-controllable physics simulation via agentic 3D motion planning fits interactive world models.
papers.title: AgentDreamer: Agentic 3D Motion Reasoning for Text-Controllable Physics Simulation
papers.tldr: AgentDreamer uses an agent-generated 3D motion plan to optimize differentiable physics simulations that better follow text instructions.

papers.abstract: Social world models predict how interactions develop after an action, helping agents negotiate, cooperate and mediate. In these situations, one action can lead to several plausible futures, hence predicting only one future can overlook consequential alternatives, while exploring them through repeated simulations increases inference cost. We propose DSWM, a Distributional Social World Model that predicts alternative responses, their probabilities and immediate and final outcome values in one output per candidate action. We train a 4B model on repeated simulations using supervised fine-tuning and GRPO. At inference time, the actor uses these possible consequences to choose an action. Across three seen and two unseen environments, with interaction backbones absent from training collection, DSWM achieves the best average performance on 13 of 15 metrics. Ablations show that retaining multiple futures and their predicted probabilities improves outcomes in all five environments.
authors: Viet-Thanh Pham, Thuy-Trang Vu, Zhuang Li, Lizhen Qu, Gholamreza Haffari
bullets: Models alternative responses, their probabilities, and immediate and final outcome values for each candidate action.
Trained on repeated simulations using supervised fine-tuning and GRPO.
Evaluated across three seen and two unseen environments, including interaction backbones absent from training data.
Achieves the best average performance on 13 of 15 metrics.
Ablations indicate that preserving multiple futures and their probabilities improves outcomes across all five environments.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a Distributional Social World Model that predicts alternative responses and probabilities for social interactions, fitting the definition of interactive world models.
papers.title: Anticipating Social Consequences with Distributional World Models
papers.tldr: DSWM predicts multiple likely social consequences and their values in one pass, helping agents choose better actions without costly repeated simulations.

papers.abstract: World models help agents assess the consequences of their actions before acting. Many real systems, however, involve multiple actors who make their own decisions, can evolve even when the agent takes no action, and are only partially observed through event logs. We formalize these systems as event worlds and ask whether large language models can predict future observations from the log and the agent's proposed actions. We build complementary benchmarks from human Diplomacy games and real Polymarket trades. Our hierarchical framework compares prediction with and without other actors' actions, then tests multi-step rollouts, predictions for actions never taken, and usefulness to agents. Fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when all actors' recorded actions are given. With only the agent's action, models struggle when other actors strongly affect the outcome, and larger models and longer histories help little. This gap also limits multi-step prediction and agent decisions, with models overestimating plan success. Yet imagined experience and initialization from world models can still improve policy learning. Anticipating other actors' actions remains a central challenge for event world modeling.
authors: Juntong Ni, Zewen Liu, Bohan Wang, Lige Zhang, Wei Jin
bullets: The study extends world modeling from single-actor settings to partially observed event worlds with autonomous actors and ongoing dynamics.
It evaluates LLMs on human Diplomacy games and real Polymarket trading logs.
A hierarchical framework tests prediction with or without other actors’ actions, multi-step rollouts, counterfactual actions, and agent usefulness.
Fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when all actors’ recorded actions are available, while larger models and longer histories help little when they are hidden.

Hidden-actor uncertainty harms multi-step prediction and decision quality, with models tending to overestimate plan success; imagined experience and world-model initialization can still aid policy learning.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates LLMs as event world models predicting future observations conditioned on agent actions in multi-actor environments.
papers.title: From Single-Actor Environments to Multi-Actor Event Worlds: Can LLMs Be Event World Models?
papers.tldr: LLMs can model multi-actor event worlds when other actors’ actions are visible, but struggle to anticipate unseen actors and reliably support planning.

papers.abstract: Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics. We introduce AW-0, an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture. Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands. Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution. We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries. Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness, demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.
authors: Zhuoyang Liu, Dantong Niu, Botong Zhang, Boning Shao, Jing Wang, Ruijie Zheng, Yuvan Sharma, Runyu Lu, Jiaming Liu, Renrui Zhang, Roei Herzig, Yutong Bai, Ken Goldberg, Danfei Xu, Yuke Zhu, Guanzhi Wang, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Trevor Darrell
bullets: Addresses the gap between predictive world action models and agentic systems with reusable, code-based skills.
Uses a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture with coupled code, video, and action generation streams.
Represents skills as parameterized programs while using code to structure multi-step prediction and control.
Introduces automated trajectory curation that aligns robot and human videos with programs and builds reusable skill libraries.
Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual tasks report improved task performance, language following, semantic reasoning, and robustness over VLA and WAM baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an agentic world action model coupling code-based planning with joint video and action prediction for robot manipulation, directly fitting embodied AI and world models.
papers.title: Agentic World Action Models
papers.tldr: AW-0 unifies code-based planning, future video prediction, and robot action generation to make world action models more compositional, reusable, and grounded in physical dynamics.

papers.abstract: Video world models predict future frames from past frames and actions. They serve as simulators in which agents train, plan or are evaluated, and that humans can control interactively. They generate in the latent space of a video autoencoder, whose compression sets their cost per frame and how long each action waits to take effect. Yet world models often reuse the autoencoders of text-to-video generators, built for offline generation with no agent waiting and, without their training data and code, not retrainable at another compression. We therefore ask how, where and how much a world model should compress. We build CADRE, an open family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders spanning multiple spatio-temporal compressions. Its members differ only in a small bottleneck on frozen features and share a diffusion decoder self-distilled to one or a few steps. We train the same world model on each autoencoder in two domains, manipulation and navigation, with two environments each. CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier, especially with a moving camera. Our study also leads to four findings. At strong compression, a diffusion decoder is sharper than perceptual regression. In robot manipulation, temporal compression is more effective in the autoencoder than in the world model. Manipulation and navigation call for opposite compressions: temporal compression costs little when the camera is still, and spatial compression when it moves. Surprisingly, with a still camera, coarser spatial tokens hurt motion far more than image quality. Code, models and a live demo are at https://kyutai.org/blog/2026-10-21-cadre
authors: Adrien Ramanana Rahary, Yutong Bai, Nicolas Dufour, Patrick P\'erez, David Picard
bullets: World-model autoencoders determine both per-frame computation and how quickly actions affect predictions.
CADRE is a family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders covering multiple spatial and temporal compression levels.
The same world model was evaluated across manipulation and navigation domains with multiple environments per domain.
CADRE achieves most of the latency–quality frontier, particularly in moving-camera settings.
Findings include sharper reconstruction from diffusion decoding under strong compression and different optimal compression choices for manipulation versus navigation.
papers.selection_reason: Rethinks video autoencoders for interactive world models with causal diffusion representation autoencoders; directly relevant to video and interactive world models.
papers.title: Rethinking Video Autoencoders for Interactive World Models
papers.tldr: CADRE shows that video-autoencoder compression should be tailored to interactive world-model latency and environment dynamics, rather than inherited from offline video generators.

papers.abstract: Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object's mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes. To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene's actual physical behavior. PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead. We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate. The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.
authors: Yunhao Luo, Wentao He, Yinpei Dai, Hyelin Nam, Hongze Fu, Joyce Chai, Nima Fazeli, Jeong Joon Park
bullets: Addresses physics ambiguity—such as mass distribution, damping, and friction—that causes prediction drift in novel scenes.
Encodes an exploratory interaction clip into a compact physics descriptor token for in-context conditioning.
Trains end-to-end using only latent prediction loss, without analytical physics modeling or physics annotations.
Reuses the descriptor across rollouts with negligible inference overhead.
Across four environments, improves rollout accuracy and visual planning success; descriptors generalize beyond training physics ranges.
papers.selection_reason: In-context physics calibration for action-conditioned world models via compact descriptor tokens.
papers.title: PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models
papers.tldr: PhysiCalWorld calibrates world models to scene-specific physics from a brief exploratory interaction, improving predictions and visual planning without fine-tuning or explicit physics labels.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used for planning, where a planner ranks candidate actions by returns imagined by the model. However, these models are judged mainly by how well they render frames, even though a visually faithful rollout can still assign the wrong return.
