papers.tldr: Agima trains a single multimodal agent to imagine action outcomes, compare possible futures, and plan before acting in environments with sparse feedback or irreversible actions.

papers.abstract: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.
authors: Zhaoyang Wang, Qianhui Wu, Haorui Wang, Simon Yu, Baolin Peng, Canwen Xu, Hao Cheng, Wenlin Yao, Boyi Liu, Yite Wang, Jianfeng Gao, Huaxiu Yao
bullets: Motivation: Training agents through real-world computer interaction is difficult to scale and poses security risks.

Method: Generates executable environments supporting graphical interfaces, MCP services, and command-line interaction, with execution-based gates for solvability, difficulty, and verifier reliability.
Scope: Produces 341 long-horizon environment–task pairs, some requiring more than 100 steps and remaining difficult for frontier models.
Results: Qwen models trained only in WildAWM worlds show substantial gains across eight out-of-distribution web, claw, and computer-use benchmarks.
Availability: The pipeline uses open-source models and its code is publicly released.
papers.selection_reason: Synthesizes controllable interactive computer-use environments for agent training, with execution-based quality gates; relevant to interactive world/environment modeling for agents.
papers.title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis
papers.tldr: WildAWM synthesizes challenging, verifiable computer-use environments across GUIs, tool services, and command lines, enabling open-source-model training that generalizes to unseen tasks.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future video and generate actions, yet remain sensitive to task-irrelevant visual perturbations, i.e., changes in visual appearance that should not affect robot behavior. We identify a gap in conventional WAM training: video prediction encourages representations to preserve appearance information, while action generation does not explicitly enforce invariance to task-irrelevant appearance. Data augmentation exposes WAMs to such perturbations but does not require perturbed and nominal observations to produce consistent action representations, and alignment with external pretrained features does not guarantee the desired invariance. To address this gap, we propose PICA-WAM, a self-supervised training framework that casts perturbation invariance as an auxiliary cross-appearance self-alignment task for WAMs. An exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher processes the nominal observation to provide a deeper-layer target, while the online WAM processes a perturbed observation and aligns its shallower-layer action representation to this target through a lightweight projection head. Across four strong WAMs evaluated on RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-Plus, EBench, and a real robot, PICA-WAM consistently improves robustness under visual perturbations, preserves nominal performance in simulation, and raises the real robot success rate. PICA-WAM further reduces the sensitivity of video features to task-irrelevant appearance and its propagation into actions, as shown by paired layer-wise diagnostics. Code: https://github.com/YudeZou/PICA-WAM-release
authors: Yude Zou, Yifei Yao, Guanbo Jiao, Jianming Ma, Guanjie Zheng, Xing Gao
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between appearance-sensitive video prediction and invariance-required action generation in WAMs.
Uses an EMA teacher on nominal observations and aligns perturbed-observation action features through a lightweight projection head.
Evaluated across four WAMs, RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-Plus, EBench, and a real robot.
Consistently improves robustness to visual perturbations, preserves simulated nominal performance, and increases real-robot success.
Layer-wise diagnostics show reduced appearance sensitivity in video features and its propagation into actions.
papers.selection_reason: Improves visual perturbation invariance in world action models for robot behavior, relevant to world models and robot learning.
papers.title: PICA-WAM: Visual Perturbation Invariance via Cross-Appearance Self-Alignment in World Action Models
papers.tldr: PICA-WAM improves WAM robustness to task-irrelevant visual changes by self-aligning action representations across nominal and perturbed observations.

papers.abstract: Existing world models can generate action-conditioned video from a single image. Many focus on camera movement, allowing users to explore the generated scene. However, navigation alone does not ensure that an action follows persistent rules when its outcome depends on state that is invisible in the current frame. We present Stateful Harness, a framework that separates world evolution from video rendering to support stateful and rule-governed interaction. It maintains an evolving world state under specified rules, renders each resulting event with a frozen video model, and uses the generated clip to update the world state for the next turn. At each turn, the harness resolves the action selected by the user and compiles the resulting event into an instruction, while a preview clip from an editable 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. To evaluate rule compliance, we build WorldState-Bench, a benchmark of 50 counterfactual twin pairs that share an initial frame and action but differ in hidden state and required outcome. Under rule-only prompting, the best of the 11 evaluated video backends produces the required endings for both cases in 32% of pairs. For MiniMax-H3, specifying the required endings raises this rate from 32% to 64%, while the full harness reaches 92% with the same frozen model. These results support separating rule execution from video rendering for world interactions with hidden state.
authors: Chan Yan Ki, Yanran Zhang, Wenzhao Zheng, Xiaofeng Wang, Zheng Zhu, Lei Chen, Jie Zhou, Jiwen Lu
bullets: Existing action-conditioned video models support navigation but may violate persistent rules when key state is invisible in the frame.
The framework tracks evolving world state, resolves user actions under specified rules, and uses a frozen video model to render each event and inform the next turn.
WorldState-Bench evaluates rule compliance using 50 counterfactual twin pairs with identical initial frames and actions but different hidden states.
Across 11 video backends, the best model succeeds on both required endings in 32% of pairs with rule-only prompting; the full harness reaches 92% with the same frozen model.
The approach targets interactive worlds where correct outcomes depend on hidden state, rather than visual appearance alone.
papers.selection_reason: Stateful rule-governed world interaction framework with hidden-state benchmark, directly relevant to interactive world models.
papers.title: State World Models: Execute the Rules, Generate the Pixels
papers.tldr: Stateful Harness separates rule-based world evolution from video rendering to make generated interactions obey hidden-state-dependent outcomes.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.
authors: Adrian Remonda, Jiajun Xi, Nicklas Hansen, Marcus Greiff, Thomas Lew, John Talbot, John Subosits, Xiaolong Wang
bullets: Addresses the high cost and safety risks of collecting extensive real-world RL data.
Pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulation trajectories.
Uses uncertainty-regularized planning to correct simulation-to-reality mismatch during online adaptation.
Adapts faster across track and surface changes in simulation, with lower lap times and fewer failures than baselines.
Demonstrates reliable few-shot adaptation on a full-size autonomous race car with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.
papers.selection_reason: Model-based RL with simulation priors and online adaptation for autonomous racing; fits world models, embodied navigation, and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Simulation Priors for Rapid Adaptation in Model-Based RL for Autonomous Racing
papers.tldr: PIA uses biased simulation experience plus limited real-world interaction to rapidly adapt model-based RL controllers for autonomous racing.

papers.abstract: Generating reusable driving environments requires both controllable future observations and an explicit representation that supports rendering from different viewpoints, yet existing methods still recover explicit scenes from generated RGB videos through optimization for each sequence. To overcome these limitations, we present Drive2Gauss, a feedforward framework that converts jointly generated RGB, metric depth, and dynamic flow into dynamic 4D Gaussian scenes. A Multimodal Video Generator predicts the three modalities from reference multiview images and future control signals. Furthermore, we introduce a Gaussian Query Decoder that uses depth to initialize sparse 3D queries and flow to associate the queries across time, and integrates appearance information through spatiotemporal feature aggregation and iterative query refinement. The reconstruction stage operates in a single feedforward pass without optimization for each scene. Extensive results on nuScenes demonstrate that our approach attains an FID of 6.38 and an FVD of 12.43 for future RGB generation, a PSNR of 29.91 dB when reconstructing its generated observations, and supports both direct rendering under lateral camera shifts and downstream video fixing. Code and more visualizations are available at https://zttt04. github.io/Drive2Gauss_page/.
authors: Tong Zhao, Zhiyuan Han, Lin Chen, Bowen Xie, Yunxi Qiao, Bohan Li, Weiqing Xiao, Gen Li, Shu Han, Xuyang Dai, Cheng Bi, Hao Zhao, Chaojian Li
bullets: Addresses the need for reusable, controllable driving environments with explicit novel-view rendering.
A multimodal video generator predicts future RGB, metric depth, and dynamic flow from multiview references and control signals.
A Gaussian Query Decoder initializes 3D queries from depth, links them over time using flow, and refines them with spatiotemporal appearance features.
On nuScenes, it reports FID 6.38, FVD 12.43, and 29.91 dB PSNR for reconstructing generated observations.
Supports rendering under lateral camera shifts and downstream video fixing; evaluation is demonstrated on nuScenes and generated observations.
papers.selection_reason: Feedforward 4D Gaussian reconstruction from multimodal generative driving videos conditioned on control signals; action-conditioned world generation and 3D scene recovery.
papers.title: Drive2Gauss: FeedForward 4D Gaussian Reconstruction from Multimodal Generative Driving Videos
papers.tldr: Drive2Gauss feedforwardly reconstructs controllable dynamic 4D Gaussian driving scenes from multimodal generated videos without per-scene optimization.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) typically represent the world through latent embeddings from pretrained video models, which entangle heterogeneous aspects of the world, from how it looks (e.g., texture and color) to how it is physically configured (e.g., occupancy and pose). This raises an underexplored question: $\textbf{what should constitute the state of a WAM?}$ We argue that the world state should separate how the world appears from how the world evolves under action: the former captures semantic context, while the latter is governed by physical state. To this end, we propose $\textbf{PrismWAM}$, which decouples physics from semantics while jointly modeling state and action. PrismWAM factorizes an embodied task into a $\mathrm{Semantic\ Planning}\rightarrow\mathrm{Physical\ Rollout}\rightarrow\mathrm{Executable\ Action}$ pipeline: given only the initial RGB observation, semantic planning learns to predict the final goal image, while physical rollout predicts the fine-grained evolution toward this goal in depth space; executable actions are then generated from the depth rollout. Without any embodied action pretraining or additional data augmentation, PrismWAM achieves strong manipulation performance in both simulation and the real world. Notably, PrismWAM even surpasses a broad range of models with large-scale embodied action pretraining (e.g., OpenWAM-$\alpha$). More broadly, we reframe World Action Models from modeling how the world looks to how it responds to action, paving the way for action-centric world models grounded in occupancy, flow, tactile sensing, proprioception, and beyond.
authors: Tianyu Xin, Wanqi Zhong, Bowen Hu, Zhangchi Guo, Lijie Wang, Yiming Wang, Haoran Liao, Heyang Yu, Xiaoyu Tian, Zhiding Yu, Yiming Li
bullets: Identifies entangled visual and physical representations as a key challenge in World Action Models.
Factorizes tasks into semantic planning, physical rollout, and executable action generation.
Predicts the goal image from the initial RGB observation, then models fine-grained evolution in depth space.
Achieves strong manipulation performance in simulation and the real world without embodied action pretraining or extra data augmentation.
Advocates action-centric world models grounded in physical state rather than appearance alone.
papers.selection_reason: Decouples physics and semantics in world action models, predicting goal images and depth rollouts to generate executable actions for manipulation.
papers.title: PrismWAM: Decoupling State Representations in World Action Models
papers.tldr: PrismWAM separates semantic appearance from physical dynamics to plan and execute embodied actions more effectively.

papers.abstract: Building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse 3D worlds is a central research direction toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene and transfers poorly to new environments, leaving general embodied agents for open-world settings under-explored. We refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), whose defining property is the ability to understand diverse visual environments and execute general actions in open-world conditions. To advance EWA research, we study open-world embodied navigation-planning and release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset of over 200K samples spanning diverse scenes. Each example is equipped with multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions. The dataset also provides unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics, supporting offline pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. Beyond offline supervision, a defining characteristic of an EWA is its interaction with the environment; training solely on offline data is therefore insufficient, especially for generalizing to scenes not covered in the training distribution. Building dedicated real interactive environments, however, is often prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a novel training scheme that employs a video world model as a low-cost environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training of the EWA within it. Empirically, pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially improves the open-world embodied planning ability of the EWA, and further RL post-training inside a world model yields clear gains on out-of-distribution scenes. The dataset, baseline checkpoints, and training and evaluation code are available at https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/EmbodiedWorld-200K/.
authors: X. Feng, J. Tang, Z. Lin, L. Chen, S. Shao, Q. Lu, K. Huang
bullets: Targets embodied agents that can understand diverse 3D environments and perform general actions beyond single-scene tasks.
Provides over 200K navigation-planning samples across diverse scenes with low-level motion and high-level semantic annotations.
Introduces unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics for offline pretraining and fair assessment.
Uses a video world model as a low-cost proxy environment for interactive RL post-training.
Pretraining improves open-world planning, while world-model RL further improves performance on out-of-distribution scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied navigation-planning dataset with interactive video world models for RL post-training directly fits embodied AI and world models.
papers.title: EmbodiedWorld-200K: Toward Embodied World Agents via Embodied-Planning Dataset and Interactive World Models
papers.tldr: EmbodiedWorld-200K advances open-world embodied agents with a 200K-sample planning dataset and video-world-model-based interactive RL.

papers.abstract: Game world models have made rapid progress toward real-time interactive generation. Yet action control is still predominantly implemented as feature conditioning, leaving the model to learn from training data how each action should move the visual world. This formulation is poorly matched to a broad class of planar-camera worlds, such as top-down and isometric games. In these worlds, player motion induces a geometrically well-defined planar camera displacement. We observe that the key to spatially consistent control in such worlds is to represent the effect of each action directly in world coordinates. To this end, we introduce ActionRoPE, a parameter-free action interface that converts action-driven camera displacement into world-coordinate rotary positions. As a result, tokens corresponding to the same world location retain the same positional address across time. These world coordinates further expose a spatial asymmetry in generation: regions covered by the initial observation are geometrically known, while newly revealed regions remain to be synthesized. We therefore propose Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS), which assigns token-wise denoising schedules according to this known-new structure. It allows observed regions to stabilize earlier, while new content is generated with reference to them. Compared with four representative action-conditioning mechanisms, our approach follows the commanded motion more faithfully and reduces the revisit drift by 66% over the strongest baseline. The same interface transfers across video backbones from 1.3B to 33B parameters and to out-of-distribution scenes. Project Page: https://teawhite.cn/ActionRoPE/
authors: Zhiyang Deng, Yuzhe Wu, Zijun Lin, Yeying Jin
bullets: Addresses the limitations of feature-based action conditioning, which requires models to learn action-to-motion geometry from data.
Uses a parameter-free interface that converts action-induced camera displacement into world-coordinate rotary positions, preserving consistent token locations across time.
Introduces Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling to stabilize observed regions earlier while synthesizing newly revealed content using them as reference.
More faithfully follows commanded motion and reduces revisit drift by 66% versus the strongest of four representative baselines.
Transfers across video backbones from 1.3B to 33B parameters and to out-of-distribution scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces ActionRoPE, a method for spatially consistent control in game world models by representing actions as world coordinates. This directly addresses action-conditioned generation and controllable world models.
papers.title: ActionRoPE: action as coordinates for spatially consistent control in planar-camera game world models
papers.tldr: ActionRoPE improves spatially consistent control in planar-camera game world models by encoding actions as world-coordinate positional shifts and scheduling denoising based on observed versus newly revealed regions.

papers.abstract: Time-series models increasingly condition on known future inputs. In controlled systems, some of these inputs are actions that can be changed, compared, and optimized before execution. A model must therefore do more than predict the realized future: it must predict how outcomes change under different actions from the same observed history and support reliable comparison of candidate plans. We introduce ActTime, an action-conditioned world model for time series. Over the observed history, ActTime updates variable-specific latent states through an action-conditioned transition and corrects them using observations. It then rolls the same transition forward under candidate actions to generate future trajectories. Training uses only factual trajectories, without paired alternative-action outcomes or planning supervision. We construct a simulator-grounded evaluation suite across building energy, traffic, greenhouse climate, and inventory management, covering factual prediction, intervention-effect prediction, offline decision making, and closed-loop planning. ActTime ranks first in 12 of 16 domain-task settings. Across eight methods, the mean pairwise model-ranking reversal rate is 17.8% between factual prediction and intervention fidelity, and rises to 28.4% between intervention fidelity and decision ranking. These results show that factual accuracy, intervention fidelity, and decision quality are related but not interchangeable.
authors: Xinxing Zhou, Xiaojie Yuan, Yanlong Wen, Ming Jin
bullets: Targets controlled time series where future actions can be compared and optimized before execution.
Maintains variable-specific latent states, updates them with an action-conditioned transition and observations, then rolls them forward under candidate actions.
Trains without paired counterfactual outcomes or planning supervision.
Evaluated on building energy, traffic, greenhouse climate, and inventory-management simulators across prediction, intervention, decision, and planning tasks.
Ranks first in 12 of 16 domain-task settings; model rankings often change across factual prediction, intervention fidelity, and decision quality.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned world modeling for time series directly fits interactive world models.
papers.title: ActTime: Action-Conditioned World Modeling for Time Series
papers.tldr: ActTime learns to simulate how different actions change future time-series outcomes, using only observed factual trajectories, and shows that prediction accuracy does not guarantee reliable intervention or decision quality.

papers.abstract: Streaming video world models generate the future chunk by chunk, conditioned on their own past and a stream of actions. Trained on short clips, they drift once a rollout exceeds the training horizon, as prediction errors re-enter the context and compound. A common remedy is to train the model on its own rollouts via distribution matching distillation (DMD). For action-conditioned world models, the teacher becomes a bottleneck: an external video model is agnostic to the actions, whereas the model's own pretrained network drifts in the same manner as the student. We observe that a long rollout need not match a teacher, provided it remains a realistic continuation of its own scene that follows the commanded actions. Realism and scene fidelity can be measured against real-data statistics, which remain valid at any horizon, while action following is preserved by the model's conditional generation loss. We propose Fr\'echet Forcing, which fine-tunes a world model together with its deployed multi-step sampler under three constraints. Generative anchoring applies the flow-matching loss after a self-generated history ending on real data. Context fidelity, a Fr\'echet distance (FD) on latent statistics of the free rollout centred on each clip's own ground truth, keeps every rollout faithful to its scene. Reality matching, an FD to real frames in a frozen perceptual space, keeps the generated frames realistic. Because all three targets are derived from short real clips without comparing a rollout against a long recorded future, training requires no teacher, no online critic and no long videos. Fine-tuning MiniWorld-1B, pretrained on 253-frame clips, for at most 36 GPU-hours on 381-frame clips yields rollouts that remain stable beyond 4,000 frames and continue to follow their actions in both robot manipulation and camera-controlled exploration.
authors: Yian Zhao, Yu Yan, Hongcan Guo, Ruochong Zheng, Jian Zhang, Jie Chen
bullets: Addresses compounding errors and drift in long-horizon autoregressive video rollouts.
Fine-tunes the deployed multi-step sampler using generative anchoring, context-fidelity Fréchet distance, and reality-matching Fréchet distance.
Uses statistics from short real clips, avoiding external teachers, online critics, and recorded long futures.
Applied to MiniWorld-1B, the method produced stable rollouts beyond 4,000 frames while continuing to follow actions in manipulation and camera-controlled exploration.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Fréchet Forcing to train long-horizon streaming world models from short clips by enforcing realism and context fidelity without requiring a teacher model or long videos.
papers.title: Frechet Forcing: Training Long-Horizon Streaming World Models from Short Clips
papers.tldr: Fréchet Forcing trains action-conditioned streaming world models to remain realistic, scene-consistent, and action-following far beyond their short-clip training horizon without requiring a teacher or long videos.

papers.abstract: World models offer increasingly rich environments for exploration, yet intervening in a world while observing the consequences from freely chosen viewpoints remains challenging. We tackle these challenges by introducing UniState, a framework for controllable world simulation built on a unified world-state representation. This representation unifies spatial memory and user interventions. Users specify object motion directly within spatial memory, while independently choosing the camera trajectory from which the resulting world state is observed. This unification makes the relationship between the scene and the requested changes explicit, removing ambiguity between object motion and viewpoint change from the control specification. Crucially, specifying an intervention does not require prescribing every resulting movement: the video model can synthesize additional motion within controlled objects and plausible interactions with their surroundings. We develop training and sampling strategies that help generated videos follow the specified object motion and camera trajectory while preserving this capacity to generate responses beyond the prescribed transformations. Experiments demonstrate more accurate joint object and camera control than the existing methods, alongside qualitative evidence that intervention-induced scene changes persist across rollouts.
authors: Jaeseok Jeong, Kyungmook Choi, Sohyun Chung, Youngsik Yun, Youngjung Uh
bullets: Addresses ambiguity between object motion and viewpoint changes in interactive world models.
Represents spatial memory and user interventions together, while allowing camera trajectories to be chosen independently.
Uses training and sampling strategies to follow specified object and camera motion while synthesizing plausible additional interactions.
Experiments show more accurate joint object-camera control than existing methods.
Qualitative results indicate that intervention-induced scene changes persist across rollouts.
papers.selection_reason: Controllable world simulation with unified spatial memory and interventions; directly fits interactive world models.
papers.title: UniState: Unifying Memory and Intervention for Controllable World Simulation
papers.tldr: UniState enables controllable world simulation by jointly specifying object interventions and camera viewpoints in a unified world-state representation.

papers.abstract: Controllable video generation has recently achieved impressive visual quality, yet existing control paradigms remain poorly suited to embodied navigation. Text prompts are spatially ambiguous, while camera-trajectory control relies on low-level motion specifications that are unintuitive for human users and difficult to manipulate. In this work, we introduce Map2Vid, a novel task that reformulates embodied navigation video generation as a BEV-map-to-video synthesis problem, together with a large-scale benchmark for systematic evaluation. By using BEV maps, which provide a visual representation of global scene layout and intended navigation routes, Map2Vid enables human-friendly navigation video generation. To support this task, we construct a dedicated dataset with over 100K navigation sequences across 61 indoor scenes, each paired with egocentric videos, BEV maps, camera trajectories and language instructions. We further develop a unified framework that integrates multiple control signals, together with a curriculum training strategy that progressively weakens non-map inputs, enabling flexible inference under both full conditioning and map-only input. Extensive experiments across multiple foundation generation models demonstrate that controllable navigation video generation via BEV map is a viable and promising direction.
authors: Yulin Dai, Yuqian Fu, Tianwen Qian, Zhen Xing, Bojia Zi, Xiaoling Wang
bullets: Reframes embodied navigation video generation as bird’s-eye-view (BEV) map-to-video synthesis.
Provides a benchmark and dataset with over 100K navigation sequences across 61 indoor scenes.
Pairs egocentric videos with BEV maps, camera trajectories, and language instructions.
Uses a unified multi-signal control framework with curriculum training that supports full conditioning or map-only inference.
Experiments across multiple foundation video-generation models show BEV-map control is viable for navigation video generation.
papers.selection_reason: BEV-map-conditioned egocentric navigation video generation; relevant to interactive world models and video generation.
papers.title: Map2Vid: Embodied Navigation Video Generation with Human-Friendly Motion Control
papers.tldr: Map2Vid introduces BEV-map-controlled video generation to make embodied navigation videos more intuitive to specify and evaluate.

papers.abstract: Digital medicine now captures data that traces individual health trajectories and reveals population health dynamics through electronic health records, claims, remote monitoring, wearable devices, mobile devices, social sensing data, medical images, etc. But much of its modeling still centers on task-specific, outcome-specific, and prediction-specific estimation. The next frontier is not simply better prediction, but action in an evolving health world shaped by multiple decision-makers, heterogeneous populations, resource constraints, and feedback in care delivery. This is why digital medicine now needs world models: not only to estimate what will happen, but to represent how actions change what can happen next -- whom to prioritize, how to allocate scarce resources, how to adapt care across subgroups, and how interventions reshape future health trajectories and population dynamics. We call such a model population health world model (PHWM): a more foundational representation of an evolving health world in which health states, individual trajectories, population health dynamics, interventions, constraints, and feedback are intrinsically coupled. Building a PHWM endows three unmet structural gaps in current digital medicine: dynamic health-state modeling, population-level intervention intelligence, and validation, equity, and governance for action-oriented use. We argue that addressing these gaps requires three minimal capabilities: representation learning under action-dependent observation, multi-scale intervention intelligence, and validation with explicit decision boundaries, while highlighting the importance of social, contextual, and public-health sensing data for action-oriented digital medicine.
authors: Xike Xie, Yu Li, Weizhong Yang, Amalie Dyda, Shaohua Kevin Zhou
bullets: Current digital medicine is largely task-, outcome-, and prediction-focused, limiting action-oriented decision-making.
A PHWM jointly represents health states, individual trajectories, population dynamics, interventions, resource constraints, and care-delivery feedback.
It targets three gaps: dynamic health-state modeling, population-level intervention intelligence, and validation, equity, and governance for action.
The proposed minimum capabilities are action-dependent observation learning, multi-scale intervention intelligence, and validation tied to explicit decision boundaries.
Social, contextual, and public-health sensing data are highlighted as important for action-oriented digital medicine.
papers.selection_reason: Population health world model with action-conditioned intervention dynamics.
papers.title: From Prediction to Action: Population Health World Model for Digital Medicine
papers.tldr: Population health world models aim to move digital medicine beyond predicting outcomes toward modeling how interventions, constraints, and feedback reshape individual and population health.

papers.abstract: Reliable long-horizon prediction remains a central challenge for embodied world models. Although recent generative models can synthesize visually plausible action-conditioned futures, their latent dynamics are typically learned through unconstrained transition modules, which may gradually deviate from coherent physical evolution as predictions are recursively rolled forward. We investigate whether explicitly structuring latent state evolution can improve the stability and utility of such imagined trajectories. To this end, we introduce HWM, a structured dynamics framework that represents backbone latents in a learned phase space consisting of generalized coordinates and momenta. Future states are propagated through dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics and mapped back to the original latent representation through a learnable inverse interface. The resulting formulation can be integrated into existing world-model architectures without redesigning their perception or decoding components, while multi-step transition supervision encourages the structured rollout to remain aligned with the latent trajectories induced by real observations. Controlled simulation experiments show that HWM produces more accurate estimates of velocity, acceleration, and jerk and substantially reduces long-horizon energy drift relative to unstructured latent dynamics. We further evaluate the approach across three distinct embodied world-model settings, covering single-arm multi-view prediction with Ctrl-World, dual-arm single-view prediction with EVAC, and task-oriented single-arm prediction with Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B. On RoboCasa, incorporating HWM into Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B yields a 2.7% relative improvement in task success. On real-world AgiBot World trajectories, it improves nDTW by 9.7% with Ctrl-World and Logic by 8.4% with EVAC.
authors: Kevin Chen, Yu-Wei Zhan, Haoran Liang, Sen Cui, Changshui Zhang
bullets: Problem: Unconstrained latent transitions can drift from coherent physical evolution during recursive long-horizon prediction.
Method: Represent latent states with generalized coordinates and momenta, propagate them using dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics, and map them back through a learnable inverse interface.
Training integration: HWM can augment existing world models without changing their perception or decoding components, while multi-step supervision aligns imagined and observed latent trajectories.
Results: HWM improves velocity, acceleration, and jerk estimates and reduces long-horizon energy drift in controlled simulations.
Embodied evaluations show gains across three settings, including 2.7% higher task success on RoboCasa, 9.7% higher nDTW with Ctrl-World, and 8.4% higher Logic with EVAC.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces HWM, a structured dynamics framework using Hamiltonian mechanics for long-horizon prediction in embodied world models, directly addressing latent action and interactive world modeling.
papers.title: Structured Latent Dynamics for Long-Horizon Embodied World Models
papers.tldr: HWM stabilizes long-horizon embodied world-model rollouts by enforcing structured dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics in latent space, improving physical consistency and downstream performance.

papers.abstract: GUI world models are increasingly used to improve action selection by predicting the consequences of candidate actions, but it is unclear how much of the resulting gain comes from prediction itself rather than from the evaluator that interprets those predictions. We study this attribution problem through controlled interventions on GUI action selection. With candidates and predictions held fixed, lookahead gains can change with how the prediction is presented to the evaluator, so end-to-end gains cannot be attributed to prediction alone. We then introduce Direct Action Ranking (DAR), which learns from reference actions to score candidates without generating future screens, and compare it with a prediction-augmented variant under matched supervision. Predicted successors add no detectable ranking signal once evaluation is learned directly. Without retraining, DAR improves AndroidWorld task success by 5.8--16.4 points across three proposers, outperforms world-model lookahead, and transfers zero-shot to unseen apps, where every prediction-conditioned configuration falls below proposer confidence. These results suggest that GUI world models should be evaluated by their decision value, the incremental action-selection value of their predictions beyond a strong direct evaluator, rather than by prediction fidelity or end-to-end lookahead gain alone.
authors: Sizhe Tang, Hanhan Zhou, Jeffrey Svajlenko, Rashmi Gangadharaiah
bullets: Lookahead gains depend on how predicted screens are presented to the evaluator, so they cannot be attributed to prediction alone.
Direct Action Ranking (DAR) scores candidate actions from reference actions without generating future screens.
Under matched supervision, adding predicted successors provides no detectable ranking signal beyond DAR.
Without retraining, DAR improves AndroidWorld success by 5.8–16.4 points across three proposers and transfers zero-shot to unseen apps.
The study argues that world models should be assessed by incremental decision value, not prediction fidelity or lookahead gains alone.
papers.selection_reason: Directly studies decision value of GUI world models for action selection, relevant to interactive world models.
papers.title: Beyond Next-Screen Prediction: The Decision Value of GUI World Models
papers.tldr: GUI world-model predictions may add little decision value beyond a strong evaluator that directly ranks candidate actions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA), video-action (VA), and world action models (WAMs) form the backbone of modern physical AI systems, yet their real-time single-batch inference remains a defining bottleneck. Latency is dominated not by individual kernel computation, but by system-level overhead: thousands of short kernel launches, intermediate data movement across operator boundaries, and redundant recomputation across consecutive decisions. General-purpose graph compilers cannot address these costs, as they optimize individual calls in isolation and lack visibility into cross-call state semantics and global pipeline structure. We present FLASHRT-PAI, a low-latency inference engine built around model-hardware pipeline co-design rather than isolated kernel optimization. FLASHRT-PAI combines three core mechanisms: deep kernel fusion with launch overlap eliminates inter-operator boundaries and launch gaps; an execution contract formalizes the pipeline's stage DAG, update rates, and named buffers to enable cross-decision state reuse and selective refresh; and execution-state capsules enable fast snapshot, restore, and fork of persistent pipeline state. The system also supports drop-in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models via parity- and latency-gated kernel replacement. Evaluation covers six policies on RTX 5090 and four on Jetson AGX Thor. At matched 16-bit precision, FLASHRT-PAI is 1.3-3.7x faster than official compiled paths. Combining pipeline co-design with reduced precision delivers 3.38-12.66x speedup over official eager implementations. In LIBERO-10, four-bit pi0.5 achieves 94.04% success on Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, compared with 92.4% for the measured official FP16 reference. FLASHRT-PAI is open source, distributed via Hugging Face Kernel Hub, and its opt-in pi0.5 kernels have been adopted into the LeRobot framework.
authors: Liang Su, David Chen, Jason Li, Kevin Guo, Teresa Lv
bullets: Targets real-time single-batch inference bottlenecks from kernel-launch overhead, data movement, and redundant recomputation across decisions.
Uses deep kernel fusion with launch overlap, an execution contract for cross-decision state reuse, and execution-state capsules for fast snapshot, restore, and fork operations.
Supports drop-in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models through parity- and latency-gated kernel replacement.
Across evaluated policies and hardware, achieves 1.3–3.7× speedup at matched 16-bit precision and 3.38–12.66× over official eager implementations with reduced precision.
In LIBERO-10, four-bit pi0.5 reaches 94.04% success on Jetson AGX Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, near or above the reported FP16 reference.
papers.selection_reason: Low-latency inference engine for VLA and world action models, directly relevant to embodied AI and efficient AI.
papers.title: FlashRT-PAI: Fast Kernels Are Not Fast Pipelines for Physical AI Inference
papers.tldr: FLASHRT-PAI accelerates physical-AI inference by optimizing the entire execution pipeline—not just individual kernels—achieving substantial speedups while preserving task performance.

papers.abstract: Abstract Action-conditioned world models for contact-rich manipulation require data that captures how contact forms, slides, and releases under varying force. Such data are slow to collect through robot teleoperation, which often lacks force feedback and is constrained by gripper geometry. We ask whether these dynamics can instead be learned from human physical interaction and transferred to a robot. We present ACTS, a visuo-tactile world model trained only on human interaction data. Operators manipulate handheld GelSight sensors while we record third-person and wrist video, tactile images, 6-DoF sensor motion, and tactile-derived normal force, yielding React, a 4.9-hour bimanual dataset across three objects. We represent actions at the tactile sensor as motion augmented by force change, providing a shared action space for human collection and robot execution. ACTS jointly predicts future scene, wrist, and tactile observations. On held-out human data, ACTS improves scene-view prediction by 0.7-2.0 dB PSNR over the stronger of two visuo-tactile world models trained from scratch on React. Without fine-tuning, in the robot teleoperation rollouts we inspected, predicted tactile imprints still appear and disappear with recorded contact. Visual transfer is less robust: camera predictions exceed frame copying on PushT, are mixed on Rope, and fall below it on Motherboard, while wrist views can blur or hallucinate structure. These results suggest that contact dynamics transfer more reliably than visual appearance from human to robot.
authors: Yuxiang Ma, Weihan Xu, Pengfei Ye, Anna Mei, Yuxin Ray Song, Tingle Li, Haonan Chen, Edward H. Adelson
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of collecting contact-rich robot data with force feedback and varied gripper geometry.
Trains a world model on 4.9 hours of bimanual human interaction using video, tactile images, sensor motion, and force.
Represents actions as tactile-sensor motion plus force change, creating a shared human–robot action space.
Jointly predicts scene, wrist, and tactile observations; scene prediction improves by 0.7–2.0 dB PSNR over scratch-trained baselines on held-out human data.
In robot rollouts, contact imprints transfer qualitatively, while visual and wrist-view predictions are inconsistent across tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Visuo-tactile world model trained on human physical interaction for contact-rich manipulation.
papers.title: ACTS: Learning Visuo-Tactile World Models from Human Physical Interaction
papers.tldr: ACTS learns visuo-tactile contact dynamics from human manipulation and transfers them to robot interaction without fine-tuning, with stronger tactile than visual transfer.

papers.abstract: A key design choice in visual world models is what information the latent state is encouraged to preserve. Models that learn a latent space with only a latent-prediction objective adapt to environment dynamics, but the predictive objective alone admits collapsed solutions and provides no explicit constraint on the visual information retained by the latent. Models built directly on pretrained visual features inherit a strong visual prior, but tie prediction and planning to a frozen state space. We propose Anchor-WM, which instead uses pretrained visual features as a teacher for learning a compact latent state rather than as the world-model state itself. Anchor-WM learns this compact latent with action-conditioned dynamics, while distilling the dense DINO representations through a training-only distillation head. This encourages the compact latent to retain visual information captured by the pretrained representation while discouraging representational collapse. At inference, the DINO encoder and distillation head are discarded, allowing prediction and planning to operate entirely in the learned latent space. Anchor-WM achieves the best average success rate across the four evaluated environments while enabling substantially faster planning than world models operating directly on DINO patch features. These results show that pretrained visual features can effectively guide world-model learning without defining the state space used for prediction and planning.
authors: Yanbo Wang, Nan Lin, Wendelin B\"ohmer, Javier Alonso-Mora
bullets: Addresses latent-state collapse and the loss of visual information in prediction-only world models.
Learns an action-conditioned compact latent while distilling dense DINO representations through a temporary training head.
Discards the DINO encoder and distillation head at inference, enabling planning entirely in the learned latent space.
Achieves the best average success rate across four evaluated environments and substantially faster planning than models using DINO patch features.
Shows that pretrained visual features can guide, rather than define, the state space for visual world models.
papers.selection_reason: Compact latent world model with action-conditioned dynamics and visual planning; fits latent and interactive world models.
papers.title: Pretrained Features as Teachers, Not States: Compact Latent World Models for Visual Planning
papers.tldr: Anchor-WM uses pretrained DINO features as a training-time teacher to learn a compact latent world-model state that supports effective visual planning without relying on DINO features at inference.

papers.abstract: Latent world models such as V-JEPA 2 forecast in the feature space of a video encoder, but one look at an object does not reveal how hard it is to rotate, how much it bounces or how much it slides. People find out by trying: a few pokes reveal how an object responds. IMPULSE, named after the impulse response it infers, gives a predictor in frozen V-JEPA 2 feature space the same ability. A Bayesian contact memory summarizes three short calibration pushes, a predicted object pose carries it into the predictor, and a lightweight random-Fourier pose head lets the predictor use the pose. On 512 fresh objects, in a pre-specified held-out confirmation with models sealed before the data existed, the memory lowers the 1-second feature-forecast error by 11.6-12.8% relative to the same predictor without experience, for all 8 training seeds, with a 95% seed-and-object interval excluding zero. The gain also holds for 128 objects with out-of-range physics (11.7-14.0%), and the full extension beats a plain predictor by 15.5-16.6%. An information-ladder argument, exact for ideal predictors, shows that physics reaches the features only through motion, so we measure how much the pathway lets pose help. On fresh objects, the Fourier head roughly triples the gain of a perfect memory over plain pose tokens (2.8-3.2x). Raw push measurements fed through the same pathway give a similar gain, so the Bayesian summary is not required; it condenses the trials into eight interpretable numbers. The gain is absent at contact onset and grows afterwards.
bullets: Addresses the limitation that a single visual observation does not reveal an object’s physical response.
Uses a Bayesian contact memory of three calibration pushes, predicted pose, and a lightweight random-Fourier pose head in frozen V-JEPA 2 feature space.
On 512 held-out objects, contact memory reduces 1-second feature-forecast error by 11.6–12.8% across all 8 seeds; gains also hold for 128 out-of-range-physics objects.
The full extension improves over a plain predictor by 15.5–16.6%; gains emerge after contact rather than at contact onset.
Raw push measurements perform similarly, while the Bayesian summary compresses trials into eight interpretable values.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned prediction in a latent video feature space is an interactive world model contribution.
papers.title: IMPULSE: Push First, Then Predict in V-JEPA 2 Feature Space
papers.tldr: IMPULSE improves V-JEPA 2 feature forecasting by probing objects with three pushes, remembering their responses, and conditioning predictions on pose.

papers.abstract: We present RhinoNet, a simplicial complex-based point cloud neural network, that creates a geometry-preserving embedding of high-dimensional point clouds. RhinoNet takes collections of datasets, also called {\em data cohorts}, and processes each dataset (point cloud) within the cohort as a simplicial complex. These simplicial complexes have datapoints as vertices and edges learned by Vietoris-Rips filtration. Using simplicial wavelets and MLP layers, RhinoNet computes a vector representation of each dataset in a latent space produced by an autoencoder. The latent space is optimized such that an optimal transport distance between pairs of point clouds is preserved between the latent representations. We apply RhinoNet to single-cell datasets collected on patients---a common source of such high-dimensional data. RhinoNet creates a patient level representation, known in biological contexts as a phenoscape. We establish that RhinoNet generates organized phenoscapes, whereas other methods such as static maps do not. Next we show that we can generate entire point clouds by sampling and decoding this phenoscape. We show two modes of generation via 1) latent flow matching and 2) geodesic interpolation in latent space, followed by a decoding back into the point cloud space. RhinoNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on single-cell and spatial data cohorts relative to tested baselines. Overall, RhinoNet lifts the concepts of representation learning and generative modeling to the point cloud or population level and defines a neural model for phenoscaping.
authors: Siddharth Viswanath, Hiren Madhu, Eddie Cavallin, Benjamin Jones, Alistair Wilkinson, Christopher Tape, Michael Perlmutter, Rex Ying, Ian Adelstein, Smita Krishnaswamy
bullets: Processes each dataset as a Vietoris–Rips simplicial complex with datapoints as vertices and learned edges.
Uses simplicial wavelets, MLP layers, and an autoencoder to encode datasets into a latent phenoscape.
Optimizes latent representations to preserve optimal-transport distances between point clouds.
Generates point clouds through latent flow matching or geodesic interpolation followed by decoding.
Applied to single-cell and spatial data cohorts, achieving state-of-the-art performance against tested baselines and producing organized phenoscap es.
papers.selection_reason: Connects geometric topological analysis to latent point-cloud models and environment generation; relevant to 3D representation and world-model-style latent dynamics.
papers.title: RhinoNet: Unsupervised Learning for Phenoscaping and Generation of High Dimensional Point Clouds
papers.tldr: RhinoNet learns geometry-preserving, patient-level representations of high-dimensional point-cloud datasets and can generate new point clouds from the learned latent space.

papers.abstract: Visual navigation requires goal directed planning informed by predictions of environment dynamics. Representative navigation world model methods propose complete action candidates before predicting consequences for selection or search updates. For each candidate, predictions primarily evaluate proposed actions rather than guide its stepwise construction. To this end, we propose InJepa, an intention first planning paradigm centered on latent states. A goal conditioned JEPA proposes latent intentions, and an action conditioned JEPA continually predicts future latent states. Both operate in a shared latent space to align their predictive representations. Within each candidate, predicted consequences feed into the next intention proposal and action inference, forming a closed loop of intention, action, and consequence. This extends the world model's role beyond evaluation to leading candidate construction through latent intentions. We evaluate InJepa through closed loop image goal navigation in Habitat MP3D. The results show effective multistep navigation through intention guided action generation and consequence feedback. Experiments across encoders further support applicability across visual representations. These findings support latent intentions as the central planning object and show that world models can directly guide plan construction through coordinated reasoning about intentions and consequences. Code is available at https://github.com/zhuxun132/InJepa.
authors: Siming Zhou, Bowen Ma, Ruiran Du, Pengcheng Zheng, Sheng Zheng, Dongshen Han, Zhijie Li, Wei Dong, Fan Mo, Chaoning Zhang
bullets: Targets the limitation of methods that generate complete action candidates before using world-model predictions for evaluation.
Uses a goal-conditioned JEPA to propose latent intentions and an action-conditioned JEPA to predict future latent states.
Feeds predicted consequences back into subsequent intention proposals and action inference in a closed loop.
Evaluated on closed-loop image-goal navigation in Habitat MP3D, demonstrating effective multistep navigation.
Results across encoders support applicability across different visual representations.
papers.selection_reason: Latent-intention planning with coupled JEPA world models for visual navigation; fits embodied navigation and latent-action world models.
papers.title: InJePA: Intention-First Latent Planning with Coupled JEPA World Models for Visual Navigation
papers.tldr: InJePA improves visual navigation by using shared latent intentions and predicted consequences to construct action plans step by step.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems have achieved rapid progress by learning unified policies that map sensor observations directly to driving trajectories. However, once deployed, these systems typically remain frozen: they may repeat similar decisions in similar scenes, and failures can only be addressed through costly data collection and retraining. This sharply contrasts with human drivers, who improve lifelong through experience, memory, and reflection. In this work, we ask whether autonomous driving systems can achieve similar post-deployment self-evolution to human drivers. We propose EvoAD, a self-evolving autonomous driving framework via latent world-model guided post-hoc reflection. EvoAD stores driving experiences in a bird's-eye-view feature memory pool, retrieves scene-relevant precedents according to geometric and semantic similarity, and uses a latent world model to evaluate the future consequences of candidate trajectories in a compact planning-oriented space. Instead of treating memory as external textual contexts or using world models only for pre-action simulation, EvoAD transforms executed driving outcomes into reusable improvement signals for future decisions. This enables the system to diagnose how prior trajectories could have been improved and to refine behavior in similar future scenarios without retraining the base driving policy. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 show consistent improvements across reflection rounds and state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating the potential of world models as reflective mechanisms for post-deployment self-evolution in autonomous driving.
authors: Junjie Yang, Qiming Zhang, Yuyan Li, Shuqi Shen, Yusong Huang, Yanggang Sheng, Wenpeng Xu, Ziyi Shi, Tianshun Li, Yijie Chen, Yujia Wang, Jun Ma, Xinhu Zheng, Hongliang Lu, Hai Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of frozen end-to-end driving policies that cannot learn from deployment failures without costly retraining.
Stores past experiences in a bird’s-eye-view feature memory and retrieves relevant precedents using geometric and semantic similarity.
Uses a latent world model to assess the future consequences of candidate trajectories in a compact planning-oriented space.

Experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 report consistent gains across reflection rounds and state-of-the-art performance.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving autonomous driving with latent world-model reflection and embodied driving memory.
papers.title: EvoAD: Self-Evolving Autonomous Driving via Latent World-Model Guided Post-hoc Reflection
papers.tldr: EvoAD enables autonomous driving systems to improve after deployment by reflecting on past driving outcomes with a latent world model, without retraining the base policy.

papers.abstract: We introduce a predictive world model for electronic health records (EHR) that represents patient histories as action conditioned latent trajectories. Rather than modeling clinical events solely through autoregressive token prediction, our framework explicitly separates patient states from observed clinical actions and learns their evolution through a state and action conditioned transition operator. At its core is a state dependent linearization predictor that propagates local changes in latent patient state, enabling time resolved prediction, multi step rollout, and action conditioned simulation. Empirically, we show that generated latent trajectories preserve downstream predictive signal, temporal structure, and subgroup level statistical relationships present in encoder derived representations. We further decode free running rollouts into the original clinical feature space and evaluate future clinical measurements against observed values using task matched forecasting baselines, demonstrating that the learned dynamics retain predictive information beyond latent space agreement. Across binary classification and time to event tasks, EHR WM achieves competitive, though task dependent, performance relative to substantially larger EHR foundation models while using a 30x smaller parameter footprint. Finally, perturbing observed action sequences produces corresponding changes in generated trajectories, demonstrating the action sensitivity of the learned dynamics. Together, these results support world modeling as a complementary framework for learning explicit, time indexed representations of patient evolution from longitudinal EHR.
authors: Simon A. Lee, Jiahang Hank Sha, Soomin Chung, Kai Akamatsu, Eran Halperin, Jeffrey N. Chiang

papers.title: Forecasting Patient Trajectories from the Electronic Health Records with Action-Conditioned World Models
papers.tldr: An action-conditioned world model forecasts and simulates patient evolution from EHR histories using compact latent trajectories.

papers.abstract: Latent world models learn action-conditioned state transitions in a compact representation space, providing a predictive model for visual planning and control. However, planning with these models typically requires costly test-time optimization over action sequences. We propose to replace this online search with a goal-conditioned inverse model that directly predicts actions from current and goal observations. A key challenge is that action prediction alone neither ensures that goal representations encode action-relevant information nor that predicted actions are consistent with the learned latent prediction model. We introduce Hindsight Inverse JEPA Planning (HIJP), a search-free framework that addresses both aspects during training. HIJP relabels future observations along offline trajectories as goals, providing action supervision across multiple temporal horizons. By retaining gradients through the goal representations, this supervision directly shapes the visual representation. HIJP further feeds predicted actions into the latent predictor model and aligns the resulting next-state representations with encoded successor observations, enforcing action-transition consistency. At inference time, the inverse dynamics model and latent predictor models are applied alternately to generate multi-step action sequences without online search. Across four visual control tasks, HIJP achieves 86.8% overall success and a 1.9-16.5x planning speedup over search-based planning.
authors: Guanchen Du, Jinhao Du, Yanpeng Sun, Shan Zhang, Na Zhao, Zechao Li
bullets: Latent world-model planning usually requires costly test-time optimization over action sequences.
HIJP uses future observations as hindsight goals to train an inverse model across multiple planning horizons.
Gradients through goal representations make visual features more action-relevant.
Predicted actions are checked against latent state transitions to enforce inverse-model/world-model consistency.
Across four visual control tasks, HIJP reaches 86.8% overall success and provides a 1.9–16.5× planning speedup over search-based methods.
papers.selection_reason: Search-free planning with latent world models and action-conditioned transitions; fits world-model subtopics.
papers.title: Beyond Action Prediction: Learning Search-Free Planning in Latent Space
papers.tldr: HIJP enables search-free visual planning by learning goal-conditioned actions that remain consistent with a latent world model, achieving strong control performance with substantially faster planning.

papers.abstract: A memory test for a video world model should say whether the scene was set, whether the asked change was carried out, and whether the last frame shows the result. Current tests fold these into one number, so a low score is easy to read as forgetting. When the change is not carried out, the hidden state transition cannot appear, so the test is not really a test of memory. We introduce MIST, an evaluation that separates the change from the memory it should leave behind. The model first sets the scene while the change stays hidden, and only later is asked to show it, with leakage before that point kept under control. This separation locates the bottleneck: the model sets the scene but does not carry out the instructed change. The same gap appears in general memory evaluations. On that basis we propose M3-Agent (Make the Missing Move), which recursively revises the details of the input instruction so that the model successfully carries out the requested instruction. Relative to the baseline, it more than triples the MIST reveal score. On the benchmarks, WRBench's score T rises by 26.1% and MBench-T's score U by 52.7%. The method meets the problem from the execution side: it shows what the frozen model can do once the move is stated, and it sets a stricter baseline.
authors: Weiyang Jin, Jiwen Yu, Sihan Xu, Yuwei Niu, Xihui Liu
bullets: Existing memory tests conflate scene setup, executing a change, and showing its result, making failures easy to misdiagnose as forgetting.
MIST hides the requested change during scene setup and tests whether the model later reveals it, while controlling information leakage.
MIST finds that models can set the scene but often fail to execute the instructed change, a gap also seen in broader memory evaluations.
M3-Agent recursively revises instruction details to help the frozen model carry out the missing action.
M3-Agent more than triples MIST reveal score and improves WRBench T by 26.1% and MBench-T U by 52.7%.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses memory failures in video world models and improves instruction execution, directly relevant to evaluating and improving interactive video world models.
papers.title: Execution Before Memory: Diagnosing Memory Failures in Video World Models
papers.tldr: MIST separates execution from memory in video world models, revealing that failures often stem from not carrying out the instructed change; M3-Agent addresses this by revising instructions and substantially improves reveal performance.

papers.abstract: Video world models must capture how a scene evolves beyond the current camera view to generate consistent observations when its content reappears. Existing approaches rely on observation history, static point clouds, or image caches constructed from past frames. These representations are often expensive and, more importantly, cannot update dynamic scene content outside the field of view: generated vehicles and pedestrians may be forgotten after leaving the field of view or reappear in physically inaccurate states. We represent an evolving scene through synchronized videos from reference-camera rigs, each comprising eight cameras that jointly cover the surrounding scene. We connect these rigs in a graph and propagate video generation between neighboring rigs to coordinate scene dynamics across locations and time. We introduce Momentum, a two-stage pipeline: WorldUpdate jointly generates reference-camera videos as a shared memory of scene dynamics, and WorldInteract grounds camera-controlled video generation in this evolving memory, allowing moving content to remain represented outside the target view and reappear consistently. To support training and evaluation, we develop a CARLA pipeline that captures synchronized videos from reference camera rigs and a moving target camera, together with an evaluation framework measuring consistency within the generated world state and the target observations.Experiments on generated street scenes show that grounding target videos in scene dynamics generated by Momentum improves dynamic scene consistency by 126.2% in unseen scenes over static image conditioning, while also improving visual fidelity. Our models and source code will be made publicly available.
authors: Nedko Savov, Stefan Maria Ailuro, Danda Pani Paudel, Yilun Du, Xi Wang, Luc Van Gool
bullets: Addresses the problem of forgetting or inaccurately replaying vehicles and pedestrians outside the field of view.
Uses synchronized eight-camera reference rigs connected in a graph to propagate scene dynamics across locations and time.
WorldUpdate generates shared reference-camera video memories; WorldInteract conditions target-camera generation on this evolving memory.
A CARLA-based pipeline and evaluation framework assess consistency of generated world states and target observations.
On generated street scenes, Momentum improved dynamic scene consistency by 126.2% in unseen scenes over static image conditioning, with improved visual fidelity.
papers.selection_reason: Persistent scene-dynamics memory for consistent video world models; fits video and interactive world models.
papers.title: Momentum: Persistent Dynamics for Video World Models
papers.tldr: Momentum builds a persistent, graph-connected video memory that keeps dynamic scene elements consistent as they move outside and re-enter the camera view.

papers.abstract: Rapid progress in embodied intelligence has enabled increasingly capable robots to follow language instructions and manipulate diverse objects. However, strong results in structured environments do not automatically transfer to open-world conditions, where clutter, occlusion, and changing viewpoints can obscure the spatial relationships required for action. To address this perceptual gap, a virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced. AWAM, an Active World-Action Model actively plans where to observe and imagines what will be seen along the planned trajectory before acting. Task-related virtual camera motion is predicted and used as a structured query into a geometry-conditioned world model, producing a reusable spatial prior for manipulation, which is later compressed into a fixed memory and fused with live observations through cross-attention for diffusion-based action prediction. AWAM achieves competitive success rates with 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials. These results support improved robustness to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts, addressing part of the gap between structured manipulation and less controlled environments.
authors: Jiawei Geng, Zhenyang Liu, Yuzheng Wu, Yanwei Fu
bullets: Addresses failures caused by occlusion, clutter, and changing viewpoints in open-world manipulation.
Predicts task-related virtual camera motion and queries a geometry-conditioned world model to generate spatial priors.
Compresses the imagined prior into fixed memory and fuses it with live observations for diffusion-based action prediction.
Reports success rates of 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials.
The demonstrated robustness is scoped to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts.
papers.selection_reason: Active world-action model with trajectory-conditioned view imagination for manipulation; fits world modeling and VLA.
papers.title: AWAM: Active Trajectory-Conditioned View Imagination for Robust Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: AWAM improves robot manipulation in cluttered and occluded settings by actively imagining task-relevant views along planned trajectories before acting.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate AI research, including language-model (LM) development, offering a potential path toward recursive self-improvement. However, turning experimental feedback into a learned ability to propose effective improvements across models faces two challenges. First, training such an ability with real feedback is expensive: reinforcement learning (RL) requires evaluating tens of thousands of proposals, each potentially requiring a full model-training run. Even at ten GPU-hours per run, reward collection alone would consume hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours, motivating a cheaper surrogate. Second, surrogate feedback can become unreliable as policy optimization favors overestimated proposals when the proposal distribution shifts. To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective LM improvement proposals. To provide scalable feedback, we use a research world model (RWM), a frozen LLM that predicts proposal gains from real experimental records provided in context, as the reward model for RL. To maintain feedback reliability, we periodically execute current-policy proposals ranked highly by the RWM and add their measured outcomes to its context. Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, real-execution evaluations on held-out tasks show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform GPT-6-sol, even when GPT-6-sol is given 300 real experimental records in context, while requiring 33% lower data-generation cost. LM2LM also generalizes to a model family unseen during training.
authors: Minhua Lin, Zijun Wang, Zewen Liu, Zhaotian Weng, Bing He, Zhan Shi, Benoit Dumoulin, Xiang Zhang, Suhang Wang, Hanqing Lu

Uses a frozen LLM research world model to predict proposal gains from experimental records and provide RL rewards.

papers.title: Language Models Learn to Improve Language Models
papers.tldr: LM2LM trains language models to propose effective language-model improvements using a learned research world model as scalable feedback, with periodic real experiments to keep that feedback reliable.

papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict actions and future world states, but long-horizon manipulation further requires language reasoning to plan subtask objectives, assess execution progress, and guide action selection. We present LAW, a closed-loop VLM--WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. Within the LAW agent, a hybrid-expert vision-language model plans the remaining subtasks, estimates the values of and fuses actions proposed by a world-action model, and asynchronously assesses execution status to support continued execution and subtask transitions. Within the world-action model, Mixture-of-Transformer Experts integrates modality-specific and shared computation for joint video--action modeling. Dual-stream hierarchical visual memory maintains temporal context for both models, while subtask-local value learning aligns action evaluation with semantic objectives and preserves supervision from successful prefixes of failed trajectories. LAW achieves 94.21% average success across 50 RoboTwin tasks. Replacing the WAM backbone with OpenWAM-$alpha$ further raises the average success rate to 95.56%, establishing a new open-source state of the art on RoboTwin. Despite having only 2B parameters, our VLM also outperforms variants using Embodied-R1.5 and GPT-5.5 High. On three long-horizon real-robot tasks, LAW achieves 65% average success, compared with 28.33% for $pi_{0.5}$ and 25% for Fast-WAM.
authors: Jiajun Cao, Kai Tang, Bohua Zhang, Zezhong Qian, Ying Li, Xiaozhu Ju, Xiaobao Wei, Jiaming Liu, Yang Ding, Sixiang Chen, Yiding Sun, Siyuan Qian, Tinghao Wang, Jixian Wu, Yichen Guo, Yi Zhang, Shilong Zou, Yong Dai, Jian Tang, Shanghang Zhang

Achieves 94.21% average success across 50 RoboTwin tasks, rising to 95.56% with OpenWAM-α.
Reaches 65% average success on three long-horizon real-robot tasks, versus 28.33% for π₀.₅ and 25% for Fast-WAM.

papers.title: LAW: Unifying Language, Action, and World Modeling for Agentic Physical Intelligence
papers.tldr: LAW unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling to improve long-horizon robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: We present LY-GWM-RoboCasa-Human300, a policy that combines a Human300-fine-tuned GR00T-N1.5 action generator, an action-conditioned graph dynamics model, and a learned binary state-reward scorer. At inference, the policy samples four action chunks, predicts the future latent features and robot state for each, and executes the candidate with the highest predicted-state reward logit. Predictions therefore influence the actions sent to the environment. The evaluated system uses a 16-step prediction horizon and keeps all three components frozen during evaluation. In the local evaluation on 50 RoboCasa 1.0.1 tasks in the pretrain kitchen split, with 50 episodes per task, the system records 207/2,500 successes (8.28%), compared with 181/2,500 (7.24%) in the historical self-trained GR00T-N1.5 baseline. The observed difference is 26 successes, or 1.04 percentage points. The atomic group improves from 141/900 to 150/900. Separately, the RoboCasa maintainers re-evaluated the submission and reported 354/1,500 successes (23.6%) across 50 tasks, with leaderboard rates of 48.3%, 16.3%, and 3.1% for Atomic-Seen, Composite-Seen, and Composite-Unseen. The local and official results are reported separately; their difference is not attributed to a model improvement. Recorded local audits identify 212,700 changed environment-input chunks, including 28,223 in atomic tasks. We describe the actual training stages, implemented inference mechanism, evaluation provenance, and public reproduction entrypoints. These results document an active prediction-and-selection system and a positive historical difference.
authors: TianLiang Ma, Ting Ma, ZhongYuan Ma

papers.title: LY-GWM-RoboCasa-Human300: Prediction-Guided Action Selection with a Graph Dynamics Model
