bullets: Addresses the problem that imitating all deployment actions can reinforce failures, while discarding failures loses information about physical interactions and their consequences.
Uses a closed-loop world-action model trained on rollouts from its own and other policies across successes, suboptimal behavior, and failures.
Combines source-dependent noise sampling, quality steering, and quality-weighted supervision to learn from full video data while regulating action imitation.
Video and action tokens interact during parallel denoising, enabling predicted consequences to directly inform action generation.
Across three deployment-and-training rounds, success on RoboChallenge Table30-V2 rose from 23.67% to 43.33%; gains were also reported on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and shirt folding.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop policy improvement from deployment rollouts with action-conditioned world modeling, relevant to robot learning/manipulation, interactive world models, and continual/online learning.
papers.title: LoopWAM: Closed-Loop Generalist Policy Improvement from Deployment Rollouts
papers.tldr: LoopWAM improves generalist robot policies by learning from mixed-quality deployment rollouts in a closed loop, substantially increasing task success without additional embodied pretraining.

papers.abstract: We introduce WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) against paired real-world executions. Given the same initial observation and low-level action sequence, WorldOracle asks whether a predicted rollout reproduces what happens in the real world, including physical consequences and task-state transitions. We evaluate models along four complementary dimensions: physical state correctness, interaction spatial alignment, key interaction area fidelity, and multi-view action coherence. To support this evaluation, we curate real-world training and evaluation suites that cover different interaction dynamics and embodiments. The evaluation suite contains long, multi-segment episodes with both successful and failed executions, enabling evaluation across varied action outcomes and behavior distributions. Experiments on seven representative ACWMs reveal distinct model strengths and failure modes. WorldOracle provides a systematic foundation for measuring and advancing action-conditioned world modeling for manipulation. We will release the datasets, evaluation code, and leaderboard.
authors: Haoyi Duan, Liliang Chen, Nan Wang, Yang Zhang, Yuhang Lu, Xiaotong Chen, Wei-Cheng Tseng, Shenyuan Gao, Zhaoshuo Li, Jingyi Jin, Pooya Jannaty, Dhruv Shah, Yuke Zhu, Ming-Yu Liu, Maoqing Yao, Guanghui Ren
bullets: Evaluates predicted rollouts against paired real executions, including physical consequences and task-state transitions.
Measures physical state correctness, spatial interaction alignment, key interaction-area fidelity, and multi-view action coherence.
Includes varied interaction dynamics, embodiments, long multi-segment episodes, and both successful and failed executions.
Experiments with seven representative models expose distinct strengths and failure modes.
Datasets, evaluation code, and a leaderboard are planned for release.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for action-conditioned world models against real-world manipulation executions, directly relevant to interactive world models and embodied manipulation.
papers.title: WorldOracle: Benchmarking Action-Conditioned World Models against Real-World Executions
papers.tldr: WorldOracle benchmarks whether action-conditioned world models accurately predict real-world manipulation outcomes from the same initial observation and action sequence.

papers.abstract: A robot needs a world model that predicts how its actions will change the scene and a policy that chooses those actions. Models are usually built and evaluated for only one of these roles, and every robot records its actions in its own format. We ask whether one robot world model can serve both roles across different bodies, and what makes this work. We present GreenWAM, a world foundation model for robotics, together with the recipe that produces it: (1) a shared anatomical action space that describes 20 robot families, from bimanual arms to dexterous humanoids, in common joint coordinates; (2) joint training on these families in visual, action-conditioned and world-action modes; and (3) policies that split an action expert off the generator. As a world model, GreenWAM attains top-tier trajectory, depth and 3D accuracy on WorldArena 1.0, ahead of every world-action model and video generator in our comparison. As a policy, it scores among the top entries of the RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard, reaches the highest zero-shot LIBERO-plus success among the compared methods and is competitive with dedicated vision-language-action and world-action policies on CALVIN and LIBERO. We further adapt GreenWAM to a real humanoid, where it succeeds more often than policies adapted from $\pi_{0.5}$ and from Cosmos 3 Edge, and distill it into a single-step policy for real-time control. Controlled experiments yield three findings: robot specialization improves world prediction and control together; an action expert helps when split off at the start of adaptation; and keeping world-model modes during policy adaptation preserves robustness to scene changes.
authors: Gennady Sidorov, Valerii Kornilov, Denis Grankin, Polina Fedotova, Aleksey Postnikov
bullets: Addresses the challenge of building one model for robots with different bodies and action formats.
Uses a shared anatomical action space covering 20 robot families and trains jointly in visual, action-conditioned, and world-action modes.
Separates an action expert from the generator to derive policies, including a distilled single-step policy for real-time control.
Achieves top-tier WorldArena 1.0 world-model accuracy and strong results across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-plus, CALVIN, and LIBERO.
Real-robot adaptation to a humanoid outperforms the cited adapted baselines; specialization and retaining world-model modes improve robustness.
papers.selection_reason: A world foundation model for robotics trained across robot families in action-conditioned and world-action modes, serving both prediction and policy roles.
papers.title: GreenWAM: A World Foundation Model for Robotics
papers.tldr: GreenWAM is a cross-robot world foundation model that supports both scene prediction and action selection through shared actions, joint training, and adaptable policies.

papers.abstract: World models (WMs) and world-action models (WAMs) focus on future world prediction and executable action generation, respectively. Although these models learn shared physical dynamics and interaction semantics from embodied trajectories, they are typically trained in isolation, which restricts knowledge reuse between prediction and control. The central challenge is therefore to develop a unified learning framework that shares these dynamics while preserving the distinct modeling capabilities required by each paradigm. We propose UniW(A)M, a mixture-of-experts world-(action) model built upon diffusion Transformers that unifies action-conditioned world modeling and diverse WAM variants. Shared experts capture common dynamics, while atomic capability experts are reused across interfaces so that each interface keeps its own conditional pathway. At deployment, a plug-in adaptive interface router (PAIR) learns from a small subset of target-task chunk scenarios to select a suitable WAM interface for each execution chunk, balancing task success and execution efficiency while keeping the backbone frozen. We evaluate UniW(A)M on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and three real-world manipulation tasks, where it achieves 88.3% average real-world success versus 76.7% for the strongest baseline. On WorldArena, it leads action-conditioned world modeling on all three tasks. AC-WM co-training contributes to action generation on every action interface and PAIR raises OOD success from 63.3% to 76.7%.
authors: Jingbo Xu, Jianjie Fang, Zhuohang Li, Zihao Song, Zhaolu Wang, Xvyuan Liu, Xin Zhang, Haisheng Su, Yinzhou Tang, Chen Gao, Wei Wu, Yong Li
bullets: Addresses isolated training of world models and world-action models, which limits reuse of learned dynamics and interaction semantics.
Uses diffusion Transformers with shared experts for common dynamics and capability-specific experts that preserve each interface’s conditional behavior.
Introduces PAIR, a plug-in router that selects WAM interfaces from a small set of target-task scenarios while keeping the backbone frozen.
Achieves 88.3% average real-world success versus 76.7% for the strongest baseline across three manipulation tasks.
Co-training improves action generation across all tested interfaces, while PAIR increases OOD success from 63.3% to 76.7%.
papers.selection_reason: Unifies action-conditioned world modeling and world-action models with a mixture-of-experts diffusion framework, directly relevant to interactive world models.
papers.title: UniW(A)M: A Unified Mixture-of-Experts Framework for World and World-Action Models
papers.tldr: UniW(A)M unifies world modeling and action generation with shared mixture-of-experts dynamics and adaptive interface routing, improving simulated and real-world manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform manipulation tasks using camera images and language instructions, but object slip or visual occlusion can disrupt execution. Recovery is typically learned during policy training or delegated to a monitor that triggers a scripted repair after detecting a failure. We introduce ForkCast, a predictive recovery framework that compares counterfactual futures to determine whether and how to intervene in a frozen VLA policy. At each decision point, ForkCast evaluates three candidates: executing the policy's nominal action chunk (Commit), adjusting the camera viewpoint (Reobserve), and replanning the arm trajectory (Replan). A candidate-conditioned world model forecasts the latent outcome of each candidate at a common future horizon, and a shared task-progress head scores the predicted outcomes. By evaluating the policy's own continuation alongside the repair candidates, a single comparison based on task progress determines both whether and how to intervene, without a failure detector, an intervention threshold, or updates to the VLA backbone. On five simulated RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with injected occlusion and object slip, ForkCast increases pooled success from 13.3% for the frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ policy to 30.0% and transfers to two additional VLA backbones without updating ForkCast. After adaptation on real-robot candidate rollouts, ForkCast also improves success over the base policy under both clean and visibility-limited conditions. Code will be released to benefit the research community.
authors: Chenru Wen, Huajian Zeng, Haokai Ding, Jian Kang, Anqing Duan, Dawei Zhou, Dezhen Song, Xingxing Zuo
bullets: Addresses manipulation failures caused by object slip and visual occlusion without retraining the VLA backbone.
Uses a candidate-conditioned world model to forecast common-horizon outcomes for Commit, Reobserve, and Replan.
A shared task-progress head selects whether to intervene and which recovery action to use, without a failure detector or intervention threshold.
On five simulated RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, pooled success increased from 13.3% to 30.0% for the frozen π₀.₅ policy.
Transferred to two additional VLA backbones and improved real-robot success under clean and visibility-limited conditions after candidate-rollout adaptation.
papers.selection_reason: Uses candidate-conditioned latent world models and counterfactual futures to recover VLA policies from failures.
papers.title: ForkCast: Predictive Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Policies via Counterfactual Futures
papers.tldr: ForkCast enables a frozen vision-language-action policy to recover from slip and occlusion by comparing predicted outcomes of continuing, reobserving, or replanning.

papers.abstract: Latent planners often rank candidate action sequences by terminal Euclidean distance to a goal latent. Exact agreement with transition distance would make this score ideal, but is stronger than planning requires: along a transition-shortest rollout, the essential requirement is that latent distance does not reverse true transition progress. We show that this pathwise no-reversal requirement is precisely the classical self-approaching condition. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to identify self-approachingness as a planner-facing compatibility condition for terminal Euclidean latent planning and to connect its violation to an exact finite-horizon candidate-order reversal. Because visual world models predict discrete latent sequences, we analyze their polygonal interpolation. We prove that an acute bend creates a nonempty region in which terminal Euclidean distance ranks a transition-worse candidate ahead of one that makes genuine progress, even under exact rollouts. We further interpret latent dimension as angular capacity through a classical spherical-code bound. A controlled six-branch experiment, including a zero-padded three-dimensional baseline, validates the predicted ordering failure and separates angular arrangement from ambient dimensionality.
authors: Junlin Wu, Wen Fan, Dandan Zhang
bullets: Frames pathwise no-reversal of latent distance as the classical self-approaching condition.
Proves that acute bends can cause terminal Euclidean scoring to prefer a worse candidate over a genuinely progressing one, even with exact rollouts.
Analyzes discrete world-model predictions through polygonal interpolation.
Relates latent dimensionality to angular capacity via a spherical-code bound.
A controlled six-branch experiment, including a zero-padded 3D baseline, validates ordering failures and distinguishes angular arrangement from ambient dimension.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical and empirical analysis of latent geometry for planning in world models, introducing self-approachingness as a planner compatibility condition.
papers.title: Order-Consistent Latent Geometry for Reliable Short-Horizon Planning in World Models
papers.tldr: The paper shows that reliable short-horizon latent planning requires distances to preserve progress along shortest transition paths, and identifies self-approaching geometry as the key condition.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies excel at generalist robotic manipulation but generate actions without explicitly modeling their environmental consequences. World action models (WAMs) incorporate future prediction, yet most rely on costly video generation, while latent alternatives either use predicted futures only as auxiliary targets or infer latent actions from suboptimal visual transitions through costly large-scale video pretraining. We introduce WAVE-0 (World-model-Augmented VLA Execution), a framework that bridges VLAs and WAMs through a lightweight latent world model. By connecting the semantic understanding of pretrained VLAs with explicit future prediction, WAVE-0 allows anticipated action consequences to directly guide action generation. Built on a pretrained VLA, its 257M world model translates VLM-generated latent action plans into predicted future representations that condition the action expert, unifying latent planning, future prediction, and action generation. The world model is trained directly on ground-truth robot actions with a counterfactual ranking objective, requiring neither pixel reconstruction nor large-scale video pretraining. WAVE-0 achieves success rates of 91.47% on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.7% on LIBERO, along with 88.0%, 61.4%, and 75.0% on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and LIBERO-Para, respectively. On real-world tasks, it improves the success rate of $\pi_{0.5}$ from 38.3% to 73.3%. These results demonstrate strong manipulation performance and generalization across diverse distribution shifts.
authors: Haomin Wang, Anqiong Ji, Ke Wang, Zhongshan Liu, Ru Ying, Ran Zheng, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit environmental consequence modeling in VLA policies without relying on costly video generation or large-scale video pretraining.
Uses a 257M-parameter world model to translate VLM-generated latent action plans into predicted future representations that condition action generation.
Trains the world model directly from ground-truth robot actions with a counterfactual ranking objective, avoiding pixel reconstruction.
Reports strong simulation performance across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and its distribution-shift variants.
Improves real-world success for π0.5 from 38.3% to 73.3%, demonstrating better generalization across distribution shifts.
papers.selection_reason: Bridges VLA policies with latent future prediction, unifying latent planning, world modeling, and action generation for manipulation.
papers.title: WAVE-0: Bridging VLA Policies and WAMs with Lightweight Latent Future Prediction
papers.tldr: WAVE-0 augments a pretrained VLA with a lightweight latent world model that predicts action consequences to guide robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: World models have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied AI, yet existing systems often remain fragmented in the modalities they model and the functions they support. In particular, visual dynamics, geometric structure, and executable action are commonly coupled through separate interfaces or downstream modules rather than being jointly represented and evolved within a shared dynamics model. In this work, we present Thinker-WM, a unified multimodal world model that jointly models and generates RGB, metric depth, and robot action through a shared intermediate Unified Dynamics Transformer with modality-specific encoders and decoders. The model performs multimodal unification at the representation level: appearance, geometry, and action are transformed into a common dynamic representation and jointly evolved by shared parameters, while their distinct output structures are preserved. The same parameterization supports multiple functions, including joint video-action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action-conditioned generation, video-to-action generation, and inverse dynamics. To examine whether the shared representation captures action-related information, we introduce a lightweight motion probe that shows the frozen visual representation contains recoverable motion information. Thinker-WM is trained on a heterogeneous corpus comprising approximately 20K hours of egocentric video, 10K hours of real-robot data, and 1K hours of simulation data, including approximately 4K hours of real-robot data with aligned depth supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance across embodied world-model evaluations. Thinker-WM ranks first on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad and WorldArena, while controlled studies further demonstrate the benefits of action conditioning, geometric interaction, and multi-function training within the shared representation.
authors: Thinker Team, Peng Gao, Jichao Jiao, Chen Liao, Daqin Luo, Yiming Ma, Baiyu Pan, Hailin Shi, Jiyuan Wang, Xiangming Xu, Xiongwei Zhao
bullets: Addresses fragmented world models that handle modalities and functions through separate interfaces or modules.
Uses modality-specific encoders and decoders around a shared Unified Dynamics Transformer that jointly evolves RGB, metric depth, and action representations.
Supports joint video-action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action-conditioned generation, video-to-action generation, and inverse dynamics.
A motion probe indicates that frozen visual representations retain recoverable action-related motion information.
Trained on heterogeneous egocentric-video, real-robot, and simulation data; the abstract reports top results on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad, and WorldArena.
papers.selection_reason: Unified multimodal world model jointly modeling RGB, depth, and robot action for embodied intelligence, with strong relevance to world models, embodied action, and spatial representation.
papers.title: Thinker-WM: A Unified World Model with Shared Multimodal Representations for Embodied Intelligence
papers.tldr: Thinker-WM unifies visual appearance, depth geometry, and robot actions in one shared world model for prediction, generation, and control-related tasks.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models have emerged as a foundation for long-horizon world rollout. However, when extended far beyond their training windows, these models suffer from progressive drift: visual quality deteriorates, motion becomes inconsistent, and object identity gradually collapses as generated frames are recursively reused as context. We study a supervision-horizon gap: short-horizon distillation leaves later rollout states without direct supervision. We show that matching short-window marginals need not determine long-horizon behavior, while longer on-policy trajectories expose delayed failures to training. This motivates temporal manifold matching at scale for long-horizon world models. Building on this insight, we introduce LongForcing, a distillation approach that scales teacher supervision to long student self-rollouts. LongForcing preserves the short-horizon teacher-forcing and causal ODE-distillation stages, while replacing the realscore teacher in the final distribution-matching stage with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher. The long-horizon teacher supervises extended student self-rollouts using the standard distribution-matching formulation, without modifying the student architecture or increasing inference cost. We evaluate LongForcing on text-to-video generation and interactive action-conditioned world models, achieving a VBench Quality score of 85.52 and improving WorldRoamBench 60s action score by 23.9 points in first-person ablations. Qualitative stress tests further sample interactive rollouts up to 24 hours, far beyond the training horizon. These results suggest that scaling supervision along the temporal axis is a practical step toward long-horizon world models. The project website and code are at https://github.com/Fantasy-AMAP/LongForcing.
authors: Ziyu Zhu, Zhaoxu Sun, Fan Jiang, Mengchao Wang, Junfeng Ni, Ting-Bing Xu, Zhicheng Liu, Mu Xu
bullets: Targets progressive visual degradation, motion inconsistency, and object-identity collapse beyond the training horizon.
Identifies a supervision-horizon gap: short-window distillation does not constrain delayed rollout failures.
Extends temporal manifold matching by replacing the final-stage realscore teacher with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher.
Preserves the student architecture and inference cost while supervising long self-rollouts.
Reports a VBench Quality score of 85.52, a 23.9-point improvement on the WorldRoamBench 60s action score in first-person ablations, and qualitative rollouts up to 24 hours.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes long-horizon world rollout via temporal manifold matching for autoregressive video diffusion, directly relevant to world models and video generation.
papers.title: LongForcing: Scaling Temporal Manifold Matching for Long-Horizon World Rollout
papers.tldr: LongForcing reduces long-horizon video and world-model drift by training on extended student self-rollouts with a bidirectional teacher.

papers.abstract: World-model-based visual navigation enables action planning by predicting future states under candidate trajectories. However, long-horizon rollout remains challenging: models are often trained with ground-truth visual histories but deployed in closed-loop prediction, and evaluating many candidates with step-by-step rollout is computationally expensive. We propose SkipWorld, a latent skip planning framework for efficient visual navigation. SkipWorld introduces three components: (i) Latent AutoRoll, which trains a world model to recursively roll out future states in latent space, reducing the mismatch between training and closed-loop inference; (ii) SkipDistill, which distills the latent autoregressive model into a skip world model that directly predicts long-stride future latent states; and (iii) Skip-then-Refine Planning, a dual-model coarse-to-fine planner that first filters candidate trajectories with the skip model and then reranks selected candidates with the stronger autoregressive model. This design preserves accurate trajectory evaluation while reducing redundant rollout computation. Experiments on RECON, HuRoN, SCAND, and TartanDrive show that, compared with NWM, SkipWorld reduces the average ATE by 4.2% and RPE by 2.7%, while decreasing planning time by 62.4% with a 2.7-fold speedup.
authors: Yifei Yang, Zehua Fan, Zike Yan, Zhongyu Li, Yan Wang
bullets: Addresses closed-loop rollout mismatch and the high cost of evaluating many candidate trajectories.
Latent AutoRoll trains recursive latent-space prediction to better match deployment conditions.
SkipDistill creates a skip world model that directly predicts long-stride future latent states.
Skip-then-Refine Planning combines fast coarse filtering with accurate autoregressive reranking.
On four benchmarks, it reduces ATE by 4.2%, RPE by 2.7%, and planning time by 62.4%, achieving a 2.7× speedup versus NWM.
papers.selection_reason: Latent skip planning with distilled world models for efficient closed-loop visual navigation.
papers.title: SkipWorld: Latent Skip Planning with Distilled World Models for Efficient Visual Navigation
papers.tldr: SkipWorld accelerates visual navigation planning by using distilled latent skip predictions for coarse filtering before autoregressive refinement, improving accuracy while greatly reducing computation.

papers.abstract: Visually similar actions can produce contact loss, jamming, slippage, or irreversible damage, while tactile feedback may arrive after a critical transition. Contact-rich manipulation therefore requires generative policies to anticipate and evaluate whether candidate actions will produce desirable contact outcomes, then adjust action generation before execution. We present ForeTac, a predictive contact-guidance framework organized as a represent-predict-evaluate-guide loop. ForeTac encodes the current tactile state, predicts the tactile consequences of a candidate action sequence, and evaluates the predicted trajectory using a contact-quality objective learned from successful and failed physical interactions. At deployment, its gradient propagates through the tactile predictor to guide action generation while the pretrained model parameters remain frozen. We evaluate ForeTac on four real-robot tasks (planar and curved-surface wiping, card swiping, and fragile-object grasping) with diffusion and flow-matching policies. Across these tasks, ForeTac raises the average task success rate from 36.3% to 71.3% and the average contact success rate (CSR) from 20.0% to 66.3% compared with vision-only Diffusion Policy. Component analyses support the tactile representation and action-conditioned foresight, and show that predicted touch preserves contact-quality ordering. Project page: https://foretac.github.io/.
authors: Zhiyuan Chen, Shuai Chen, Haoran Zhou, Yizhe Zhao, Kaiyuan Yang, Zhixiang Duan, Shaoqing Xu, Ran Cao, Diyun Xiang, Yangwei You
bullets: Addresses contact loss, jamming, slippage, and damage caused by delayed tactile feedback.
Uses a represent–predict–evaluate–guide loop with tactile-state encoding and action-conditioned tactile foresight.
Guides action generation by backpropagating a learned contact-quality objective through the tactile predictor while keeping pretrained policies frozen.
Evaluated on four real-robot tasks with diffusion and flow-matching policies.
Improves average task success from 36.3% to 71.3% and contact success from 20.0% to 66.3% versus vision-only Diffusion Policy.
papers.selection_reason: Predictive contact guidance for generative robot policies using action-conditioned tactile foresight and contact-quality evaluation.
papers.title: ForeTac: Predictive Contact Guidance for Generative Robot Policies
papers.tldr: ForeTac improves contact-rich robot manipulation by predicting tactile outcomes and guiding generative policies before execution.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) built on pretrained video generation models adapt quickly to new robotic tasks, but they forget previously learned tasks under sequential fine-tuning. Experience replay (ER) mitigates such forgetting by rehearsing data of previous tasks, yet this data is often unavailable in robotics, where a policy is deployed as weights only and its training data is not shared along with it. In this work, we ask whether a WAM can achieve data-free continual learning by regenerating its own past. Our key observation is that a WAM can indeed autoregressively regenerate complete rollouts of previously learned tasks and replay them to mitigate forgetting. However, replaying such raw rollouts still lags far behind replaying real data, which we attribute to two issues. First, the WAM is unable to recognize task completion and keeps generating purposeless motion after the task is done. Second, under open-loop generation, the generated actions gradually drift away from the generated observations. To address both issues, we present rectified generative replay (R$^2$-WAM), which truncates generated rollouts at task completion with an agentic evaluator and filters out rollouts whose actions are physically inconsistent with the observations. On the four LIBERO suites and five real-world tasks, R$^2$-WAM reduces forgetting by over 90% relative to sequential fine-tuning and nearly matches ER without accessing any data from previous tasks. Our analysis further reveals that forgetting in WAMs concentrates in inverse dynamics modeling: a forgotten WAM still produces visually plausible observations of previous tasks while its generated actions fail.
authors: Kaipeng Fang, Hangxu Liu, Chaojian Shi, Yunsong Zhou, Hongzi Zhu, Minyi Guo, Jingkuan Song, Lianli Gao
bullets: Problem: Sequentially fine-tuning world action models on new robotic tasks causes forgetting, while prior-task training data may be unavailable.
Method: The model autoregressively regenerates past-task rollouts, truncates them at task completion, and filters action–observation inconsistencies.
Contribution: Rectified generative replay (R²-WAM) supports continual learning without storing or accessing previous data.
Result: Across four LIBERO suites and five real-world tasks, it reduces forgetting by over 90% versus sequential fine-tuning and nearly matches experience replay.
Finding: Forgetting is concentrated in inverse-dynamics modeling; observations can remain visually plausible while generated actions fail.
papers.selection_reason: Data-free continual learning for world action models via rectified generative replay; directly targets world models and continual adaptation.
papers.title: Data-Free Continual Learning for World Action Model with Rectified Generative Replay
papers.tldr: R²-WAM enables data-free continual learning by replaying self-generated, task-complete, physically consistent rollouts to substantially reduce forgetting in world action models.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models can reduce costly real-robot interaction in reinforcement learning for Vision-Language-Action models (VLA-RL), but hallucinations can mislead policy optimization. Extending them to richer VLA interfaces and long-horizon tasks raises challenges in spatiotemporal and cross-modal consistency, exploration-reliability balance in RL, and compounding rollout errors. We present WoVR+, extending WoVR's hallucination-aware WM-RL framework by redesigning the learned environment and imagined interaction protocol: A VLA-interface-aligned world model provides multi-view prediction and proprioceptive updates while mitigating hallucinations. Chunk-wise noise preserves flow-based policy exploration while limiting prediction-degrading action jitter. For long-horizon tasks, stage-local imagined training combines stage-entry resets, stage-specific rewards, local horizons, and controllable sampling to shorten generated prefixes and balance training across stages. WoVR+ improves success over SFT by 21.09% and 16.7% on RoboTwin and 6 real-robot tasks. Long-horizon phone-packaging success rises from 30% to 75%. Videos are available at https://youmo445.github.io/WoVR_Plus.github.io/.
authors: Shangqing Zhou, Zhennan Jiang, Ning Ma, Xin Fu, Yupeng Zheng, Shuai Tian, Huangrui Li, Jiahao Liu, Chao Yu, Zhongpu Xia, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao
bullets: Targets hallucinations, cross-modal consistency, exploration reliability, and compounding errors in world-model-based VLA-RL.
Uses a VLA-aligned world model with multi-view prediction and proprioceptive updates to improve imagined interactions.
Applies chunk-wise action noise to preserve exploration while limiting prediction-degrading jitter.
Trains long-horizon tasks stage by stage using resets, stage-specific rewards, local horizons, and controllable sampling.
Reports higher success than SFT on RoboTwin and six real-robot tasks; phone-packaging success increases from 30% to 75%.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned world model as simulator for VLA policy RL, directly relevant to interactive world models and vision-language-action.
papers.title: WoVR+: World Model as Reliable Simulator for Versatile VLA Policy Optimization with RL
papers.tldr: WoVR+ improves VLA policy optimization with a hallucination-aware world model and stage-local imagined RL, reducing reliance on costly real-robot interaction.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and world models have demonstrated strong capabilities in semantic understanding and future scene evolution for autonomous driving. However, effectively integrating both capabilities for trajectory generation remains challenging. In this work, we propose DriveWLA, a unified World-Language-Action model based on Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) that jointly models semantic understanding, future scene dynamics, and trajectory generation. DriveWLA consists of three experts: a World Expert for future prediction, a Language Expert for semantic understanding, and an Action Expert for trajectory generation. We further introduce Cross-Expert Attention, which enables controlled information flow across experts while aligning semantic and dynamic representations. To improve trajectory generation beyond imitation learning, we apply Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning post-training to refine the Action Expert. Extensive experiments show that DriveWLA achieves superior performance in both open-loop and closed-loop evaluation. DriveWLA achieves 92.3 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, demonstrating strong performance among VLM-based and world-model-based planners. Without specific fine-tuning, DriveWLA further demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive. These results validate the effectiveness of our unified World-Language-Action modeling, establishing DriveWLA as a generalizable framework for autonomous driving.
authors: Shuzheng Wang, Haoxuan Li, Shengzhen Li, Chenxi Wu, Yajing Sun, Lu Hou, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Uses a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture with separate World, Language, and Action experts.
Introduces Cross-Expert Attention to align semantic and dynamic representations through controlled information exchange.
Applies Flow-GRPO reinforcement-learning post-training to improve trajectory generation beyond imitation learning.
Reports 92.3 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, with strong open- and closed-loop performance.
Shows zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive without specific fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Unified world-language-action model for autonomous driving, directly covering trajectory generation, future dynamics, and semantic understanding.
papers.title: DriveWLA: Unifying Future Dynamics and Scene Semantics through World-Language-Action Modeling for Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: DriveWLA unifies scene semantics, future dynamics, and trajectory generation in one World-Language-Action model for autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Occupancy world models provide a structured, metric representation of future driving scenes, making them a promising basis for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing occupancy-aware planners typically couple occupancy prediction and action generation through either hierarchical coupling or parallel multi-task learning. Hierarchical methods use occupancy either as a fully predicted future preceding action generation or as an action-conditioned rollout for trajectory evaluation, whereas parallel multi-task methods predict occupancy alongside planning through a separate branch or auxiliary objective. These interfaces retain either an explicit generation order or a role asymmetry, limiting reciprocal interaction between world prediction and action generation during trajectory formation. We propose OccWAM, an occupancy-native world-action model that jointly generates dense future occupancy and continuous ego trajectories via flow matching conditioned on scene representations. Building on this joint formulation, we introduce scene-to-ego world-action flow matching, a two-stage formulation. The first stage predicts scene-centric occupancy together with an absolute ego trajectory, providing a stable representation of future scene evolution. The same predicted world is then re-indexed into the future ego frames induced by the initial trajectory, where ego motion is represented through adjacent pose increments and a second joint flow refines ego-centric occupancy and motion for action-aligned planning. Unlike video-based world-action models, OccWAM preserves explicit semantic geometry for direct planning reasoning without pixel synthesis. Extensive experiments on Bench2Drive and nuScenes demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in closed-loop driving, open-loop planning, and future occupancy prediction.
authors: Qihang Huang, Wenhui Huang, Collister Chua, Shiyu Fang, Zhan Chen, Songyan Zhang, Zhidong Wang, Daiying Tian, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses limited reciprocal interaction in hierarchical and parallel occupancy-aware planning methods.
Generates dense scene occupancy and continuous ego trajectories jointly from scene representations.
First predicts scene-centric occupancy and an absolute ego trajectory, then refines ego-centric occupancy and motion in future ego frames.
Uses explicit semantic geometry rather than pixel synthesis for direct planning reasoning.
Reports state-of-the-art results in closed-loop driving, open-loop planning, and future occupancy prediction on Bench2Drive and nuScenes.
papers.selection_reason: OccWAM proposes a joint occupancy and trajectory generation model via flow matching for autonomous driving, preserving semantic geometry for planning.
papers.title: OccWAM: Occupancy World-Action Models with Joint Scene-to-Ego Flow Matching
papers.tldr: OccWAM jointly predicts future occupancy and ego trajectories through two-stage scene-to-ego flow matching for geometry-aware autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Recent coding large language models (LLMs) can synthesize dynamic 4D worlds from natural language, but the resulting content remains a visual artifact. It lacks physical semantics such as the collision geometry, mass, friction, inertia, and joint structure, required to enable it to simulate the physical world, and its dynamics are scripted to look plausible rather than designed to execute. What is needed is an executable world: one that a physics engine can load and step, resolving contact physically. We present Code2Worlds-2, an extension of Code2Worlds that turns 4D world generation into an embodied world simulation. We keep the original dual-stream generation pipeline intact and append two modules. First, a SimReady Scene Compiler that turns a generated visual scene into a simulator-compatible representation: it assigns collision meshes via convex decomposition, estimates physical attributes with a vision-language model, infers a lightweight support graph, instantiates the engine's contact, friction, and dynamics constraints, and applies a gravity settling pass, before exporting the scene as MuJoCo MJCF. Second, a Simulator-in-the-Loop 4D Refiner that implements an automated agent harness-a compile, simulate, critique and refine loop-that converts visual dynamics into executable rigid and articulated dynamics and evolves the physical settings rather than only the code, replacing the purely visual motion critic with a simulator critic that inspects penetration depth, collision pairs, stability, contact forces, joint limits, and robot reachability. We further propose SimCode4D, a state-based benchmark with five task templates for evaluating embodied simulation. Experiments on SimCode4D and across natural, indoor, industrial, urban, and service scenes show that Code2Worlds-2 produces physically plausible, simulator-compatible, and robot-interactable scenes.
authors: Haoyu Zhang, Siming Li, Zeyu Zhang, Yi Zhang, Tat-Seng Chua, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually plausible generated worlds and scenes with physical semantics needed for simulation.
Adds a SimReady Scene Compiler that infers collision geometry, physical properties, support relations, and dynamics constraints, then exports MuJoCo MJCF.
Introduces a Simulator-in-the-Loop 4D Refiner that iteratively compiles, simulates, critiques, and adjusts physical settings.
Uses simulator feedback on contacts, penetration, stability, forces, joint limits, and robot reachability instead of only visual motion critique.
Proposes SimCode4D, a five-template state-based benchmark, and evaluates scenes across natural, indoor, industrial, urban, and service settings.
papers.selection_reason: Generates physically executable embodied world simulations with simulator-in-the-loop refinement; fits interactive world models.
papers.title: Code2Worlds-2: Physically Plausible Agent Harness for Embodied World Simulation
papers.tldr: Code2Worlds-2 converts visually generated 4D worlds into physically executable, robot-interactable simulations through scene compilation and simulator-guided refinement.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use generative visual representations to condition robot actions, yet how these representations organize action-relevant information remains poorly understood. We identify persistent high-norm spatial outliers in WAM representations and find that their action relevance persists even after normalization and K/V projection attenuate their extreme magnitude. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RegisterWAM, which adds learnable non-spatial registers to the world model and uses them directly for action conditioning. Registers alone do not fully eliminate spatial outliers; pairing them with observation flow-matching (FM) loss supervision suppresses spatial outliers while concentrating high-norm responses in registers. Beyond this reorganization, observation FM loss supervision also improves action learning without registers, motivating an additional noised-observation FM objective that learns current-scene recovery from corrupted inputs. The resulting model achieves 81.64\% success on LIBERO-Plus without additional embodied pretraining data or foundation models, reaches 93.0\% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, and improves real-world manipulation performance.
authors: Yiwei Zhang, Yantai Yang, Jin Gao, Jin Lou, Andong Chen, Yufei Liu, Boyang Xing, Yuchen Zhu, Weiming Hu, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: WAMs contain persistent high-norm spatial outliers that remain action-relevant even after normalization and K/V projection.
RegisterWAM adds non-spatial learnable registers for action conditioning, while observation flow-matching supervision suppresses spatial outliers and concentrates responses in registers.
Flow-matching supervision improves action learning even without registers, motivating a noised-observation objective for recovering current scenes from corrupted inputs.
The resulting model reports 81.64% success on LIBERO-Plus and 93.0% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, with improved real-world manipulation performance.
papers.selection_reason: RegisterWAM improves World Action Models by adding learnable non-spatial registers and using observation flow-matching supervision for better action conditioning.
papers.title: Acting Through Registers
papers.tldr: RegisterWAM reorganizes action-relevant representations into learnable registers and uses flow-matching supervision to improve robot manipulation without extra embodied pretraining data or foundation models.

papers.abstract: In outdoor environments, varying terrain and contact conditions can cause identical action commands to produce different motion outcomes for quadruped robots. Predicting these outcomes is essential for reliable navigation and informed path selection. Existing video world models can generate visually plausible futures, yet often struggle to capture robot dynamics and terrain interactions, leading to overly optimistic predictions of action outcomes. We present DR-WM, a physically consistent world model that incorporates robot-terrain contact dynamics to predict the consequences of quadruped actions. Starting from an initial RGB image, our method reconstructs scene geometry and integrates dense, dimensionless priors over terrain contact properties, calibrated using real-world action-response data. The resulting terrain model supports the simulation of physics with spatially varying contact properties such as friction. Given the initial state of the robot and candidate action sequences, we simulate its future motion and use the resulting camera trajectories and rendered geometry to guide the training of a video world model. The generated future observations are then used to update the terrain reconstruction, enabling iterative model rollouts without additional real-world images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DR-WM substantially outperforms geometry-only baselines and baselines with uniform physical parameters on key physical metrics characterizing action outcomes, while achieving the best performance among the evaluated baselines. These physically grounded predictions support more informed action selection: across 90 challenging scenarios, an 8B vision-language model augmented with DR-WM outperforms an unassisted 32B vision-language model on five of six evaluation metrics.
authors: Ruo Chen, Jiahua Pang, Yingjie Niu, Hongyi Lin, Jun Tian, Yang Zhu, Chao Li
bullets: Addresses unreliable action-outcome prediction when identical commands encounter different terrain and contact conditions.
Reconstructs geometry from an RGB image and augments it with dense priors for terrain contact properties such as friction.
Simulates candidate robot actions, uses camera trajectories and rendered geometry to train a video world model, and iteratively updates terrain estimates without new real-world images.
Outperforms geometry-only and uniform-physics baselines on physical action-outcome metrics.
Improves action selection: a 8B vision-language model using DR-WM surpasses an unassisted 32B model on five of six metrics across 90 challenging scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces DR-WM, a behavior-grounded world model for quadrupeds that integrates robot-terrain contact dynamics for physically consistent future prediction.
papers.title: From Pixels to Executable Physics: Behavior-Grounded World Models for Embodied Action Consequence Prediction
papers.tldr: DR-WM predicts quadruped action consequences more reliably by combining scene geometry with spatially varying, real-world-calibrated terrain contact dynamics.

papers.abstract: Operational mobile networks are rich in observations but poor in interventions: they continuously generate large volumes of passive telemetry, while controlled action--response trajectories remain comparatively scarce and costly to collect. This observation--intervention asymmetry is a central obstacle to building practical world models for RAN control. We address this problem with RAN-JEPA, an action-conditioned world model that separates representation learning from intervention learning. The model first learns a predictive latent representation from observation-only network data, adapts that representation to the target deployment domain, and then learns action-conditioned latent dynamics from controlled sleep/wake trajectories while keeping the encoder fixed. We evaluate RAN-JEPA using public operator performance data for pretraining and a real-equipment four-cell 5G testbed for domain adaptation, post-training, and control. Across four future 15-minute intervals, RAN-JEPA achieves lower action-conditioned prediction error than a GPT-2 world-model baseline and a mechanistic rule, while remaining close to a strong persistence reference. What-if evaluation further shows that the model produces distinct and coherent future trajectories under matched SLEEP and KEEP plans. In closed-loop control, RAN-JEPA consistently supports higher sleep ratios than the two baselines at comparable congestion cost. These results show that observation-first, action-conditioned learning can turn abundant passive telemetry and limited intervention data into a practical predictive model for energy-aware RAN control.
authors: Binghan Wu, Kai Zeng, Kai Yang, Ya-Qin Zhang, Joseph Sifakis, Ye Ouyang
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and cost of controlled action–response data in mobile networks.
Pretrains predictive representations on observation-only data, adapts them to a target domain, then learns sleep/wake-conditioned dynamics with the encoder fixed.
Evaluated with public operator data and a real-equipment four-cell 5G testbed.
Achieves lower action-conditioned prediction error than a GPT-2 world model and mechanistic rule, while remaining near a persistence baseline.
Supports higher sleep ratios at comparable congestion cost and generates distinct futures for SLEEP versus KEEP plans.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned world model for network control fits interactive world models despite non-embodied domain.
papers.title: RAN-JEPA: An Action-Conditioned World Model for Energy-efficient Mobile Network Control
papers.tldr: RAN-JEPA learns an action-conditioned latent world model from abundant passive telemetry plus limited intervention data to enable energy-aware 5G RAN control.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) are a category of policy models that ex- plicitly predict both actions and future world states. They have been shown to outperform action-only models across various robotic manipulation tasks. How- ever, representing the future with full-frame video prediction can be computation- ally expensive during both training and inference. This raises a central question: what compact state representation preserves the planning and supervision bene- fits of future prediction? In this paper, we propose BoxWAM, which replaces dense future frames with oriented bounding box trajectories of task-relevant ob- jects. By explicitly imagining object-centric future motion, our method provides a lightweight prediction target that captures the key physical changes induced by robot actions. We show that box trajectory prediction substantially reduces com- putational cost while improving action prediction performance, suggesting that object-centric compact states can serve as an efficient alternative to video-based world action modeling for robotic manipulation. Result videos can be found on https://box-wam.github.io
authors: Qinxi Yu, Wenzhou Ding, Gloria X. Wang, Albert J. Zhai, Shenlong Wang
bullets: Addresses the high training and inference cost of dense future-frame prediction in world action models.
Represents task-relevant object motion with object-centric oriented bounding-box trajectories.
Uses predicted future object motion as a compact planning and supervision signal.
Reports substantially lower computational cost and improved action prediction performance.
Focuses on robotic manipulation; the abstract does not specify datasets or numeric results.
papers.selection_reason: Replaces video future prediction with object-box trajectories in world action models for manipulation; fits interactive world models and robot learning.
papers.title: Box-WAM: Box Trajectories as Compact State Representations for World Action Models
papers.tldr: Box-WAM uses oriented bounding-box trajectories instead of future video frames to make world action models more efficient while improving action prediction for robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Precise control of movement across various robotic embodiments is a longstanding challenge. Modeling complex robotic structures requires significant time, dedicated sensors, and manual labeling. Recent advancements in 4D representation learning offer an interesting alternative: can we leverage 4D features lifted from 2D observations to densely map a robot's spatial movement based on the action signal? To this end, we propose Act4R, a framework that builds on 3D foundation model to predict a robot's 3D scene flow with any given action. Act4R introduces a Spatial-Action Encoder, which encodes the current 2D robot state and its action signals into embeddings that represent future robot state in 3D. Then, both the current and future spatial embeddings are decoded into point maps to estimate action-conditioned scene flow. To effectively learn the mapping between action and future state, Act4R introduces spatial-action fusion in its transformer-based encoder, and a spatial alignment loss that guides the encoder for future flow prediction. After training on some samples of a given embodiment, Act4R can perform inverse control by optimizing the signal to achieve the desired scene flow. We evaluate Act4R on a public real-world dataset and synthetic data collected in simulator. Experiments on various robotic platforms show that Act4R outperforms the previous SoTA in scene flow prediction. Our method also performs better in inverse control, both on the action accuracy metric and in closed-loop control in simulation.
authors: Zhaoliang Zhang, Chenhao Yu, Zhimin Shao, Xijun Liu, Cheng Peng
bullets: Addresses the costly modeling, sensing, and labeling required for precise control across robot embodiments.
Uses a 3D foundation model with a Spatial-Action Encoder to combine 2D robot observations and actions into future 3D spatial embeddings.
Decodes current and future embeddings into point maps and estimates action-conditioned 3D scene flow.
Introduces spatial-action fusion and a spatial alignment loss to improve future-flow prediction.
Outperforms prior state of the art in scene-flow prediction and improves inverse control on real-world and simulated data.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Act4R, a 3D foundation model framework that predicts action-conditioned 3D scene flow from 2D observations, effectively bridging world models and robot control.
papers.title: Act4R: Action-conditioned 4D reconstruction for kinematics-free control
papers.tldr: Act4R predicts 3D robot motion from action signals and enables inverse control without explicit kinematics models or dedicated sensing.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled plausible interactive environments, yet long-horizon generation places a fundamental demand on visual memory: the previously observed world must remain consistent as the model continues to generate. Existing autoregressive approaches often implicitly rely on the generative model itself to retain such information, leading to spatial memory decay beyond the active context. We introduce World-T3, a camera-controlled video world model with a test-time training memory that consolidates past observations into dedicated model parameters. To robustly update this memory, we propose a recursive least-squares rule that incrementally absorbs novel visual features via online pose-keyed memory updates. Our TTT memory reads out previously observed scene features from the fast-weight state by camera pose, enabling consistent generation with constant storage and per-step computation regardless of rollout length. To facilitate real-time interactive generation with this robust memory, we further distill the autoregressive model into a few-step generator via dual-teacher distribution matching. On a long-horizon revisit benchmark, World-T3 raises revisit PSNR from 13.52 to 18.31 dB and reduces absolute rotation error from 3.344 to 1.075 relative to the strongest baseline on both metrics, while sustaining 20.6 FPS at 1280 x 704 on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU.
authors: Junyi Wu, Zekun Li, Chenhongyi Yang, Chen Guo, Lingchen Yang, Yongan Zhang, Xinyi Zhang, Hongbing Hu, Bartek Rymkowski, Srinath Sridhar, Yan Yan, Xijie Huang
bullets: Addresses spatial memory decay when autoregressive world models generate beyond their active context.
Uses recursive least squares to update fast-weight memory with newly observed visual features keyed by camera pose.
Reads stored scene features with constant storage and per-step computation regardless of rollout length.
Distills the autoregressive model into a few-step generator using dual-teacher distribution matching for interactive speed.
Improves revisit PSNR from 13.52 to 18.31 dB and absolute rotation error from 3.344 to 1.075, while reaching 20.6 FPS at 1280×704 on one NVIDIA B200 GPU.
papers.selection_reason: Camera-controlled video world model with test-time training as persistent memory, fitting video world models, interactive world models, and test-time learning.
papers.title: World-T3: Test-Time Training as Persistent Memory for Real-Time Video World Models
papers.tldr: World-T3 gives real-time video world models persistent, pose-keyed test-time memory to preserve scene consistency during long-horizon generation.

papers.abstract: To reconstruct a predictive 4D representation of the physical world from monocular video captured by a moving camera, we jointly reconstruct dynamic Gaussian radiance fields and infer their underlying physical dynamics. This paper proposes \emph{Physical SLAM}, a physics-aware method for constructing 4D Gaussian fields of deformable objects and predicting their future state when subjected to external actions, given a sequence of RGB-D images. Our method separates the scene into a static background Gaussian field for camera localization and a dynamic object Gaussian field driven by a spring--mass physical model of elastic deformation, inertia, and damping. To integrate visual observations with physical dynamics, we introduce virtual observation forces that gradually pull simulated surface nodes toward observed depth points, avoiding abrupt replacement of simulated node positions. Meanwhile, the physical parameters of the spring--mass model are updated from simulation errors aggregated over the full reconstruction observation window, enabling the reconstructed dynamics to align with observations. To couple appearance, geometry, and physics, we further design a physics-aware Gaussian transformation and surface alignment strategy, where dynamic Gaussians are transformed along the deforming physical surface of the spring--mass model and constrained to remain aligned with the surface during rendering-based optimization. The resulting representation supports observed-frame rendering and action-conditioned simulation, extending SLAM maps to describe how deformable objects respond to manipulation. On the PhysTwin benchmark, our method improves reconstruction and prediction PSNR over PhysTwin by 10.4\% and 11.0\%, respectively. On the TUM RGB-D benchmark, it reduces average camera tracking error by 20.6\%, improves SSIM by 3.6\%, and reduces LPIPS by 8.3\% compared with 4DGS-SLAM.
authors: Guangming Wang, Zhishuo Liu, Haibing Wu, Wanli Ma, Yixiong Jing, Olaf Wysocki, Brian Sheil
bullets: Addresses predictive 4D mapping of dynamic, deformable scenes from moving-camera RGB-D video.
Separates static background and dynamic object Gaussian fields, using the former for localization and a spring–mass model for deformation, inertia, and damping.
Uses virtual observation forces to smoothly align simulated surface nodes with depth observations and updates physical parameters over the observation window.
Transforms dynamic Gaussians along the simulated deforming surface while enforcing surface alignment during rendering optimization.
Improves reconstruction and prediction PSNR on PhysTwin, and tracking, SSIM, and LPIPS on TUM RGB-D, relative to the cited baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Builds physics-aware 4D Gaussian scene representations that support action-conditioned future simulation, fitting interactive world-model interests.
papers.title: Physical SLAM: Physics-aware Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping
papers.tldr: Physical SLAM reconstructs deformable objects’ 4D Gaussian representations while learning their physics, enabling camera tracking, rendering, and action-conditioned future-state prediction.

papers.abstract: Multi-player interactive world models aim to simulate shared environments from multiple players' perspectives, but achieving robust generation while scaling to more players remains challenging. Existing approaches that rely on fully-connected communication (e.g., Solaris) incur quadratic attention costs as the number of players grows, while centralized approaches (e.g., $\gamma$-World) suffer from interference between unrelated events in a shared global representation. To address these challenges, we present Multics, a multi-player video generation framework with hierarchical communication that structures information exchange across player, group, and global levels. This hierarchy introduces group tokens into self-attention as intermediate group-level representations that aggregate locally relevant player information. These tokens connect to global tokens for cross-group communication, while the hierarchical topology limits direct mixing between unrelated local events. Group-token parameters are shared across group slots, allowing the same communication module to accommodate varying numbers of players without introducing new group-specific parameters. We further propose budget-constrained dynamic grouping based on recent camera trajectories, which adaptively groups relevant players while limiting unnecessary communication. Experiments demonstrate that Multics achieves state-of-the-art performance in 4- and 6-player settings, with improved cross-player consistency, player-specific action and camera controllability, and interference robustness. Moreover, Multics generalizes from 4-player training to 6-, 8-, and 10-player inference without retraining, while reducing self-attention computation compared with fully-connected communication.
authors: Kaiyi Huang, Wangbo Yu, Yukun Huang, Jiwen Yu, Kunhao Liu, Donglin Yang, Wenbo Hu, Ying Shan, Xihui Liu
bullets: Addresses quadratic communication costs and interference from unrelated events as player count grows.
Uses player-, group-, and global-level communication, with shared group tokens linking local information to global context.
Dynamically groups relevant players from recent camera trajectories under a communication budget.
Achieves state-of-the-art results in 4- and 6-player settings with stronger consistency, controllability, and interference robustness.
Generalizes from 4-player training to 6-, 8-, and 10-player inference without retraining while reducing self-attention computation.
papers.selection_reason: Presents Multics, a multi-player world model with hierarchical communication, addressing scalability and interference in interactive world simulations.
papers.title: Multics: Generative Multi-Player World Model with Hierarchical Communication
papers.tldr: Multics generates scalable multi-player worlds by using hierarchical, dynamically formed communication groups instead of fully connecting all players.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising alternative for embodied intelligence by jointly predicting future world states and robot actions. However, their heavy visual encoding and iterative generative inference incur substantial latency, limiting their applicability to high-frequency closed-loop control. Existing training-free acceleration methods typically optimize a single stage, yielding limited speedups or degraded control under aggressive reuse. In this work, we systematically profile the inference overhead of WAMs and observe abundant redundancy across Transformer computation, diffusion denoising, and consecutive policy queries. However, the safe removal of such redundancy depends strongly on its impact on action prediction and control sensitivity. Based on these observations, we introduce \textbf{MARS}, a training-free and plug-and-play framework for multi-level WAM acceleration. MARS selectively removes low-impact attention computation, adaptively accelerates diffusion inference according to motion granularity, and speculatively reuses predicted future visual representations across consecutive queries with online verification. Together, these complementary mechanisms provide remarkable acceleration while limiting approximation error. Extensive experiments across LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, and RoboCasa show that MARS achieves up to $4.00\times$, $3.94\times$, and $2.10\times$ end-to-end speedups, respectively, while maintaining task success rate close to the original policy. Moreover, MARS generalizes across different model backbones and across simulation and real-robot experiments, substantially improving the efficiency--performance trade-off of WAM inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MARS.
authors: Zengyuan Zuo, Yongchang Zhang, Guangyu Zhao, Tianze Zhang, Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: WAMs are slowed by heavy visual encoding, iterative diffusion inference, and repeated policy queries, limiting high-frequency control.
MARS is training-free and plug-and-play, targeting redundancy in Transformer attention, diffusion denoising, and consecutive queries.
It removes low-impact attention computation, adapts diffusion effort to motion granularity, and reuses future visual features with online verification.
Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, and RoboCasa report up to 4.00×, 3.94×, and 2.10× speedups, respectively.
The approach transfers across model backbones and simulation-to-real-robot settings, though its scope is demonstrated on the evaluated WAM tasks and systems.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes MARS, a training-free framework for accelerating World Action Models (WAMs) through multi-level optimization, directly contributing to efficient interactive world models.
papers.title: MARS: Systematic Multi-Level Acceleration for World Action Models
papers.tldr: MARS accelerates World Action Model inference at multiple levels, achieving up to 4× end-to-end speedup while keeping task success close to the original policy.

papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) now reason about space well enough to program robots, yet the world models behind robot policies are implicit, held in network weights or predicted video, and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. We present D-World, an explicit world-language-action model built on the Sense, Plan and Act decomposition. A perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code. A planning agent searches for actions in simulation and, after each executed action chunk, revises the twin's object states and named physical parameters against what the robot measured. A parameter revision is accepted only if replaying the latest chunk does not increase any measured residual beyond its tolerance, and every chunk is checked in the updated twin before it runs. Structural mismatches return to perception for reconstruction. We call this measurement-grounded cycle of correction and revision recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which the LLM stays frozen while the world it acts in improves. We model the choice of actions that both advance the task and expose model error as a dual control problem and show that the cost of incorporating evidence into the twin sets the threshold at which probing pays, so cheap local revision counteracts the turn-off of cautious controllers. Each episode runs a real-to-sim-to-real loop, and its recorded twins can be refitted and re-rendered offline into higher-fidelity environments for post-training. Because perception and planning communicate only through the twin and language, either can be replaced by a learned model, and since inference dominates the loop, the loop speeds up with faster models. On a dual-arm robot, towel and toaster tasks show local revisions, such as one reducing the bread's rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm, that let execution continue without reconstruction.
bullets: Addresses the opacity and lack of direct correction in implicit robot world models.
Uses a Sense–Plan–Act architecture where perception builds an executable scene twin and planning searches for actions in simulation.
Revises object states and physical parameters after each action chunk, accepting updates only when replayed measurements remain within residual tolerances.
Frames information-seeking actions as dual control, balancing task progress with exposing and correcting model errors.
Demonstrates real-to-sim-to-real operation on dual-arm towel and toaster tasks, including local corrections that avoid full scene reconstruction.
papers.selection_reason: Explicit world-language-action model with digital-twin self-improvement for robot manipulation and planning.
papers.title: D-World: An Explicit World-Language-Action Model with Recursive Self-Improvement under Dual Control
papers.tldr: D-World enables robots to improve an explicit, inspectable digital twin through measurement-grounded planning and execution, without updating the underlying LLM.

papers.abstract: Clinical decisions depend on anticipating how a patient's condition will evolve as treatment is adjusted and new evidence becomes available. Existing medical world models capture patient-state evolution, but often define the evolving state around a particular modality or task, limiting reuse as inputs or prediction targets change. These models also retain history through observation sequences or recurrent or latent summaries rather than exposing preceding patient states and clinical actions as an ordered transition context. This distinction matters because similar current measurements may follow different recent changes, treatment exposures, and observed responses. To tackle these limitations, we propose PatientWM, a clinical world-model framework built around a unified patient state and sequential latent history. Availability-aware encoders integrate observations available at each decision time into the patient state, while typed decoders produce task-specific clinical readouts without defining the state around any single target. PatientWM further conditions each next-state prediction on the current state and supplied action together with a bounded, ordered history of preceding latent patient states and clinical actions, preserving recent treatment and response context. Experiments across MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and three external clinical datasets show superior performance in clinical prediction, multi-step forecasting, and action-planning evaluation. Transfer experiments further demonstrate the generalizability of PatientWM's patient state. Together, these results establish its ability to forecast clinical evolution and support planning.
authors: Ziwen Kan, Jie Peng, Bo Yan, Davis Hobley, Zheng Zhang, Yu Tian, Tianlong Chen, Song Wang
bullets: Addresses the limited reuse of modality- or task-specific clinical world models.
Builds unified patient states from observations available at each decision time.
Uses typed decoders for task-specific clinical readouts without defining the state around one target.
Predicts next states from the current state, clinical action, and bounded history of prior states and actions.
Shows strong performance across clinical prediction, multi-step forecasting, action planning, and transfer evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Clinical world model that predicts patient-state evolution conditioned on current state and clinical actions, fitting interactive world models.
papers.title: PatientWM: Towards Generalizable Clinical World Models via Unified Patient States
papers.tldr: PatientWM models clinical evolution with a reusable patient state and ordered latent history to improve prediction, forecasting, and treatment planning across datasets.

papers.abstract: Relational learning typically predicts from a database state, but decision making asks a different question: how will that state change under an action? In operational systems, the answer depends on system-specific dynamics that may not be visible in the database itself. We view each such system as a relational "world" and ask whether a model can infer how it behaves from observed executions. We introduce TabWM (Tabular World Model) and WorldRel, a generator of executable relational worlds for pretraining. Given executions from an unseen world, TabWM uses them as context to predict the sparse structured edits caused by a new action without parameter updates. Across 512 held-out worlds, complete-edit F1 rises from 0.016 with no observed executions to 0.685 with 64, where a correct edit must match its operation, relational location, and value. Because these predictions are explicit relational edits, they can be applied recursively to imagine candidate futures and compare actions before they are taken. Broader search over these predicted futures improves the realized return of selected action sequences. Together, these results suggest that relational dynamics can be learned in context, broadening relational learning from modeling system state to modeling how that state changes under action.
bullets: Motivation: Relational models usually predict states, but decision making requires predicting state changes under actions whose dynamics may be system-specific.
Method: TabWM uses executions from an unseen world as context, without parameter updates, to predict sparse structured edits for new actions.
WorldRel is introduced as a generator of executable relational worlds for pretraining.
Across 512 held-out worlds, complete-edit F1 increases from 0.016 with no executions to 0.685 with 64 observed executions.
Predicted edits can be recursively composed to imagine futures; broader search over them improves the realized return of selected action sequences.
papers.selection_reason: Learns relational world dynamics from executions and predicts action-induced edits; fits interactive world models.
papers.title: Relational Learning as World Modeling
papers.tldr: TabWM learns unseen relational-world dynamics from observed executions and predicts how actions will change database state, enabling better action planning.

papers.abstract: Cross-task generalization remains difficult for world action models (WAMs), even when their predicted futures depict plausible manipulation. This gap can be attributed directly: we make this gap directly testable by decoupling a WAM into a world model and an inverse-dynamics model (IDM), then holding the IDM fixed while replacing the source of future images. We introduce Align Once, Evaluate Everywhere (AoE), a camera-space inverse-dynamics model pretrained on large-scale robot data, which provides this recovery interface for different future sources across tasks and environments. Through it, we find that actions recovered from recorded futures of unseen tasks execute almost as well as replayed demonstrations, whereas futures predicted by world models collapse across benchmarks. The failures are not generic: they concentrate on the gripper and interaction geometry while generation capacity is spent on task-irrelevant background. This diagnosis suggests that supervision should target exactly these regions. We therefore introduce the vision-to-action (VITA) loss, which passes generated futures through the frozen AoE and penalizes discrepancies in the recovered actions, redirecting generation toward action-relevant detail. Across two world models and three manipulation benchmarks, this simple change raises the execution success of generated futures from near zero to 47.0%. The same loss also transfers to WAMs and yields consistent gains in native control.
authors: Chen Zhao, Zipeng Ye, Yihan Lin, Yuchen Xie, Jing Zhang
bullets: AoE decouples world models from inverse-dynamics models by holding the IDM fixed while swapping future-image sources.
Actions recovered from recorded futures of unseen tasks nearly match replayed demonstrations, but actions from predicted futures fail across benchmarks.
World-model errors concentrate on gripper and interaction geometry, while generation focuses on task-irrelevant backgrounds.
The VITA loss uses frozen AoE-recovered actions to emphasize action-relevant visual details.
Across two world models and three manipulation benchmarks, VITA raises generated-future execution success from near zero to 47.0% and improves native control.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and improves cross-task generalization in world action models using a VITA loss, central to world model research.
papers.title: What Limits Cross-Task Generalization in World Action Models?
papers.tldr: Cross-task failure in world action models stems mainly from poor prediction of gripper interaction geometry, and action-based supervision substantially improves control from generated futures.

papers.abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments, it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.
authors: Ke Gui, Chenghao Shi, Ziyue Wang, Longwen Chen, Xieyuanli Chen, Huimin Lu
bullets: Addresses image-goal navigation when targets are outside the current view and persistent spatial memory is required.
