Uses learned scene-coordinate localization to anchor current, goal, and history frames in a shared reference frame.
Jointly predicts future states and actions in latent space, avoiding pixel reconstruction and CEM-style planning.
Reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2% across four trajectory prediction benchmarks.
Improves closed-loop success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and SPL from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-grounded world action model for image-goal navigation with latent state-action prediction and persistent spatial memory.
papers.title: G$^2$WAM: World Action Models for Efficient and Geometry Grounded Image-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: G$^2$WAM enables efficient image-goal navigation by combining geometry-grounded spatial memory with latent world-action modeling, improving trajectory prediction and navigation success without explicit 3D reconstruction or costly planning.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are often pretrained via imitation learning, making reinforcement learning (RL) post-training important when deployment moves beyond demonstration coverage. Existing refinement paradigms expose a reliability--efficiency tension: model-free refinement avoids simulator bias but is interaction-intensive, whereas model-based refinement can exploit unreliable imagination even as its simulator adapts. We propose Model-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (MERL), a trust-calibrated framework that couples policy optimization with an online-updated simulator comprising a world model and a reward proxy head. Across stages, simulator reliability controls the imagined-data ratio and rollout horizon; within rollouts, chunk-level trust controls replay selection and optimization weight. For recursive imagination without exact grounded continuations, a residual predictor estimates trust without querying future ground truth. On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, MERL reaches 79.7% average success, improves high-threshold learning speed by 10.9% over the matched model-free control, and outperforms same-protocol external baselines across three training seeds. Fixed-data adaptation from 50 demonstrations per task achieves 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.
authors: Wenzhan Li, Yiran Qin, Heng Zhou, Huirui Wang, Yulan Guo, Ruimao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–reliability trade-off between interaction-heavy model-free refinement and potentially biased model-based refinement.
Couples policy optimization with an online-updated world model and reward proxy, using simulator reliability to adjust imagined-data ratios and rollout horizons.
Uses chunk-level trust for replay selection and optimization weighting, with a residual predictor for recursive imagination without future ground-truth queries.
On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, achieves 79.7% average success and 10.9% faster high-threshold learning than matched model-free control.
With 50 demonstrations per task, reaches 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.
papers.selection_reason: VLA RL post-training with a trust-calibrated evolving world-model simulator directly fits embodied robot learning and interactive world models.
papers.title: Trust-Calibrated VLA Policy Post-Training with Evolving Imagination
papers.tldr: MERL improves VLA reinforcement-learning post-training by dynamically trusting and weighting imagined experience as its learned simulator evolves.

papers.abstract: The growing use of language models for forecasting motivates a broader evaluation of their world-model capabilities. Such evaluation must go beyond predictive accuracy to assess hidden-state inference and intervention prediction. Real-world forecasting benchmarks offer limited access to hidden-state ground truth and controlled experiments. We introduce CivWorldBench, a benchmark built on a multi-agent strategy game engine with recorded internal states, controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts. Its 1,900 decision points from 475 worlds support three task levels: association forecasting, belief inference, and intervention prediction. Reference predictors support attributable evaluation of capability gaps, with an expert harness and empirical ceiling estimates contextualizing scores. Stored trajectories make intermediate predictions verifiable, while agent-play experiments test whether world-model capabilities support decision-making. The main panel comprises eleven frontier language models. Composite benchmark scores correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels, more closely than with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a proxy for real-world forecasting capability. Strong association forecasts do not consistently extend to belief inference or intervention prediction, and effect magnitudes remain poorly calibrated despite informative direction predictions. Process verification reveals errors missed by final-answer evaluation, and structured reasoning improves intervention prediction for the strongest model in the process study. Agent-play experiments identify useful assisted plans and motivate evaluating decision-relevant capabilities beyond association forecasting. These findings identify hidden-state inference, intermediate-state prediction, and effect calibration as priorities for world-model training.
authors: Ang Li, Haofei Yu, Zhengwei Tao, Liang Chen, Kuan Li, Miaomiao Li, Chenran Cai, Bin Liang, Jiaxuan You, Kam-Fai Wong
bullets: Benchmark uses a strategy-game engine with recorded states, controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts across 1,900 decision points from 475 worlds.
It evaluates association forecasting, belief inference, and intervention prediction, with reference predictors, expert harnesses, and estimated performance ceilings.
Scores correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards, while strong association forecasting does not reliably transfer to hidden-state or intervention tasks.
Models often predict intervention directions correctly but poorly calibrate effect magnitudes; process verification uncovers errors missed by final answers.
Agent-play studies find useful assisted plans and highlight the need to evaluate decision-relevant world-model capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces CivWorldBench, a benchmark for evaluating language world models in multi-agent sandbox worlds, focusing on belief inference and intervention prediction. Relevant to world model evaluation and dynamics.
papers.title: CivWorldBench: Evaluating Language World Models in Structured Multi-Agent Sandbox Worlds
papers.tldr: CivWorldBench evaluates language-model world models beyond forecasting accuracy by testing hidden-state inference and intervention prediction in controlled multi-agent worlds.

papers.abstract: Recent world action models draw on video generation priors to jointly predict future observations and robot actions. Adapting these priors to control requires determining how future predictions should guide policy learning. RAP-WAM combines predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations (RAP) with future-supervised queries and Coupled Action Projection for policy learning. Predictive rehearsal trains on model-generated inputs while retaining recorded targets, and accumulates recurring errors into a spatial prior. We perturb actions and measure changes in video predictions. Action-response-based spatiotemporal credit assignment combines these responses, prediction error, and the rehearsal prior to allocate visual supervision; spatially aggregating the responses determines supervision intensity across future action steps. No separate scoring network or deployment-time probe is required. The base learns from a video-pretrained backbone without intermediate pretraining on external embodied data. We evaluate the fixed base and its agent-refined, task-conditioned system. On 42 RoboDojo tasks, their average success rates are 12.85% and 15.62%, with Scores of 17.86 and 20.59. Across 15 real-robot tasks, the complete system achieves 89.00% task-macro-average success, exceeding the strongest of five baselines by 37.67 percentage points. Across 315 fixed-output simulation windows, 45.21% of response-top20 positions fall outside error-top20, revealing information beyond prediction error.
authors: Yuanpeng He, Ceyao Zhang, Fangjing Li, Kefei Zhu, Lijian Li, Yueheng Li, Tianjia He, Wenpin Jiao, Zhi Jin, Yaodong Yang, Yuanpei Chen
bullets: Addresses how future video predictions should guide policy learning in world-action models.
Uses predictive rehearsal, action-response perturbations, future-supervised queries, and Coupled Action Projection.
Allocates visual supervision using prediction error, action responses, and a spatial rehearsal prior without a separate scoring network or deployment-time probe.
On 42 RoboDojo tasks, average success was 12.85% for the fixed base and 15.62% after agent refinement.
On 15 real-robot tasks, the complete system achieved 89.00% task-macro-average success, 37.67 percentage points above the strongest of five baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Learns world-action models from video prediction and uses action perturbations to guide robot policies, directly relevant to world models and embodied learning.
papers.title: RAP-WAM: Learning World-Action Models through Predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations
papers.tldr: RAP-WAM learns robot control from video-pretrained world-action models by combining predictive rehearsal with action perturbations for targeted future supervision.

papers.abstract: Video-based interactive world models aim to enable real-time, user-controllable environments. Yet most existing systems are trained and rolled out at a fixed temporal rate, limiting both runtime-rate adaptation and physical-horizon coverage -- a limitation we term temporal-rate coupling. Specifically, when runtime generation throughput differs from the learned temporal rate, the generated world evolves unintentionally more slowly or quickly. Moreover, using a single temporal rate imposes an inherent trade-off between temporal granularity and physical horizon: higher rates capture finer motion but cover a shorter duration under a fixed context window. To address both limitations, we introduce Rate-Adaptive Rollout (RAR), a framework that enables interactive world models to roll out at controllable temporal rates. At its core, Stride-RoPE aligns latent frames sampled at different rates on a shared physical-time coordinate, enabling consistent multi-rate rollout, unseen-rate generalization, and online rate switching without discarding history. Meanwhile, RAR uses multi-stride video sampling to enable joint learning of fine-grained dynamics and long-horizon evolution. Across action- and camera-controlled environments, RAR achieves temporally consistent multi-rate rollout and online rate switching while preserving high-rate generation quality and extending physical horizons under matched training budgets. RAR also transfers to pretrained world models while preserving perceptual quality.
authors: Yaoyang Liu, Dongyu Yan, Yihua Du, Shengju Qian, Zeke Xie, Xin Wang, Ying-Cong Chen, Long Chen
bullets: Addresses temporal-rate coupling: fixed training and rollout rates can cause unintended slowdowns or speedups and limit horizon coverage.
Uses Stride-RoPE to align latent frames across sampling rates on a shared physical-time coordinate.
Supports unseen-rate generalization and online rate switching without discarding prior history.
Multi-stride video sampling jointly learns fine-grained dynamics and long-horizon evolution.
Demonstrates consistent multi-rate rollout, preserved high-rate quality, longer horizons, and transfer to pretrained models across action- and camera-controlled environments.
papers.selection_reason: Rate-adaptive rollout for interactive world models; directly targets controllable multi-rate world simulation.
papers.title: RAR: Rate-Adaptive Rollout for Time-Consistent Interactive World Models
papers.tldr: RAR enables interactive world models to generate temporally consistent video at controllable rates while supporting both fine motion and longer physical horizons.

papers.abstract: We propose the task of Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting: predicting the spatiotemporal evolution of a future dense 3D liquid velocity field conditioned on how a solid object moves through it. This task provides an upstream physical forecasting primitive for systems that need to reason about motion-conditioned liquid response, including robotic liquid manipulation, digital twins, and rigid-fluid video generation. Existing works have made efforts in predicting flow around static or prescribed solid geometries and synthesizing visually plausible fluid motion. Yet these approaches provide limited coverage for interactive liquid dynamics, as they are not capable of forecasting how a moving solid induces a future full-domain liquid response. In this forecasting scenario, the hydrodynamic effect is condensed near an evolving liquid-solid interface, but the prediction target is a global spatiotemporal rollout. To address this challenge, we propose a two-level recurrent forecasting framework, TIDE/TIDES: TIDE isolates localized interface-driven forecasting, while TIDES adds transport-aware coupling and explicit stabilization to reduce accumulated rollout error. Across adapted neighboring baselines, controlled component ablations, motion/size OOD tests, and long-horizon evaluation, TIDES achieves the best forecasting performance and the ablations identify localized interaction, transport coupling, and stabilization as the key contributors. Together, our task formulation, benchmark, and TIDE/TIDES study establish a controlled foundation for moving-solid-conditioned dense liquid forecasting. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jongwonryu/TIDE-TIDES.
authors: Jongwon Ryu, Sunjae Yoon, Junyeong Kim
bullets: Targets global, spatiotemporal liquid-flow rollouts conditioned on solid-object motion, addressing a gap in interactive fluid forecasting.
TIDE models localized, interface-driven effects, while TIDES adds transport-aware coupling and explicit stabilization for rollout robustness.
Experiments include baseline comparisons, component ablations, motion/size out-of-distribution tests, and long-horizon evaluation.
TIDES achieves the best reported forecasting performance, with localized interaction, transport coupling, and stabilization identified as key contributors.
The task, benchmark, and code provide a foundation for robotics, digital twins, and rigid-fluid video generation.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned spatiotemporal liquid forecasting is an interactive world model.
papers.title: Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting under Moving-Solid Interaction
papers.tldr: Introduces a benchmark and recurrent framework for forecasting dense 4D liquid velocity fields under moving-solid interactions.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models must capture how multiple participants jointly change a shared environment while observing different parts of it. Competitive games make this challenge concrete: players cooperate and compete, while fog of war, team vision and camera placement determine what each can see. Modeling these interactions requires data that connect individual observations and actions to shared state and events. We introduce the Esports World Model Dataset (EWM), a collection of human gameplay spanning StarCraft II, Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2, with 3,053 games and maps and approximately 4,880 player-view hours, including estimated hours for the ongoing CS2 extension. It includes 4,628 completed StarCraft II views, all ten perspectives for 303 Dota 2 matches, and up to ten views per round in CS2. Across these views, replay-clock alignment connects rendered video with game-native actions, structured state and events from the same match. The three games expose complementary observation conditions: private fog of war, shared team vision and first-person viewpoints. In StarCraft II, player-specific entity records further distinguish live observations from remembered snapshots and link co-observed entities across opposing views. Together with temporal alignment, these records allow researchers to distinguish legitimate information differences from disagreement about shared state. By connecting human decisions, shared dynamics and player-specific information, EWM supports research toward jointly controlled multiplayer world models and interactive environments populated by teammates and opponents learned from human play.
authors: Weiyu Ma, Zeyuan Gong, Xuhui Liu, Wenxuan Zhang, Jian Ding, Xinyu Cui, Jian Zhao, Mohamed Elhoseiny
bullets: Covers human gameplay from StarCraft II, Dota 2, and Counter-Strike 2 across 3,053 games and maps and approximately 4,880 player-view hours.
Aligns rendered video with game-native actions, structured state, and events using replay clocks.
Captures complementary information settings: private fog of war, shared team vision, and first-person views.
Includes StarCraft II records that distinguish live observations from remembered snapshots and link entities across opposing views.
Supports studying how teammates and opponents jointly affect shared environments despite differing observations.
papers.selection_reason: Dataset specifically designed for interactive world models with multi-agent observations, actions, and shared state.
papers.title: Esports World Model Dataset
papers.tldr: EWM is a multimodal esports dataset linking multiple players’ views, actions, and shared game state to support multiplayer world-model research.

papers.abstract: Behavioral foundation models (BFMs) provide humanoids with reusable repertoires of whole-body behaviors; in real-world humanoid control, the same behavioral intent may require fundamentally different motions under different terrain constraints. Covering such variation with terrain-matched demonstrations requires enumerating a combinatorial space of behaviors and terrain geometries. We introduce P-BFM, a perceptive behavioral foundation model that factorizes humanoid control into terrain-invariant intent and terrain-conditioned realization. A forward-backward representation maps motion references, target states, and reward functions into a shared intent space without terrain information, while a perceptive policy learns how to realize each intent under the surrounding terrain geometry. We further identify a complementary limitation of purely latent control: behavioral latents can preserve local motion patterns while losing precise global progress. We therefore introduce Explicit Root Instructions (ERI), which separates global transport (e.g., heading and planar velocity) from behavioral intent, while leaving local whole-body adaptation to the perceptive policy. This decomposition leads to a characteristic capability absent from conventional BFMs: one fixed intent induces different, terrain-appropriate behaviors, including changes in step height, stride, posture, foothold placement, and contacts, without terrain-specific demonstrations. Across challenging terrains, P-BFM improves motion fidelity, root-control precision, and perturbation recovery over strong baselines. A single frozen policy further supports motion tracking, goal reaching, reward inference, teleoperation, and terrain-aware recovery, and transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 using onboard depth sensing.
authors: Xue Wang, Yitang Li, Yiming Zhang, Siqin Wang, Junhan Sun, Zhihao Liu, Yaojie Shen, Jingbo Yuan, Hao Zhao, Qingdu Li
bullets: Factorizes control into terrain-invariant behavioral intent and terrain-conditioned motion realization.
Uses a forward-backward representation to map motion references, target states, and rewards into a shared intent space.
Adds Explicit Root Instructions to preserve precise global transport while the policy handles local whole-body adaptation.
Adapts step height, stride, posture, footholds, and contacts across challenging terrains, improving fidelity, root control, and perturbation recovery.
A single frozen policy supports tracking, goal reaching, reward inference, teleoperation, and recovery, with zero-shot transfer to a Unitree G1 using depth sensing.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces P-BFM, a perceptive behavioral foundation model for humanoid control that factors intent and terrain-conditioned realization, enabling zero-shot transfer to new terrains.
papers.title: P-BFM: Perceptive Behavioral Foundation Models for Humanoid Control via Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: P-BFM enables humanoids to execute the same behavioral intent with terrain-appropriate whole-body motions, without terrain-specific demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Surgical world models must turn prospective robot actions into visually faithful, structurally consistent instrument motion. We introduce SurgCast, which predicts future instrument skeletons from current structure, robot state, and future actions, then uses the forecast to control video generation. Dual-path injection combines skeleton geometry with derived, instrument-specific motion descriptors through geometric residuals and conditioning modulation. Both paths complement native action conditioning and are retained in a four-step causal student. On SutureBot and SRTH-Porcine-Cholei, the teacher and student improve all seven reported quality and instrument-consistency metrics over their respective direct-action baselines; teacher FVD decreases by 37.6% and 67.3%. Ablations show that future actions improve skeleton prediction and that combining both injection paths performs best across all six metrics under predicted skeletons. These results support using predicted articulated structure and its motion semantics as a control interface for surgical video prediction. Project videos and examples are available at https://surgcast.netlify.app/.
authors: Wanhao Liu, Rulin Zhou, Liangjing Shao, Zhaocheng Lin, Dongyue Li, Jinsong Lin, Guoheng Ma, Hangheng Yang, Zhiqing Tang, Jing Chen, Panshuo Li, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Predicts future instrument skeletons from current structure, robot state, and planned actions.
Injects skeleton geometry and instrument-specific motion descriptors through complementary conditioning paths.
Uses a four-step causal student to retain both injection paths alongside native action conditioning.
Improves all reported quality and instrument-consistency metrics over direct-action baselines on SutureBot and SRTH-Porcine-Cholei.
Teacher FVD decreases by 37.6% and 67.3% on the two evaluated datasets; ablations favor combining both paths.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned future skeleton prediction and controllable surgical video generation directly fit interactive world models.
papers.title: SurgCast: Action-Conditioned Future Skeletons for Controllable Surgical World Models
papers.tldr: SurgCast forecasts action-conditioned instrument skeletons to make surgical video generation more controllable and structurally consistent.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs), often built upon pretrained video-generation world models, have emerged as a promising framework for general-purpose and open-ended robot control. However, their real-world deployment often suffers from discontinuous and jerky execution. Existing methods typically address this issue by either improving inference efficiency or enhancing action continuity across prediction chunks, without jointly addressing both challenges. To bridge this gap, we propose StreamingWAM, a streaming-diffusion framework for WAM-based robot control. StreamingWAM combines a noise ladder for chunk-wise action prediction, a prefix rollout module for cross-chunk continuity, and dense video-history memory for temporally consistent conditioning. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that StreamingWAM improves action continuity across static and dynamic settings, achieving competitive performance while reducing steady-state replanning latency to 72.9 ms in simulation and 57.3 ms on the real robot. The method also produces smoother action transitions, while the streaming staircase reduces sensitivity to the execution horizon K.
authors: Shaojie Ren, Jingwen Sun, Zezhi Liu, Hongjin Chen, Xin Jin, Wei Zou, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Addresses jerky, discontinuous execution in World Action Model-based robot control.
Uses chunk-wise staircase flow matching with a noise ladder for streaming action prediction.
Combines prefix rollouts and dense video-history memory for cross-chunk temporal consistency.
Evaluated in simulation and real-world tasks, with steady-state replanning latency of 72.9 ms and 57.3 ms, respectively.
Produces smoother transitions and reduces sensitivity to the execution horizon K.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming world action model for robot control.
papers.title: StreamingWAM: Streaming World Action Modeling via Chunk-Wise Staircase Flow Matching
papers.tldr: StreamingWAM enables smoother, lower-latency robot control by jointly improving streaming inference and continuity between action chunks.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in large language models have made software engineering agents capable of tackling complex coding tasks. Within a containerized environment, a coding agent receives tool responses or execution results, and determines its later actions by those earlier results. However, most existing coding agents never look ahead: their policies do not anticipate the consequences of actions, and the terminal reward barely attributes a failure to certain earlier steps, so an ill-judged edit can corrupt the repository state irreversibly before any signal arrives. Recent code world models aim to address these challenges, but they are either trained and then frozen before reinforcement learning (RL), or reduced to an auxiliary next-token loss on the environment's outputs. We present ANTE (Anticipate, Then Execute), an agentic RL framework that verifies the policy's pre-action predictions by real execution and turns them into per-step credit for its actions and trust-or-abstain decisions. With an internal belief stated before each action, Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) turns the settled predictions into per-step advantages by anchoring credit on the policy's own forecasts. To turn the trained forecasts into better actions at inference, thereby facilitating effective test-time scaling, ANTE-TTO (test-time optimization) selects among candidate actions without an external scorer. ANTE raises Qwen3-32B from 25.0% to 57.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, 6.2% above a matched GRPO baseline trained without the belief state; its world model's accuracy climbs from 44% to 69% during RL, and the learned foresight capability transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains. In summary, we aim to build a code world model that knows what has happened, what holds now, and what the next action will achieve.
authors: Yi Ge, Kangrui Ruan, Jifan Chen, Manish Prajapat, Christian Bock, Xiaoyang Wang, Rein Houthooft, Aritra Sengupta, Varun Kumar
bullets: Coding agents often act reactively, making early mistakes that can irreversibly damage repository state before terminal feedback arrives.
ANTE has agents state an internal belief before each action, then verifies it through execution to provide per-step credit and support trust-or-abstain decisions.
Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) converts verified forecasts into action advantages during reinforcement learning.
ANTE-TTO uses the learned forecasts to select among candidate actions at inference without an external scorer.
On SWE-bench Verified, ANTE improves Qwen3-32B pass@1 from 25.0% to 57.2%; its world-model accuracy rises from 44% to 69% and transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains.
papers.selection_reason: Learns verified internal world models for coding agents and uses them for per-step credit and test-time optimization.
papers.title: ANTE: Anticipate, Then Execute -- Learning Internal World Models for Coding Agents from Verified Beliefs
papers.tldr: ANTE trains coding agents to predict the consequences of actions before execution, using verified beliefs for finer-grained learning and improved decision-making.

papers.abstract: Evaluating robot manipulation policies through repeated physical trials is costly. We study whether an action-conditioned world model can serve as a closed-loop test environment whose policy success rates track those on real robots. Beyond realistic video, the model must return the camera views and proprioceptive state needed for the policy's next action and preserve failed-action outcomes to avoid overestimating policy capability. We introduce ProWorld, a world model that jointly predicts multi-view video and robot state, then feeds both back to a frozen policy for repeated interaction. ProWorld comprises a shared transformer for joint video-state flow prediction and Shared-Time View Encoding to distinguish cameras while preserving temporal synchronization. To reduce interaction hallucinations that turn missed grasps into successful lifts, we augment training with failed interactions collected in high-fidelity simulation, reducing inflated success rates in the generated environment. ProWorld achieves the highest overall TriWorldBench score among the compared methods. Across three policies and four local manipulation tasks, it attains a Pearson correlation of 0.95 and a Spearman correlation of 0.94 between generated and real success rates. These results support joint visual-proprioceptive feedback and failure-aware training as a basis for world-model-based policy evaluation.
authors: Zijun Wang, Tianyi Yan, Haokun Lin, Panwen Hu, Bohang He, Siyu Ren, Xiaoyu Guo, Weijia Liufu, Shuoshuo Xue, Fengjiao Chen, Zipeng Ye, Xuezhi Cao, Zutao Jiang, Hanhui Li, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Targets the high cost of evaluating manipulation policies through repeated real-robot trials.
Jointly predicts synchronized multi-view video and robot proprioceptive state for feedback to a frozen policy.
Uses a shared transformer and Shared-Time View Encoding to model multiple cameras and temporal alignment.
Trains on failed interactions to reduce hallucinated recoveries that inflate simulated policy success.
Across three policies and four local manipulation tasks, generated and real success rates correlate strongly (Pearson 0.95; Spearman 0.94).
papers.selection_reason: Develops ProWorld, an action-conditioned world model that predicts multi-view video and proprioceptive state for closed-loop policy evaluation, incorporating failure-aware training to reduce hallucinations.
papers.title: ProWorld: Multi-View World Model with Proprioceptive Feedback for Closed-Loop Policy Evaluation
papers.tldr: ProWorld is a multi-view, proprioceptive world model that enables closed-loop robot policy evaluation while preserving realistic failure outcomes.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models directly in latent space, but unconstrained autoregressive predictors may contract the latent distribution over long rollouts. We introduce Symplectic Hamiltonian JEPA (LeHami), which replaces the standard predictor with an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over a structured latent state (q, p) integrated using an exactly symplectic leapfrog step. This construction preserves phase-space volume at every rollout step and rules out uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and merging of distinct latent states, independently of the learned parameters or action sequence. We obtain the momentum-like component from temporal derivatives of the learned position-like representation, providing an explicit second-order state for prediction and control. On conservative and actuated visual pendulum environments, LeHami substantially improves long-horizon velocity prediction over an unconstrained JEPA world model and empirically maintains constant latent volume where the baseline contracts. The learned flow also supports accurate integration at unseen sub-frame step sizes and numerical time reversal. These results show how geometric structure can provide inference-time guarantees that are complementary to representation regularization in latent world models.
authors: Romina Yalovetzky, Randall Balestriero, Yann LeCun
bullets: Addresses latent-space contraction in unconstrained autoregressive JEPAs during long rollouts.
Uses an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over position–momentum latents, integrated with an exactly symplectic leapfrog step.
Guarantees phase-space volume preservation and prevents uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and state merging.
Improves long-horizon velocity prediction over an unconstrained JEPA on conservative and actuated visual pendulums.
Supports unseen sub-frame integration and numerical time reversal, though the reported scope is limited to pendulum environments.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned latent world model with symplectic structure fits interactive world-model interests.
papers.title: LeHami: Symplectic Latent Dynamics for World Models
papers.tldr: LeHami improves long-horizon latent world-model rollouts by enforcing Hamiltonian, volume-preserving dynamics in a structured latent space.

papers.abstract: Tool-using agents alternate between model generation and tool execution, waiting for each tool call to complete before starting the next generation. This sequential execution is costly during agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which requires large batches of multi-turn rollouts. We introduce ObsSpec, an observation speculation pipeline for agentic RL that uses a small world model to predict tool outputs while the environment executes, allowing the policy to begin its next generation early. ObsSpec retains speculative work only when the predicted and actual observations match exactly, making rollout collection lossless, while co-training keeps the world model up to date as the policy learns. On terminal-use tasks, predictions from a 0.6B world model exactly match actual observations in 66.4% of attempts and arrive roughly 16 times faster. Using these predictions, ObsSpec reduces agent latency by 9.3% and 14.2% for 8B and 32B policies. Across controlled experiments, we characterize the regimes in which ObsSpec reduces agent latency under shared policy resources. Finally, because ObsSpec overlaps policy generation with tool execution, it is architecturally compatible with existing techniques for accelerating RL. Code is available at https://github.com/kylemontgomery1/verl-recipe/tree/obsspec/obsspec.
authors: Kyle Montgomery, Wang Zhang, Chenguang Wang
bullets: Targets the latency caused by sequential policy generation and tool execution in multi-turn agentic RL.
Uses a small co-trained world model to predict tool outputs, letting the policy start generating before execution finishes.
Keeps speculative generations only when predictions exactly match actual observations, avoiding rollout changes.
A 0.6B world model matches terminal-use observations in 66.4% of attempts and predicts them about 16× faster.
Reduces agent latency by 9.3% for 8B policies and 14.2% for 32B policies in reported experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Uses a co-trained world model to speculate tool observations and accelerate agentic RL rollouts.
papers.title: ObsSpec: Accelerating Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Observation Speculation
papers.tldr: ObsSpec speeds up agentic RL rollouts by speculating tool observations in parallel with tool execution while preserving lossless training.

papers.abstract: By predicting future states, latent world models provide rich self-supervision for end-to-end driving, but often inherit dense features from pretrained visual encoders as their world-state interface. This creates a mismatch: visual pretraining produces information-rich, spatially dense features, but their adaptation for motion-conditioned world modeling and planning is deferred to downstream training. The dense grid also makes future prediction more computationally expensive as visual resolution increases. We therefore argue that video pretraining should directly learn state representations suited to downstream world modeling and planning, rather than relying on downstream training to adapt inherited visual features. We propose ***MORE***, a V-JEPA framework that learns **M**otion-**O**riented **RE**gisters during video pretraining as a shared state interface for driving world models and planning. MORE injects temporally aligned ego motion into a small set of registers and uses them as the sole context for masked patch prediction, channeling dense patch-level supervision through a compact state bottleneck. A complementary blockwise register-masking objective further shapes predictive structure in the register space. During downstream training, the same register space defines the future states predicted by the world model and provides shared scene memory for trajectory generation and scoring. On NAVSIM-v2, MORE outperforms the state of the art by 1.6 in EPDMS, while achieving superior efficiency with only 1/10 the inference latency of DriveLaW. These results support learning the state interface for world modeling and planning directly during video pretraining.
authors: Yingdong Gu, Haoyu Wang, Shaocheng Yan, Zhenjun Zhao, Hao Han, Pengcheng Shi, Xianfei Li, Qinghua Tan, Wenlong Liao, Tao He, Jiayuan Li, Pai Peng
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between dense visual features and the compact, motion-conditioned states needed for driving prediction and planning.
Uses a V-JEPA framework that injects temporally aligned ego motion into a small set of registers and predicts masked patches from only those registers.
Adds blockwise register masking to structure predictive information within the register space.
Reuses the registers as future world-model states and shared scene memory for trajectory generation and scoring.
On NAVSIM-v2, reports a 1.6 EPDMS improvement over the state of the art and 1/10 DriveLaW’s inference latency.
papers.selection_reason: Learns motion-oriented registers as a shared state interface for driving world models and planning, conditioned on ego motion.
papers.title: MORE: Learning Motion-Oriented Registers for Driving World Models and Planning
papers.tldr: MORE pretrains compact, motion-aware registers as a shared state interface for efficient driving world modeling and planning.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive world models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for sample efficient decision making, yet their open loop rollouts often exhibit increasing drift that leads to error accumulation even within a relatively small planning horizon. Hierarchical temporal abstraction is a natural candidate to mitigate such drift by reducing the effective prediction horizon; however, existing hierarchical designs can introduce added structural and conceptual complexity, sometimes making them difficult to control and limiting gains over flat baselines. To this end, we introduce MHWA (Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action model), which employs a strided high level context channel to reduce global context update frequency, effectively curbing the propagation of compounding drift. Crucially, via context aware routing, the gating network dynamically reconfigures a low level mixture of experts by using both global context and current observations, thereby enabling flexible high-low coordination, helping alleviate interference commonly observed in static hierarchies. Empirically, using RLiable's seed-by-game aggregation, MHWA (77M parameters) achieves an IQM human normalized score (HNS) of 0.884 across three training seeds on a 14-game Atari subset using 10% subsampled offline data, outperforming a matched JOWA-70M baseline (0.529) and achieving numerically comparable performance to JOWA-150M while using nearly half the parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.
authors: Pengcheng Pan, Guoqing Ma, Yuhan Zhang, Yang Chen, Yichen Liu, Ziheng Li, Shan Yu
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and rollout drift that limit open-loop planning in autoregressive world models.
Uses a strided high-level context channel to reduce global context update frequency and shorten the effective prediction horizon.
Dynamically routes a low-level mixture of experts using global context and current observations for flexible high-low coordination.
On a 14-game Atari subset with 10% offline data, achieves 0.884 IQM HNS across three seeds, versus 0.529 for matched JOWA-70M.
Matches JOWA-150M numerically while using 77M parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.
papers.selection_reason: Autoregressive world-action model for decision making with hierarchical temporal abstraction fits interactive world models.
papers.title: MHWA: Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action Model
papers.tldr: MHWA reduces drift in autoregressive world-model rollouts through multi-timescale hierarchical context and dynamic expert routing, achieving strong Atari performance with substantially lower compute than a larger baseline.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine action generation with future prediction, allowing predicted futures to support action evaluation and robot decision making. However, the future associated with a candidate action may contain action-induced and environment-driven changes. Directly evaluating the predicted future may not fully characterize the future change associated with the candidate action. For example, a candidate action that worsens a favorable environmental future may still yield a favorable outcome, while one that improves an unfavorable environmental future may still yield an unfavorable outcome. To analyze this issue, we formulate a Structural Causal Model (SCM) for action evaluation in WAMs. The SCM formalizes how action-induced and environment-driven changes jointly shape future evaluation, and reveals a backdoor path through which environmental evolution can also affect the future evaluation associated with a candidate action. Intervention and backdoor adjustment account for this path, providing a causal basis for characterizing the future change associated with each candidate action. Based on this analysis, we propose Causal Action-Gain World Action Model (CAG-WAM). For each candidate action, CAG-WAM predicts an action-conditioned future and an environmental future under the same current observation, and defines their evaluation difference as causal action gain (CAG) for characterizing the future change associated with the candidate action. During training, we incorporate CAG into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to guide robot policy learning. During inference, we evaluate the initial action with CAG and, when needed, revise it using predicted future information. Experiments on multiple benchmarks support the effectiveness of CAG-WAM.
authors: Peizheng Guo, Cheng Zhang, Xingyu Zhang, Changwen Zheng, Wenwen Qiang
bullets: WAMs can misjudge actions when predicted futures mix action-induced and environment-driven changes.
An SCM uses intervention and backdoor adjustment to isolate each candidate action’s future change.
CAG-WAM compares action-conditioned and environment-only futures to compute causal action gain (CAG).
CAG guides GRPO-based policy learning and supports inference-time action revision.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks support its effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Causal action-gain world action model for robot manipulation; fits robot learning and interactive world models.
papers.title: CAG-WAM: Causal Action-Gain World Action Models for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: CAG-WAM uses causal modeling to separate action-driven effects from environmental changes, improving action evaluation and policy learning for robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Latent world-model planning has shown promising results in goal-conditioned robotic manipulation, but remains challenging for long-horizon planning due to limited temporal guidance and inefficient action search. A distant visual goal provides little guidance for preparatory actions, while uninformed action sampling makes local optimization inefficient. We propose PILOT (Policy-Initialized Local Optimization with Temporal subgoals), which uses a video model to generate intermediate visual subgoals and a learned policy to initialize the cross-entropy method (CEM). CEM refines candidate action sequences toward each subgoal using an action-conditioned world model in a receding-horizon control loop. In our primary real-robot evaluation across four UR5e manipulation tasks, PILOT achieves 68.8% success, compared with 55.0% without policy initialization, 13.8% for policy-only execution, and 0.0% for direct final-goal planning. Simulation results show that these gains persist over longer horizons: PILOT exceeds direct execution of the same policy by 30 percentage points on long Push-T tasks and by 22 percentage points on LIBERO-10. Policy initialization also accelerates local optimization: on Push-T, CEM matches the cost reached by generic initialization after 10 iterations in only 4 iterations and reduces the final planning cost by 24.1% under the same sampling budget. These results show that combining temporal subgoals with policy-guided action search improves both long-horizon task execution and local planning efficiency. Videos are available on the webpage: https://pilot-planner.github.io/.
authors: Yang Liu, Hanchen Cui, Karthik Desingh
bullets: Addresses weak temporal guidance and inefficient action search in latent world-model planning.
Uses a video model to generate intermediate visual subgoals and a learned policy to initialize CEM action-sequence optimization.
Refines actions with an action-conditioned world model in a receding-horizon control loop.
Achieves 68.8% success across four real-robot UR5e tasks, outperforming ablated alternatives reported in the abstract.
Simulation results indicate improved long-horizon execution and faster, lower-cost local optimization.
papers.selection_reason: Combines video-generated visual subgoals and policy-initialized CEM with an action-conditioned world model for long-horizon robot manipulation.
papers.title: PILOT: Guiding Long-Horizon World-Model Planning for Robot Manipulation with Visual Subgoals and Policy Priors
papers.tldr: PILOT improves long-horizon robot manipulation by combining video-generated visual subgoals with policy-initialized action planning.

papers.abstract: Humans and animals do not learn vision from a fixed set of data: they move, interact, and learn from the visual consequences of their actions. Motivated by this developmental view, we study whether robots can improve visual learning by actively collecting experience through curiosity-driven interaction. We introduce DySCOVER, a self-supervised framework for active robot visual learning. A robot observes RGB frames, learns a visual autoencoder that encodes and reconstructs them, and trains a recurrent world model to predict the next visual latent state conditioned on the current state and action. The agent's policy is trained only with intrinsic rewards: reconstruction error encourages visually novel observations, while the world model's error encourages transitions whose consequences are not yet predictable. This prediction error biases the policy toward more intricate trajectories that enrich the agent's set of experiences with observations beyond those encouraged by visual novelty alone. Our experiments conducted with robotic arms as the embodied agents show that adding predictive curiosity improves the vision model over using visual curiosity alone. Across variations in initial conditions, experience capacity, embodiment, and scene content, adding predictive curiosity consistently improved visual learning. These results show that predictive curiosity can improve active visual learning beyond reconstruction-based curiosity alone.
authors: Stelios Zarifis, Panagiotis Filntisis, George Retsinas, Petros Maragos
bullets: Robots actively gather visual experience instead of learning from a fixed dataset.
A visual autoencoder reconstructs RGB observations, while a recurrent world model predicts future visual latents from states and actions.
Intrinsic rewards combine reconstruction error with prediction error to drive curiosity-based exploration.
Robot-arm experiments show predictive curiosity consistently improves visual learning over reconstruction-based curiosity alone.
The study evaluates varied initial conditions, experience capacities, embodiments, and scene contents.
papers.selection_reason: Curiosity-driven robot visual learning uses an action-conditioned recurrent world model and intrinsic rewards, fitting robot learning and interactive world models.
papers.title: Learning to See through Action: Predictive Curiosity for Robots
papers.tldr: DySCOVER helps robots learn better visual representations by seeking both visually novel observations and unpredictable action consequences.

papers.abstract: Pixel-space world models have recently emerged as a promising approach for GUI agents, predicting future screens prior to execution and subsequently re-perceiving them for action selection. However, this two-stage paradigm faces two key challenges in GUI environments: (L1) the high computational cost of pixel reconstruction and (L2) the need to reconstruct large and diverse appearance-level details beyond what is required for action selection. In practice, this screen-generation objective can induce an identity shortcut problem, where future-state prediction largely preserves the current state rather than capturing action-induced changes. In this work, we reformulate GUI world modeling by shifting the prediction target from full-screen reconstruction to action-induced future information in latent space. Concretely, we leverage a large multimodal model as the latent world model, whose shared representations support two dedicated heads for both action selection and predictive transition modeling. The action head directly translates these latent representations into action selection, while the transition head captures action-conditioned future information. To mitigate the identity shortcut, we further introduce an action-aware contrastive objective that encourages the transition representations to capture discriminative action-induced changes. Extensive experiments across offline and online GUI settings show that our method achieves up to 31.9% and 40.6% relative gains in success rate over pixel-space world models, respectively, while substantially reducing inference latency by up to 98.9%. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/latent2world.
authors: Seungjun Yu, Hojun Choi, Seojeong Park, Jaeyo Shin, Hyunjung Shim
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and unnecessary visual detail of pixel-space GUI world models.
Uses a large multimodal model with shared latent representations and separate action-selection and transition-prediction heads.
Introduces an action-aware contrastive objective to avoid identity shortcuts and emphasize action-induced changes.
Reports up to 31.9% relative gains offline and 40.6% online over pixel-space world models, with up to 98.9% lower inference latency.
Evaluated in both offline and online GUI settings; the abstract does not specify task or dataset scope.
papers.selection_reason: Latent action-conditioned world model for GUI agents, directly fits interactive world models.
papers.title: Latent World Action Model for GUI Agents
papers.tldr: A latent-space world model for GUI agents predicts action-induced changes instead of reconstructing full screens, improving success rates while greatly reducing inference latency.

papers.abstract: We introduce ClothCode, a unified generative framework for garment state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction in a shared discrete configuration space. A material-aligned tokenizer encodes garment configuration as residual vector-quantized patch tokens, while task-specific Masked Generative Transformers predict these tokens through parallel confidence-guided refinement. Across three garment templates, ClothCode reduces mean displacement error by 26.6% for state estimation and 37.0% for dynamics prediction relative to the strongest baselines. Dynamics prediction requires only 16.7 ms per window, compared with 556.2 ms for diffusion. Integrated into the same model-predictive controller, ClothCode improves real-world folding and flattening success from 56.7% to 78.9%. Further results and videos are available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ClothCode-DE32
authors: Yingdong Ru, Lipeng Zhuang, Shiyu Fan, Zhuo He, Florent P. Audonnet, Gerardo Aragon Camarasa

Applies task-specific Masked Generative Transformers with parallel confidence-guided refinement for state estimation and dynamics prediction.

papers.title: ClothCode: Generative Modeling for Garment State Estimation and Dynamics Prediction
papers.tldr: ClothCode is a unified generative model that estimates garment states and predicts action-conditioned dynamics efficiently, improving prediction accuracy and real-world folding and flattening success.

papers.abstract: Forecasting tissue deformation from future instrument motion could support predictive planning and increasingly autonomous surgical systems. We study this problem using a scene-specific differentiable surface model fitted to an observed tool-tissue interaction window. Rather than forecasting absolute simulated positions, we introduce an \textit{observation-referenced} formulation that anchors each tissue point to its last valid observation and adds only the deformation induced by the known, preplanned future tool trajectory. This reduces sensitivity to reconstruction, initialization, and persistent simulation offsets while preserving the predicted deformation response. The physical model uses differentiable, mesh-free position-based dynamics with scene-specific rigidity, attachment, region scale, and grasp coupling. We further introduce an optional \textit{observation-referenced residual model} combining graph-spectral spatial modes with periodic harmonic dynamics for structured motion not explained by the tool input. We evaluate the framework retrospectively on 12 surgical manipulation clips from three datasets. Observation referencing provides the largest gain, with a median within-clip error ratio of $0.598$ relative to the corresponding absolute simulation forecast. The optional periodic residual further improves forecasting when the remaining motion exhibits periodic structure. These results support observation-referenced deformation prediction as a practical building block for future surgical world models, digital twins, and generative simulators that must predict how tissue evolves under instrument actions.
authors: Tom Olesch, Nan Xiao, Xiongye Xiao, Jonathan C. DeLong, Fei Liu
bullets: Addresses tissue deformation forecasting from known future instrument motion for predictive and autonomous surgery.
Fits a scene-specific differentiable, mesh-free position-based dynamics model to an observed tool–tissue interaction window.
Anchors each tissue point to its last valid observation, reducing sensitivity to reconstruction, initialization, and persistent simulation offsets.
Optionally adds graph-spectral spatial modes and periodic harmonic dynamics to capture motion not explained by tool input.
Evaluated on 12 clips from three datasets; observation referencing achieved a median within-clip error ratio of 0.598 versus absolute simulation, while periodic residuals helped for periodic motion.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned tissue deformation forecasting is directly relevant to surgical world models.
papers.title: Observation-Referenced Tissue Deformation Forecasting with Tool-Driven and Residual Dynamics
papers.tldr: An observation-referenced deformation forecasting framework improves surgical tissue-motion prediction by anchoring forecasts to recent observations and modeling tool-induced changes.

papers.abstract: A robot's learned model of its own dynamics is only valid until those dynamics change: actuators wear, payloads shift, and joints stiffen. A model-based agent that keeps training as if nothing happened adapts slowly, dragged back by a replay buffer full of stale experience. We present Changepoint-Aware World Models (CAWM), a DreamerV3 agent that detects an abrupt dynamics shift from its own internal prediction error, using an online CUSUM test against a rolling baseline that fires only on abrupt change rather than on slow learning drift. It then forgets stale replay, keeping the learned representation while flushing obsolete data. On simulated locomotion under two robot-relevant shifts, doubled gravity and halved actuator gain, CAWM recovers substantially faster than passive retraining. It also beats a strong baseline that respawns a fresh dynamics model on detection, the deep-world-model analogue of model-bank methods. With the response triggered at the shift, CAWM gains +95 to +153 return in the first 30k post-shift frames over three seeds, while matching that respawn at asymptote. Running the detector in closed loop reproduces this gain on the gravity shift. The benefit holds across both shift types, and is largest when the shift is severe enough that old data is genuinely obsolete.
bullets: Targets slow adaptation after actuator wear, payload changes, or joint stiffening make stored experience obsolete.
Uses DreamerV3 with an online CUSUM test on internal prediction error to detect abrupt shifts without reacting to gradual learning drift.
Flushes obsolete replay data instead of retraining from stale experience or replacing the entire dynamics model.
On simulated locomotion with doubled gravity or halved actuator gain, it recovers faster than passive retraining and fresh-model respawning.
With shift-triggered detection, it gains 95–153 return in the first 30k post-shift frames over three seeds and matches respawning at asymptote; benefits are largest for severe shifts.
papers.selection_reason: Detects dynamics shifts in model-based RL and forgets stale replay, directly relevant to world models, online adaptation, and robot learning.
papers.title: Changepoint-Aware World Models: Detecting Dynamics Shifts and Recovering by Forgetting Stale Replay in Model-Based RL
papers.tldr: CAWM detects abrupt robot-dynamics changes and rapidly adapts by discarding stale replay while preserving its learned representation.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon autonomous research has shown promise in accelerating scientific progress through sustained cycles of hypothesis generation, implementation, and validation. However, this Generate-Execute-Feedback paradigm relies on reactive trial-and-error, where costly and time-consuming executions introduce severe feedback delays, throttling evolutionary progress under explosively expanding search space. To address this challenge, we propose JANUS, a framework that unifies future outcomes forecasting and past experience reflection through a Predict-Verify-Evolve loop driven by a co-evolving world model. Within an evolving graph, the research agent proposes candidates while world model scores them by forecasting value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility, then accordingly selects, refines, or prunes branches prior to execution. After receiving ground-truth feedback, JANUS distills experience into evolving skills: hierarchical skills for research agent, exploration-strategy skills for world model, and their coordination protocols. This mechanism enables continual co-evolution: the research agent sharpens candidate generation while the world model refines its predictive judgment over extended horizons. Extensive evaluations on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks demonstrate that JANUS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving both higher evolving efficiency and ceiling.
bullets: Targets feedback delays and inefficient trial-and-error in Generate–Execute–Feedback research loops.
Uses a Predict–Verify–Evolve loop within an evolving graph to forecast value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility.
Selects, refines, or prunes candidate branches before execution, then incorporates ground-truth feedback.
Co-evolves hierarchical research skills, exploration strategies, and coordination protocols for the agent and world model.
Evaluations on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks report higher evolving efficiency and ceiling than state-of-the-art baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes co-evolving world models that forecast action-conditioned outcomes for long-horizon research agents.
papers.title: JANUS: Enhancing Long-Horizon Autonomous Research with Co-Evolving World Models
papers.tldr: JANUS accelerates long-horizon autonomous research by using a co-evolving world model to predict, filter, and improve research candidates before costly execution.

papers.abstract: Ultrasound (US) acquisition depends on the operator's ability to interpret anatomy and anticipate how the view will change with probe motion. Many robotic US navigation methods select actions without explicitly predicting these anatomical changes. We propose SonoGraph-WM, an action- and goal-conditioned world model for anticipatory probe navigation. The model represents anatomy as scene graphs (SGs), capturing visible structures, their geometry, and spatial relationships without synthesizing US images. Given a history of SGs and probe poses, a unified Transformer jointly predicts future SGs and poses. A receding-horizon planner recursively imagines candidate trajectories, selects the shortest predicted path reaching a goal graph, and follows it over a short execution horizon before replanning from new observations. To reduce reliance on tracked and anatomically annotated US sequences, we generate aligned SG--pose training data from computed tomography (CT) label maps along surface-constrained probe trajectories. On four held-out CT cases, spatial relation F1 remains above 93% over 20 prediction steps, and closed-loop navigation achieves 77.50% and 75.00% success for the gallbladder and pancreas, respectively, using annotation-derived SGs. In robot--phantom navigation experiments with label-map-derived SGs, the planner reached the target view in 73.7% of trials. These findings support CT-supervised anatomical world modeling for probe planning and highlight the importance of frequent observation updates for reliable navigation. Project Page: https://noseefood.github.io/us-sonograph-wm/
bullets: Represents ultrasound anatomy as scene graphs of visible structures, geometry, and spatial relationships instead of synthesizing images.

CT label maps generate aligned scene-graph/pose training data, reducing dependence on tracked and anatomically annotated ultrasound sequences.
On held-out CT cases, spatial-relation F1 stayed above 93% for 20 prediction steps; navigation success was 77.50% for the gallbladder and 75.00% for the pancreas.
Robot–phantom trials reached target views in 73.7% of cases, with results emphasizing frequent observation updates for reliable navigation.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned scene-graph world model for anticipatory robotic ultrasound navigation; aligns with interactive world models and robot navigation.
papers.title: Scanning While Imagining: A Scene-Graph World Model for Robotic Ultrasound Navigation
papers.tldr: SonoGraph-WM enables anticipatory robotic ultrasound navigation by predicting future anatomical scene graphs and probe poses, then planning through imagined trajectories.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot's actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource-constrained edge devices. We present SmolWAM, a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B-parameter Cosmos Policy by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk's attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified-flow step. Trained in 3.6 GPU-hours, SmolWAM succeeds in 95.5% of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57 ms and 2.3 TFLOP per 16-action chunk with 2.4 GiB of GPU memory, 11x faster than its teacher with 18.5x fewer FLOPs and 3.2x less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion.
authors: Timi Owolabi, Hikmah Olawore, Frances Adelakun, Ayotomiwa Oyewumi
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of video-diffusion world-action models on resource-constrained edge devices.
Rebuilds a pretrained 2B-parameter model’s inference interface using visual latents, cached text features, 12 transformer blocks, and a single rectified-flow step.
Achieves 95.5% success across 400 LIBERO episodes with 57 ms inference latency and 2.4 GiB of GPU memory.
Runs 11× faster than its teacher while using 18.5× fewer FLOPs and 3.2× less memory.
Its world head retains the ability to forecast scene motion.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient latent world-action model for robotic manipulation; fits VLA, manipulation, interactive world modeling, and edge-device efficiency.
papers.title: SmolWAM: A Latent World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation on Edge Devices
papers.tldr: SmolWAM compresses a large world-action model into an edge-friendly latent model that rapidly predicts robot actions and future scene observations.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models offer a promising foundation for generalist robotic intelligence by predicting the consequences of actions. However, existing robotic datasets provide limited coverage of the diverse interaction dynamics required for generalizable world modeling. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer complementary interaction experience, yet the embodiment gap between human hands and robotic manipulators hinders effective cross-embodiment learning. Meanwhile, the predominance of successful demonstrations leaves failure dynamics substantially underrepresented, limiting the ability of world models to anticipate unsuccessful executions. To address these limitations, we introduce HF-WM, an action-conditioned world model that combines Human interaction learning with Failure-aware post-training. To bridge the embodiment gap, we develop a dual-branch framework that couples video generation with auxiliary pointflow prediction, using stabilized pointflow as a unified motion representation across human and robot interactions while suppressing egocentric camera motion. To improve failure modeling, we further perform Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training on perturbed actions derived from successful demonstrations, guided by action alignment and physical plausibility rewards, enabling the model to learn plausible failure dynamics without paired ground-truth videos. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HF-WM achieves state-of-the-art performance in action-conditioned video generation and exhibits strong utility for policy evaluation in downstream robotic tasks.
authors: Peiyan Tu, Cong Wang, Hanxin Zhu, Xin Jin, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Addresses limited interaction diversity, the human–robot embodiment gap, and the underrepresentation of failures in robot datasets.
Uses a dual-branch model combining action-conditioned video generation with auxiliary pointflow prediction.
Employs stabilized pointflow to represent motion across human and robot interactions while reducing egocentric camera-motion effects.
Applies GRPO post-training to perturbed actions, guided by action-alignment and physical-plausibility rewards, without paired failure videos.
Experiments report state-of-the-art action-conditioned video generation and strong utility for downstream robotic policy evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned world model learning from human videos and modeling failure dynamics.
papers.title: Beyond Successful Robot Demonstrations: Learning from Human Interactions and Modeling Failure Dynamics
papers.tldr: HF-WM improves robotic world modeling by learning from human interactions and synthesizing failure dynamics from perturbed successful demonstrations.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) inherit powerful priors from pretrained video generation models, but their variational autoencoder (VAE) representations are optimized for visual reconstruction rather than manipulation. External visual representations can improve manipulation, but existing methods couple representation choices with different integration mechanisms, obscuring their individual effects. We systematically compare visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations under controlled settings. Our study yields three main findings. First, strong general-purpose visual representations provide broader robustness gains and can match or outperform representations pretrained for specific visual capabilities. Second, channel-wise joint prediction achieves the highest average success rate; further analyses suggest that future-feature prediction and the action expert's effective use of added visual information contribute to its gains. Third, additional sources should be selected for the task-relevant information they contribute beyond existing representations, as the same source can help one combination but harm another. However, even the best evaluated composition provides a smaller additional gain than the initial improvement from adding a strong general-purpose representation to the VAE-only baseline. We instantiate the resulting Representation Recipe as R$^2$-WAM. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop with an 84.7% success rate and reaches 92.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, improving over the VAE-only baselines by 5.9 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively. Taken together, these findings suggest that future work should prioritize stronger general-purpose visual representations and more effective mechanisms for integrating them into WAMs, with feature composition serving as a supplementary route to improvement.
authors: Kai Liu, Jiangran Lyu, Tingyu Deng, Yixin Zheng, Jingtian Wan, Wenbo Cui, Mi Yan, Yizhou Zhou, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
bullets: Compares visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations under controlled settings.
General-purpose representations provide broad robustness and can match or exceed task-specific pretrained features.
Channel-wise joint prediction has the highest average success, aided by future-feature prediction and effective use of added information.
Additional representations help only when they add task-relevant information beyond existing features; composition gains are secondary.
R²-WAM reaches 84.7% on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop and 92.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, improving over VAE-only baselines by 5.9 and 2.2 points.
papers.selection_reason: Systematic study of visual representations for action-conditioned world models in manipulation.
papers.title: What Visual Representations Do World Action Models Need?
papers.tldr: A controlled study finds that strong general-purpose visual representations, especially with channel-wise joint prediction, substantially improve World Action Models for manipulation.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn compact latent world models without pixel reconstruction. Existing JEPA pipelines typically train visual representations and action-conditioned dynamics before adding a control policy or solver. We introduce LeWAM, an end-to-end JEPA for control with: (1) a joint training objective over next latent state prediction and action flow matching, and (2) an isotropic Gaussian constraint on the latent state, enabling a single model to support direct policy execution and efficient planning by evaluating sampled actions with its learned latent dynamics. Compared with prior JEPAs in visual planning, LeWAM improves success rate from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks, and plans 32.3 times faster. On behavior cloning tasks in simulation and physical robots, LeWAM is also competitive with established methods. Interpretability analyses show that LeWAM learns control-relevant representations and action distributions effectively guiding test-time planning and control.
authors: Minghao Fu, Tavis Siebert, Eryk Halicki, Randall Balestriero
bullets: Addresses the separation of representation, dynamics, and control training in prior JEPA pipelines.
Jointly trains next-latent-state prediction with action flow matching under an isotropic Gaussian latent constraint.
Supports direct policy execution and test-time planning by scoring sampled actions through learned latent dynamics.
Improves visual-planning success from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks.
Plans 32.3× faster than prior JEPAs and remains competitive on simulated and physical-robot behavior cloning tasks.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end JEPA world model with action-conditioned latent dynamics and planning, directly relevant to world models and robot learning.
papers.title: LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs
papers.tldr: LeWAM is an end-to-end JEPA for control that jointly learns latent dynamics and action generation, enabling both direct policy execution and fast planning.

papers.abstract: World-action models have recently improved autonomous driving by jointly learning future scene prediction and trajectory generation. Most existing approaches model the future primarily through RGB appearance, and recent works have begun to incorporate geometric prediction to improve spatial understanding. However, dense geometry describes the spatial layout of the entire scene without indicating which parts are most relevant to the ego vehicle's action. For driving, the model must also identify and anticipate where it can safely move and which regions may pose collision risks. Jointly modeling action-relevant regions and future geometry can provide the policy with both driving-relevant cues and their corresponding spatial structure. We therefore propose AffordDrive3D, an affordance- and geometry-aware world-action model that jointly learns future action-relevant regions and spatial structure. In order to capture the scene semantics and driving context needed for driving affordance prediction, we build AffordDrive3D on a VLM backbone to forecast drivable areas and collision-critical regions that directly affect ego motion, while predicting future geometry from RGB world-model latents. On NAVSIM, AffordDrive3D achieves state-of-the-art performance with 91.3 PDMS and 89.9 EPDMS, demonstrating the effectiveness of jointly modeling future affordances and geometry for trajectory planning.
authors: Tianhui Cai, Xinglong Sun, Chao Fang, Zhenxin Li, Rui Song, Jose M. Alvarez, Yunxiang Mao, Jiaqi Ma, Langechuan Liu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of RGB- and geometry-focused world-action models that lack action-relevant spatial cues.
Uses a VLM backbone to forecast drivable areas and collision-critical regions affecting ego motion.
Predicts future geometry from RGB world-model latents alongside future affordances.
Achieves 91.3 PDMS and 89.9 EPDMS on NAVSIM, reported as state-of-the-art.
Focuses on affordance and geometry prediction for driving-relevant spatial understanding.
papers.selection_reason: Affordance- and geometry-aware world-action model for autonomous driving trajectory planning with spatial understanding.
papers.title: AffordDrive3D: Affordance-Aware World-Action Modeling with Spatial Understanding
papers.tldr: AffordDrive3D improves autonomous-driving trajectory planning by jointly predicting future driving affordances and scene geometry.

papers.abstract: World models enable agents to plan by predicting future states of the environment, but their predictions can become unreliable when test-time dynamics differ from those seen during training. We present JEPA-TTT, which adapts the latent dynamics predictor of a pretrained action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture world model throughout test time. Self-supervised updates accumulate across episodes, while the visual encoder and reward head remain fixed, preserving the pretrained representation and task objective. Planning requires neither a goal image nor online environment reward. JEPA-TTT uses dense replay, which forms prediction windows at every temporal offset, retains them in a growing buffer, and samples minibatches from that buffer for predictor updates. Across eight dynamics shifts in four continuous-control environments, JEPA-TTT improves planning on every shift. After 500 test-time episodes, it reduces autoregressive latent prediction error by 83% on average and improves planning performance by 153% over the frozen JEPA world model. These results show that persistent self-supervised test-time training can adapt a pretrained latent world model under changed dynamics.
bullets: Addresses unreliable world-model predictions when test-time dynamics shift from training conditions.
Updates only the action-conditioned latent dynamics predictor; the visual encoder and reward head remain fixed.
Uses self-supervised dense replay with prediction windows collected across temporal offsets and episodes.
Requires neither goal images nor online environment rewards for planning.

Across eight shifts in four continuous-control environments, it improved planning on every shift, reducing latent prediction error by 83% and increasing planning performance by 153% after 500 episodes.
papers.selection_reason: Adapts an action-conditioned latent world model via persistent test-time training for planning under dynamics shifts.
papers.title: JEPA-TTT: Persistent Test-Time Training of Latent World Models for Planning under Dynamics Shifts
papers.tldr: JEPA-TTT persistently adapts a pretrained latent world model during deployment, improving prediction and planning under changed environment dynamics.

papers.abstract: We present DreamTrue, a multi-view, cross-embodiment robot world model for action-faithful and physically plausible video prediction. Training such a model on existing robot datasets faces two obstacles: imprecise calibration can impair action following, while limited coverage of unsuccessful interactions can bias predictions toward successful outcomes. To improve action following across embodiments, we render action trajectories into image-space conditions and introduce offline geometric calibration to align these conditions with the target videos. To broaden interaction coverage, we introduce counterfactual post-training, modifying recorded action trajectories and generating future videos under a wider range of actions and contact configurations. To provide feedback on these predictions without paired ground-truth futures, we construct a human-annotated video dataset covering robot, object, and interaction defects and use it to train an embodied video reward model. Its scores guide reinforcement-learning post-training toward more physically plausible interaction outcomes. On AgiBot, DreamTrue attains state-of-the-art action following, while reducing the human-assessed interaction defect rate from from 48.12% to 6.25%. Notably, our model ranks first in the world model track of the AgiBot World Challenge 2026. The project page can be found at https://brave-eai.github.io/DreamTrue.
